hand/cobordism-theory.html:
The Chromatic Filter: Heights, Primes, and the Structure of Stable Homotopy

The transition from Complex Cobordism (MU) to the broader landscape of stable homotopy theory is governed by the concept of chromatic filtration. While Part 4 mentioned the Morava stabilizer group, a serious aspirant must understand the mechanism of this filtration. The Adams-Novikov Spectral Sequence (ANSS) does not merely compute groups; it organizes them by the height of the formal group law associated with the cohomology theory used as the coefficient ring.

The key insight is that MU_* acts as a universal coefficient ring, but when we localize at a prime p, the structure simplifies based on the height h. For a fixed prime p, the possible heights range from 1 to n = (p-1)/2. The chromatic tower stratifies the stable homotopy category into layers where each layer is controlled by the Morava K-theory K(n). A critical exception to the "universal" nature of MU occurs in the context of rational homotopy theory: over the rationals (Q), all formal group laws become isomorphic to the additive law, collapsing the chromatic complexity. This means π_*(MU) ⊗ Q is simply a polynomial ring on even generators, losing all torsion information. The examiner often twists this by asking for computations in the p-local category versus the rational category, or by presenting a problem where a genus vanishes rationally but not integrally.

Consider the landmark result of Quillen regarding the isomorphism between the Lazard ring and π_*(MU). This isomorphism holds over Z, but the map from the Lazard ring to the coefficient ring of any other complex-oriented theory E factors through MU. The exception arises in non-complex oriented theories like Real cobordism (KO) or K-theory (KU), where the formal group laws are not 1-dimensional over Z but rather have different periodicities and torsion structures (e.g., KU has a height 1 formal group law at every prime). The examiner may present a diagram chase involving the map MU → KU and ask you to identify the kernel, which relates to the image of the J-homomorphism.

In applied scenarios, this depth is crucial for understanding why certain invariants vanish. For instance, the Â-genus vanishes on manifolds with positive scalar curvature because the Dirac operator has no kernel (Lichnerowicz). In the chromatic context, this relates to the fact that the image of J consists of elements detected by K-theory (height 1), while higher chromatic layers correspond to more complex geometric structures like string manifolds and elliptic cohomology.

Technique: Analyzing the Kernel of the Map MU → KU
Let E be a complex-oriented cohomology theory with formal group law F_E. Suppose we have a map f: MU → E inducing an isomorphism on rational homotopy groups. If p=3, determine the structure of the kernel of the induced map on coefficient rings modulo p-torsion, given that E corresponds to height 1.
The map MU → KU induces a map on formal group laws from the universal law F_U to the multiplicative law F_KU(x,y) = x + y + xy. Over Z[1/2], these are related by an isomorphism, but over Z_p for p odd, they differ by torsion. At p=3, height 1 theories correspond to elliptic curves with j-invariant having specific properties. The kernel of MU_* → KU_* is generated by the elements corresponding to the difference in the formal group laws. Specifically, the kernel is a free module over MU_*/p generated by certain divided power classes. For p=3, the height 1 condition implies the formal group law has a specific reduction type. The kernel consists of elements that vanish when reduced modulo the ideal defining the multiplicative law. A standard result states that for KU, the image of J is finite cyclic at odd primes. Thus, the kernel captures the "missing" torsion information not detected by K-theory.
Exam-Day Strategy: The Rational vs. p-Local Trap
When solving problems involving cobordism rings or spectral sequences, always check the coefficient ring first. If the problem involves rational coefficients, ignore all torsion and formal group law complexities; treat everything as polynomial algebras on even variables. If the problem mentions "p-local" or specific primes (like p=2 or p=3), immediately switch to considering heights and Morava K-theories. A common mistake is applying the Lazard ring isomorphism over Q without realizing it collapses to a trivial statement. Always state your coefficient ring assumptions explicitly in your solution.

Topological Modular Forms: The Bridge Between Geometry and Number Theory

Moving beyond MU, the next frontier is Topological Modular Forms (TMF). This theory represents the universal elliptic cohomology. The construction relies on the work of Hopkins-Miller and Goerss-Hopkins-Miller. Unlike MU, which is associated with the unitary group BU, TMF is associated with the moduli stack of elliptic curves. The coefficient ring π_*(TMF) is the ring of integral modular forms. A critical distinction from MU is that TMF has non-trivial homotopy groups in negative degrees (unlike MU which is concentrated in even degrees starting at 0, though MU itself is periodic-like in structure but not periodic). Actually, MU is concentrated in even degrees, while TMF is also concentrated in even degrees but with different torsion properties.

The Witten genus is a map from the bordism ring of string manifolds to modular forms. The Ando-Hopkins-Rezk theorem establishes an orientation MString → TMF. This implies that every string manifold admits a TMF-orientation. The examiner often tests the understanding of the obstruction classes. For a manifold to admit a Witten genus, it must be a "string manifold," meaning w1 = 0, w2 = 0, and p1/2 = 0 (the first Pontryagin class divided by 2 must vanish). This condition is the topological constraint. If these conditions are not met, the Witten genus is not defined or vanishes. A classic trap is assuming that any oriented manifold admits a Witten genus; only string manifolds do.

In the context of the Stolz-Teichner program, the connection to quantum field theory provides a physical intuition: 0-dimensional SUSY theories compute K-theory, while 1-dimensional theories compute TMF. This hierarchy is essential for advanced problems where one must identify which cohomology theory corresponds to a given physical dimension or symmetry group. The exception here is that TMF is not a ring spectrum in the strictest sense over all integers without localization; its structure is deeply tied to the arithmetic of modular forms, specifically the level structure and congruence subgroups.

Technique: Verifying String Manifold Conditions
Given a closed oriented 8-manifold M with Pontryagin classes p1(M) = 4x and p2(M) = y, determine if M can support a Witten genus. Assume the manifold is simply connected.
To support a Witten genus, M must be a string manifold. The conditions are w1=0 (satisfied by oriented), w2=0, and p1/2 = 0 in H4(M; Z). Here p1(M) is given as 4x. For p1/2 to vanish in integer cohomology, we need the class 2x to be zero. If x represents a non-torsion generator of H4(M; Z), then 2x ≠ 0. Thus, if p1 = 4x where x is not torsion, the condition p1/2 = 0 fails because 2x is not zero in Z-coefficients. Therefore, this specific manifold does not admit a Witten genus unless x is a torsion element of order 2. The examiner might provide p1 = 4t where t is torsion; then p1/2 = 2t could be zero if t has order 2. Always check the integrality of the divided class.
Exam-Day Strategy: Modular Forms Arithmetic
When dealing with TMF or Witten genus problems, remember that the target ring is modular forms. If a question asks for the value of a genus on a specific manifold, and the answer choices involve modular forms, check the weight and level. The Witten genus maps to weight 12c modular forms for an 8c-manifold. If the input data (Pontryagin classes) does not match the required divisibility conditions for modular forms (e.g., denominators in q-expansions), the answer might be zero or undefined. Do not force a polynomial fit if the arithmetic constraints of modular forms are violated.

Comparisons and Exceptions: MU, KO, and the Image of J

A deep understanding requires comparing the major cohomology theories: MU (Complex Cobordism), KU (K-theory), and KO (Real K-theory). MU is complex-oriented with a universal formal group law. KU has a multiplicative formal group law over Z[1/2]. KO is real-oriented but not complex-oriented in the same way; its formal group law is defined over Z/2Z or requires careful handling of the Bott periodicity.

The Image of J is a landmark concept connecting these theories. It consists of elements in the stable homotopy groups of spheres π_k^S that come from K-theory (specifically KU). The image of J is finite cyclic at odd primes and has specific structure at p=2. A critical exception is that the Image of J vanishes rationally, but is non-trivial integrally.

Landweber Exact Functor Theorem and the Construction of Cohomology Theories

The Landweber Exact Functor Theorem provides the primary mechanism for turning a formal group law into a homology or cohomology theory. Given a graded commutative ring R and a formal group law F over R, one asks whether the functor X ↦ MU_*(X) ⊗MU_* R, where the MU_*-module structure is induced by the map MU_* → R classifying F, defines a homology theory. The theorem states that this functor is a homology theory if and only if the sequence (p, v1, v2, …) is regular in R for each prime p, where the v_i are the Hazewinkel (or Araki) generators of the p-typical formal group law associated to F. Regularity means that each v_i is a non-zero-divisor modulo the ideal generated by p, v1, …, vi-1. When the condition holds, the resulting theory is Landweber exact and inherits a great deal of structure from MU, including a complex orientation and a well-behaved Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence.

In practice, verifying Landweber exactness reduces to checking the regularity of the p-typical coefficients in the coefficient ring. For example, the Brown-Peterson spectrum BP has coefficient ring Z_(p)[v1, v2, …] with |v_i| = 2(p^i - 1). The sequence (p, v1, v2, …) is regular by construction, so BP is Landweber exact. Similarly, the Johnson-Wilson theories E(n) have coefficients Z_(p)[v1, …, vn-1, v_n±1] and are Landweber exact because inverting v_n preserves regularity. On the other hand, the Morava K-theories K(n) have coefficients F_p[v_n±1]; the sequence (p, v1, …, vn-1) is not regular because p = 0 in F_p, so K(n) is not Landweber exact in the classical sense. Instead, K(n) arises as a Bousfield localization of a Landweber exact theory.

The theorem also has a cohomological version: if the homology theory is Landweber exact, the associated cohomology theory is representable by a ring spectrum and satisfies a Künneth isomorphism for finite complexes. This makes Landweber exact theories the workhorses of chromatic homotopy theory. Many computations, such as the Adams-Novikov E2-term, are performed in the category of Landweber exact MU_*-modules. The theorem also clarifies why certain formal group laws, like the additive or multiplicative ones, give rise to familiar theories: the additive law corresponds to ordinary homology (where the sequence is (p) and regularity holds trivially), while the multiplicative law corresponds to K-theory after inverting the Bott element.

An important subtlety is that Landweber exactness is a condition on the p-typicalization of the formal group law. A formal group law over a ring R may be Landweber exact at some primes but not others. The theorem applies prime by prime, and a theory is globally Landweber exact only if it is exact at every prime. This prime-by-prime behavior underlies the chromatic filtration, where each height n formal group law contributes a layer that is detected by Morava K-theory K(n). Understanding the regularity condition is therefore essential for constructing new cohomology theories and for analyzing the algebraic geometry of the moduli stack of formal groups.

Morava K-Theories and the Chromatic Filtration

Morava K-theories K(n) form a family of extraordinary cohomology theories indexed by a prime p and an integer n ≥ 0. Their coefficient rings are K(n)_* = F_p[v_n±1] with |v_n| = 2(p^n - 1). The formal group law associated to K(n) has height exactly n, meaning that the p-series [p](x) = v_n xp^n + higher terms. This height is the key invariant in the chromatic viewpoint: the moduli stack of formal groups stratifies by height, and each stratum corresponds to a layer in the chromatic filtration of the stable homotopy category. The theory K(0) is rational homology, K(1) is closely related to p-adic K-theory, and higher K(n) detect increasingly subtle torsion phenomena.

A fundamental property of Morava K-theories is that they are field theories in the sense of stable homotopy: every module spectrum over K(n) is a wedge of suspensions of K(n). This implies that the K(n)-based Adams-Novikov spectral sequence collapses at the E2-page for many computations. Moreover, the Bousfield class of K(n) is minimal among non-zero Bousfield classes, and the telescope conjecture (still open for n ≥ 2) predicts that the localization with respect to a v_n self-map of a finite spectrum coincides with K(n)-localization. The chromatic convergence theorem of Ravenel states that the stable homotopy groups of a finite spectrum can be recovered from the tower of K(n)-localizations, providing a powerful computational framework.

The construction of K(n) can be approached via the Landweber Exact Functor Theorem applied to the formal group law of height n over F_p, but the resulting theory is only a homology theory after a suitable completion. Alternatively, K(n) can be obtained as the Bousfield localization of the Johnson-Wilson theory E(n) with respect to a v_n self-map. The coefficient ring of E(n) is Z_(p)[v1, …, vn-1, v_n±1], and the map E(n) → K(n) kills v1, …, vn-1 and reduces coefficients modulo p. This relationship shows that K(n) is a quotient of a Landweber exact theory, which explains why K(n) itself is not Landweber exact but still inherits many good properties.

In applications, Morava K-theories are used to detect nilpotence and periodicity. The nilpotence theorem of Devinatz, Hopkins, and Smith states that a map of ring spectra is nilpotent if and only if it is nilpotent on K(n)-homology for all n. The periodicity theorem guarantees the existence of v_n self-maps on finite spectra of type n, which are detected by K(n). These theorems are the cornerstone of the chromatic program and provide the theoretical justification for the filtration. For an examiner, a typical question might ask to identify the height of a formal group law given its p-series, or to explain why K(n) is not Landweber exact while E(n) is. Mastery of the coefficient rings, the height filtration, and the relationship between E(n) and K(n) is essential for advanced problems in stable homotopy theory.

Technique: Verifying Landweber Exactness for a p-Typical Formal Group Law
Let R = Z_(p)[v1, v2]/(v12) with |v1| = 2(p-1), |v2| = 2(p2-1). Consider the p-typical formal group law over R with Hazewinkel generators v1, v2. Determine whether the associated homology theory is Landweber exact.
To apply the Landweber Exact Functor Theorem we must check the regularity of the sequence (p, v1, v2) in R. First, p is a non-zero-divisor in Z_(p)[v1, v2] and remains so in the quotient because the ideal (v12) does not contain any multiple of p. Next, we examine v1 modulo (p). In R/(p) = F_p[v1, v2]/(v12), the element v1 is nilpotent (v12 = 0) but not zero. A nilpotent element in a commutative ring is a zero-divisor (since v1·v1 = 0). Therefore v1 is a zero-divisor in R/(p), violating the regularity condition. Consequently the sequence (p, v1, v2) is not regular, and the homology theory defined by this formal group law is not Landweber exact. The failure occurs because the relation v12 = 0 introduces torsion that obstructs the exactness of the functor.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a problem asks to construct a cohomology theory from a formal group law, first check the regularity of the sequence (p, v1, v2, …) in the coefficient ring. If the sequence is regular, the Landweber Exact Functor Theorem guarantees a homology theory; otherwise, the construction fails or requires a derived version. Remember that nilpotent elements in the mod p reduction immediately break regularity, so any relation that makes a v_i nilpotent modulo p is a red flag.

The Adams-Novikov Spectral Sequence and Cobordism

The Adams-Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) is the primary computational tool for stable homotopy groups of spheres using complex cobordism. Its E2-page is ExtMU_*MUs,t(MU_*, MU_*), where MU_*MU is the Hopf algebroid corepresenting the automorphisms of the universal formal group law. The spectral sequence converges to the p-completed stable homotopy groups πt-s^S^∧_p. The connection to cobordism is direct: MU_* is the coefficient ring of complex cobordism, and the comodule structure on MU_*X encodes the action of the formal group law on the cobordism groups of X. The ANSS can be viewed as a sophisticated version of the classical Adams spectral sequence, replacing mod p homology with MU-homology.

A key feature of the ANSS is its relationship to the chromatic filtration. The E2-term can be filtered by the height of the formal group law, leading to the chromatic spectral sequence. The v_n-periodic families in the stable homotopy groups correspond to permanent cycles in the ANSS that are detected by Morava K-theory K(n). The differentials in the ANSS are often understood via the geometry of the moduli stack of formal groups; for instance, the d3 differential on the Greek letter elements is related to the obstruction to lifting a height n formal group law to height n+1. Computations of the ANSS for low stems have been carried out extensively by Ravenel and others, revealing patterns such as the alpha, beta, and gamma families.

In practice, the ANSS is used to compute the stable homotopy groups of finite complexes as well as spheres. For a finite spectrum X, the E2-page is ExtMU_*MU(MU_*, MU_*X). The MU_*MU-comodule structure on MU_*X is determined by the action of the formal group law on the cobordism classes of submanifolds. This makes the ANSS a bridge between geometric cobordism data and algebraic Ext groups. A typical exam question might ask to set up the ANSS for a specific spectrum, such as the mod p Moore spectrum, and to identify the first few differentials using known results about the cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group.

An important technical point is that the ANSS is a spectral sequence of modules over the ring π_*^S, and its convergence is conditional on the nilpotence theorem. The nilpotence theorem ensures that any element that is nilpotent in the E_∞-page actually represents a nilpotent map of spectra, which guarantees that the spectral sequence converges to the correct homotopy groups. Without nilpotence, there could be phantom maps that are invisible to the ANSS. The periodicity theorem then provides the v_n self-maps that generate the periodic families detected in the ANSS. Together, these theorems justify the chromatic approach and make the ANSS a reliable computational device.

Quillen's Theorem on the Universal Formal Group Law

Daniel Quillen's theorem, proved in 1969, establishes that the formal group law associated to complex cobordism MU is universal. Concretely, for any commutative ring R and any formal group law F over R, there exists a unique ring homomorphism θ: MU_* → R such that the pushforward of the universal formal group law F_MU along θ is isomorphic to F. This means that MU_* = Z[x1, x2, …] (with |x_i| = 2i) carries the universal formal group law, and the Lazard ring L, which classifies formal group laws, is canonically isomorphic to MU_*. Quillen's proof uses the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence and the fact that MU is a complex-oriented ring spectrum whose coefficient ring is polynomial on generators in even degrees.

The universality has profound consequences. It identifies the moduli stack of formal groups M_fg with the stack Spec MU_* / Spec MU_*MU, where MU_*MU corepresents the automorphism group of the universal formal group law. This geometric perspective underlies the entire chromatic program: the height stratification of M_fg corresponds to the chromatic filtration of the stable homotopy category. Moreover, any complex-oriented cohomology theory E gives a map MU → E, which corresponds to a point of M_fg over π_*E. The Landweber Exact Functor Theorem can then be reinterpreted as a condition for a quasi-coherent sheaf on M_fg to define a homology theory.

Quillen's theorem also implies that the coefficient ring of any complex-oriented theory is a quotient of MU_* by an ideal generated by the coefficients of the formal group law. For example, the multiplicative formal group law corresponds to the map MU_* → Z[β±1] sending the universal law to the multiplicative one; the kernel is generated by the elements that enforce the relation x +_F y = x + y + βxy. This map factors through the complex K-theory spectrum KU, and the resulting formal group law is the multiplicative one of height 1 at each prime. Similarly, the additive formal group law corresponds to ordinary homology, where the map kills all positive-degree generators.

In an examination setting, a common task is to compute the map on coefficients induced by a given formal group law. For instance, given the p-typical formal group law with Hazewinkel generators v1, v2, …, one must express the universal generators x_i in terms of the v_i. The relationship is given by the Hazewinkel formula: v_n = p xp^n-1 + … (polynomial in earlier x_i). Understanding this translation is essential for working with the Adams-Novikov E2-term, where the cobar complex is built from MU_*MU = MU_*[b1, b2, …] and the b_i are related to the x_i via the coproduct. Quillen's theorem guarantees that any computation done in MU_* can be transported to any other complex-oriented theory via the classifying map.

The Nilpotence and Periodicity Theorems in Stable Homotopy

The nilpotence theorem, proved by Devinatz, Hopkins, and Smith in 1988, states that a map f: Σ^k X → X of finite spectra is nilpotent (some iterate is null-homotopic) if and only if its Morava K-theory homology K(n)_*(f) is nilpotent for all n ≥ 0 and all primes p. This theorem provides a powerful detection mechanism: to prove a map is nilpotent, it suffices to check its effect on each Morava K-theory. The proof uses the thick subcategory theorem, which classifies thick subcategories of finite spectra by their type (the smallest n such that K(n)_*X ≠ 0). The nilpotence theorem then follows by showing that a map that is zero on all K(n) must be zero in the stable homotopy category after a finite number of iterations.

The periodicity theorem, also due to Hopkins and Smith, asserts that for each finite spectrum X of type n, there exists a v_n self-map: a map v: Σ^d X → X such that K(n)_*(v) is an isomorphism and K(m)_*(v) = 0 for m ≠ n. Such a map induces periodicity in the K(n)-local homotopy groups of X. The existence of v_n self-maps is the homotopical analogue of the algebraic fact that the Morava stabilizer group has cohomological periodicity. The periodicity theorem is proved by constructing a suitable map using the geometry of the Lubin-Tate deformation space of the height n formal group law.

Together, the nilpotence and periodicity theorems form the backbone of the chromatic convergence theorem. The chromatic tower for a finite spectrum X is the sequence of Bousfield localizations L_n X with respect to the wedge of K(0) ∨ … ∨ K(n). The nilpotence theorem ensures that the fiber of L_n X → Ln-1 X is a wedge of suspensions of K(n), and the periodicity theorem provides the v_n self-maps that generate the homotopy groups of these fibers. The chromatic convergence theorem then states that the homotopy limit of the tower recovers the p-completion of X. This gives a complete qualitative picture of the stable homotopy category of finite spectra.

For exam purposes, it is crucial to understand the statements and the logical dependencies: the thick subcategory theorem → nilpotence theorem → periodicity theorem → chromatic convergence. A typical question might ask to explain why the nilpotence theorem fails for infinite spectra, or to describe how a v_n self-map is used to compute the K(n)-local homotopy groups of a type n spectrum. Another common trap is to confuse the nilpotence theorem (which concerns maps of finite spectra) with the nilpotence of elements in the stable homotopy groups of spheres; the latter is a corollary but requires the additional input that the sphere spectrum is finite. Mastery of these theorems and their interplay is a hallmark of advanced knowledge in stable homotopy theory.

  • Assuming that every formal group law yields a Landweber exact theory; the regularity condition on (p, v1, v2, …) is necessary and often fails when relations introduce nilpotent elements modulo p.
  • Confusing the coefficient rings of Morava K-theory K(n) and Johnson-Wilson theory E(n); K(n) has coefficients F_p[v_n±1] while E(n) has Z_(p)[v1, …, vn-1, v_n±1], and only E(n) is Landweber exact.
  • Treating the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence as unconditionally convergent without invoking the nilpotence theorem; convergence to the correct homotopy groups relies on the nilpotence of phantom maps.
  • Misidentifying the height of a formal group law from its p-series; the height is the smallest n such that the coefficient of xp^n is a unit, not merely non-zero.
  • Believing that Quillen's theorem implies MU_* is the Lazard ring only after tensoring with Q; the isomorphism holds integrally and is a theorem, not a definition.
  • Overlooking that the periodicity theorem guarantees v_n self-maps only for finite spectra of type n; infinite spectra or spectra of lower type do not admit such maps.
  • Neglecting the prime-by-prime nature of Landweber exactness; a theory may be exact at one prime but not another, and global exactness requires exactness at all primes.

These advanced topics form the core of modern chromatic homotopy theory and are essential for solving high-level problems in stable homotopy and cobordism.
