This equivalence is compatible with the A∞-structure on both sides, where the composition of morphisms corresponds to the convolution of microsupports.

Worked Computation: Wrapped Fukaya Category of T*S1
Compute the wrapped Fukaya category W(T*S1) and identify its generators and morphism spaces.
T*S1 is symplectomorphic to the cylinder S1 × ℝ with symplectic form dθ ∧ dp. The zero section S1 × {0} is a compact exact Lagrangian. The wrapped Fukaya category is generated by the zero section L0 and a cotangent fiber Lp = {θ0} × ℝ. The morphism spaces are: CW*(L0, L0) = C*(S1) = k ⊕ k[1] (cohomology of the circle), CW*(Lp, Lp) = k (the fiber is contractible), CW*(L0, Lp) = k (one intersection point), CW*(Lp, L0) = k (one intersection point). The A∞-operations: μ2 on CW*(L0, L0) is the cup product on C*(S1), which is trivial in positive degrees. The wrapped Floer cohomology HW*(L0, L0) = H*(S1) ⊗ k[u] where u has degree 2 (the Reeb chord on the boundary at infinity). The category is equivalent to the category of constructible sheaves on S1, where L0 corresponds to the constant sheaf kS1 and Lp corresponds to the skyscraper sheaf at a point.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Arboreal Models
When a question asks about the wrapped Fukaya category of a Weinstein manifold, check if the skeleton is arboreal. If the singularities are Ak, Dk, or E-type, the category is generated by cocores and the endomorphism algebra is the Ginzburg dg-algebra of the corresponding quiver. For cotangent bundles, immediately recall the Nadler-Zaslow equivalence: W(T*M) ≃ Shc(M). The stop Λ controls which sheaves appear — singular support disjoint from Λ. Memorize the A1 case: T*S1 has wrapped category generated by zero section and fiber, with HW*(L0, L0) = H*(S1) ⊗ k[u], deg u = 2.

Fukaya Categories with Bulk Deformations and the Curved A∞-Structure

When Lagrangian submanifolds are not exact, or when one considers the Fukaya category of a closed symplectic manifold, the A∞-operations acquire curvature terms. A bulk deformation is a choice of a cohomology class b ∈ H2(X; Λ0) where Λ0 is the Novikov ring; it modifies the symplectic area of pseudoholomorphic disks by adding ∫u b. The curved A∞-algebra associated to a Lagrangian L has operations μkb for k ≥ 0, where μ0b = ∑β nβ Tω(β) e∫β b is the curvature term counting pseudoholomorphic disks with boundary on L. The Maurer-Cartan equation for a bounding cochain b ∈ CF1(L, L) ⊗ Λ+ is ∑k≥0 μkb(b, ..., b) = 0. Solutions to this equation correspond to objects of the Fukaya category — Lagrangians equipped with a bounding cochain that cancels the obstruction to defining Floer cohomology. The Fukaya category of a closed symplectic manifold X is defined as the category of pairs (L, b) where L is a relatively spin Lagrangian and b is a weak bounding cochain satisfying the Maurer-Cartan equation modulo Tλ for some λ > 0. The morphism spaces are the Floer complexes CF*((L0, b0), (L1, b1)) with differential twisted by the bounding cochains. The A∞-operations are defined by counting pseudoholomorphic polygons with boundary marked points weighted by the bounding cochains. The bulk deformation b ∈ H2(X; Λ0) enters as a universal deformation parameter: the operations μkb depend on b, and the Maurer-Cartan equation becomes ∑k≥0 μkb(b, ..., b) = 0. The potential function W(b) = ∑k≥0 (1/(k+1)) ⟨μkb(b, ..., b), b⟩ is the Landau-Ginzburg superpotential; its critical points correspond to objects of the Fukaya category. For toric Fano manifolds, the bulk-deformed Fukaya category is equivalent to the category of matrix factorizations of the Landau-Ginzburg superpotential on the mirror torus, as proved by Cho, Oh, and others.

Mirror Symmetry for Fano Varieties and the Landau-Ginzburg Model

For a Fano manifold X (c1(X) > 0), the mirror is not a Calabi-Yau manifold but a Landau-Ginzburg model (Y, W) where Y is a non-compact Calabi-Yau manifold (often a torus (ℂ*)n) and W: Y → ℂ is a holomorphic superpotential. Homological mirror symmetry for Fano varieties, conjectured by Kontsevich and developed by Auroux, Abouzaid, Seidel, and others, states that the Fukaya category F(X) is equivalent to the category of matrix factorizations MF(Y, W) or the derived category of singularities Dsg(W-1(0)). The superpotential W is constructed by counting pseudoholomorphic disks with boundary on a Lagrangian torus fiber of a toric degeneration of X. For ℙ2, the mirror is ((ℂ*)2, W = x + y + 1/xy). The Fukaya category F(ℙ2) is generated by the Clifford torus LCl and its Hamiltonian perturbations. The endomorphism algebra of LCl is the Clifford algebra Cl3, and the A∞-structure matches the Yoneda algebra of the skyscraper sheaf in MF(Y, W). For a general toric Fano manifold X, the mirror superpotential is W = ∑i=1m zvi where vi are the primitive normal vectors to the facets of the moment polytope. The bulk-deformed Fukaya category with bulk parameter b ∈ H2(X) corresponds to the category of matrix factorizations of Wb = W + ∑ bi zvi. The equivalence is constructed by associating to each Lagrangian torus fiber Lu a matrix factorization of W given by the Koszul complex of the equations ∂W/∂zi = 0. The critical points of W correspond to the eigenvalues of the quantum product by c1(X) on QH*(X). The closed-open string map CO: QH*(X) → HH*(F(X)) sends the quantum cohomology ring to the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category; for Fano varieties, this map is an isomorphism after inverting the quantum parameter, reflecting the fact that the Fukaya category is smooth and proper.

The Fukaya Category and Extended Topological Field Theory

The Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold X can be organized into a 2-dimensional extended topological field theory (TQFT) valued in the (∞,2)-category of A∞-categories. Following the cobordism hypothesis of Baez-Dolan and Lurie, a fully extended 2D TQFT is determined by its value on a point, which is a fully dualizable object in the target (∞,2)-category. The Fukaya category F(X) is not fully dualizable in the (∞,2)-category of A∞-categories, but the wrapped Fukaya category W(X) of a Liouville domain X is expected to be fully dualizable, with dual given by W(X-) where X- is X with the opposite symplectic form. The value of the TQFT on a circle is the Hochschild homology HH*(F(X)), which carries a Connes' B-operator and an S1-action. The value on a pair of pants is the A∞-bimodule structure on the diagonal bimodule. The open-closed string map OC: HH*(F(X)) → QH*(X) and the closed-open string map CO: QH*(X) → HH*(F(X)) are the maps induced by the TQFT on the disk with one interior marked point and the disk with one boundary marked point, respectively. The Cardy condition, which states that OC ∘ CO is the quantum product by the fundamental class, is the sewing constraint for the disk with two boundary marked points and one interior marked point. The Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold with boundary, developed by Abouzaid and others, assigns to a Lagrangian cobordism between Legendrians in the contact boundary an A∞-bimodule between the wrapped Fukaya categories of the ends. This fits into the framework of factorization homology: the Fukaya category is the factorization homology of the Ran space of X with coefficients in the E2-algebra of chains on the based loop space. The relationship with the geometric Langlands program arises because the Fukaya category of the Hitchin moduli space MH(G, C) for a complex reductive group G and a Riemann surface C is expected to be equivalent to the category of D-modules on the moduli stack of G-local systems on C, and this equivalence is realized by a 4D TQFT (the Kapustin-Witten twist of N=4 super Yang-Mills) compactified on C.

  • Confusing the arboreal skeleton (a singular Lagrangian in a Weinstein manifold) with the stop (a Legendrian in the contact boundary); the skeleton generates the wrapped category, the stop defines the partially wrapped category.
  • Assuming the Nadler-Zaslow equivalence W(T*M) ≃ Shc(M) holds for all M without the constructibility condition; the microsupport of a constructible sheaf must be a conical Lagrangian, and the equivalence requires the stop at infinity to be the unit cotangent bundle.
  • Treating the curved A∞-structure as a standard A∞-structure; the curvature term μ0 is non-zero, the Maurer-Cartan equation must be satisfied, and the differential squares to the commutator with the curvature.
  • Believing the mirror of a Fano variety is a Calabi-Yau manifold; it is a Landau-Ginzburg model (Y, W) with a non-trivial superpotential W, and the equivalence is with matrix factorizations MF(Y, W), not DbCoh(Y).
  • Overlooking that the closed-open map CO: QH*(X) → HH*(F(X)) is not always an isomorphism; for Fano varieties it is an isomorphism after inverting the quantum parameter, but for general symplectic manifolds it has a kernel related to the symplectic cohomology.
  • Assuming the Fukaya category of a closed symplectic manifold is defined without bounding cochains; objects are pairs (L, b) where b solves the Maurer-Cartan equation, and the category is only defined over the Novikov ring.
  • Mixing up the wrapped Fukaya category W(X) of a Liouville domain with the compact Fukaya category F(X); the former has non-compact Lagrangians and is generated by cocores, the latter requires compact exact Lagrangians and is generated by the zero section in cotangent bundles.

Lagrangian Correspondences and Functoriality in Fukaya Categories

A Lagrangian correspondence from a symplectic manifold X to a symplectic manifold Y is a Lagrangian submanifold L ⊂ X⁻ × Y, where X⁻ denotes X with the opposite symplectic form. Given such a correspondence, one can define an A∞-functor ΦL : F(X) → F(Y) by counting pseudoholomorphic quilts with seams mapped to L. The quilt construction, developed by Wehrheim and Woodward, replaces the single polygon count of the A∞-structure with a count of quilted surfaces whose patches map to X or Y and whose seams map to L. The resulting functor respects composition up to homotopy: if L₁ ⊂ X⁻ × Y and L₂ ⊂ Y⁻ × Z are transverse correspondences, then the geometric composition L₂ ∘ L₁ ⊂ X⁻ × Z induces a functor homotopic to ΦL₂ ∘ ΦL₁. This functoriality is essential for the categorical formulation of the symplectic category, where objects are symplectic manifolds and morphisms are Lagrangian correspondences modulo Hamiltonian isotopy. The construction also yields a categorical action of the mapping class group on the Fukaya category of a surface: a Dehn twist about a curve γ corresponds to the Lagrangian correspondence given by the graph of the Dehn twist in T*S¹ × T*S¹, and the associated functor is the spherical twist around the Lagrangian sphere representing γ. In the wrapped setting, correspondences with non‑compact ends define functors between wrapped Fukaya categories, and the composition law holds after completing with respect to the wrapped Floer complex. A key technical point is the need for a clean intersection condition at the seams to avoid bubbling of holomorphic discs with boundary on the correspondence; this is achieved by perturbing the almost complex structure on the product or by using the geometric composition when it is embedded.

Spherical Twists, Braid Group Actions, and the Seidel–Thomas Construction

A spherical object in an A∞-category is an object S whose endomorphism algebra is isomorphic to the cohomology algebra of a sphere H*(Sn), concentrated in degrees 0 and n. In the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold of real dimension 2n, a Lagrangian sphere L ≅ Sn with vanishing Maslov class gives a spherical object. Seidel and Thomas constructed an autoequivalence TS of the derived Fukaya category, called the spherical twist, by taking the cone of the evaluation map Hom(S, −) ⊗ S → Id. On the geometric level, TL is realized by the generalized Dehn twist along L, a symplectomorphism supported in a neighbourhood of L that acts on the Fukaya category by sending a Lagrangian K to the Lagrangian obtained by iterating the Dehn twist along L applied to K. When a collection of spherical Lagrangians L₁, …, Lr intersect according to the Dynkin diagram of a simply‑laced Lie algebra, the associated spherical twists satisfy the braid relations of the corresponding Artin group. This yields a categorical action of the braid group on the Fukaya category, which under homological mirror symmetry corresponds to the action of the braid group on the derived category of coherent sheaves via spherical twists of spherical objects (e.g., the action on DbCoh(Y) for a K3 surface). The Seidel–Thomas construction also provides a bridge to the theory of stability conditions: the spherical twist acts on the space of Bridgeland stability conditions by a reflection in the wall associated to the spherical object. In the context of the Fukaya–Seidel category of a Lefschetz fibration, the vanishing cycles are spherical objects, and the monodromy of the fibration is expressed as a product of spherical twists, giving a categorical incarnation of the Picard–Lefschetz formula.

Worked Example: Spherical Twist on the Fukaya Category of the A2 Milnor Fibre
Let X be the Milnor fibre of the A2 singularity, symplectomorphic to the cotangent bundle T*S² with a single Lagrangian sphere L (the zero section). Compute the action of the spherical twist TL on the object L itself in the derived Fukaya category.
The endomorphism algebra of L is H*(S²) = k ⊕ k[−2]. The evaluation map Hom(L, L) ⊗ L → L is the identity in degree 0 and zero in degree −2. Its cone is the complex L → L[2] with the identity map in degree 0, which is quasi‑isomorphic to the zero object. Hence TL(L) ≅ 0 in the derived category. Geometrically, the Dehn twist along the zero section of T*S² is Hamiltonian isotopic to the identity, so it sends the zero section to a Lagrangian that is exact isotopic to the zero section, but the Floer complex with itself is acyclic, confirming the categorical result.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the effect of a spherical twist on a spherical object, remember that the twist always sends the spherical object to zero in the derived category. For a collection of spherical objects forming an ADE configuration, write down the braid relations explicitly: TiTjTi = TjTiTj for adjacent nodes, and TiTj = TjTi for non‑adjacent nodes. This pattern appears frequently in mirror symmetry computations for K3 surfaces and ADE singularities.

Equivariant Fukaya Categories and Hamiltonian Group Actions

When a compact Lie group G acts on a symplectic manifold X by Hamiltonian symplectomorphisms with moment map μ : X → g*, one can define an equivariant Fukaya category FG(X) whose objects are G-equivariant Lagrangian branes: a Lagrangian submanifold L ⊂ X together with a lift of the G-action to the grading and spin structures, and a G-equivariant local system. Morphism spaces are the G-equivariant Floer cohomology groups HF*G(L₀, L₁), computed by counting G-invariant pseudoholomorphic strips or by using the Borel construction X ×G EG. The A∞-operations are defined by counting G-invariant pseudoholomorphic polygons, which is equivalent to working in the symplectic quotient X//0 G = μ⁻¹(0)/G when 0 is a regular value and the action is free. In that case, there is a quasi‑equivalence FG(X) ≃ F(X//0 G) established by the symplectic reduction functor, which sends a G-equivariant Lagrangian L to its image L//0 G in the quotient. When the action is not free, one must work with the derived symplectic quotient or with the category of G-equivariant matrix factorizations of the moment map, leading to the categorical Kirwan surjectivity theorem of Ginzburg and others. The equivariant Fukaya category also carries a natural action of the representation category Rep(G) by tensoring the local system, making it a module category over Rep(G). This structure is crucial for the geometric Langlands correspondence, where the Fukaya category of the Hitchin moduli space MH(G, C) is expected to be equivalent to the category of D-modules on the moduli stack of G-local systems, and the G-action corresponds to the Hecke operators.

Mirror Symmetry for Log Calabi–Yau Varieties and the Gross–Hacking–Keel Program

A log Calabi–Yau variety is a pair (Y, D) where Y is a smooth projective variety and D is a reduced simple normal crossing divisor such that KY + D ∼ 0. The mirror of a log Calabi–Yau is a Landau–Ginzburg model (X, W) where X is a non‑compact Calabi–Yau manifold and W : X → C is a proper holomorphic function with critical points corresponding to the strata of D. Gross, Hacking, and Keel constructed the mirror by degenerating Y to a union of toric varieties glued along toric strata, then applying the SYZ fibration on each piece and gluing the dual tori. The resulting mirror X carries a natural cluster structure, and the superpotential W is a sum of theta functions associated to the boundary divisors. Homological mirror symmetry in this setting predicts an equivalence DbCoh(Y, D) ≃ MF(X, W), where the left side is the derived category of coherent sheaves on Y with support conditions along D (or equivalently the wrapped Fukaya category of the complement Y D), and the right side is the category of matrix factorizations of W. The Fukaya category of the mirror X is generated by Lagrangian sections of the SYZ fibration, which correspond to line bundles on Y, and by Lagrangian thimbles emanating from the critical points of W, which correspond to structure sheaves of the strata of D. The cluster mutation of the mirror corresponds to the wall‑crossing of stability conditions on the Fukaya category, and the scattering diagram of the Gross–Siebert program appears as the wall‑crossing diagram for the A∞-structure. This program has been completed for surfaces (the log Calabi–Yau surfaces are exactly the complements of anti‑canonical divisors in del Pezzo surfaces) and for higher‑dimensional cluster varieties.

Categorical Crepant Resolution Conjecture and Fukaya Categories of Orbifolds

The categorical crepant resolution conjecture, formulated by Kuznetsov and extended by Ruan, predicts that for a Gorenstein orbifold X with a crepant resolution π : Y → X, there is an equivalence between the derived category of coherent sheaves on Y and the derived category of G-equivariant coherent sheaves on a suitable resolution of the inertia stack of X. In symplectic geometry, the mirror statement involves the Fukaya category of the symplectic orbifold X and the Fukaya category of its crepant resolution Y. When X is a global quotient M/G by a finite group G acting symplectically, the Fukaya category of the orbifold is defined using G-equivariant Lagrangians in M and orbifold Floer cohomology, which includes contributions from twisted sectors labelled by conjugacy classes of G. The crepant resolution Y is often obtained by a sequence of blow‑ups along G-invariant submanifolds; the exceptional divisors are Lagrangian spheres whose spherical twists generate the kernel of the pull‑back functor π* : F(X) → F(Y). The conjecture asserts that π* is fully faithful and its essential image is the right orthogonal to the subcategory generated by the exceptional Lagrangians. This has been proved for Hilbert schemes of points on C² (the McKay correspondence for G ⊂ SL(2, C)) by Seidel and Thomas, and for certain toric orbifolds by Abouzaid, Auroux, and Katzarkov using the Gross–Siebert program. The categorical McKay correspondence also appears in the context of Fukaya categories of symplectic manifolds with singularities, where the singularities are modeled on Cⁿ/G and the resolution is a crepant partial resolution.

  • Confusing the geometric composition of Lagrangian correspondences with the categorical composition of the associated functors; the former is only defined when the intersection is clean, while the latter always exists via quilt counts.
  • Assuming every Lagrangian sphere gives a spherical object; the Maslov class must vanish and the minimal Maslov number must be at least 2 for the endomorphism algebra to be isomorphic to H*(Sn).
  • Treating the equivariant Fukaya category as simply the Fukaya category of the symplectic quotient; this holds only when the moment map is regular and the action is free, otherwise one must use the derived quotient or matrix factorizations.
  • Believing the mirror of a log Calabi–Yau is always a compact Calabi–Yau; it is a non‑compact Landau–Ginzburg model with a proper superpotential, and the equivalence is with matrix factorizations, not with the derived category of the compactification.
  • Overlooking the role of twisted sectors in orbifold Fukaya categories; the inertia stack contributes additional objects that correspond to the exceptional divisors in the crepant resolution.
  • Mixing up the spherical twist functor with the Dehn twist symplectomorphism; the former is an autoequivalence of the derived category, the latter is a symplectomorphism that induces the former only after passing to the Fukaya category.
  • Assuming the categorical crepant resolution conjecture holds for all Gorenstein orbifolds; it is known only for specific classes (toric, Hilbert schemes, certain quotient singularities) and fails in general without additional derived equivalence hypotheses.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Mapping Tori and Monodromy

A symplectic mapping torus is constructed from a symplectomorphism φ of a compact symplectic manifold (M,ω) by forming the quotient of M×[0,1] by the relation (x,1)∼(φ(x),0). The resulting manifold carries a natural symplectic form provided φ is Hamiltonian isotopic to the identity; otherwise one obtains a symplectic fibration over the circle with monodromy φ. The Fukaya category of the mapping torus encodes the dynamics of φ through the action of the monodromy on the Fukaya category of the fiber. Concretely, there is an A∞-functor Φ:F(M)→F(M) induced by the graph of φ viewed as a Lagrangian correspondence in M×M̄. The Fukaya category of the mapping torus is equivalent to the homotopy fixed‑point category of Φ, i.e. the category of modules over the A∞-algebra of Φ‑equivariant objects. This perspective links symplectic mapping class group actions to autoequivalences of Fukaya categories and underlies the construction of symplectic Khovanov homology via mapping tori of Dehn twists. When φ is a Dehn twist along a Lagrangian sphere L, the functor Φ is the spherical twist T_L, and the mapping torus is the total space of a Lefschetz fibration with a single critical point. The resulting Fukaya category is generated by the vanishing cycle L and its iterated twists, reproducing the braid group action on the derived category of the mirror. For higher‑dimensional monodromies, the fixed‑point category can be computed via a spectral sequence whose E₂‑page is the Hochschild cohomology of F(M) with coefficients in the bimodule defined by Φ. This spectral sequence degenerates when φ is symplectically isotopic to the identity, reflecting the fact that the mapping torus is then symplectomorphic to M×S¹ and its Fukaya category splits as a tensor product F(M)⊗F(S¹). The monodromy also controls the wrapped Fukaya category of the mapping torus: the stop at infinity is the graph of φ, and the wrapped category is the localization of F(M) at the morphisms inverted by Φ. These results have been applied to compute Fukaya categories of symplectic 4‑manifolds obtained by Luttinger surgery, where the monodromy is a product of Dehn twists along Lagrangian tori.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Sums and the Gluing Formula

The symplectic sum (or Gompf sum) of two symplectic manifolds (X₁,ω₁) and (X₂,ω₂) along a common symplectic hypersurface (V,ω_V) produces a new symplectic manifold X=X₁#_V X₂. The Fukaya category of X can be described by a gluing formula that expresses F(X) as a homotopy pushout of the Fukaya categories of the pieces relative to V. More precisely, let F(X_i,V) denote the relative Fukaya category whose objects are Lagrangians in X_i that intersect V cleanly and are equipped with a trivialization of their normal bundle along V. There are restriction functors res_i:F(X_i,V)→F(V) sending a Lagrangian to its intersection with V. The gluing theorem states that F(X) is quasi‑equivalent to the homotopy fiber product F(X₁,V)×F(V)^h F(X₂,V). In the language of A∞-categories, this means that objects of F(X) are pairs (L₁,L₂) with an isomorphism res₁(L₁)≅res₂(L₂) in F(V), and morphism spaces are given by a mapping cone construction that counts holomorphic strips with boundary on the two sides meeting at V. The formula has been proved for exact symplectic sums by Abouzaid and for closed sums under monotonicity assumptions by Maulik and others. A key technical tool is the stretched neck analysis: one degenerates the symplectic form on X by inserting a long cylindrical neck modeled on V×[−R,R] and studies the limit of pseudoholomorphic curves as R→∞. The limiting configurations are holomorphic buildings with levels in the completions of X₁V and X₂V, matched along asymptotic Reeb orbits in the symplectization of V. The matching conditions are encoded by the relative Fukaya categories and the restriction functors. The gluing formula has immediate applications: it computes the Fukaya category of a symplectic hypersurface complement, relates the Fukaya category of a blow‑up to that of the original manifold, and provides a categorical interpretation of the symplectic sum formula for Gromov–Witten invariants. In mirror symmetry, the gluing formula corresponds to the gluing of Landau–Ginzburg models along a common fiber, and the homotopy pushout of matrix factorization categories reproduces the derived category of the mirror variety.

Worked Example: Gluing Two Copies of T* S² Along the Zero Section
Let X₁=X₂=T* S² with the standard exact symplectic form, and let V be the zero section S². Compute the Fukaya category of the symplectic sum X=X₁#_V X₂.
The Fukaya category of T* S² is generated by the zero section S² and the cotangent fiber T*_p S². The relative category F(T* S²,S²) has the same objects, and the restriction functor sends S² to the identity object in F(S²) (which is just the category of vector spaces) and sends the fiber to the zero object because the fiber is disjoint from the zero section. In the homotopy fiber product, an object is a pair (L₁,L₂) with an isomorphism of their restrictions. Since the fiber restricts to zero, any pair involving a fiber on one side forces the other side to also restrict to zero, which is impossible for the zero section. Hence the only objects are (S²,S²) with the identity isomorphism. The endomorphism algebra of this object is the tensor product of the endomorphism algebras of S² in each copy, i.e. H*(S²)⊗H*(S²)≅H*(S²×S²). This matches the known fact that the symplectic sum of two copies of T* S² along the zero section is symplectomorphic to T* (S²×S²) and its Fukaya category is generated by the zero section S²×S². The computation illustrates how the gluing formula reduces to a simple algebraic fiber product when the restriction functors are essentially projections.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Fukaya category of a symplectic sum, first identify the relative categories and the restriction functors. Write down the homotopy fiber product diagram and simplify using known generators of the pieces. Remember that the zero section restricts to the unit object in F(V) while fibers often restrict to zero. This pattern appears repeatedly in blow‑up and hypersurface complement computations.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Cuts and the Surgery Exact Triangle

A symplectic cut is the inverse operation to the symplectic sum: given a Hamiltonian circle action on a symplectic manifold (X,ω) with moment map μ:X→ℝ, one cuts X at a regular level μ=c and collapses the S¹‑orbits in the level set to obtain a symplectic manifold X_c with a new divisor V≅μ-1(c)/S¹. The Fukaya category of X_c fits into an exact triangle of A∞-categories relating F(X), F(X_c), and the Fukaya category of the divisor V. This triangle is the categorical shadow of the surgery exact sequence in symplectic homology and of the long exact sequence in Floer cohomology for Dehn twists. Concretely, there is a functor i_*:F(V)→F(X_c) induced by the inclusion of the divisor, and a functor j^*:F(X_c)→F(X) induced by the inclusion of the complement. The composition j^*∘i_* is zero, and the cone of the natural transformation id→i_*∘j^* is quasi‑isomorphic to the functor given by the spherical twist around the Lagrangian sphere that appears as the vanishing cycle of the cut. When the circle action is semi‑free and the fixed point set is a symplectic submanifold, the vanishing cycle is a Lagrangian sphere in X_c whose spherical twist generates the kernel of j^*. The exact triangle then reads F(V)→F(X_c)→F(X)→F(V)[1]. This formalism has been used to compute Fukaya categories of toric varieties by iterated cuts, to prove the homological mirror symmetry for toric Fano varieties, and to relate the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold to that of its symplectic reduction. In the wrapped setting, the cut corresponds to adding a stop at the divisor, and the exact triangle becomes a localization sequence for wrapped Fukaya categories. The surgery exact triangle also underlies the proof that the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold with a Hamiltonian S¹‑action is generated by the fixed point components and the descending manifolds of the moment map.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Blow-ups and the Exceptional Lagrangian Spheres

Blowing up a symplectic manifold (X,ω) at a point replaces the point by an exceptional divisor E≅ℂPn-1 with symplectic form ω_E=ω|E. The Fukaya category of the blow‑up X̃ is related to F(X) by a semi‑orthogonal decomposition: F(X̃) is generated by the pull‑back of F(X) together with a collection of exceptional Lagrangian spheres L_E in the preimage of the exceptional divisor. Each L_E is a Lagrangian sphere in X̃ that intersects E transversely at a single point and is disjoint from the proper transform of any submanifold not passing through the blown‑up point. The endomorphism algebra of L_E is the cohomology algebra H*(Sn-1) (or H*(S2n-1) in the monotone case), making L_E a spherical object. The spherical twist TL_E acts as an autoequivalence of F(X̃) and its kernel is precisely the subcategory generated by the pull‑backs of objects supported at the blown‑up point. The semi‑orthogonal decomposition takes the form ⟨F(X), L_E⟩ where the left orthogonal of L_E is the essential image of the pull‑back functor π^*:F(X)→F(X̃). This decomposition has been proved for exact blow‑ups by Auroux and for monotone blow‑ups by Seidel. It implies that the Fukaya category of a blow‑up at k points is generated by π^*F(X) and k exceptional spheres, with mutual morphisms given by the intersection pairing of the corresponding exceptional divisors. In mirror symmetry, the blow‑up corresponds to a mutation of the Landau–Ginzburg superpotential, and the exceptional spheres correspond to the new vanishing cycles created by the mutation. The categorical blow‑up formula also underlies the proof of the categorical crepant resolution conjecture for toric orbifolds, where the resolution is a sequence of blow‑ups and the exceptional spheres generate the kernel of the pull‑back functor from the orbifold Fukaya category to the resolved one.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Lefschetz Fibrations and the Vanishing Cycle Category

A symplectic Lefschetz fibration π:E→D² over the disk with fiber (M,ω) and isolated non‑degenerate critical points gives rise to a directed A∞-category called the vanishing cycle category VC(π). Its objects are the vanishing cycles L_i⊂M, one for each critical value, equipped with a grading and a spin structure. Morphism spaces are the Floer cohomology groups HF*(L_i,L_j) computed in the fiber M, and the A∞-operations count pseudoholomorphic polygons in M with boundary on the vanishing cycles. The Fukaya category of the total space E is quasi‑equivalent to the category of twisted complexes over VC(π), i.e. the derived category of right A∞-modules over VC(π). This equivalence, due to Seidel, is the symplectic counterpart of the statement that the derived category of coherent sheaves on a Landau–Ginzburg model is generated by the matrix factorizations of the superpotential. The directed nature of VC(π) reflects the ordering of critical values along a path in the base; changing the path induces a mutation of the vanishing cycles, which corresponds to a spherical twist in the Fukaya category of E. When the fibration is extended to a Lefschetz fibration over S², the total space is a closed symplectic manifold and its Fukaya category is the homotopy fixed‑point category of the monodromy autoequivalence of F(M) given by the product of spherical twists around the vanishing cycles. This monodromy is the symplectic monodromy of the fibration, and its action on F(M) encodes the global topology of E. The vanishing cycle category also controls the wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of a smooth fiber: the stop at infinity is the union of the vanishing cycles, and the wrapped category is the localization of F(M) at the morphisms inverted by the monodromy. These results have been used to compute Fukaya categories of hypersurfaces in projective space, of symplectic 4‑manifolds obtained by plumbing, and to prove homological mirror symmetry for quintic threefolds by matching the vanishing cycle category with the category of matrix factorizations of the Fermat superpotential.

  • Confusing the homotopy fiber product in the symplectic sum formula with the ordinary fiber product of categories; the former requires a derived intersection of restriction functors and cannot be replaced by a strict pullback.
  • Assuming every Lagrangian sphere in a blow‑up is exceptional; the sphere must have minimal Maslov number at least two and vanish Maslov class to be spherical.
  • Treating the symplectic cut exact triangle as a short exact sequence of triangulated categories without checking that the functors are exact and that the cone is indeed the spherical twist.
  • Overlooking the grading and spin structure requirements on vanishing cycles; without them the A∞-operations in the vanishing cycle category are not well defined.
  • Believing the monodromy of a Lefschetz fibration is always a product of Dehn twists in the symplectic mapping class group; in higher dimensions the monodromy is a product of generalized Dehn twists along Lagrangian spheres, which may not generate the whole mapping class group.
  • Neglecting the role of the stop in the wrapped Fukaya category of a mapping torus; the stop is the graph of the monodromy, and omitting it leads to an incorrect description of the wrapped category.
  • Mixing up the categorical blow‑up formula with the geometric blow‑up formula for quantum cohomology; the former is a semi‑orthogonal decomposition of A∞-categories, the latter is a direct sum decomposition of vector spaces with a modified product.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Hypersurfaces and the Donaldson Divisor

Let X be a closed symplectic manifold of dimension 2n with a symplectic form ω representing an integral cohomology class. For a sufficiently large integer k, the line bundle L⊗k admits a section s whose zero set D = s−1(0) is a smooth symplectic hypersurface of dimension 2n−2, by Donaldson's theorem on symplectic submanifolds. The Fukaya category F(D) of the Donaldson divisor D is related to F(X) through a restriction functor res : F(X) → F(D) defined on objects by intersecting a Lagrangian L ⊂ X with D after a Hamiltonian perturbation making the intersection transverse. On morphisms, res is induced by the inclusion of Floer complexes CF*(L0, L1) → CF*(L0 ∩ D, L1 ∩ D) counting pseudoholomorphic strips in X with boundary on L0, L1 that intersect D at prescribed points. The functor res is an A∞-functor whose higher components count polygons with one interior marked point mapping to D. When D is an ample divisor, the restriction functor admits a left adjoint i! : F(D) → F(X) given by parallel transport of Lagrangians in D along the normal direction, and a right adjoint i! given by the same construction with reversed orientation. The composition res ∘ i! is quasi-isomorphic to the identity on F(D), while i! ∘ res is the monodromy of the Lefschetz fibration obtained by blowing up X along D and projecting to ℙ1. In the monotone setting, Seidel proved that the cone of the natural transformation id → i! ∘ res is the spherical twist around the Lagrangian sphere given by the vanishing cycle of the blow-up. This yields a semi-orthogonal decomposition F(X) = ⟨i!F(D), ker(res)⟩ where the kernel is generated by the exceptional Lagrangian sphere. For Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces, the restriction functor relates the Fukaya category of the hypersurface to the category of matrix factorizations of the Landau–Ginzburg superpotential on the mirror, providing a categorical interpretation of the hyperplane section property in mirror symmetry.

The Fukaya Category of the Symplectic Torus and Homological Mirror Symmetry for Tori

The symplectic torus T2n = ℝ2n/ℤ2n with a constant symplectic form ω = Σ dpi ∧ dqi has a Fukaya category F(T2n) whose objects are Lagrangian subtori with flat unitary connections (local systems). Every Lagrangian submanifold in T2n is Hamiltonian isotopic to a linear subtorus LΛ = Λ ⊗ ℝ/Λ for some primitive sublattice Λ ⊂ ℤ2n, equipped with a grading and a spin structure. The Floer cohomology HF*(LΛ0, LΛ1) is isomorphic to the cohomology of the intersection LΛ0 ∩ LΛ1, which is a finite union of tori of dimension equal to the rank of Λ0 ∩ Λ1. The A∞-operations count pseudoholomorphic polygons in T2n, which lift to affine polygons in ℝ2n with vertices on the lifts of the Lagrangians. Because the universal cover is ℝ2n, all pseudoholomorphic polygons are constant, so the A∞-structure is formal: mk = 0 for k ≥ 3, and m2 is the cup product on cohomology twisted by the holonomies of the local systems. The derived Fukaya category DπF(T2n) is therefore equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the dual complex torus T2n∨ = Hom(ℤ2n, ℂ×) with its natural complex structure determined by ω. This equivalence, proved by Polishchuk and Zaslow for n = 1 and by Fukaya for general n, is the original and simplest case of homological mirror symmetry. The mirror map sends a Lagrangian torus LΛ with local system ∇ to the skyscraper sheaf at the point of T2n∨ corresponding to the holonomy of ∇ along Λ. More generally, a Lagrangian submanifold with a non-trivial Maslov class corresponds to a complex of sheaves supported on a subtorus of T2n∨. The HMS equivalence intertwines the tensor product of local systems on the symplectic side with the derived tensor product of sheaves on the mirror side, and the duality functor L ↦ L∨ on the Fukaya category corresponds to the derived dual RHom(−, O) on the mirror. For non-constant symplectic forms, the Fukaya category is quasi-equivalent to the category of modules over a non-commutative torus algebra, and mirror symmetry relates it to the derived category of a non-commutative complex torus.

Worked Problem: Restriction to a Donaldson Divisor
Let X = ℙ2 with the Fubini–Study form ωFS, and let D ⊂ X be a smooth cubic curve (a symplectic hypersurface of degree 3). Let L ⊂ X be the Clifford torus, a monotone Lagrangian torus. Compute the restriction res(L) in F(D) and describe the morphism space HF*(res(L), res(L)).
The Clifford torus L ⊂ ℙ2 is the set of points [|z0| : |z1| : |z2|] with |z0| = |z1| = |z2|. It intersects a generic cubic curve D in 3 points (by Bézout's theorem, since L has degree 1 in the sense of symplectic intersection with D ∼ 3H). After a Hamiltonian perturbation, L ∩ D consists of 3 transverse intersection points. Each point is a Lagrangian 0-sphere in D (which is a Riemann surface of genus 1). The restriction res(L) is the direct sum of these 3 points, each equipped with the induced grading and spin structure. The Floer cohomology HF*(res(L), res(L)) is the direct sum over pairs of intersection points of the Floer cohomology between the corresponding 0-spheres. Since D is a torus, the Floer cohomology between two distinct points is zero (no pseudoholomorphic strips between distinct points on a torus with the standard complex structure), while the self-Floer cohomology of each point is H*(pt) = ℤ in degree 0. Thus HF*(res(L), res(L)) ≅ ℤ3 concentrated in degree 0. The A∞-structure is formal because D is a torus, so the endomorphism algebra of res(L) is the commutative algebra ℤ3 with componentwise multiplication.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Formal Fukaya Categories
When a symplectic manifold has a global Darboux chart (e.g., cotangent bundles, tori, Liouville domains with trivial topology), the Fukaya category is often formal: all higher A∞-operations vanish. Check whether the universal cover is ℝ2n with a constant symplectic form — if yes, pseudoholomorphic polygons lift to affine polygons and are constant by the maximum principle. This reduces computations to classical topology (intersection numbers, cup products). On exams, if you are asked to compute mk for k ≥ 3 on a torus or cotangent fiber, the answer is zero. Use this to save time and avoid overcomputing.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Manifolds with Cylindrical Ends and Symplectic Cohomology

A Liouville domain (W, λ) is a compact symplectic manifold with boundary such that the Liouville vector field Z defined by ιZdλ = λ points strictly outward along ∂W. Its completion Ŵ = W ∪∂W ([1, ∞) × ∂W) is a symplectic manifold with cylindrical ends, where the symplectic form is d(rλ) on the cylindrical part with radial coordinate r ≥ 1. The wrapped Fukaya category W(W) is defined using Lagrangians that are either compact and exact in W or non-compact and asymptotic to Legendrian submanifolds in ∂W at infinity. Its morphism spaces are the wrapped Floer cohomology groups HW*(L0, L1), defined as the direct limit over Hamiltonians H with slope → ∞ at infinity of the Floer cohomology HF*(H). The symplectic cohomology SH*(W) is the wrapped Floer cohomology of the empty Lagrangian, equivalently the Hochschild cohomology HH*(W(W), W(W)). There is a canonical open-closed string map OC : HH*(W(W)) → SH*(W) which is an isomorphism for many Liouville domains (e.g., cotangent bundles, Weinstein manifolds). The Viterbo restriction map SH*(W) → H*+n(W, ∂W) fits into a long exact sequence with the symplectic cohomology of the filling and the contact homology of the boundary. For a Weinstein manifold, the wrapped Fukaya category is generated by the cocores of the critical handles, and SH*(W) is computed by the Morse–Bott complex of the Reeb orbits on ∂W. The symplectic cohomology carries a Batalin–Vilkovisky algebra structure (a Gerstenhaber algebra with a degree −1 operator Δ satisfying Δ2 = 0 and the BV identity), which corresponds under mirror symmetry to the BV structure on the Hochschild cohomology of the mirror category. The cylindrical end also allows the definition of the Fukaya category of the symplectic completion Ŵ, which is the localization of W(W) at the morphisms inverted by the monodromy of the Reeb flow. When W is a plumbing of cotangent bundles of spheres, the wrapped Fukaya category is quasi-equivalent to the category of modules over the Ginzburg algebra of the corresponding quiver, and SH*(W) is the Hochschild cohomology of that algebra.

The Fukaya Category and the Fukaya Category of the Mirror: HMS for Elliptic Curves and K3 Surfaces

For an elliptic curve Eτ = ℂ/(ℤ + τℤ) with Im(τ) > 0, the mirror is the symplectic torus T2 with symplectic form ω = Im(τ) dp ∧ dq. Homological mirror symmetry, proved by Polishchuk–Zaslow, states that DπF(T2) ≃ DbCoh(Eτ). The equivalence sends a Lagrangian circle with slope p/q and holonomy e2πiθ to the line bundle O(p, q) ⊗ tθ on Eτ, where tθ is translation by θ. The Fourier–Mukai transform on the mirror side corresponds to the symplectic automorphism of T2 given by the matrix (0 −1 1 0) in SL(2, ℤ). For a K3 surface X with a symplectic form ω and a complex structure I such that ω is of type (1,1), the mirror is another K3 surface X∨ with the roles of the symplectic and complex structures exchanged. The Fukaya category F(X) is generated by Lagrangian spheres (vanishing cycles of Lefschetz fibrations) and Lagrangian tori (fibers of elliptic fibrations). The derived category DbCoh(X∨) is generated by spherical objects (structure sheaves of (−2)-curves) and line bundles. Homological mirror symmetry for K3 surfaces, proved by Seidel for the quartic K3 and by Sheridan for general polarized K3s, states that DπF(X) ≃ DbCoh(X∨). The equivalence matches the spherical twist around a Lagrangian sphere L ⊂ X with the spherical twist around the structure sheaf OC of the corresponding (−2)-curve C ⊂ X∨. The autoequivalence group of DπF(X) contains the symplectic mapping class group of X, which is generated by Dehn twists along Lagrangian spheres. On the mirror side, this corresponds to the group of autoequivalences of DbCoh(X∨) generated by spherical twists and tensoring by line bundles. The stability manifold of DπF(X) (Bridgeland stability conditions) is identified with the complexified Kähler moduli space of X∨, and the wall-crossing formula for stability conditions matches the wall-crossing for counts of pseudoholomorphic disks in X.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Manifolds with Contact Boundaries and the Contact Category

Let (Y, ξ = ker α) be a contact manifold of dimension 2n−1 with contact form α. Its symplectization is ℝ × Y with symplectic form d(etα). A Legendrian submanifold Λ ⊂ Y gives rise to a Lagrangian cylinder ℝ × Λ in the symplectization. The contact category C(Y, ξ) is an A∞-category whose objects are Legendrian submanifolds with gradings and spin structures, and whose morphism spaces are the Legendrian contact homology LCH*(Λ0, Λ1) defined by counting pseudoholomorphic disks in ℝ × Y with boundary on ℝ × Λ0, ℝ × Λ1 and punctures asymptotic to Reeb chords. The A∞-operations count polygons with boundary on multiple Legendrian cylinders. There is a fully faithful A∞-functor C(Y, ξ) → W(W) from the contact category of the boundary of a Liouville domain W to its wrapped Fukaya category, sending a Legendrian Λ to its Lagrangian cone in W. This functor is part of a localization sequence relating the wrapped Fukaya category of W to the Fukaya category of the closed symplectic manifold obtained by capping off W with a symplectic filling. The contact category also appears as the category of boundary conditions for the topological string on a Liouville domain: the open-closed map HH*(C(Y)) → SH*(W) factors through the symplectic cohomology of the filling. For a contact manifold that is the boundary of a Weinstein domain, the contact category is generated by the Legendrian spheres given by the attaching spheres of the critical handles. The Legendrian contact homology of these spheres computes the Chekanov–Eliashberg DGA, and the contact category is quasi-equivalent to the category of modules over this DGA. In dimension 3, the contact category of the standard contact S3 is generated by the Legendrian unknot, and its endomorphism algebra is the Chekanov–Eliashberg algebra of the unknot, which is formal and quasi-isomorphic to the homology of the based loop space of S2. The contact category provides a categorical invariant of contact structures that is finer than contact homology and detects overtwistedness: an overtwisted contact manifold has a contractible Legendrian unknot whose Chekanov–Eliashberg algebra is acyclic, making the contact category trivial.

  • Confusing the restriction functor to a Donaldson divisor with the pullback functor in a Lefschetz fibration; the former is defined by intersection with a hypersurface, the latter by parallel transport along a fibration, and they satisfy different adjunction properties.
  • Assuming the Fukaya category of a torus is always formal; formality holds for constant symplectic forms on T2n but fails for non-constant forms where pseudoholomorphic polygons can be non-trivial.
  • Treating symplectic cohomology as the same as quantum cohomology; SH* is the wrapped Floer cohomology of the empty Lagrangian on a Liouville domain, while quantum cohomology is the Floer cohomology of the diagonal in a closed symplectic manifold — they are related by the Viterbo map but differ in general.
  • Believing HMS for K3 surfaces is a direct generalization of the elliptic curve case; the K3 Fukaya category has both spherical objects (Lagrangian spheres) and non-spherical objects (Lagrangian tori), and the equivalence requires matching the full autoequivalence group, not just the spherical twists.
  • Overlooking the grading and spin structure requirements on Legendrians in the contact category; without a grading, the Legendrian contact homology differential is not well-defined, and without a spin structure, the orientation of moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic disks is ambiguous.
  • Confusing the contact category with the category of Legendrian isotopy classes; the contact category is an A∞-category with morphisms given by Legendrian contact homology, while the set of Legendrian isotopy classes is just the set of objects up to equivalence — the categorical structure encodes much more information.
  • Assuming the open-closed map from the contact category to symplectic cohomology is always an isomorphism; it is an isomorphism for subcritical Weinstein domains but fails for critical ones, where the kernel and cokernel detect the presence of non-trivial Lagrangian disks.

Advanced Analysis: The Gopakumar–Vafa Conjecture and Integer Refinement

The standard WDVV equations and the Mirror Theorem provide genus-zero Gromov–Witten (GW) invariants, which are rational numbers. However, a serious aspirant must understand that these rational numbers are not fundamental; they are shadows of deeper integer structures. The breakthrough came with the Gopakumar–Vafa (GV) conjecture, which posits that GW invariants can be re-expressed as a sum over integers n_i and BPS states. This is crucial because GW invariants depend on the choice of Kähler class and exhibit wall-crossing behavior when the moduli space topology changes, whereas GV invariants are topological constants.

Mechanism: The GV formula relates the generating function of GW invariants to a sum over BPS states. Specifically, if Nβ is the GW invariant for curve class β, the GV conjecture states that there exist integers n_i such that:

Σβ Nβ qdeg(β) = Σk ≥ 0 Σi n_i (-2)^k sinh((k+1) t)

Landmark Case: The quintic threefold. For the quintic, the genus-zero GW potential F0 matches the hypergeometric series from the mirror side. When expanded, the coefficients N_d (instanton numbers) are rational. The GV conjecture asserts that these rationals arise from integer counts of stable sheaves or curves in a Calabi–Yau compactification. For example, the number 2875 for lines on the quintic is an integer, but higher degree invariants like N2 (conics) involve denominators that are resolved by the GV integers.

Technique: Extracting GV Integers from Rational GW Data
Question: The genus-zero GW potential for the quintic is given by F0 = Σ N_d q^d. Given N1 = 2875, express the term for d=1 in the GV form involving sinh(t) and explain why the coefficient must be an integer if the mirror symmetry holds exactly.
Solution: The GW potential is F0 = Σd N_d q^d. Substituting q = eit, the term for d=1 is 2875 eit. In the GV formula, this corresponds to terms involving sinh(t) = (e^t - e-t)/2. The full expansion involves a sum over BPS states. The key insight is that while N_d are rational, the underlying integers n_i count stable objects in the derived category or moduli of sheaves. The "twist" examiners use is asking you to identify that for specific curve classes, the GW invariant equals the GV integer directly (up to a sign factor), but for others, it is a weighted sum. You must recognize that N_d are not arbitrary rationals but encode integer BPS counts.
Exam-Day Strategy: The "Rational Trap"
When calculating a GW invariant for the quintic, never assume the result is an integer. If you calculate a rational number with a large denominator (e.g., involving 2 or 6), do not panic. Instead, recall that this is expected behavior for genus-zero invariants before GV refinement. The examiner may ask you to convert this rational sum into the GV form to prove it satisfies the integrality conjecture. Always check if the question asks for the "virtual count" (GW) or the "topological invariant" (GV).

Categorical Mirror Symmetry: Fukaya Categories and Homological Duality

The original Mirror Theorem was enumerative, but modern mathematics has shifted to categorical mirror symmetry. This section covers Kontsevich's Homological Mirror Symmetry (HMS), which states an equivalence between the derived category of coherent sheaves on a Calabi–Yau X (D^b(X)) and the Fukaya category of its mirror check{X} (Fuk(check{X})).

Mechanism: The A-model (symplectic side, Fukaya category) captures Lagrangian submanifolds and their Floer cohomology. The B-model (complex side, derived category) captures holomorphic vector bundles. HMS asserts these categories are equivalent as triangulated categories. This is far deeper than counting curves; it equates the algebraic structure of the mirror with the symplectic topology of the original.

Comparison: Standard Mirror Symmetry (Givental) computes numbers (GW invariants). HMS computes categories. The Fukaya category objects are Lagrangian branes. Their intersection theory computes Floer cohomology, which corresponds to Ext groups in the derived category of the mirror.

Exceptions and Nuances: This equivalence is conjectural for general Calabi–Yau threefolds but proven for specific cases like abelian varieties or K3 surfaces. A critical exception arises in the presence of orbifold singularities; the Fukaya category must be defined as an "orbifold" Fukaya category to match the derived category of the singular mirror.

Technique: Mapping Objects via HMS
Question: In the context of Homological Mirror Symmetry, identify the correspondence between a line bundle O_X(L) in the derived category D^b(X) and an object in the Fukaya category of the mirror check{X}. How does this relate to the GW potential?
Solution: Under HMS, the derived category D^b(X) corresponds to the Fukaya category Fuk(check{X}). A line bundle (or more generally, a coherent sheaf) in D^b(X) corresponds to a Lagrangian submanifold (often with local system coefficients) in check{X}. Specifically, the structure sheaf O_X often maps to a specific Lagrangian sphere or torus. The GW potential is essentially the generating function of the Euler characteristics of the Hom complexes between these objects. If you know the category equivalence, you can reconstruct the enumerative invariants without explicit integration, as the algebraic structure of the Fukaya category encodes the same data.

Wall-Crossing and Stability Conditions: Beyond the Large Volume Limit

The standard GW invariants are computed in the "large volume limit" where the Kähler parameters are positive, ensuring stability of holomorphic curves.

Quantum Differential Equations and the Dubrovin Connection

The quantum cohomology ring carries a natural flat connection known as the Dubrovin connection. For a smooth projective variety X with quantum product ⋆ depending on Kähler parameters t = (t1, …, tr), the connection acts on the trivial bundle over the Kähler moduli space with fibre H∗(X, ℂ). In coordinates it reads ∇∂/∂ti = ∂/∂ti + (1/z) (Ti ⋆), where z is the formal parameter and Ti a basis of H2(X). Flatness of ∇ is equivalent to the WDVV equations and encodes the associativity of the quantum product. The fundamental solution matrix of this connection is the J-function, a generating series of genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants with one descendant insertion. Explicitly, J(t, z) = et/z (1 + Σd≠0 qd Σn≥0 ⟨τn(γ)⟩0,1,d z−n−1). The J-function satisfies the quantum differential equations (QDE) ∇ J = 0 and provides the bridge between enumerative geometry and the theory of integrable systems. For Fano varieties the QDE are regular singular at z = 0 and irregular at z = ∞; their monodromy data define the Frobenius manifold structure. In the case of projective space ℙn the QDE reduce to the hypergeometric equation (z d/dz)n+1 J = q J, whose solutions are the classical hypergeometric series. For Calabi–Yau threefolds the QDE are of order equal to the dimension of Heven and their solutions exhibit the mirror map as the ratio of two periods. The Dubrovin connection also underlies the construction of the quantum D-module, a holonomic D-module on the Kähler moduli space whose solutions are precisely the J-function and its derivatives. This perspective is essential for the proof of the mirror theorem via the Givental formalism, where the J-function of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model is identified with the J-function of the original variety after a change of variables.

Topological Recursion and the Eynard–Orantin Formalism

Topological recursion, introduced by Eynard and Orantin, provides a universal mechanism to compute all‑genus Gromov–Witten invariants from a spectral curve. A spectral curve consists of a Riemann surface Σ, a meromorphic function x on Σ, a meromorphic 1‑form y dx, and the Bergman kernel B(p, q) — the unique symmetric bidifferential with a double pole on the diagonal and no other singularities. The recursion produces symmetric multidifferentials Wg,n(p1, …, pn) for all genera g ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1, starting from the initial data W0,1 = y dx and W0,2 = B. The recursion formula is Wg,n+1(p0, p1, …, pn) = Σα Resp→α [ ∫pσ(p) B(p0, ·) / (2 (y(p) − y(σ(p))) dx(p)) ] × ( Wg−1,n+2(p, σ(p), p1, …, pn) + Σ′ Wg1,|I|+1(p, pI) Wg2,|J|+1(σ(p), pJ) ), where the sum runs over branch points α of x, σ is the local involution, and the primed sum runs over stable splittings. For toric Calabi–Yau threefolds the mirror curve provides the spectral curve, and the Wg,n compute the open and closed Gromov–Witten invariants. In particular, the genus‑zero free energy F0 is recovered from W0,1 by integration, and higher genus free energies Fg are obtained from Wg,0 = (1/(2g−2)) Σα Resp→α (Φ(p) Wg,1(p)), where Φ is a primitive of y dx. The formalism also yields the Gopakumar–Vafa invariants via the expansion of Wg,n in the framing parameter. A key feature is the polynomiality of Wg,n in the Bergman kernel, which implies that the invariants are determined by a finite set of initial data. This property underlies the proof of the remodeling conjecture for toric Calabi–Yau geometries and provides an algorithmic tool for high‑genus computations that bypasses the virtual localization formula.

Technique: Extracting Genus‑One Invariants from the Spectral Curve
Given the mirror curve of the resolved conifold defined by x + y + 1 = 0 with x, y ∈ ℂ×, the spectral curve data are Σ = ℂ×, x = log X, y = log Y, and the standard Bergman kernel B(p,q) = dp dq / (p−q)2. Compute the genus‑one free energy F1 using the Eynard–Orantin formula F1 = (1/24) Σα log ( (dx/dp)(α) (dy/dp)(α) ) − (1/24) log ( ∏α (dx/dp)(α) ) where the sum runs over branch points of x.
For the conifold the projection x = log X has no branch points on ℂ×; however, after compactifying to ℙ1 the map x has two simple ramification points at X = 0 and X = ∞. At X = 0, dx/dp = 1/X diverges, and similarly at ∞. The regularized product of derivatives yields a factor of 1. The Eynard–Orantin formula then gives F1 = −(1/12) log Q, where Q = e−t is the Kähler parameter. This matches the known genus‑one Gromov–Witten invariant of the resolved conifold, confirming that the spectral curve correctly encodes the enumerative geometry.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Recognising the Spectral Curve
When a problem asks for higher‑genus invariants of a toric Calabi–Yau threefold, first write down the mirror curve from the toric diagram. Identify the projection x and the differential y dx. The branch points of x are the only data needed to start the recursion. If the curve is hyperelliptic, the Bergman kernel is the standard one on the hyperelliptic Riemann surface. Remember that the genus‑one free energy has a universal expression in terms of the discriminant of x; memorise the formula F1 = −(1/12) log Δ + constant. This shortcut saves time compared to performing the full residue computation.

Open Gromov–Witten Invariants and Disk Potentials

Open Gromov–Witten invariants count holomorphic maps from bordered Riemann surfaces (disks, annuli) to a symplectic manifold X with Lagrangian boundary conditions on a Lagrangian submanifold L. The genus‑zero open potential W(u) = Σβ nβ e⟨∂β, u⟩ is a generating function of disk invariants nβ ∈ ℚ, where β ∈ H2(X, L) and u are flat coordinates on H1(L). For a toric Fano manifold equipped with a toric Lagrangian fiber L ⊂ X, the disk potential coincides with the Landau–Ginzburg superpotential of the mirror. The coefficients nβ are computed by the open mirror theorem (Chan–Lau–Leung–Tseng) which expresses them as residues of the mirror period integrals. In the A‑model, the disk invariants satisfy the open WDVV equations, a set of quadratic relations among the structure constants of the open Frobenius manifold. These relations are equivalent to the Maurer–Cartan equation for the bounding cochain in the Fukaya category. For the quintic threefold with a real Lagrangian ℝℙ3 ⊂ ℙ4, the disk potential is W = Σd odd Nd qd/2, where Nd are the genus‑zero closed invariants. The open‑closed map sends the disk class to the closed insertion τ0(pt) and intertwines the open and closed quantum products. A striking application is the computation of the Ooguri–Vafa invariants for knots in the resolved conifold: the open potential reproduces the colored HOMFLY polynomial after the identification q = e−gs. The integrality of open invariants is conjectured to follow from the existence of a categorification via the Fukaya category, where disk counts are Euler characteristics of morphism spaces between Lagrangian branes.

Quantum K‑Theory and the q‑Difference Equations

Quantum K‑theory replaces the quantum cohomology ring by a deformation of the K‑theory ring of a smooth projective variety X. The product ⋆q depends on a parameter q (not to be confused with the Novikov variable) and is defined by structure constants ⟨α, β, γ⟩0,3,dK = χ( M0,3(X, d), ev1∗α ⊗ ev2∗β ⊗ ev3∗γ ⊗ Ovir ), where χ denotes the holomorphic Euler characteristic and Ovir the virtual structure sheaf. The resulting ring is associative and commutative, and its associativity is encoded in the quantum K‑theoretic WDVV equations. The fundamental solution of the quantum K‑theory connection is the K-theoretic J-function JK(t, q) = Σd qd Σn≥0 ⟨τn(γ)⟩0,1,dK (1−q−1)n. Unlike the cohomological case, JK satisfies a system of q‑difference equations rather than differential equations. For X = ℙn the q‑difference equation reads (1 − q−1 z ∂/∂z)n+1 JK = q JK, whose solutions are the q‑hypergeometric series. The q‑difference module is a holonomic module over the algebra of q‑difference operators, and its monodromy (Stokes) data define a Frobenius manifold structure on the K‑theoretic moduli space. The limit q → 1 recovers the quantum cohomology Dubrovin connection after the identification z = ℏ/(1−q). Quantum K‑theory also admits a mirror description: the mirror of a toric variety is a Landau–Ginzburg model with a q‑difference superpotential, and the mirror theorem (Givental–Lee) identifies the K‑theoretic J-function with the oscillatory integral of the mirror. This framework has been used to prove the quantum K‑theoretic version of the Crepant Transformation Conjecture for toric orbifolds.

Applications to Enumerative Geometry of Fano Varieties

Fano varieties, whose anticanonical bundle is ample, provide a testing ground where quantum cohomology is semisimple and the Dubrovin connection has regular singularities. The classification of smooth Fano threefolds by Iskovskikh and Mori–Mukai yields 105 deformation families, each with a known quantum cohomology ring. For a Fano threefold X of Picard rank one, the quantum product is determined by a single parameter q and the three‑point invariants ⟨H, H, H⟩0,3,d where H is the ample generator of H2. The genus‑zero potential F0 satisfies a Picard–Fuchs equation of order equal to dim Heven(X). For example, the cubic threefold has quantum differential equation (θ4 − 5 q (5θ+1)(5θ+2)(5θ+3)(5θ+4)) J = 0 with θ = q d/dq. The mirror map is obtained by solving this equation and identifying the flat coordinate t = log q + Σ ad qd. The semisimplicity of the quantum cohomology implies that the total descendant potential is uniquely reconstructed from the genus‑zero data via the Givental–Teleman formula. This reconstruction yields all‑genus Gromov–Witten invariants without further geometric input. In practice, one computes the R‑matrix from the fundamental solution of the Dubrovin connection and applies the quantization formula to obtain the higher‑genus potentials. For the del Pezzo surface dP3 (blow‑up of ℙ2 at three points) the quantum cohomology is semisimple, and the genus‑one free energy is F1 = −(1/24) log det(∂i∂j F0) + constant, matching the BCOV holomorphic anomaly prediction. These results illustrate how the abstract axioms of Frobenius manifolds translate into concrete enumerative predictions for Fano varieties.

  • Confusing the Novikov variable q with the quantum K‑theory parameter q; they play completely different roles.
  • Assuming the Dubrovin connection is always regular singular; for non‑Fano varieties it has irregular singularities at z = ∞.
  • Neglecting the framing dependence in topological recursion; the choice of framing changes the open invariants by a known factor.
  • Applying the closed WDVV equations to open invariants without the open‑closed map; the open WDVV involve boundary insertions.
  • Forgetting that the quantum K‑theory J‑function satisfies q‑difference equations, not differential equations; the limit q → 1 must be taken carefully.
  • Treating the Gopakumar–Vafa integers as directly equal to genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants for all curve classes; they are related by a universal transformation involving multiple covers.
  • These traps highlight the most frequent conceptual errors in advanced quantum cohomology problems.

Higher Genus Gromov–Witten Theory and the Holomorphic Anomaly Equation

Genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants determine the quantum product and the Frobenius manifold structure, but the full topological string partition function requires all genera. The genus‑g free energy Fg is defined by the generating series of connected Gromov–Witten invariants with arbitrary insertions. For a Calabi–Yau threefold X the BCOV holomorphic anomaly equation governs the anti‑holomorphic dependence of Fg on the complex structure moduli. In the A‑model language the equation reads ∂īFg = ½ Cījk ( DjDkFg‑1 + Σh=1g‑1 DjFh DkFg‑h ), where Cījk is the complex conjugate of the Yukawa coupling and D denotes the covariant derivative with respect to the Weil–Petersson metric. The equation is recursive in genus and expresses the failure of holomorphicity of the higher‑genus amplitudes. The boundary conditions at the large volume limit (the “holomorphic limit”) fix the holomorphic ambiguity, which is a polynomial in the generators of the ring of modular forms of the mirror family. For the quintic threefold the ambiguity at each genus is a polynomial of degree 3g‑3 in the Eisenstein series E2, E4, E6. The solution of the holomorphic anomaly equations together with the gap condition at the conifold point and the known behaviour at the orbifold point yields all‑genus Gromov–Witten invariants for the quintic up to genus 51. The same formalism extends to non‑Calabi–Yau targets: for Fano varieties the anomaly equation acquires a source term proportional to the first Chern class, and the recursion can be solved using the Givental–Teleman reconstruction from the semisimple quantum cohomology. In practice, the holomorphic anomaly provides a powerful computational tool that bypasses the virtual localization on the moduli space of stable maps at higher genus.

The Crepant Transformation Conjecture and Orbifold Quantum Cohomology

The Crepant Transformation Conjecture (CTC) asserts that the Gromov–Witten theory of a smooth variety Y obtained by a crepant resolution of an orbifold X is equivalent to the orbifold Gromov–Witten theory of X after an analytic continuation in the Kähler parameters and a linear change of variables (the “crepant transformation”). For a global quotient orbifold X = [M/G] with G finite, the orbifold quantum cohomology ring H∗orb(X) is defined using the inertia stack and the age‑shifted grading. The quantum product is deformed by orbifold Gromov–Witten invariants ⟨α,β,γ⟩orb0,3,d which count stable maps from orbicurves with twisted sectors. The CTC was proved for toric orbifolds by Coates–Iritani–Jiang and for the local ℙ1 orbifold by Bryan–Graber. In the toric case the mirror theorem identifies the orbifold J‑function with the J‑function of the resolution after a change of variables qi ↦ (−1)age qi and a symplectic transformation given by the I‑function. The conjecture also predicts an equality of the total ancestor potentials (the Givental quantization of the genus‑zero data) after the same analytic continuation. A concrete illustration is the resolution of the An‑1 surface singularity ℂ2/ℤn. The orbifold quantum cohomology of ℂ2/ℤn is semisimple and its Dubrovin connection coincides with that of the minimal resolution after the identification of the Kähler parameters with the root lattice of type An‑1. The CTC has been extended to the quantum K‑theory setting (Givental–Lee) and to the categorical level (Kawamata, Halpern‑Leistner–Shipman), where it becomes an equivalence of derived categories of coherent sheaves. The conjecture remains open for non‑toric crepant resolutions such as the flop of a threefold, where the analytic continuation involves wall‑crossing in the space of stability conditions.

Worked Example: Orbifold Quantum Product for ℂ2/ℤ3
Compute the orbifold quantum product of the two non‑trivial twisted sector classes φ1, φ2 in H∗orb(ℂ2/ℤ3) and verify that it matches the quantum product of the corresponding exceptional divisor classes in the minimal resolution after the crepant transformation.
The inertia stack of ℂ2/ℤ3 has three components: the untwisted sector 1 and two twisted sectors φ1, φ2 of age 1/3 and 2/3. The orbifold quantum product is determined by the three‑point invariants ⟨φi, φj, φk⟩orb0,3,0. By the orbifold topological recursion relations these invariants equal the classical cup product on the inertia stack, which gives φ1 ⋆ φ1 = φ2, φ1 ⋆ φ2 = 1, φ2 ⋆ φ2 = φ1. The minimal resolution Y is the total space of O(−3) → ℙ1 with exceptional divisor E ≅ ℙ1. The quantum cohomology of Y is generated by the hyperplane class H of the base and the fiber class F. The crepant transformation identifies φ1 E, φ2 H − E. The quantum product on Y satisfies E ⋆ E = −3 F, E ⋆ (H−E) = F, (H−E) ⋆ (H−E) = −3 F. After the change of variables qY = −qorb the two rings become isomorphic, confirming the CTC for this example.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the crepant transformation, first write down the orbifold inertia stack and the age grading. Then state the analytic continuation rule q ↦ (−1)age q and the linear change of basis between twisted sectors and exceptional divisor classes. Cite the Coates–Iritani–Jiang theorem for toric orbifolds; this is the standard reference examiners expect.

Quantum Cohomology of Grassmannians and the Quantum Schubert Calculus

The quantum cohomology ring QH∗(Gr(k,n)) of the Grassmannian of k‑planes in ℂn is a deformation of the classical Schubert calculus. The Schubert classes σλ indexed by partitions λ fitting inside a k × (n−k) rectangle form a ℤ‑basis. The quantum product σλ ⋆ σμ = Σν,d ⟨σλ, σμ, σν∨⟩0,3,d qd σν is governed by the three‑point, genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants, which are known to be non‑negative integers (the quantum Littlewood–Richardson coefficients). Bertram’s quantum Pieri rule gives a combinatorial description for multiplying by a special Schubert class σ(r): σλ ⋆ σ(r) = Σ σμ + q Σ σν, where the first sum runs over classical Pieri expansions and the second sum runs over “quantum” partitions obtained by removing a rim hook of length n from λ and adding r boxes. The full quantum Littlewood–Richardson rule was established by Buch, Kresch, and Tamvakis using the quantum‑to‑classical principle: the coefficient of qd σν in σλ ⋆ σμ equals the classical Littlewood–Richardson coefficient for a triple of partitions in a larger Grassmannian Gr(k, n+d). This principle reduces quantum computations to classical ones. The quantum cohomology ring is presented as ℤ[q][σ1,…,σk] / Iq, where Iq is the ideal generated by the quantum Giambelli relations. The ring is semisimple for generic q, and its eigenvalues are given by the Bethe ansatz equations for the XXX spin chain, linking quantum Schubert calculus to integrable systems. The quantum K‑theory of Grassmannians (Buch–Mihalcea) replaces the quantum parameter q by a K‑theoretic parameter and the product satisfies a q‑difference version of the Pieri rule. These structures have been used to compute Gromov–Witten invariants of flag varieties via the quantum Chevalley formula and to prove the Peterson isomorphism between QH∗(G/P) and the homology of the Peterson variety.

Localization Techniques: Torus Actions and the Virtual Localization Formula

The virtual localization formula of Graber and Pandharipande expresses Gromov–Witten invariants of a smooth projective variety X with a torus T‑action as a sum over T‑fixed loci in the moduli space of stable maps M̄g,n(X,β). Each fixed locus corresponds to a decorated graph Γ whose vertices are T‑fixed points in X, edges are T‑invariant curves, and legs are marked points. The contribution of a graph is a rational function in the equivariant parameters λ1,…,λr given by the product over vertices of 1 / eT(Obv) times the product over edges of 1 / (we(λi−λj)) where we is the weight of the T‑action on the normal bundle of the invariant curve. The virtual normal bundle splits into moving and fixed parts; the moving part contributes the inverse equivariant Euler class, while the fixed part yields the virtual fundamental class of the fixed locus. For toric varieties the fixed loci are isolated, and the formula reduces to a sum over trees of rational functions that can be evaluated by residue calculus. This technique yields closed formulas for the J‑function of toric varieties (Givental’s mirror theorem) and for the quantum product of flag varieties (Kim’s quantum Giambelli formula). In the non‑toric case, such as the Grassmannian, the fixed loci are products of smaller Grassmannians, and the localization sum can be organized using the quantum‑to‑classical principle. The virtual localization formula also underlies the computation of open Gromov–Witten invariants with Lagrangian boundary conditions, where the fixed loci involve maps to T‑invariant disks. A common pitfall is forgetting the contribution of the virtual normal bundle at vertices with non‑trivial automorphisms; the correct factor is 1 / |Aut(Γ)| times the inverse equivariant Euler class of the moving part of the obstruction bundle.

Integrable Systems and Quantum Cohomology: The Toda Lattice and KP Hierarchy

The genus‑zero Gromov–Witten potential of a Fano variety satisfies the WDVV equations, which are the associativity conditions for the quantum product. Dubrovin showed that the WDVV equations are equivalent to the existence of a flat identity and a flat metric on the Frobenius manifold, and that the hierarchy of commuting Hamiltonian flows on the loop space of the Frobenius manifold is the principal hierarchy of a topological field theory. For ℙn the principal hierarchy coincides with the n‑th Gelfand–Dickey hierarchy, which is a reduction of the KP hierarchy. The tau‑function of the KP hierarchy generates the genus‑zero descendant invariants via the string and dilaton equations. At higher genus, the total descendant potential Z = exp( Σg≥0 ℏg‑1 Fg ) is conjectured to be a tau‑function of an integrable hierarchy (the “quantum” hierarchy). For ℙ1 the total potential is the tau‑function of the 2‑Toda lattice hierarchy, as proved by Okounkov and Pandharipande using the infinite wedge formalism. The Lax operator of the Toda lattice is L = Λ + u + v Λ−1, where Λ is the shift operator, and the quantum cohomology relation (Λ + Λ−1) = q translates into the spectral curve of the Toda lattice. The Givental quantization formalism identifies the R‑matrix of the Frobenius manifold with the symplectic transformation that maps the trivial tau‑function to the total descendant potential. This provides a reconstruction of all‑genus invariants from genus‑zero data for any semisimple Frobenius manifold (Givental–Teleman theorem). The integrable systems perspective also yields the Virasoro constraints for the total potential: the operators Lm = Σk≥0 (k+½) tk ∂/∂tk+m + ½ Σa+b=m‑1 ∂²/∂ta∂tb + (1/16) δm,−1 annihilate Z. These constraints are equivalent to the topological recursion relations and the string equation. For non‑Fano targets such as the quintic threefold, the relevant integrable system is the B‑model Kodaira–Spencer theory of gravity, whose partition function satisfies the holomorphic anomaly equations rather than the KP hierarchy.

  • Confusing the equivariant parameters in virtual localization with the Novikov variables; they belong to different rings and must not be identified.
  • Assuming the quantum Littlewood–Richardson coefficients are always positive for any Grassmannian; positivity holds for Grassmannians but fails for general flag varieties.
  • Neglecting the age shift in orbifold quantum cohomology; the degree of a twisted sector class is its classical degree plus twice its age.
  • Applying the holomorphic anomaly equation to non‑Calabi–Yau targets without the Chern class source term; the recursion then produces incorrect amplitudes.
  • Treating the Toda lattice Lax operator as a matrix of size equal to the rank of the quantum cohomology; the correct size is the dimension of the Frobenius manifold.
  • Forgetting that the crepant transformation involves an analytic continuation in the Kähler moduli space, not merely a linear change of basis.
  • Misidentifying the quantum parameter q in the quantum Pieri rule with the equivariant weight of a torus action; they transform differently under mirror symmetry.

Quantum Lefschetz Theorem and Quantum Cohomology of Complete Intersections

The quantum Lefschetz theorem gives a precise relationship between the Gromov–Witten invariants of a smooth projective variety X and those of a smooth complete intersection Y defined by a regular section of a convex vector bundle E on X. Convexity means that for every stable map f: ℙ¹ → X the higher cohomology H¹(ℙ¹, f*E) vanishes. Under this hypothesis the virtual fundamental class of the moduli space of stable maps to Y is the restriction of the virtual class of X capped with the top Chern class of the obstruction bundle R¹π*ev*E. The theorem states that the genus‑zero Gromov–Witten potential of Y can be obtained from the J‑function of X by applying the differential operator ∏i=1r ∏m=1di (c1(Ei) + mℏ) where E = ⊕i Ei and di = c1(Ei)·β.
