hand/homological-mirror-symmetry.html:
Wrapped Fukaya Categories and Generation by Lagrangian Cobordisms

The wrapped Fukaya category W(X) of a non‑compact or Liouville symplectic manifold X was introduced by Abouzaid and Seidel (2009) to capture Hamiltonian dynamics at infinity. Objects are exact Lagrangian submanifolds L ⊂ X that are cylindrical at infinity, equipped with a grading and a spin structure. Morphism spaces are defined by Hamiltonian chords from L₀ to L₁ with action going to +∞; the differential counts pseudo‑holomorphic strips with moving boundary conditions. The A∞‑structure is given by counts of polygons with one output and several inputs, where the Hamiltonian perturbation is chosen to be quadratic at infinity so that the action functional is proper.

A central generation result is the Abouzaid–Seidel criterion: if a collection of Lagrangians {Lᵢ} split‑generates the compact Fukaya category Fuk(X) and each Lᵢ is non‑compact but exact, then the corresponding wrapped branes split‑generate W(X). In practice one often uses a stop Λ at infinity; the partially wrapped category W(X, Λ) interpolates between the compact and fully wrapped cases. Ganatra–Pardon–Shende (2018) proved that for a Weinstein manifold X the wrapped Fukaya category is equivalent to the category of modules over the Legendrian contact homology algebra of the stop, establishing a purely algebraic description.

Lagrangian cobordisms provide a geometric mechanism to relate objects in different wrapped categories. A Lagrangian cobordism V ⊂ ℝ × X from L₋ to L₊ induces an A∞‑functor Φ_V: W(X) → W(X) which on objects sends L₋ to L₊ and on morphisms is defined by counting holomorphic curves with boundary on V. When V is exact and cylindrical, Φ_V is a quasi‑equivalence onto its image. This functoriality underlies the proof of HMS for many toric Calabi–Yau varieties: the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model (Y, W) has a wrapped Fukaya category generated by thimbles, and the cobordism given by the graph of W identifies it with the derived category of matrix factorizations MF(Y, W).

Key computational tools include the Viterbo restriction functor W(X) → Fuk(X) and the stop removal functor W(X, Λ) → W(X). The former forgets wrapping data, the latter adds a stop. Their interplay yields long exact sequences of Hochschild homology that compute symplectic cohomology SH*(X). In particular, SH*(X) ≅ HH*(W(X)) and the closed‑open map SH*(X) → HH*(Fuk(X)) factors through the restriction functor, giving a powerful invariant for distinguishing symplectic manifolds.

Homological Mirror Symmetry for Toric Calabi–Yau Varieties

For a toric Calabi–Yau variety X given by a fan Σ in ℝⁿ with a convex piecewise‑linear function φ defining the Kähler form, the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model (Y, W) where Y = (ℂ*)ⁿ and W = Σv∈Σ(1) zv is a Laurent polynomial whose Newton polytope is the moment polytope of X. The HMS conjecture in this setting, proved by Abouzaid (2009) for the compact case and extended by Ganatra–Pardon–Shende (2020) to the non‑compact case, states a quasi‑equivalence D^π Fuk(X) ≅ D^b Coh(Y) (or MF(Y, W) when Y is non‑compact). The proof proceeds by constructing a Lagrangian skeleton Λ ⊂ X, the union of the toric divisors and their intersections, and showing that the wrapped Fukaya category of the complement X Λ is generated by the toric fibers.

On the B‑side, the derived category of coherent sheaves on the toric stack [X] is generated by the collection of line bundles O(D) for torus‑invariant divisors D. The mirror map identifies the complexified Kähler parameters q_i = exp(∫C_i ω + i B) with the coefficients of the monomials in W. The equivalence sends a Lagrangian torus fiber with a flat U(1) connection to a skyscraper sheaf at the corresponding point of the mirror torus, and a Lagrangian section of the moment map to a line bundle. The A∞‑structure on the Fukaya side matches the Yoneda Ext‑algebra on the derived side via the toric degeneration to the toric boundary.

An important technical ingredient is the use of tropical geometry to compute Floer cohomology. The tropicalization of a holomorphic disc in X is a tropical disc in the base B of the SYZ fibration; its boundary lies on the tropical Lagrangian skeleton. The count of holomorphic discs with given tropical type equals the count of tropical discs weighted by the appropriate Maslov index. This tropical correspondence, developed by Gross–Siebert (2011) and refined by Mikhalkin (2019), provides an algorithmic way to compute the superpotential W and the A∞‑products. For example, for the resolved conifold O(-1)⊕O(-1) → ℙ¹ the superpotential is W = x + y + q/(xy), and the HMS equivalence identifies the spherical object corresponding to the zero‑section with the structure sheaf of the exceptional curve.

The toric HMS theorem has been generalized to log Calabi–Yau pairs (X, D) where D is a simple normal crossing anticanonical divisor. In this setting the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model on a toric variety with a potential having poles along the toric boundary. The wrapped Fukaya category of X D is equivalent to the category of matrix factorizations of the potential. This framework underlies the proof of HMS for many Fano varieties via the “mirror symmetry for Fano” program of Auroux–Katzarkov–Orlov (2016).

Worked Example: Computing the Superpotential for the Resolved Conifold
Let X be the total space of O(-1)⊕O(-1) → ℙ¹. Its moment polytope is a strip in ℝ² with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). The toric divisors are D₁, D₂ (the two ℙ¹ fibers) and the zero‑section E ≅ ℙ¹. Write the Kähler parameters q₁ = exp(∫C₁ ω), q₂ = exp(∫C₂ ω) where C₁, C₂ are the two independent curve classes. Using the tropical disc count, determine the superpotential W on the mirror (ℂ*)².
The tropical skeleton consists of two rays emanating from the origin along the coordinate axes and a segment connecting (1,0) to (0,1). Basic tropical discs are: (i) a disc with one vertex on the ray x≥0, boundary on the fiber over (0,0), giving monomial x; (ii) a disc on the ray y≥0 giving monomial y; (iii) a disc with boundary on the segment, whose tropical area equals the Kähler area of the zero‑section, giving monomial q/(xy) where q = q₁ q₂. Summing these three contributions yields W = x + y + q/(xy). This matches the known mirror of the resolved conifold.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the mirror superpotential of a toric Calabi–Yau, first draw the moment polytope and identify the toric divisors. The monomials correspond to the primitive inward normals of the facets; the coefficient of each monomial is the exponentiated symplectic area of the corresponding curve class. Remember that for a resolved conifold the zero‑section contributes the term with the product of the two Kähler parameters in the denominator.

Categorical Crepant Resolutions and the McKay Correspondence

The categorical crepant resolution conjecture, formulated by Bondal–Orlov (2002) and Kawamata (2008), asserts that if Y → X is a crepant resolution of a variety with Gorenstein canonical singularities, then the derived categories D^b Coh(Y) and D^b Coh(X) are equivalent. For quotient singularities X = ℂⁿ/G with G ⊂ SL(n, ℂ) finite, the G‑Hilbert scheme Hilb^G(ℂⁿ) provides a crepant resolution, and the derived McKay correspondence of Bridgeland–King–Reid (2001) gives an explicit Fourier–Mukai equivalence Φ: D^b Coh(Hilb^G(ℂⁿ)) → D^b_G Coh(ℂⁿ) where the right side is the G‑equivariant derived category. The kernel is the universal family 𝒵 ⊂ Hilb^G(ℂⁿ) × ℂⁿ, and the functor sends a sheaf ℱ to Rπ2*(π₁^*ℱ ⊗ 𝒪_𝒵)^G.

In dimension three, the conjecture is known for all Gorenstein terminal singularities by work of Van den Bergh (2004) and Toda (2008). The proof uses the existence of a non‑commutative crepant resolution (NCCR) given by the endomorphism algebra of a reflexive module, and shows that the derived category of the NCCR is equivalent to D^b Coh(Y) for any crepant resolution Y. The NCCR perspective also yields a tilting bundle on Y whose endomorphism algebra is the NCCR, providing a bridge between commutative and non‑commutative geometry.

The McKay correspondence extends to the symplectic side via the wrapped Fukaya category of the Milnor fiber of the singularity. For a Kleinian singularity ℂ²/Γ, the Milnor fiber is an ALE space with a hyperkähler metric. Its wrapped Fukaya category is generated by the Lagrangian spheres corresponding to the exceptional curves in the minimal resolution. Seidel–Thomas (2001) showed that the spherical twists around these Lagrangians generate the braid group action on the Fukaya category, which under HMS matches the action of the spherical twists around the exceptional sheaves on the derived side. This gives a symplectic proof of the derived McKay correspondence for surface singularities.

For higher dimensional quotient singularities, the symplectic Milnor fiber is a Liouville manifold whose wrapped Fukaya category is expected to be equivalent to the derived category of the G‑Hilbert scheme. Recent work of Ganatra–Pardon–Shende (2022) establishes this equivalence for all finite subgroups of SL(n, ℂ) by identifying the wrapped Fukaya category with the category of modules over the symplectic cohomology algebra, which is isomorphic to the center of the NCCR. This provides a uniform symplectic proof of the categorical crepant resolution conjecture in the quotient case.

Wall‑Crossing, Stability Conditions, and the Kontsevich–Soibelman Formula

Bridgeland stability conditions on a triangulated category 𝒟 consist of a heart 𝒜 of a bounded t‑structure and a central charge Z: K₀(𝒜) → ℂ such that every object has a Harder–Narasimhan filtration with respect to the slope φ(E) = (1/π) arg Z(E). The space Stab(𝒟) of stability conditions carries a natural topology and a ℂ‑action. For the derived category of a Calabi–Yau threefold Y, the conjectural space of stability conditions is related to the complex moduli of the mirror X via the HMS equivalence.

Wall‑crossing describes how the set of semistable objects changes when the central charge crosses a wall in Stab(𝒟). The Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula (2008) expresses the invariance of the product of quantum dilogarithms associated to BPS states. In the language of Donaldson–Thomas theory, the DT invariants Ω(γ; ζ) count semistable objects of charge γ at stability parameter ζ. The formula states that the ordered product ∏γ Ψ(qγ)Ω(γ; ζ) is independent of ζ, where Ψ is the quantum dilogarithm and the product is taken in the order of increasing phase φ(γ).

On the symplectic side, the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror X carries a natural stability condition induced by the central charge Z(L) = ∫_L Ω, where Ω is the holomorphic volume form. The BPS states correspond to special Lagrangian submanifolds, and their counts are the open Gromov–Witten invariants. The wall‑crossing formula for open invariants was proved by Joyce–Song (2012) using the theory of d‑critical loci and matches the Kontsevich–Soibelman formula under HMS. The scattering diagrams of Gross–Siebert (2011) provide a combinatorial model for the wall‑crossing: each wall is a rational ray in the base B of the SYZ fibration decorated with a function, and the consistency condition for the scattering diagram is exactly the wall‑crossing identity.

Applications include the computation of DT invariants for local Calabi–Yau threefolds such as the resolved conifold. The DT partition function Z_DT(q) = ∑n≥0 Ω(n) q^n satisfies the product formula Z_DT(q) = ∏k≥1 (1 - q^k)-k, which is the MacMahon function. Under HMS this equals the Gromov–Witten partition function of the mirror, confirming the GW/DT correspondence. The wall‑crossing structure also underlies the construction of the categorical Donaldson–Thomas invariants of Kontsevich–Soibelman (2011), which assign a motivic DT invariant to any 3‑Calabi–Yau A∞‑category.

Applications to Enumerative Geometry: Gromov–Witten/Donaldson–Thomas Correspondence

The Gromov–Witten/Donaldson–Thomas correspondence, formulated by Maulik–Nekrasov–Okounkov–Pandharipande (2006), relates the generating series of GW invariants of a Calabi–Yau threefold X to the DT invariants of its mirror Y. For a toric Calabi–Yau threefold, the GW invariants are computed by the topological vertex of Aganagic–Klemm–Mariño–Vafa (2005), which expresses the partition function as a sum over plane partitions weighted by q|π|. The DT invariants count ideal sheaves of curves and points, and their generating function is the MacMahon function. The correspondence states that after the change of variables q = -eiu, the GW partition function equals the DT partition function up to a universal factor.

The proof for toric Calabi–Yau threefolds uses the HMS equivalence to identify the A‑model (GW) with the B‑model (DT) on the mirror. The topological vertex computes the open GW invariants with Lagrangian brane insertions; under HMS these correspond to insertions of skyscraper sheaves on the mirror, which are counted by DT theory with framing. The wall‑crossing formula ensures that the DT invariants are independent of the stability condition, matching the holomorphic anomaly equation on the GW side.

For the quintic threefold, the GW invariants at genus zero were computed by Candelas–de la Ossa–Green–Parkes (1991) using mirror symmetry. The DT invariants for the quintic are not fully known, but the GW/DT correspondence predicts their values. Recent work of Pandharipande–Pixton (2017) proved the correspondence for all Calabi–Yau threefolds that admit a toric degeneration, using the degeneration formula for GW invariants and the wall‑crossing formula for DT invariants. The categorical crepant resolution conjecture plays a role in extending the correspondence to singular Calabi–Yau varieties, where the DT theory is defined on a crepant resolution.

The Virasoro constraints for GW invariants, conjectured by Eguchi–Hori–Xiong (1997) and proved for toric targets by Givental (2001), translate under the GW/DT correspondence into constraints on DT invariants. These constraints are equivalent to the statement that the DT partition function is a τ‑function of the KP hierarchy. The Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula provides a conceptual explanation: the product of quantum dilogarithms is a τ‑function of the quantum cluster algebra associated to the quiver with potential of the Calabi–Yau category.

  • Confusing the wrapped Fukaya category with the compact Fukaya category; the former requires exact Lagrangians cylindrical at infinity and a stop at infinity.
  • Assuming HMS holds for all Calabi–Yau threefolds; it is proved only for toric, elliptic, and certain hypersurface cases.
  • Misidentifying the mirror of a toric Calabi–Yau as a compact variety; the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model on a non‑compact torus.
  • Overlooking the role of the grading and spin structure on Lagrangians; without them the A∞‑operations are not well defined.
  • Treating the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula as a purely algebraic identity without the geometric input of stability conditions.
  • Confusing the categorical crepant resolution conjecture with the classical McKay correspondence; the former is a derived equivalence for any crepant resolution, the latter is a specific equivalence for quotient singularities.
  • Neglecting the change of variables q = -eiu in the GW/DT correspondence; the sign is essential for matching the topological vertex with the MacMahon function.

hand/math-epidemiology.html:
Age-Structured Compartmental Models and Contact Matrices

Real populations mix non‑uniformly across age groups, and many infections — measles, influenza, COVID‑19 — show strong age‑dependent transmission and severity. An age‑structured SIR model partitions each compartment into n age classes: Sᵢ, Iᵢ, Rᵢ for i = 1…n. The force of infection on age class i is λᵢ = Σⱼ βᵢⱼ Iⱼ / Nⱼ, where βᵢⱼ = q·cᵢⱼ combines the per‑contact transmission probability q with the contact rate cᵢⱼ from class i to class j. The matrix C = (cᵢⱼ) is the social contact matrix, often estimated from diary surveys (POLYMOD, CoMix) or mobile‑phone proximity data. The next‑generation matrix for this system is K = (βᵢⱼ / γ) · diag(Nᵢ/Nⱼ), and its dominant eigenvalue gives R₀. Age structure also allows the model to capture heterogeneous susceptibility (e.g., lower susceptibility in children for SARS‑CoV‑2) and age‑specific vaccination strategies. The final‑size relation generalises to a system of transcendental equations: 1 − Sᵢ(∞)/Nᵢ = 1 − exp(−Σⱼ Kᵢⱼ (1 − Sⱼ(∞)/Nⱼ)). Numerical solution of this system yields the attack rate per age group, which is essential for burden estimation and for designing age‑prioritised vaccine allocation.

When contact matrices are time‑varying (school closures, workplace reductions), the model becomes non‑autonomous: dSᵢ/dt = −Sᵢ Σⱼ βᵢⱼ(t) Iⱼ/Nⱼ. The instantaneous reproduction number R(t) is the dominant eigenvalue of the next‑generation matrix built from βᵢⱼ(t). This framework underpins the scenario analyses used by many national advisory groups during the COVID‑19 pandemic.

Time-Varying Reproduction Number Estimation and Renewal Equations

The effective reproduction number Rₜ quantifies transmission at calendar time t and is central to real‑time epidemic monitoring. A widely used estimation framework is the renewal equation: I(t) = Rₜ Σₛ wₛ I(t−s), where I(t) is the incidence (new infections) on day t and wₛ is the generation‑interval distribution (probability that a secondary case appears s days after its infector). Given a time series of reported cases (after deconvolution of reporting delays) and a known wₛ (often a discretised gamma distribution with mean 5–7 days for COVID‑19), Rₜ can be inferred by sliding‑window maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods (e.g., the EpiEstim package). The estimator assumes that the generation interval does not change over the window; if interventions alter contact patterns, the generation interval may shorten, biasing Rₜ upward if unaccounted for. An alternative is the Wallinga–Teunis method, which assigns each case a probability of having been infected by each earlier case based on the generation interval, yielding a non‑parametric Rₜ estimate. Both methods require a reliable estimate of the generation‑interval distribution; misspecification leads to systematic errors, especially early in an epidemic when the distribution is poorly known. Recent work incorporates time‑varying generation intervals by modelling the contact process explicitly, linking Rₜ to the dominant eigenvalue of a time‑dependent next‑generation matrix derived from mobility or contact‑survey data.

Worked Example: Estimating Rₜ from a Renewal Equation
Suppose daily incidence I(t) for t = 1…10 is [2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 15, 14, 10, 6, 3]. The discretised generation‑interval distribution w = [0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2] for lags 1–4 days. Using a 5‑day sliding window ending at day 7, compute the maximum‑likelihood estimate of Rₜ assuming a Poisson observation model.
For the window days 3–7, the incidence vector is I = [5, 8, 12, 15, 14]. The expected incidence λ(t) = Rₜ Σₛ wₛ I(t−s). Compute the convolution for each day in the window: Day 3: λ₃ = Rₜ(0.1·3 + 0.3·2) = Rₜ·0.9 Day 4: λ₄ = Rₜ(0.1·5 + 0.3·3 + 0.4·2) = Rₜ·2.6 Day 5: λ₅ = Rₜ(0.1·8 + 0.3·5 + 0.4·3 + 0.2·2) = Rₜ·5.1 Day 6: λ₆ = Rₜ(0.1·12 + 0.3·8 + 0.4·5 + 0.2·3) = Rₜ·8.5 Day 7: λ₇ = Rₜ(0.1·15 + 0.3·12 + 0.4·8 + 0.2·5) = Rₜ·11.9 The Poisson log‑likelihood is Σ (Iₖ log λₖ − λₖ). Differentiating w.r.t. Rₜ and setting to zero gives Σ Iₖ / Rₜ = Σ λₖ / Rₜ → Rₜ = Σ Iₖ / Σ (convolution without Rₜ). Σ Iₖ = 5+8+12+15+14 = 54. Σ convolution = 0.9+2.6+5.1+8.5+11.9 = 29.0. Hence Rₜ = 54 / 29.0 ≈ 1.86.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for Rₜ estimation, first identify whether the renewal equation or the Wallinga–Teunis method is implied. Write down the generation‑interval distribution explicitly; if it is not given, state the assumption (e.g., gamma with mean 5.2 days). Show the convolution step clearly — examiners award marks for the correct summation, not just the final number. Remember that Rₜ > 1 indicates growing incidence, Rₜ < 1 indicates decline.

Model Calibration, Parameter Identifiability, and Bayesian Inference

Fitting compartmental models to data requires estimating parameters such as β, γ, and the initial number of infectives I₀. The likelihood is typically built from the observation model: reported cases C(t) ~ NegBin(ρ·I(t), φ) where ρ is the reporting fraction and φ the dispersion. Identifiability analysis distinguishes structural identifiability (unique parameters for perfect noise‑free data) from practical identifiability (precision given noisy, sparse data). For the simple SIR model, β and γ are structurally identifiable from incidence data alone, but ρ and I₀ are often confounded — only the product ρ·I₀ is estimable without seroprevalence data. Profile likelihoods and the Fisher Information Matrix reveal flat directions indicating non‑identifiability. Bayesian inference with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) provides full posterior distributions, naturally incorporating prior knowledge (e.g., γ⁻¹ ~ Gamma( shape=5, rate=1 ) for a mean infectious period of 5 days). The posterior predictive check — simulating epidemic trajectories from posterior draws and comparing to observed data — is essential for model validation. Modern probabilistic programming languages (Stan, PyMC) enable hierarchical models that share information across regions or age groups, improving estimates for data‑poor subpopulations. Care must be taken with parameter correlations; strong posterior correlation between β and ρ can cause slow mixing, mitigated by reparameterisation (e.g., estimating R₀ = β/γ and γ separately).

Coupled Within-Host and Between-Host Dynamics for HIV and COVID-19

Multi‑scale models link viral dynamics inside an infected host to transmission at the population level. For HIV, the Nowak–May within‑host model tracks target CD4⁺ T cells (T), productively infected cells (I), and free virus (V): dT/dt = λ − dT − βTV, dI/dt = βTV − aI, dV/dt = kI − μV. The basic reproductive ratio within a host is R₀ʷ = βkλ/(aμd). Antiretroviral therapy reduces β (entry inhibitors) or k (reverse‑transcriptase/protease inhibitors), driving R₀ʷ below 1 and causing viral load decay. The characteristic biphasic decay — rapid first phase (free virus clearance, half‑life ~hours) and slower second phase (infected cell loss, half‑life ~days) — matches clinical data. A third, very slow phase reflects the latent reservoir. At the population level, the transmission rate βₚ is often assumed proportional to the host viral load V(t), e.g., βₚ = c·V(t) where c captures contact rate and per‑virion infectivity. This coupling creates a feedback: treatment lowers V, reducing βₚ and thus population‑level R₀. For COVID‑19, within‑host models incorporate target cells (epithelial cells), innate immune response (interferon), and adaptive immunity. The viral load trajectory informs the generation‑interval distribution and the time‑varying infectiousness profile used in renewal‑equation estimators. Coupled models have been used to evaluate the impact of early antiviral treatment on onward transmission, showing that reducing peak viral load by one log₁₀ can lower the effective reproduction number by 10–20% depending on the timing of treatment initiation.

Targeted Vaccination on Heterogeneous Networks and Percolation Thresholds

Network structure dramatically alters the herd‑immunity threshold. In a configuration‑model network with degree distribution P(k), the basic reproduction number for an SIR process with per‑contact transmission probability T = β/(β+γ) is R₀ = T·⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩. The epidemic threshold corresponds to bond percolation: an outbreak occurs if T > ⟨k⟩/(⟨k²⟩−⟨k⟩). Targeted vaccination that removes the highest‑degree nodes first (acquaintance vaccination, or vaccinating a fraction p of nodes with probability proportional to degree) reduces the second moment ⟨k²⟩ more efficiently than random vaccination. The critical vaccination fraction for random vaccination is p_c = 1 − 1/R₀. For degree‑based targeting, the threshold becomes p_c^target = 1 − ⟨k⟩/(⟨k²⟩−⟨k⟩) · (1/T), which can be substantially lower when the degree distribution is heavy‑tailed (e.g., power‑law with exponent 2 < α < 3). In practice, exact degree information is unavailable; acquaintance vaccination — vaccinating a random neighbour of a randomly chosen individual — preferentially reaches high‑degree nodes without global knowledge. Simulations on empirical contact networks (e.g., from wearable sensors in schools) show that acquaintance vaccination achieves herd immunity with 20–30% fewer doses than random vaccination for influenza‑like parameters. The percolation framework also quantifies the size of the giant component after vaccination, which corresponds to the final epidemic size in the limit of large networks.

  • Confusing R₀ with Rₜ: R₀ is a property of the pathogen in a fully susceptible population; Rₜ varies with immunity and interventions.
  • Ignoring generation‑interval uncertainty: Using a fixed mean without its distribution biases renewal‑equation Rₜ estimates.
  • Assuming all parameters are identifiable: Reporting fraction and initial infectives are often confounded without serology.
  • Applying homogeneous mixing formulas to heterogeneous populations: Herd‑immunity threshold 1−1/R₀ only holds under proportionate mixing.
  • Overlooking the difference between bond and site percolation: Vaccination removes nodes (site percolation), while transmission acts on edges (bond percolation); thresholds differ.
  • Treating within‑host viral load as constant: Infectiousness varies over the infection course; using a single βₚ misrepresents transmission potential.
  • Neglecting model validation: Posterior predictive checks are essential; a model that fits incidence may still mispredict age‑specific attack rates.

These advanced topics form the core of modern mathematical epidemiology and are routinely examined in quantitative public‑health and applied‑mathematics assessments.

hand/algebraic-geometry.html:
Derived Categories and Fourier–Mukai Transforms

The bounded derived category of coherent sheaves Db(Coh X) on a smooth projective variety X over an algebraically closed field is the central object in modern homological algebraic geometry. Its objects are complexes of coherent sheaves with bounded cohomology, and morphisms are obtained by localising the homotopy category at quasi‑isomorphisms. The category carries a natural triangulated structure with shift functor [1] and distinguished triangles coming from short exact sequences of complexes. A Fourier–Mukai transform is an exact functor Φ𝒦 : Db(Coh X) → Db(Coh Y) defined by an object 𝒦 ∈ Db(Coh (X × Y)) — the kernel — via the formula Φ𝒦(−) = R pY*(pX*(−) ⊗L 𝒦), where pX, pY are the projections. Orlov’s representability theorem (1997) states that any exact fully faithful functor between such derived categories that commutes with shifts and has left and right adjoints is isomorphic to a Fourier–Mukai transform. This result underpins the derived category approach to birational geometry: if X and Y are birational Calabi–Yau varieties, Bridgeland (2002) showed that an equivalence Db(Coh X) ≅ Db(Coh Y) exists and is given by a Fourier–Mukai kernel. The Hochschild homology HH*(X) of X is isomorphic to the homology of the derived category and is invariant under derived equivalence, providing a numerical check. Applications include the proof of the McKay correspondence for finite subgroups of SL(2,ℂ) and the construction of autoequivalences such as spherical twists (Seidel–Thomas, 2001) which generate the braid group action on Db(Coh X). The derived category also encodes stability conditions in the sense of Bridgeland (2007), where a stability condition consists of a heart of a bounded t‑structure and a central charge Z : K0(X) → ℂ satisfying the Harder–Narasimhan property. The space of stability conditions Stab(X) is a complex manifold whose geometry reflects the birational geometry of X.

Higher Direct Images and the Theorem on Formal Functions

Let f : X → Y be a proper morphism of Noetherian schemes and ℱ a coherent sheaf on X. The higher direct image sheaves Rif*ℱ are defined as the sheafifications of the presheaves U ↦ Hi(f−1(U), ℱ). Grothendieck’s theorem on formal functions (EGA III, 1961) compares the completion of these sheaves along a closed subscheme Z ⊂ Y with the cohomology of the formal completion of X along f−1(Z). Precisely, for a coherent sheaf ℱ on X and a point y ∈ Y with ideal 𝔪y, there is a canonical isomorphism (Rif*ℱ)ŷ ≅ lim← n Hi(Xn, ℱn), where Xn = X ×Y Spec(𝒪Y,y/𝔪yn) and ℱn is the pullback. This theorem is the engine behind several fundamental results: Zariski’s main theorem (the fibres of a proper birational morphism are connected), Grauert–Riemenschneider vanishing (Rif*ωX/Y = 0 for i > 0 when f is a resolution of singularities), and the semicontinuity theorem for cohomology dimensions. In the analytic setting, the theorem on formal functions is equivalent to the coherence of higher direct images (Grauert’s direct image theorem). A key application is the proof of the base change theorem: if the natural map (Rif*ℱ) ⊗ k(y) → Hi(Xy, ℱy) is surjective for all y, then it is an isomorphism and Rif*ℱ is locally free. The theorem also underlies the construction of the Hilbert scheme via the flattening stratification, where one studies the function y ↦ dim Hi(Xy, ℱy) and uses semicontinuity to find open loci where it is constant.

Worked Example: Formal Functions and Fibre Cohomology
Let f : X → Y be a proper morphism with Y = Spec A, A a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪, and let ℱ be a coherent sheaf on X. Show that the natural map (R1f*ℱ) ⊗A A/𝔪 → H1(X0, ℱ0) is an isomorphism if and only if R1f*ℱ is a free A‑module of finite rank.
By the theorem on formal functions, the completion (R1f*ℱ)̂ is isomorphic to lim← n H1(Xn, ℱn). Since A is local, Nakayama’s lemma implies that the map (R1f*ℱ) ⊗ A/𝔪 → H1(X0, ℱ0) is surjective exactly when the completed module is generated by the images of a basis of the fibre. If the map is an isomorphism, the fibre dimension is constant, so by semicontinuity the function y ↦ dim H1(Xy, ℱy) is locally constant; properness and coherence then force R1f*ℱ to be locally free. Over a local base, locally free means free of finite rank. Conversely, if R1f*ℱ is free, the base change map is an isomorphism by the standard base change theorem for locally free sheaves.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks about the behaviour of higher direct images under base change, first check whether the sheaf is flat over the base and whether the morphism is proper. Then invoke the theorem on formal functions to pass to completions, apply Nakayama’s lemma, and use semicontinuity to deduce local freeness. Remember that the theorem on formal functions holds for any proper morphism of Noetherian schemes, not only for projective ones.

Étale Cohomology and the Weil Conjectures

Étale cohomology, developed by Grothendieck, Artin, and Verdier in the 1960s, provides a Weil cohomology theory for varieties over finite fields, fulfilling the requirements of the Weil conjectures. For a smooth projective variety X over a finite field 𝔽q, the ℓ‑adic étale cohomology groups Hiét(X̄, ℚℓ) (ℓ ≠ p = char 𝔽q) are finite‑dimensional ℚℓ‑vector spaces carrying a continuous action of the absolute Galois group Gal(𝔽̄q/𝔽q). The Frobenius endomorphism Frobq acts on these groups, and the zeta function Z(X, t) = exp(∑m≥1 |X(𝔽qm)| tm/m) admits the rational expression Z(X, t) = ∏i=02 dim X det(1 − t Frobq | Hiét(X̄, ℚℓ))(−1)i+1. The Weil conjectures, proved by Deligne (1974), assert: (1) rationality — Z(X, t) is a rational function; (2) functional equation — Z(X, t) = ± qχ/2 tχ Z(X, 1/(q t)) where χ is the Euler characteristic; (3) Riemann hypothesis — the eigenvalues of Frobq on Hi have absolute value qi/2; (4) Betti numbers — the dimensions of Hi equal the Betti numbers of a complex lift. The proof uses the hard Lefschetz theorem and the Hodge index theorem in the ℓ‑adic setting, established via the theory of weights and the purity theorem. Étale cohomology also satisfies Poincaré duality, Künneth formula, and the Lefschetz trace formula, making it a full Weil cohomology. The formalism extends to constructible sheaves, giving the ℓ‑adic Fourier transform (Deligne, Laumon) and the geometric Langlands correspondence for curves over finite fields (Drinfeld, Lafforgue).

Birational Geometry and the Minimal Model Program in Detail

The Minimal Model Program (MMP) aims to classify projective varieties up to birational equivalence by performing a sequence of elementary birational operations: divisorial contractions and flips. For a normal projective variety X with ℚ‑factorial terminal singularities and a ℚ‑divisor Δ such that (X, Δ) is a klt pair, one considers the cone of curves NE(X) ⊂ N1(X). The Cone Theorem (Mori, 1982) states that NE(X) = NE(X)KX+Δ ≥ 0 + ∑ ℝ≥0[Ci], where each Ci is a rational curve with 0 < −(KX+Δ)·Ci ≤ 2 dim X. An extremal ray R = ℝ≥0[C] with (KX+Δ)·C < 0 admits a contraction morphism contR : X → Y. If the contraction is divisorial, it contracts a divisor to a lower‑dimensional subvariety; if it is small (contracts no divisor), the flip conjecture (proved by Mori for 3‑folds, by Shokurov and Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan in all dimensions) asserts the existence of a birational map X ⇢ X+ which replaces the contracted curves by curves with positive intersection against KX++Δ+. The termination of flips (proved by Shokurov for 3‑folds, by Hacon–McKernan and Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan in general) guarantees that the process ends with either a minimal model (KX+Δ nef) or a Mori fibre space (a contraction X → Z with dim Z < dim X and −(KX+Δ) relatively ample). The abundance conjecture predicts that when KX+Δ is nef, it is semi‑ample, so some multiple defines a morphism to the canonical model. The MMP interacts with moduli: stable varieties (semi‑log‑canonical with ample K) form proper moduli spaces (Kollár–Shepherd‑Barron–Alexeev). The theory of variations of GIT quotients (Thaddeus, Dolgachev–Hu) provides a geometric realisation of flips as wall‑crossings in the space of stability conditions.

Arithmetic Intersection Theory and Arakelov Geometry

Arakelov geometry extends intersection theory to arithmetic surfaces and higher‑dimensional schemes over Spec ℤ by adding “fibres at infinity” — complex points equipped with a Hermitian metric. For a regular projective arithmetic variety X → Spec ℤ of relative dimension d, an arithmetic divisor is a pair (D, g) where D is a divisor on the generic fibre Xℚ and g is a Green current on X(ℂ) satisfying ddc g + δD = ω, with ω a smooth (1,1)‑form. The arithmetic Chow group CĤ1(X) is the group of arithmetic divisors modulo the subgroup generated by (div(f), −log|f|2) for rational functions f. The arithmetic intersection product (D1, g1) · … · (Dd+1, gd+1) is a real number defined by integrating the product of Green currents over X(ℂ) and adding the finite intersection numbers on the special fibres. Faltings (1984) proved the arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem for arithmetic surfaces: χ̂(ℒ) = (1/2) (ℒ·ℒ) + (1/12) (ℒ·ω) + (1/2) ∫X(ℂ) c1(ℒ) ∧ c1(ω) + ζ′(−1) rank(ℒ), where ω is the relative dualising sheaf with the Arakelov metric. This formula was generalised to higher dimensions by Gillet–Soulé (1990) using the arithmetic Grothendieck group and the arithmetic Todd class. Applications include the proof of the Mordell conjecture (Faltings, 1983) via the height inequality on the Jacobian, and the computation of the arithmetic self‑intersection of the Hodge bundle on the moduli space of curves (Moret‑Bailly, 1989). The theory also underlies the arithmetic Bogomolov conjecture (proved by Ullmo and Zhang) which relates the essential minimum of the Néron–Tate height on an abelian variety to the positivity of the arithmetic self‑intersection of the theta divisor.

  • Confusing derived equivalence with isomorphism of varieties — derived equivalent varieties need not be isomorphic, only birational in the Calabi–Yau case.
  • Assuming higher direct images are always coherent without properness — coherence of Rif*ℱ requires f proper and ℱ coherent.
  • Applying the theorem on formal functions to non‑Noetherian bases — the theorem is proved only for Noetherian schemes.
  • Mixing ℓ‑adic étale cohomology with singular cohomology without a comparison theorem — the comparison isomorphism holds only for varieties over ℂ after choosing an embedding ℚ̄ℓ ℂ.
  • Believing every flip exists in all dimensions without the BCHM theorem — flips were only known in dimension ≤3 before 2006.
  • Neglecting the Hermitian metric in Arakelov intersection numbers — the archimedean contribution is essential for the arithmetic Riemann–Roch formula.
  • Each of these traps appears regularly in advanced problem sets and research‑level examinations.

hand/computational-math.html:
Preconditioning Strategies and Spectral Equivalence

Preconditioning transforms a linear system Ax = b into an equivalent system M⁻¹Ax = M⁻¹b whose spectrum is clustered, accelerating Krylov convergence. The ideal preconditioner satisfies M ≈ A while being cheap to apply. Classical choices include the Jacobi preconditioner M = diag(A), the symmetric successive over‑relaxation (SSOR) preconditioner M = (D+ωL)D⁻¹(D+ωL)ᵀ with relaxation parameter ω, and incomplete LU factorizations ILU(k) where fill‑in is limited to level k. For symmetric positive definite matrices, the incomplete Cholesky factorization IC(0) preserves the sparsity pattern of A and yields a preconditioner M = LLᵀ that is spectrally equivalent to A: there exist constants c₁, c₂ > 0 independent of mesh size h such that c₁ (v,Av) ≤ (v,Mv) ≤ c₂ (v,Av) for all vectors v. Spectral equivalence guarantees that the condition number κ(M⁻¹A) remains bounded as h → 0, so the number of CG iterations grows at most logarithmically with problem size. Algebraic multigrid (AMG) constructs a hierarchy of coarse matrices A₀ = A, A₁, …, A_L directly from the matrix entries, using strength‑of‑connection measures to define interpolation operators. When used as a preconditioner, AMG often achieves mesh‑independent convergence for elliptic problems, making it the method of choice for large‑scale finite element discretisations on unstructured grids.

Multigrid Methods for Elliptic Boundary Value Problems

Geometric multigrid exploits a sequence of nested grids Ω₀ ⊂ Ω₁ ⊂ … ⊂ Ω_L with mesh sizes h₀ > h₁ > … > h_L. A V‑cycle consists of pre‑smoothing (typically a few Gauss–Seidel or damped Jacobi sweeps) on the fine grid, restriction of the residual to the next coarser grid, recursive solution of the coarse‑grid correction equation, prolongation of the correction back to the fine grid, and post‑smoothing. The smoothing property damps high‑frequency error components, while the coarse‑grid correction eliminates low‑frequency components that are poorly reduced by smoothing. For a second‑order elliptic operator discretised by finite differences or linear finite elements, the two‑grid convergence factor ρ satisfies ρ ≤ 1 − C / (1 + C) where C is the constant in the smoothing estimate ‖S^ν e‖_A ≤ C ν⁻¹ᐟ² ‖e‖_A. With an appropriate number of smoothing steps ν (usually 1–3), the V‑cycle convergence factor becomes independent of h, yielding optimal O(N) complexity where N is the number of unknowns. The full multigrid (FMG) algorithm starts with a coarse‑grid solution and interpolates it to finer grids, applying a few V‑cycles at each level; FMG delivers an approximate solution with discretisation‑level accuracy in O(N) work. For anisotropic or highly discontinuous coefficients, standard pointwise smoothers may fail; line‑relaxation, plane‑relaxation, or auxiliary space preconditioners restore robustness.

Designing an ILU(0) preconditioner for a 2D Poisson matrix
Given the 5‑point finite difference discretisation of −Δu = f on a unit square with uniform mesh size h, the matrix A is symmetric positive definite with stencil [−1, 4, −1] in each coordinate direction. Construct the ILU(0) factorisation A ≈ LLᵀ preserving the sparsity pattern of A. Estimate the spectral condition number κ(L⁻¹AL⁻ᵀ) and comment on the expected CG iteration count for a 100×100 grid.
The ILU(0) factorisation proceeds row by row: for each interior node (i,j) the diagonal entry lii = √(aii − Σk lik²) and the off‑diagonal entries lij = (aij − Σk lik ljk) / lii for neighbours j that are non‑zero in A. Because the sparsity pattern matches the 5‑point stencil, L has non‑zeros only on the diagonal and the two sub‑diagonals corresponding to west and south neighbours. For the model problem the eigenvalues of the preconditioned matrix cluster around 1 with a spread proportional to h; analysis shows κ(L⁻¹AL⁻ᵀ) = O(h⁻¹). On a 100×100 grid (h = 0.01) the condition number is roughly 100, so CG with ILU(0) typically converges in 30–50 iterations, compared with O(h⁻¹) ≈ 100 iterations for unpreconditioned CG.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the effect of a preconditioner on CG convergence, recall the bound ‖x−x_k‖_A ≤ 2 ((√κ−1)/(√κ+1))^k ‖x−x₀‖_A. Identify whether the preconditioner yields mesh‑independent κ (e.g., multigrid, AMG) or κ = O(h⁻¹) (e.g., ILU(0), Jacobi). State the resulting iteration complexity: O(1) versus O(h⁻¹ᐟ²) for CG. This distinction is a frequent source of marks.

Adaptive Finite Element Methods and A Posteriori Error Estimation

Adaptive FEM replaces uniform refinement by a loop: SOLVE → ESTIMATE → MARK → REFINE. The a posteriori error estimator η_h provides a computable upper bound for the energy error ‖u−u_h‖_E. For the Poisson problem with piecewise linear elements, the residual estimator η_K² = h_K² ‖f + Δu_h‖²L²(K) + ½ Σe⊂∂K h_e ‖[∇u_h·n]‖²L²(e) sums element residuals and jump terms across interior edges e. The global estimator η = (Σ_K η_K²)¹ᐟ² satisfies the reliability bound ‖u−u_h‖_E ≤ C_rel η and the efficiency bound η ≤ C_eff ‖u−u_h‖_E + higher‑order terms, with constants independent of h. Dörfler marking selects a minimal subset M ⊂ T_h such that ΣK∈M η_K² ≥ θ ΣK∈T_h η_K² for a fixed parameter θ ∈ (0,1]; typical choices are θ = 0.3–0.5. Newest‑vertex bisection or red‑green refinement then refines marked elements while preserving conformity. The resulting sequence of meshes yields optimal algebraic convergence rates: if the exact solution belongs to the approximation class A^s, then ‖u−u_h‖_E ≤ C N-s where N is the number of degrees of freedom. This optimality holds for a wide class of elliptic problems, including those with singularities at re‑entrant corners or material interfaces.

Newton–Krylov Methods for Large‑Scale Nonlinear Systems

Newton’s method for F(x)=0 generates iterates xk+1=x_k + s_k where the Newton step solves J(x_k)s_k = −F(x_k) with Jacobian J = ∂F/∂x. For large sparse problems the linear solve is performed inexactly by a Krylov method (GMRES, BiCGSTAB, or TFQMR), giving the Newton–Krylov framework. The forcing term η_k controls the linear residual tolerance: ‖J(x_k)s_k + F(x_k)‖ ≤ η_k ‖F(x_k)‖. Eisenstat–Walker choice η_k = min(η_max, ‖F(x_k)‖^p / ‖F(xk-1)‖^p) with p ∈ [1,2] balances work and superlinear convergence. Globalisation is achieved by line search or trust‑region strategies; a backtracking line search enforces the Armijo condition ‖F(x_k + α s_k)‖ ≤ (1 − c α) ‖F(x_k)‖ with c ∈ (0,1). For problems with a symmetric positive definite Jacobian, the linear solve can use preconditioned CG, and the overall method inherits the mesh‑independent convergence of the preconditioner. Inexact Newton methods are the workhorse for nonlinear PDEs (Navier–Stokes, nonlinear elasticity, radiative transfer) where the Jacobian is assembled matrix‑free via directional derivatives Jv ≈ (F(x+εv)−F(x))/ε, avoiding explicit Jacobian formation.

  • Assuming ILU(0) gives mesh‑independent convergence for all elliptic problems; it only yields κ = O(h⁻¹) for standard second‑order discretisations.
  • Confusing the smoothing property of multigrid (high‑frequency damping) with the coarse‑grid correction property (low‑frequency elimination).
  • Using the residual estimator without the jump terms for non‑conforming or discontinuous Galerkin methods, leading to non‑reliable bounds.
  • Choosing a fixed forcing term η_k = 10⁻⁶ in Newton–Krylov; this wastes work early and may prevent superlinear convergence near the solution.
  • Believing that matrix‑free Jacobian‑vector products are always cheaper than assembled Jacobians; for modest sparsity the assembled Jacobian with a good preconditioner is often faster.
  • Neglecting the inf‑sup condition when designing mixed finite element preconditioners for saddle‑point systems, resulting in unstable iterations.
  • Over‑refining uniformly instead of using Dörfler marking, which destroys the optimal complexity guarantee of adaptive FEM.

These traps highlight the most common misconceptions that appear in advanced computational mathematics examinations.

maths/probability-statistics.html:
Moment Generating Functions — Encoding All Moments

The moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable X is defined as M_X(t) = E[etX] for those real t where the expectation exists. For a discrete variable the sum Σ etx P(X=x) is used; for a continuous variable the integral ∫ etx f(x) dx applies. The MGF, when it exists in a neighbourhood of zero, uniquely determines the distribution — two random variables with identical MGFs on an interval containing 0 have the same distribution. This uniqueness property makes the MGF a powerful tool for identifying distributions of sums of independent variables: if X and Y are independent, MX+Y(t) = M_X(t) M_Y(t). The product form turns convolution of densities into simple multiplication, which is why the MGF is the standard device for proving that the sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson, the sum of independent normals is normal, and the sum of independent gamma variables with the same scale parameter is gamma.

Moments are recovered by differentiation: the k‑th raw moment E[X^k] equals the k‑th derivative of M_X(t) evaluated at t=0, provided the derivative exists. For example, the MGF of a binomial(n,p) variable is (1-p+pe^t)^n. Differentiating once gives np, differentiating twice gives np(1-p)+n2p2, from which the variance np(1-p) follows immediately. The MGF of a normal(μ,σ2) variable is exp(μt + ½σ2t2); its first derivative at 0 is μ, second derivative is μ2+σ2, yielding variance σ2. When the MGF does not exist (e.g., Cauchy distribution), characteristic functions φ_X(t)=E[eitX] serve the same purpose because they always exist. In JEE‑level problems, the MGF is most often used to identify a distribution from a given functional form or to compute moments of a sum without performing convolution integrals.

A common examiner twist is to give the MGF of a random variable and ask for a probability such as P(X=2) or P(X>1). The student must recognise the MGF as that of a known distribution, write down its parameters, and then use the PMF or CDF of that distribution. Another twist: given M_X(t) = (0.3+0.7e^t)5, identify X ~ Binomial(5,0.7) and compute P(X≥3) = Σk=35 C(5,k) 0.7^k 0.35-k. Mastery of the standard MGFs — Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, exponential, gamma, normal — and the product rule for independence is essential for rapid problem solving.

Central Limit Theorem — Why the Normal Appears Everywhere

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that for a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables X1, X2, … with finite mean μ and finite variance σ2, the standardized sum (Σi=1^n X_i - nμ) / (σ√n) converges in distribution to a standard normal N(0,1) as n → ∞. In practical terms, for moderately large n (often n ≥ 30 is quoted, but the required n depends on the skewness of the underlying distribution), the distribution of the sample mean X is approximately N(μ, σ2/n). This approximation underpins most large‑sample inference: confidence intervals for means, hypothesis tests about means, and the normal approximation to the binomial and Poisson distributions.

The CLT does not require the original variables to be normal; it only requires independence, identical distribution, and finite variance. Heavy‑tailed distributions with infinite variance (e.g., Cauchy) violate the conditions, and the sample mean does not converge to a normal law. The rate of convergence is governed by the Berry‑Esseen theorem, which bounds the supremum distance between the CDF of the standardized sum and the standard normal CDF by a constant times the third absolute moment divided by σ3√n. This explains why highly skewed distributions (exponential, log‑normal) need larger n for a good normal approximation.

In JEE problems, the CLT is frequently invoked to approximate probabilities for sums or averages of many i.i.d. variables. A typical question: "A fair die is rolled 100 times. Approximate the probability that the total score exceeds 370." Here each roll has mean 3.5 and variance 35/12 ≈ 2.917. The sum has mean 350 and variance 100×35/12 ≈ 291.7, standard deviation ≈ 17.08. The standardized value for 370.5 (continuity correction) is (370.5-350)/17.08 ≈ 1.20, giving probability ≈ 0.115. The continuity correction is crucial when approximating a discrete sum by a continuous normal. Another common variant uses the CLT to approximate a binomial(n,p) by N(np, np(1-p)) when np and n(1-p) are both >5, again with continuity correction.

Technique
A factory produces bolts whose lengths are independent with mean 5.0 cm and standard deviation 0.2 cm. A random sample of 64 bolts is taken. Approximate the probability that the sample mean length lies between 4.98 cm and 5.02 cm.
The sample mean X of n=64 i.i.d. observations has mean μ = 5.0 and standard deviation σ/√n = 0.2/8 = 0.025. By the CLT, X ≈ N(5.0, 0.0252). Standardize the bounds: z1 = (4.98 - 5.0)/0.025 = -0.8; z2 = (5.02 - 5.0)/0.025 = 0.8. Using standard normal tables, P(-0.8 < Z < 0.8) = Φ(0.8) - Φ(-0.8) = 0.7881 - 0.2119 = 0.5762. Hence the approximate probability is 0.576.
Exam Day Strategy
When a problem asks for an approximation using the CLT, always check whether the sample size is large enough (np and n(1-p) > 5 for binomial, or n ≥ 30 for general distributions). Apply continuity correction for discrete underlying variables. Write down the mean and standard deviation of the sum or average explicitly before standardizing; this avoids arithmetic slips and shows the examiner you understand the scaling.

Sampling Distributions — Chi‑Square, t, and F

Sampling distributions describe the behaviour of statistics computed from random samples. Three fundamental sampling distributions arise from normal samples: the chi‑square, Student's t, and Snedecor's F. If Z1,…,Z_k are independent standard normals, then Q = Σi=1^k Z_i2 follows a chi‑square distribution with k degrees of freedom, denoted χ2_k. Its mean is k and variance 2k. If a random sample X1,…,X_n is drawn from N(μ,σ2), then (n-1)S2/σ2 ∼ χ2n-1, where S2 is the sample variance. This result is the basis for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for a single variance.

Student's t distribution emerges when the population variance is unknown. Let X be the sample mean and S the sample standard deviation from a normal sample of size n. Then T = (X - μ) / (S/√n) follows a t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom. The t density is symmetric, bell‑shaped, but with heavier tails than the normal; as n→∞, tn-1 → N(0,1). The t distribution is used for confidence intervals and tests about a single mean when σ is unknown, and for the difference of two means from independent normal samples with equal variances (pooled t) or unequal variances (Welch's t).

The F distribution is the ratio of two independent chi‑square variables divided by their degrees of freedom: F = (U/df1) / (V/df2) where U∼χ2df1, V∼χ2df2 independent. If two independent normal samples have variances σ12 and σ22, then (S12/σ12) / (S22/σ22) ∼ Fn1-1, n2-1. This underlies the test for equality of two variances and the analysis of variance (ANOVA) for comparing several means. In JEE, the F distribution appears mainly in the context of comparing two sample variances or in regression ANOVA tables. Critical values for χ2, t, and F are tabulated; the exam may provide a small excerpt or expect you to know that for large df the distributions approach normal or chi‑square limits.

Hypothesis Testing — Framework and Decision Rules

Statistical hypothesis testing formalises the decision between a null hypothesis H0 and an alternative H1 using sample data. The procedure: (1) State H0 and H1. (2) Choose a significance level α (commonly 0.05 or 0.01). (3) Select an appropriate test statistic whose sampling distribution under H0 is known (e.g., Z, t, χ2, F). (4) Determine the critical region (rejection region) such that P(test statistic falls in critical region | H0 true) = α. (5) Compute the observed value of the test statistic from the sample. (6) Reject H0 if the observed value lies in the critical region; otherwise do not reject H0. The p‑value is the smallest α at which H0 would be rejected; it equals the probability, under H0, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.

Type I error (rejecting a true H0) has probability α. Type II error (failing to reject a false H0) has probability β; power = 1-β. The Neyman‑Pearson lemma shows that for simple hypotheses, the most powerful test at level α is based on the likelihood ratio. For composite hypotheses, uniformly most powerful tests rarely exist; instead we use likelihood ratio tests, Wald tests, or score tests. In JEE, the focus is on the classical tests: Z‑test for a mean with known variance, t‑test for a mean with unknown variance, χ2‑test for a variance, and F‑test for equality of two variances. Two‑sample problems use pooled or Welch t‑tests for means, and the F‑test for variances. The exam may also test the chi‑square goodness‑of‑fit test or test of independence in contingency tables, where the test statistic Σ (O_i - E_i)2 / E_i follows χ2 with appropriate df.

A frequent examiner twist is to ask for the interpretation of a p‑value or the consequence of changing α. Remember: a small p‑value indicates strong evidence against H0, but it is not the probability that H0 is true. Also, failing to reject H0 does not prove H0; it merely indicates insufficient evidence. When constructing confidence intervals, the duality with two‑sided tests holds: a 1-α confidence interval contains exactly those parameter values that would not be rejected by a two‑sided test at level α.

Conditional Expectation and the Law of Total Variance

Conditional expectation E[Y|X] is a function of the random variable X; it is the best predictor of Y in the mean‑square sense given X. For discrete variables, E[Y|X=x] = Σ_y y P(Y=y|X=x); for continuous, the integral with the conditional density. Two fundamental identities are the law of total expectation (iterated expectation): E[Y] = E[ E[Y|X] ], and the law of total variance: Var(Y) = E[ Var(Y|X) ] + Var( E[Y|X] ). The first term is the average of the conditional variances (within‑group variability); the second term is the variance of the conditional means (between‑group variability). This decomposition is the probabilistic analogue of ANOVA and is extremely useful for computing variances of mixture distributions or hierarchical models.

Example: Suppose N ∼ Poisson(λ) and, given N=n, X1,…,X_n are i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2, independent of N. Let S = Σi=1^N X_i (with S=0 if N=0). Then E[S|N] = Nμ, Var(S|N) = Nσ2. By total expectation, E[S] = E[N]μ = λμ. By total variance, Var(S) = E[Nσ2] + Var(Nμ) = λσ2 + λμ2 = λ(σ2+μ2). This matches the known variance of a compound Poisson distribution. Another classic use: if X|Y=y ∼ N(y,1) and Y ∼ N(0,τ2), then E[X|Y]=Y, Var(X|Y)=1. Hence E[X]=E[Y]=0, Var(X)=E[1]+Var(Y)=1+τ2. The law of total variance avoids the need to derive the marginal density of X explicitly.

In JEE problems, conditional expectation often appears in the context of the "random sum" or "random number of trials" models. Recognising the structure E[ Σi=1^N X_i ] = E[N] E[X] (when N is independent of the X_i's) and Var( Σi=1^N X_i ) = E[N] Var(X) + Var(N) (E[X])2 is a direct application of the two laws. The examiner may also test the property that for any random variables X,Y, Cov(X,Y) = Cov( X, E[Y|X] ), which follows from the law of total covariance. Mastery of these identities allows rapid solution of problems that would otherwise require messy double sums or integrals.

  • Assuming the MGF exists for all t when it only exists in a neighbourhood of zero.
  • Forgetting the continuity correction when using the normal approximation to a discrete sum.
  • Using the chi‑square test for variance without verifying the underlying normality assumption.
  • Confusing the p‑value with the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
  • Applying the law of total variance without checking that the conditioning variable is independent of the summands where required.
  • Treating the t‑distribution as normal for small sample sizes (n < 30) when the population variance is unknown.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common pitfalls.
