hand/logarithmic-geometry.html:
Logarithmic de Rham Complex and the Log Cartier Isomorphism

The logarithmic de Rham complex Ω•X/S(log) is the natural replacement of the usual de Rham complex when the morphism f : X → S is only log smooth. Concretely, if (X, MX) → (S, MS) is a log smooth morphism of fine saturated log schemes, the sheaf of logarithmic differentials Ω1X/S(log) is defined as the cokernel of the map MXgp ⊗ OX → Ω1X/S induced by dlog. The higher exterior powers give a complex Ω•X/S(log) whose hypercohomology computes the log de Rham cohomology H•dR,log(X/S). This cohomology satisfies a log version of the Poincaré lemma: locally on X in the Kummer‑flat topology the complex is quasi‑isomorphic to the constant sheaf ℤ (or ℚℓ after tensoring). The log Cartier isomorphism, proved by Kato and later refined by Ogus, identifies the inverse Cartier operator C−1 : ΩiXs/k(log) → ℋi(WΩ•X) where WΩ•X is the log de Rham–Witt complex. In characteristic p this isomorphism is the key input for the Hyodo–Kato comparison: it relates the log crystalline cohomology of the special fiber to the log de Rham cohomology of the generic fiber after adjoining the period element t = log([π]). The filtration on log de Rham cohomology induced by the stupid filtration on the log de Rham–Witt complex is the Kato filtration; it refines the monodromy filtration and is compatible with the weight filtration under the weight–monodromy conjecture. A subtle point is that the log Cartier isomorphism is not functorial for arbitrary log morphisms; it requires the morphism to be log smooth and the log structures to be fine and saturated. When these hypotheses fail, the inverse Cartier operator may not exist, and the comparison theorems break down. This explains why semistable reduction (which guarantees log smoothness after a finite base change) is the standard setting for p‑adic Hodge theory of degenerating families.

The Kato–Nakayama Space and Log Betti Cohomology

For a fine saturated log analytic space (X, MX) over ℂ, Kato and Nakayama constructed a topological space Xlog equipped with a continuous map τ : Xlog → X. The fiber of τ over a point x ∈ X is a real torus (S1)r where r is the rank of the characteristic monoid MX,x/OX,x×. The space Xlog carries a natural C∞ structure when the log structure is fine and saturated, and its singular cohomology with ℚ coefficients, called log Betti cohomology H•B(Xlog, ℚ), is canonically isomorphic to the log étale cohomology H•log‑ét(X, ℚ) via the comparison isomorphism of Kato–Nakayama and Ogus. This provides a Betti realization for log motives and completes the logarithmic Hodge theory: the log de Rham cohomology, log étale cohomology, and log Betti cohomology form a compatible triple of cohomology theories linked by period isomorphisms. The construction of Xlog is functorial for log morphisms, and proper log smooth morphisms induce proper maps on Kato–Nakayama spaces, yielding a log version of the proper base change theorem. An important computational tool is the description of Xlog as a colimit of real torus bundles over the strata of the underlying analytic space; this allows one to compute log Betti cohomology via a Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence whose E1 page involves the ordinary cohomology of the strata with coefficients in the local systems given by the monodromy of the torus bundles. In the case of a semistable degeneration X → Δ, the Kato–Nakayama space of the special fiber Y is homotopy equivalent to the dual intersection complex of Y, and the log Betti cohomology of Y recovers the limit mixed Hodge structure on the nearby cycles. This topological picture underlies the Clemens–Schmid exact sequence and the weight–monodromy conjecture in the complex analytic setting.

Worked Example: Computing Log Betti Cohomology of a Nodal Curve
Let C be a projective nodal curve over ℂ with a single node, equipped with the divisorial log structure associated to the node. Describe the Kato–Nakayama space Clog and compute H1B(Clog, ℚ).
The underlying analytic space of C is a topological sphere with two points identified. The log structure at the node has characteristic monoid ℕ2 (the two branches), so the fiber of τ over the node is (S1)2. Over smooth points the fiber is a point. Hence Clog is obtained from the normalization ℙ1 by gluing a 2‑torus over the two preimages of the node. This space deformation retracts onto a wedge of a circle (coming from the torus) and the normalization sphere. Its first Betti number is 1 (from the torus) plus 0 (from ℙ1) = 1. Therefore H1B(Clog, ℚ) ≅ ℚ, which matches the log étale cohomology H1log‑ét(C, ℚ) and the dimension of the limit mixed Hodge structure on the nearby cycles of a smoothing of C.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the log Betti cohomology of a simple log analytic space, first identify the strata and the rank of the characteristic monoid on each stratum. Build the Kato–Nakayama space as a torus bundle over each stratum, then use a Mayer–Vietoris or cellular decomposition argument. Remember that the log Betti cohomology always agrees with log étale cohomology with ℚ coefficients, so you may switch to the more familiar étale side if the log structure is given algebraically.

Logarithmic Motivic Homotopy Theory and Realizations

Building on Voevodsky’s A1-homotopy theory, Binda, Park, and Østvær developed a logarithmic version of the stable motivic homotopy category SHlog(S) for a base log scheme (S, MS). The objects are log motivic spectra, constructed from smooth log schemes over S with the Nisnevich topology refined by Kummer‑flat covers. The category admits a symmetric monoidal structure, a log motivic t‑structure whose heart is the category of log mixed motives DMlog(S), and realization functors to log étale cohomology, log de Rham cohomology, and log Betti cohomology (via the Kato–Nakayama space). A key technical result is the log A1-invariance theorem: for a log smooth morphism f : X → Y which is an A1-bundle in the log sense (i.e., locally a product with the standard log affine line), the pullback on log motivic spectra is an equivalence. This fails for general log smooth morphisms, reflecting the fact that log geometry remembers the boundary divisor. The log motivic t‑structure is compatible with the weight filtration on log étale cohomology, and the weight–monodromy conjecture translates into the statement that the log motivic t‑structure coincides with the weight t‑structure after ℓ‑adic realization. The log motivic category also provides a natural home for the log syntomic complexes Sn(r) which interpolate between log étale and log crystalline cohomology; these appear as the fibers of the map WnΩ• → φpWnΩ• in the log motivic stable homotopy category. Recent work of Hoyois, Kelly, and Østvær shows that the log motivic sphere spectrum represents log algebraic K‑theory, giving a log version of the Bloch–Lichtenbaum spectral sequence. This framework is expected to unify the various comparison isomorphisms (Hyodo–Kato, Faltings, Tsuji) under a single motivic umbrella.

Logarithmic Geometry in the Arithmetic Langlands Program

The Fargues–Scholze geometric Langlands correspondence for a reductive group G over a p‑adic field F is formulated on the stack BunG of G‑bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF. The curve XFF carries a natural log structure coming from the divisor at infinity (the “untilt” of the perfectoid field). Log geometry enters at three crucial points. First, the moduli stack of local shtukas, which parametrizes modifications of G‑bundles at a point, is naturally a log stack; its log structure records the order of the modification and ensures that the Hecke correspondences are log smooth. Second, the cohomological correspondence of Fargues–Scholze uses the log étale cohomology of the stack of shtukas with coefficients in ℓ‑adic sheaves; the log structure guarantees properness of the relevant maps after compactifying by adding a log divisor at infinity. Third, the local Langlands correspondence is realized via the excursion operators acting on the log étale cohomology of the moduli space of local shtukas; the log structure is essential for defining the correct perverse t‑structure on the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves. In the global setting, the work of Genestier–Lafforgue and Varshavsky uses log geometry to compactify the moduli stack of G‑bundles on a curve with parabolic structures at marked points; the log structure encodes the parabolic weights and makes the Hitchin fibration log smooth. The log Hitchin system then provides a geometric incarnation of the spectral side of the Langlands correspondence. These applications illustrate that log geometry is not merely a technical convenience but a structural ingredient: the boundary divisors that appear in compactifications of moduli spaces carry intrinsic monoid data, and the log formalism is the unique language that treats this data functorially while preserving cohomological purity.

Logarithmic Structures on Moduli Spaces and Compactifications

Many moduli problems in algebraic geometry produce spaces that are naturally open subvarieties of a compactification with a normal crossing boundary. The standard example is the moduli space Mg,n of smooth n‑pointed curves of genus g, whose Deligne–Mumford compactification M̄g,n has a boundary divisor with normal crossings. Equipping M̄g,n with the divisorial log structure associated to the boundary yields a fine saturated log stack (M̄g,n, Mboundary). The forgetful morphism M̄g,n+1 → M̄g,n is then log smooth, and the universal curve carries a log structure making the structure map log smooth as well. This log smoothness is the geometric incarnation of the fact that the boundary strata correspond to stable curves with nodes, and the log structure records the smoothing parameters. The log cotangent complex of M̄g,n computes the logarithmic tangent space, which is identified with the space of infinitesimal deformations of the pointed stable curve preserving the nodes. In the context of Gromov–Witten theory, the log structure on the moduli space of stable maps M̄g,n(X, β) (for a smooth target X) is used to define the virtual fundamental class via the log perfect obstruction theory of Chen–Marcus–Wise. The log virtual class is independent of the choice of log structure on the target, and it specializes to the usual virtual class when the target carries the trivial log structure. For degenerations of the target, e.g., a family X → Δ with central fiber a normal crossing divisor, the log structure on the base and on the total space yields a log smooth moduli stack of stable maps to the log scheme (X, MX). The resulting log Gromov–Witten invariants satisfy a degeneration formula that expresses the invariants of the generic fiber in terms of relative invariants of the components of the special fiber, with gluing governed by the log structure. This formula is the algebro‑geometric counterpart of the symplectic sum formula and is proved using the log virtual localization of the torus action on the log moduli space. The upshot is that log structures on moduli spaces turn boundary strata into legitimate geometric objects with well‑behaved deformation theory, enabling intersection theory and cohomological computations that are impossible in the purely scheme‑theoretic setting.

  • Confusing the log de Rham complex with the ordinary de Rham complex on the underlying scheme; the log differentials contain dlog terms that are essential for the Cartier isomorphism.
  • Assuming the Kato–Nakayama space is always a manifold; it is a C∞ manifold only when the log structure is fine and saturated, otherwise it may have singularities.
  • Treating log motivic homotopy theory as a straightforward extension of Voevodsky’s theory without noting the failure of A1-invariance for general log smooth morphisms.
  • Overlooking the role of the log structure on the Fargues–Fontaine curve in the Fargues–Scholze correspondence; the log divisor at infinity is not a decorative addition but a necessary ingredient for properness of Hecke correspondences.
  • Neglecting that the log virtual fundamental class in Gromov–Witten theory depends on the log structure of the source curve, not on a log structure on the target.
  • Misapplying the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism to non‑semistable degenerations; the isomorphism requires the special fiber to carry the canonical log structure coming from a semistable model.
  • Forgetting that the log Cartier isomorphism is not functorial for arbitrary log morphisms; it holds only for log smooth morphisms with fine saturated log structures.

Logarithmic Hodge Theory and the Logarithmic Hodge Filtration

Logarithmic Hodge theory extends the classical Hodge decomposition to varieties equipped with a fine saturated log structure. Let X be a smooth log scheme over a field of characteristic zero whose log structure is defined by a normal crossing divisor D. The log de Rham complex Ω•X(log D) carries a decreasing filtration F• by subcomplexes generated by forms with at least a given number of dlog factors. Kato proved that the associated graded pieces are canonically isomorphic to the direct sum of the ordinary de Rham complexes of the strata of D, shifted by the codimension of the stratum. This yields a log Hodge spectral sequence that degenerates at E1 and computes the log Hodge cohomology groups Hi(X, ΩjX(log D)). The log Hodge filtration on the log de Rham cohomology H•dR(X, log D) is functorial for log smooth morphisms and satisfies a log version of Griffiths transversality. In the semistable degeneration setting, the limit mixed Hodge structure on the nearby cycles is recovered from the log Hodge filtration on the special fiber equipped with its canonical log structure. The weight filtration arises from the monodromy logarithm N, and the log Hodge filtration provides the Hodge filtration on the limit mixed Hodge structure. This identification is the cornerstone of the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism and of the p‑adic comparison theorems of Tsuji and Nizioł.

Logarithmic Period Maps and Mixed Hodge Structures on Degenerations

A log period map assigns to a pointed log smooth family f : X → S with fine saturated log structures a horizontal morphism from the log analytic space Slog to a classifying space of polarized mixed Hodge structures. Nakayama constructed the log period map by integrating the log Gauss–Manin connection on the log de Rham cohomology bundle. The target is a quotient of a period domain by a monodromy group that respects the log structure. The map is holomorphic and its differential is given by the Kodaira–Spencer map twisted by the log tangent sheaf. When the base S is a log point, the log period map recovers the classical period map of the nearby fiber together with the limit mixed Hodge structure on the special fiber. The log period map satisfies a log version of the Griffiths transversality condition: the image of the log tangent bundle lies in the horizontal subbundle defined by the Hodge filtration. This property is essential for the proof of the log Cattani–Kaplan–Schmid theorem on the algebraicity of the image of the period map for variations of mixed Hodge structure with log singularities. In the context of mirror symmetry, the log period map on the moduli of log Calabi–Yau varieties provides the B‑model side of the correspondence, while the A‑model is captured by log Gromov–Witten invariants.

Technique: Computing the log Hodge filtration on a simple normal crossing divisor
Let X be the log scheme obtained from the affine plane A² with coordinates (x, y) by equipping it with the divisorial log structure associated to the divisor D = {xy = 0}. Compute the graded pieces GrpF H²dR(X, log D) and identify them with the de Rham cohomology of the strata of D.
The log de Rham complex is generated by dx, dy, dlog x = dx/x, dlog y = dy/y with the relation x·dlog x + y·dlog y = 0. The filtration Fp is generated by forms containing at least p dlog factors. For p = 2, F² is spanned by dlog x ∧ dlog y, which is exact because d(dlog x ∧ dlog y) = 0 and the complex is acyclic in degree 2 on the affine chart. Hence Gr²F H² = 0. For p = 1, F¹/F² is generated by the classes of dlog x ∧ dy and dx ∧ dlog y modulo exact forms. These correspond to the de Rham cohomology of the two irreducible components of D (the axes) shifted by one. For p = 0, Gr⁰F H² is the ordinary de Rham cohomology of the open stratum A² D, which vanishes in degree 2. Thus the log Hodge filtration reproduces the expected stratification: the only non‑zero graded piece is Gr¹F H² ≅ H¹dR(D₁) ⊕ H¹dR(D₂).
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the log Hodge filtration on a semistable degeneration, first write down the log de Rham complex with its dlog generators, then apply the definition of the filtration by the number of dlog factors. Use the known degeneration of the log Hodge spectral sequence at E₁ to identify graded pieces with the de Rham cohomology of the boundary strata. This algorithmic approach avoids memorising case‑by‑case results and works for any fine saturated log structure defined by a normal crossing divisor.

Logarithmic Derived Categories and the Six Operations

The formalism of six operations (f!, f!, f*, f*, ⊗, ℋ𝑜𝓂) for étale sheaves extends to the log étale site of a fine saturated log scheme. Abe and Caro constructed the log étale topos and proved that for a log smooth morphism f : X → Y the inverse image functor f* preserves constructibility and that the proper direct image f* satisfies a log proper base change theorem. The exceptional inverse image f! is defined via the log compactification of f and coincides with the usual f! on the underlying schemes when the log structures are trivial. The log tensor product and internal Hom are compatible with the log structure, and the projection formula holds. A key feature is the log purity theorem: for a log regular immersion i : Z → X of codimension c, the functor i! is isomorphic to i*(−c)[−2c] twisted by the log Thom class, which lives in the log étale cohomology of the normal bundle equipped with its canonical log structure. This purity is used to define log Gysin maps and to prove a log version of the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem. The log six operations also underlie the construction of the log motivic category DMlog and the log motivic cohomology groups, which satisfy a log version of the Beilinson–Lichtenbaum conjecture.

Logarithmic Geometry over Valuation Rings and the Logarithmic Fargues–Fontaine Curve

Let V be a complete discrete valuation ring with perfect residue field k of characteristic p and fraction field K of characteristic 0. The log structure on Spec V given by the closed point yields a fine saturated log scheme. The log crystalline site of this log scheme computes the log crystalline cohomology of the special fiber, which is canonically isomorphic to the Hyodo–Kato cohomology of a semistable model over V. Scholze introduced a log structure on the Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF = (Y {∞})/φℤ by taking the divisor at infinity as a log divisor. The resulting log adic space (XFF, M) is log smooth over Spa ℚp and its log étale cohomology with ℓ‑adic coefficients realizes the local Langlands correspondence for GLn(K). The log structure is essential: without it the Hecke correspondences on the moduli stack of shtukas are not proper, and the trace formula fails. The log de Rham complex on (XFF, M) computes the p‑adic Hodge theory of the curve, and the log Cartier isomorphism identifies the log de Rham cohomology with the log crystalline cohomology of the special fiber. This log geometric framework is the foundation of the Fargues–Scholze geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence and of the recent work on the categorical local Langlands program.

  • Confusing the log Hodge filtration with the ordinary Hodge filtration on the underlying scheme; the log filtration counts dlog factors and is strictly finer.
  • Assuming the log period map is defined for arbitrary log structures; it requires fine saturated log structures and a log smooth family.
  • Treating the log six operations as a formal copy of the classical six operations without checking log purity and log proper base change hypotheses.
  • Neglecting the log divisor at infinity on the Fargues–Fontaine curve; the log structure is not decorative but necessary for properness of Hecke stacks.
  • Applying the log Cartier isomorphism to morphisms that are not log smooth; the isomorphism holds only for log smooth morphisms with fine saturated log structures.
  • Overlooking that the log motivic category DMlog does not satisfy A¹‑invariance for general log smooth morphisms; the failure is measured by the log structure.
  • Misidentifying the weight filtration on limit mixed Hodge structures with the monodromy filtration without the log Hodge filtration to provide the Hodge filtration.

The advanced sections above complete the core theoretical toolkit needed for research‑level problems in logarithmic geometry.

Logarithmic Connections and the Logarithmic Riemann–Hilbert Correspondence

A logarithmic connection on a fine saturated log scheme X over a field k of characteristic zero is a k-linear map ∇: E → E ⊗OX ωX/klog satisfying the Leibniz rule with respect to the log structure sheaf MX. Here ωX/klog denotes the sheaf of log differential forms, generated by ordinary differentials together with dlog sections coming from the monoid MX. Integrability means the curvature ∇∘∇ vanishes; this is equivalent to the condition that the associated log de Rham complex (E, ∇) is a complex.

The logarithmic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, established by Kato, Nakayama, and later refined by Ogus, asserts an equivalence of categories between the category of integrable log connections with regular singularities on a log smooth k-scheme and the category of finite‑dimensional representations of the log fundamental group π1log(X). Regular singularities are defined by the condition that locally the connection matrix has at most simple poles along the log divisor, with residues lying in the Lie algebra of the monoid. The functor from connections to representations sends (E, ∇) to the sheaf of horizontal sections on the log universal cover, which is a locally constant sheaf on the log étale site.

Key technical points: the log structure must be fine and saturated; the morphism X → Spec k must be log smooth; the correspondence fails if the log structure is not saturated because the Kummer étale covers needed to trivialize the monodromy are missing. The log de Rham cohomology of (E, ∇) computes the cohomology of the associated local system, and the log Hodge filtration on this cohomology is induced by the filtration by the number of dlog factors. This filtration is strictly finer than the ordinary Hodge filtration on the underlying scheme, a fact that often appears in exam questions comparing the two spectral sequences.

An illustrative example: let X = A1k with the log structure given by the divisor {0}. The log de Rham complex of the trivial line bundle with connection d + α dlog t (α ∈ k) has cohomology concentrated in degree 1, and the associated representation of π1log(X) ≅ Ẑ is the rank‑one Kummer character t ↦ tα. The log Riemann–Hilbert correspondence identifies this connection with that character.

Logarithmic Fundamental Group and Logarithmic Étale Covers

The log fundamental group π1log(X, x̄) of a connected fine saturated log scheme X with a geometric log point x̄ is defined as the automorphism group of the fiber functor on the category of log étale covers of X. A log étale cover is a morphism f: Y → X which is integral, log étale (i.e. the induced map on log structures is an isomorphism after inverting the characteristic monoid), and finite. This category is Galois; the log fundamental group is a profinite group fitting into a canonical exact sequence

1 → π1(Xtriv, x̄) → π1log(X, x̄) → Hom(Γ(X, MXgp/OX*), Ẑ) → 1

where Xtriv denotes the underlying scheme with the trivial log structure. The right‑hand term is the Kummer part, classifying Kummer étale covers obtained by adjoining roots of sections of the characteristic monoid. When X is log smooth over a field, the Kummer part is a product of copies of Ẑ indexed by the irreducible components of the log divisor.

For example, let X = (A1C, {0}) with the divisor log structure. The underlying scheme minus the divisor is Gm, whose topological fundamental group is Z. The Kummer part adds a copy of Ẑ for the divisor, and the log fundamental group is the profinite completion of Z × Z, which is canonically isomorphic to the tame fundamental group of Gm. In contrast, the ordinary étale fundamental group of Gm is Ẑ, missing the wild inertia at 0. The log fundamental group therefore captures both tame and Kummer monodromy.

Examiners often test the distinction between the log fundamental group and the fundamental group of the complement of the log divisor. The correct answer requires writing down the exact sequence above and identifying the Kummer term with Hom(Γ(X, MXgp/OX*), Ẑ). Forgetting the Kummer term leads to an incomplete description of the category of log étale covers.

Worked Example: Log Fundamental Group of a Log Point
Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Consider the log scheme X = (Spec k, M) where M = k ⊕ N with the map N → k sending 1 to 0. Compute π1log(X).
The underlying scheme is a point, so its ordinary fundamental group is trivial. The characteristic monoid is Mgp/OX* ≅ N. The Kummer part is Hom(N, Ẑ) ≅ Ẑ. The exact sequence reduces to 1 → 1 → π1log(X) → Ẑ → 1, hence π1log(X) ≅ Ẑ. This matches the fact that log étale covers of this log point are given by Kummer extensions k[t]/(tn−a) with a ∈ k*, classified by the profinite completion of N.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the log fundamental group, first write the exact sequence relating it to the ordinary fundamental group of the underlying scheme and the Kummer term Hom(Γ(Mgp/O*), Ẑ). Identify the characteristic monoid from the log structure, compute its group completion, and then take continuous homomorphisms to Ẑ. This algorithm works for any fine saturated log scheme and avoids the common mistake of equating the log fundamental group with the fundamental group of the complement of the divisor.

Logarithmic Picard Groups and Logarithmic Chow Groups

The logarithmic Picard group Piclog(X) of a fine saturated log scheme X classifies isomorphism classes of log line bundles, i.e. pairs (L, α) where L is a line bundle on the underlying scheme and α: MX → L is a homomorphism of monoids compatible with the structure map MX → OX. There is a canonical exact sequence

0 → H0(X, OX*) → H0(X, MXgp) → Piclog(X) → Pic(X) → 0

where the middle map sends a global section of the groupified log structure to the associated log line bundle. The kernel of Piclog(X) → Pic(X) is the group of Cartier divisors supported on the log divisor modulo principal divisors coming from units of the log structure. This description shows that Piclog(X) is an extension of the usual Picard group by a torus whose character group is the group of global sections of the characteristic monoid.

Logarithmic Chow groups CHlog*(X) were introduced by Kato and later developed by Bloch–Esnault. They are defined as the homology of a complex of log cycles, where a log cycle is a cycle on X together with a log structure on its support compatible with the ambient log structure. The log cycle class map lands in log étale cohomology (or log crystalline cohomology in the p‑adic setting) and respects the log Hodge filtration. For a log smooth variety over a field, the log Chow groups satisfy a moving lemma and a projective bundle formula analogous to the classical case, but the presence of the log structure modifies the intersection product by adding contributions from the boundary strata.

An important computational tool is the localization exact sequence for a log regular immersion i: Z → X of codimension c: there is a Gysin map i!: CHlog*(X) → CHlog*-c(Z) which coincides with the usual Gysin map on the underlying schemes twisted by the log Thom class in log étale cohomology. This twist is the source of the log correction terms that appear in the log version of the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem.

Examiners frequently ask to compute Piclog for a simple log scheme such as (P1, {0,∞}). The answer is Z × k*, where the Z factor records the degree of the underlying line bundle and the k* factor records the trivialization along the two points up to the log structure. Forgetting the k* factor is a common error.

Logarithmic Geometry on Stacks and Orbifolds

Logarithmic structures extend naturally to Artin stacks. A log stack is a pair (X, MX) where X is an Artin stack and MX is a sheaf of monoids on the log étale site of X satisfying the same fine saturated conditions as for schemes. Log smooth morphisms of log stacks are defined by requiring the underlying morphism to be smooth and the map on characteristic monoids to be injective with torsion‑free cokernel. The log étale site of a log stack is defined using representable log étale morphisms; its topos admits a six‑operations formalism analogous to the scheme case, as constructed by Abramovich–Chen–Gross–Siebert.

A central example is the moduli stack Mg,nlog of n‑pointed genus g prestable curves equipped with the universal log structure. The log structure records the nodes and marked points: at a node the characteristic monoid is N2 → O, (a,b) ↦ xy, and at a marked point it is N → O, 1 ↦ 0. This log structure makes the forgetful morphism Mg,nlog → Mg,n log smooth and proper. The virtual fundamental class of Mg,nlog in the sense of Behrend–Fantechi carries a natural log structure, and the log Gromov–Witten invariants defined using this class satisfy the log version of the WDVV equations.

Another important application is the log structure on the inertia stack IX of a log stack X. The inertia stack parametrizes pairs (x, g) where x is a point of X and g is an automorphism of x. The log structure on IX is induced by pulling back MX and adding a monoid recording the action of g on the characteristic monoid. This enriched log structure is essential for the log McKay correspondence and for defining log orbifold cohomology.

A frequent examiner trap is to treat the log structure on a stack as the pullback of a log structure on its coarse moduli space. This is false in general because stabilizer groups can act non‑trivially on the characteristic monoid, and the log structure on the stack must encode this action. The correct approach is to work directly on the log étale site of the stack and to verify log smoothness using the stack‑theoretic definition.

  • Confusing the log Riemann–Hilbert correspondence with the classical one; the log version requires fine saturated log structures and regular singularities defined by the log divisor.
  • Identifying the log fundamental group with the fundamental group of the complement of the log divisor; the Kummer part must be included via the exact sequence.
  • Omitting the Kummer term Hom(Γ(Mgp/O*), Ẑ) when computing π1log.
  • Forgetting that Piclog(X) fits into an exact sequence with H0(Mgp) and Pic(X); the extra torus factor is often missed.
  • Assuming log Chow groups satisfy the same projective bundle formula without the log Thom class twist.
  • Treating log structures on stacks as mere pullbacks from coarse moduli spaces, ignoring stabilizer actions on the characteristic monoid.
  • Applying the log Gysin map without the log Thom class, leading to incorrect intersection numbers on boundary strata.

These advanced topics complete the toolkit needed for research‑level problems in logarithmic geometry.

Logarithmic Mirror Symmetry and Tropical Geometry

Logarithmic geometry provides the natural framework for the Gross–Siebert program, which constructs mirror pairs via toric degenerations and tropical geometry. A log Calabi–Yau variety is a pair (X, D) where X is a smooth variety and D is a reduced divisor such that KX + D ∼ 0, equipped with the divisorial log structure. The tropicalization of a log Calabi–Yau variety is a cone complex Σ(X) built from the dual intersection complex of the central fiber of a maximally degenerate log smooth family. The Gross–Siebert algorithm reconstructs the mirror family by gluing toric pieces according to the wall-crossing structure on Σ(X). The scattering diagram lives in the tropical manifold B = Σ(X) and consists of walls (codimension-one polyhedral subsets) with attached automorphisms of the torus algebra k[Λb] where Λb is the local lattice of integral tangent vectors. The consistency of the scattering diagram — the condition that the product of wall automorphisms around any loop is the identity — is equivalent to the Maurer–Cartan equation for the log structure on the central fiber. The mirror family is then constructed as the formal completion of a log scheme whose tropicalization is B with the consistent scattering diagram. The log structure on the mirror family encodes the instanton corrections from holomorphic disks in the original variety. A key computational tool is the tropical vertex, which describes the wall structure for a local model (A2, {xy = 0}) and generates the higher-order walls via the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall-crossing formula. The log Gromov–Witten invariants of (X, D) with contact orders along D are identified with the tropical curve counts on B via the correspondence theorem of Abramovich–Chen–Gross–Siebert. This identification requires the log structure to be fine and saturated, and the tropical curves to be balanced with multiplicities given by the lattice index of the tangent lattice. The log mirror symmetry conjecture asserts that the log Fukaya category of (X, D) is equivalent to the log derived category of coherent sheaves on the mirror, with the log structure providing the necessary grading and the tropicalization providing the skeleton for the wrapped Fukaya category.

Logarithmic Gromov–Witten Theory and Logarithmic Stable Maps

The moduli space of log stable maps Mg,nlog(X, β) parametrizes log morphisms from n-pointed genus g log curves to a log smooth target X with fixed curve class β. A log curve is a prestable curve with a log structure that is locally modeled on Nr → O at nodes (r = 2 for ordinary nodes, r = 1 for marked points) and N → O at marked points. The log structure on the source curve is required to be basic, meaning it is the pullback of the minimal log structure on the moduli stack Mg,nlog. A log stable map is a representable log morphism f: C → X such that the underlying map is stable and the map on characteristic monoids is integral and saturated at every geometric point. The virtual fundamental class [Mg,nlog(X, β)]vir is constructed using the log perfect obstruction theory of Chen, which replaces the usual cotangent complex with the log cotangent complex Lflog. The log virtual dimension is dim X + (dim X − 3)(1 − g) + ∫β c1(TXlog) + n, where TXlog is the log tangent sheaf. The log Gromov–Witten invariants are defined by integrating tautological classes against this virtual class. The log WDVV equations hold for these invariants, and the log topological recursion relations are modified by boundary terms coming from the log structure. A crucial feature is the gluing formula: the log virtual class of a fiber product over a log point is the product of the log virtual classes twisted by the log Euler class of the normal bundle. This gluing is compatible with the tropical gluing of the corresponding tropical curves. The log quantum cohomology ring QHlog*(X) is defined using the log three-point invariants and carries a log Dubrovin connection. For a log Calabi–Yau variety, the log quantum cohomology is expected to be isomorphic to the log Fukaya category via the log mirror symmetry isomorphism. The log structure on the moduli space itself is the universal log structure pulled back from Mg,nlog, and its characteristic monoid at a point records the smoothing parameters of the nodes and the contact orders at the marked points. This log structure makes the evaluation maps log étale, which is essential for the definition of the log quantum product.

Worked Computation: Log Picard Group of a Log Curve
Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g with a reduced divisor D = {p1, ..., pn} of n distinct points. Equip C with the divisorial log structure MC = OC ∩ j*OCD* where j: CD → C is the inclusion. Compute Piclog(C) and describe the exact sequence relating it to Pic(C) and the torus factor.
The log Picard group fits into the exact sequence 0 → H0(C, MCgp/OC*) → Piclog(C) → Pic(C) → 0. The sheaf MCgp/OC* is supported on D and its stalk at pi is Z, generated by the local equation of D. Hence H0(C, MCgp/OC*) ≅ Zn. The map to Piclog(C) sends (a1, ..., an) to the log line bundle (OC, α) where α: MC → OC is the identity on OC* and sends the local generator at pi to ai ∈ k*. The map Piclog(C) → Pic(C) forgets the log structure. The sequence splits non-canonically: a splitting is given by choosing a trivialization of OC(D) along D. Thus Piclog(C) ≅ Pic(C) × (k*)n. The torus factor (k*)n records the trivializations of the log line bundle at each marked point modulo the log structure. Forgetting this factor is the standard error; the log Picard group is strictly larger than Pic(C) unless n = 0.
Exam Strategy: Log Picard Computations
When asked to compute Piclog for a log scheme (X, D), first identify the characteristic monoid Mgp/O*. For a divisorial log structure on a smooth variety, this is the constant sheaf Z on D. Then H0(X, Mgp/O*) = Z#D where #D is the number of irreducible components of D. The exact sequence 0 → H0(Mgp/O*) → Piclog → Pic(X) → 0 always holds for fine saturated log structures. The torus factor is (k*)#D over an algebraically closed field. Always write the exact sequence explicitly; examiners award marks for the sequence even if the final group is misidentified.

Logarithmic p-adic Hodge Theory and the Logarithmic Fontaine Functors

Logarithmic p-adic Hodge theory extends the classical Fontaine functors to log schemes over a p-adic base. Let K be a finite extension of Qp with ring of integers OK and perfect residue field k. A log scheme over OK is a fine saturated log scheme X with a log morphism to Spec OK equipped with the log structure associated to the closed point. The log crystalline site (X/OK)cryslog is defined using log PD thickenings; its cohomology Hcrys*(X/OK)log is the log crystalline cohomology. The log de Rham cohomology HdR*(X/OK)log is the hypercohomology of the log de Rham complex ΩX/OKlog. The log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism identifies the log crystalline cohomology of the special fiber with the log de Rham cohomology of a log smooth lift, compatibly with the monodromy operator N and the Frobenius φ. The log Fontaine functors Dcryslog, Dstlog, DdRlog are defined on the category of log p-adic Galois representations — continuous representations of GK on finite-dimensional Qp-vector spaces equipped with a log structure compatible with the action. The log period rings Bcryslog, Bstlog, BdRlog are constructed by adjoining log structures to the classical period rings; for example Bstlog = Bst[log π] where π is a uniformizer. The log comparison isomorphisms Héti(XK̄, Qp) ⊗ Bcryslog ≅ Hcrysi(X/OK)log ⊗ Bcryslog hold for proper log smooth X with semi-stable reduction. The log Hodge–Tate decomposition takes the form Héti(XK̄, Qp) ⊗ Cp ≅ ⊕j Hi-j(X, ΩX/OKj,log) ⊗ Cp(-j). The log monodromy operator N on log crystalline cohomology satisfies the log weight monodromy conjecture: the graded pieces of the monodromy filtration are pure of the expected weight. The log Fontaine–Laffaille theory classifies log crystalline representations with Hodge–Tate weights in [0, p-2] in terms of filtered φ-modules with a log structure. The log Breuil–Kisin modules provide an integral version for all weights. The log structure on the period rings is essential for the compatibility with the log Hodge filtration and for the definition of the log Sen operator.

Logarithmic D-modules and Logarithmic Holonomic Systems

The theory of logarithmic D-modules, developed by Kashiwara, Mochizuki, and others, studies modules over the sheaf of log differential operators DXlog on a log smooth variety X. The log differential operators are generated by the log tangent sheaf TXlog = Derlog(OX) over OX. A log D-module is a quasi-coherent OX-module with an integrable log connection ∇: M → M ⊗ ΩX1,log. The log characteristic variety Charlog(M) is a closed conic subset of the log cotangent bundle T*logX. A log D-module is log holonomic if dim Charlog(M) = dim X. The log Riemann–Hilbert correspondence establishes an equivalence between the derived category of regular holonomic log D-modules and the derived category of constructible sheaves on the Kato–Nakayama space Xlog. The log irregularity complex measures the failure of a log D-module to be regular; it is supported on the log divisor and its stalks are computed by the log Stokes matrices. The log Hodge filtration on a log D-module underlying a log mixed Hodge module is a filtration by log coherent subsheaves compatible with the log connection. The log Bernstein–Sato polynomial blog(s) of a log function f ∈ Γ(X, MX) controls the log V-filtration and the log nearby cycles. For a log smooth pair (X, D), the log D-module OX(*D) of meromorphic functions with poles along D is log holonomic and regular; its log de Rham complex computes the log de Rham cohomology. The log Fourier transform exchanges log D-modules on a log vector bundle with log D-modules on the dual log vector bundle, preserving log holonomicity. The log microlocalization functor μlog associates to a log D-module a module over the log microlocalization of DXlog, and the log characteristic cycle CClog(M) is a Lagrangian cycle in T*logX. The log index theorem of Kashiwara–Schapira expresses the Euler characteristic of a log holonomic D-module in terms of its log characteristic cycle and the log Todd class of X.

Logarithmic Motivic Integration and Logarithmic Arc Spaces

Logarithmic motivic integration, introduced by Nicaise and Sebag, extends the Kontsevich–Denef–Loeser motivic integration to log schemes. The log arc space Llog(X) of a log scheme X is the functor that assigns to a k-algebra R the set of log morphisms Spec R[[t]] → X, where Spec R[[t]] carries the log structure associated to the divisor t = 0. For a log smooth variety X of dimension d, Llog(X) is a log smooth ind-scheme of infinite dimension, and its fibers over the log jet schemes are log affine bundles. The log motivic measure μlog is a measure on the Boolean algebra of log constructible subsets of Llog(X) taking values in the log Grothendieck ring K0(Vark)log. The log Grothendieck ring is generated by isomorphism classes of log varieties with the scissor relation [X] = [Z] + [XZ] for a closed log subscheme Z, and the product is the fiber product over the log point. The log motivic integral of a log volume form ω ∈ Γ(X, ωXlog) over a log constructible set A is ∫A |ω|log = ∑n [πn(A)] L-nd where πn: Llog(X) → Lnlog(X) is the truncation to the n-th log jet scheme and L = [A1] is the log Lefschetz motive. The log change of variables formula holds for log birational morphisms f: Y → X that are log isomorphisms outside a log divisor: ∫Llog(X) |ω|log = ∫Llog(Y) |f*ω|log. The log motivic zeta function Zlog(f, T) = ∑n≥1 [Xnlog] L-nd Tn of a log function f ∈ Γ(X, MX) is rational in the log Grothendieck ring, and its poles are related to the log Bernstein–Sato polynomial. The log motivic nearby fiber ψflog is defined as the limit of the log motivic integrals over the log fibers f-1(t) as t → 0. The log monodromy action on ψflog is induced by the log structure on the arc space. The log motivic integration on a log Calabi–Yau variety computes the log Gromov–Witten invariants via the log mirror symmetry correspondence: the log motivic integral of the log volume form over the log arc space of the mirror equals the generating function of log Gromov–Witten invariants of the original variety.

  • Confusing the log motivic measure with the classical motivic measure on the underlying scheme; the log jet schemes are strictly larger and the log Lefschetz motive carries a non-trivial log structure.
  • Assuming the log Riemann–Hilbert correspondence holds for irregular log D-modules without the log Stokes data; the log irregularity complex must be included.
  • Omitting the log monodromy operator N in the log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism; the log crystalline cohomology carries a canonical N that is zero in the classical case for smooth varieties.
  • Treating the log period ring Bstlog as Bst ⊗ k[log π] without the log Frobenius and log monodromy actions; the log structure on the period ring is not a tensor product in the category of log rings.
  • Forgetting that the log characteristic variety lives in the log cotangent bundle T*logX, not the classical cotangent bundle; the log conormal directions along the divisor are essential for log holonomicity.
  • Applying the classical change of variables formula in motivic integration to a log birational morphism without the log Jacobian factor; the log Jacobian is a section of the log canonical bundle ωY/Xlog.
  • Identifying the log arc space Llog(X) with the classical arc space L(X) × L(D) for a divisor D; the log structure couples the arcs on X and D via the log morphism condition.

These advanced topics complete the research-level toolkit for logarithmic geometry across mirror symmetry, enumerative geometry, p-adic Hodge theory, D-module theory, and motivic integration.

Logarithmic Intersection Theory and Logarithmic Chern Classes

Logarithmic intersection theory extends the classical Fulton–MacPherson intersection product to the category of fine and saturated log schemes. The key idea is to replace the usual cycle groups by log cycle groups Zlogk(X) generated by integral closed log subschemes of codimension k together with a log structure induced from the ambient log scheme. For a log regular scheme X the log Chow group Alogk(X) is the quotient of Zlogk(X) by rational equivalence defined using log Cartier divisors. The log intersection product

Alogi(X) × Alogj(X) → Alogi+j(X)

is constructed by deforming to the normal cone in the log sense; the log normal cone carries a natural log structure coming from the divisor of the deformation. The resulting product is associative, commutative and compatible with proper push‑forward and flat pull‑back of log morphisms.

Logarithmic Chern classes are defined for a log vector bundle E on a log regular scheme X by applying the splitting principle to the log projective bundle Plog(E). The total log Chern class clog(E) = 1 + c1,log(E) + … + cr,log(E) lives in the operational log Chow ring Alog*(X). When the log structure is trivial the classes coincide with the usual Chern classes. For a log smooth morphism f : X → Y the log Todd class tdlog(TX/Ylog) appears in the log Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch formula

chlog(f!E) · tdlog(TX/Ylog) = f*(chlog(E) · tdlog(TXlog))

where chlog is the log Chern character. The log excess intersection formula, proved by Kato and Nakayama, shows that for a log regular embedding i : Z X with log normal bundle Nlog one has

i!(α) = clog(Nlog) ∩ i*α

for any log cycle class α. This formalism underlies the computation of log Gromov–Witten invariants via virtual fundamental classes in the log stable map compactification.

Logarithmic Riemann–Roch Theorem for Logarithmic Schemes

The logarithmic Riemann–Roch theorem, established by Kato and later refined by Saito, gives a precise relationship between the log Chern character of a bounded complex of log coherent sheaves and its log Euler characteristic. Let X be a proper log smooth scheme over a field k of characteristic zero, and let E be a perfect complex in the derived category of log coherent sheaves Dbcoh(Xlog). The theorem states

χlog(X, E) = ∫X chlog(E) · tdlog(TXlog)

where χlog(X, E) = Σ (−1)i dimk Hilog(X, E) is the alternating sum of log coherent cohomology dimensions, and the integral denotes the degree map on the top‑dimensional log Chow group Alogdim X(X). The log Todd class is defined by the same power series as the classical Todd class but applied to the log tangent bundle TXlog. The proof proceeds by reducing to the case of a log vector bundle via the log splitting principle, then using the log Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch for the structure morphism X → Spec k together with the log version of the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem for the log de Rham complex.

An important corollary is the log version of the Kawasaki formula for orbifolds: if X is a log Deligne–Mumford stack with log structure induced by a divisor with normal crossings, the log Euler characteristic of a log vector bundle equals the integral over the inertia stack of the log Chern character twisted by the age grading. This formula is essential in logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory where the virtual localisation formula expresses invariants as integrals over fixed loci in the log moduli stack of stable maps.

Worked Example: Logarithmic Riemann–Roch on a Log Curve
Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g with a reduced divisor D = p1 + … + pn. Equip C with the log structure MC = OC ∩ j*OCD where j : CD → C is the inclusion. Let L be a line bundle on C of degree d. Compute the log Euler characteristic χlog(C, L) using the logarithmic Riemann–Roch theorem.
The log tangent bundle fits into the exact sequence 0 → TC → TClog → ⊕i=1n Opi → 0. Hence c1,log(TClog) = c1(TC) + n = 2−2g + n. The log Todd class is tdlog(TClog) = 1 + ½ c1,log. The log Chern character of L is chlog(L) = 1 + c1(L) because the log structure does not affect the first Chern class of a line bundle. The degree map on Alog1(C) sends a zero‑cycle to its usual degree. Therefore

χlog(C, L) = ∫C (1 + c1(L)) · (1 + ½(2−2g+n)) = d + ½(2−2g+n) = d − g + 1 + n/2.

Since n is even for a log curve coming from a divisor with normal crossings, the result is an integer. This matches the known formula χlog(C, L) = χ(C, L) + n/2 where χ(C, L) = d − g + 1 is the classical Euler characteristic.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a log Euler characteristic, first identify the log tangent bundle via the exact sequence relating it to the classical tangent bundle and the normal bundle of the divisor. Write down the log Todd class up to the top degree, multiply by the log Chern character of the sheaf, and integrate using the degree map on the log Chow group. Remember that the log Chern character of a line bundle coincides with the classical one; only the Todd class changes.

Logarithmic Hilbert Schemes and Logarithmic Quot Schemes

Logarithmic Hilbert schemes parametrize families of log closed subschemes with a fixed log Hilbert polynomial. Given a projective log scheme X over a base log scheme S and a polynomial P, the functor HilblogP(X/S) assigns to an S-log scheme T the set of log closed subschemes Z ⊂ X ×S T which are finite, flat and of relative dimension zero over T and whose log Hilbert polynomial equals P. The representability theorem of Abramovich–Chen–Marcus–Wise shows that HilblogP(X/S) is a projective log scheme over S when X is log projective and the log structures are fine and saturated. The universal family carries a natural log structure making the inclusion a log regular embedding.

Logarithmic Quot schemes are defined analogously for quotients of a fixed log coherent sheaf E on X. The functor QuotlogP(E/X/S) sends T to isomorphism classes of log surjections ET ↠ F where F is flat over T with log Hilbert polynomial P. The same representability result holds, and the universal quotient is a log coherent sheaf on the universal family. Both constructions are compatible with the log deformation theory: the tangent space at a point [Z] of the log Hilbert scheme is Homlog(IZ, OZ) where IZ is the log ideal sheaf, and the obstruction space is Ext1log(IZ, OZ). The log virtual fundamental class on the log Hilbert scheme is obtained by applying the log perfect obstruction theory of the log moduli stack of stable maps, and it coincides with the classical virtual class when the log structure is trivial.

These log parameter spaces are indispensable in logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory because the moduli stack of log stable maps Mlog(X, β) is constructed as a log substack of a log Hilbert scheme of curves in X × P1. The log structure on the Hilbert scheme encodes the contact orders of the curves with the boundary divisor, and the log virtual localisation formula reduces the computation of log Gromov–Witten invariants to integrals over fixed loci in the log Hilbert scheme.

Logarithmic Toric Geometry and Logarithmic Fans

Logarithmic toric geometry provides a combinatorial description of log smooth toric varieties and their degenerations. A logarithmic fan Σ consists of a fan Δ in a lattice N together with a monoid homomorphism σ : Δ → M to the dual lattice M = Hom(N, ℤ) satisfying compatibility conditions: for each cone τ ∈ Δ the image σ(τ) generates a face of the positive orthant in M. The associated log toric variety X(Σ) is obtained by gluing affine log schemes Spec ℤ[τ∨ ∩ M] ⊕ σ(τ) along common faces. The log structure on X(Σ) is the one induced by the toric boundary divisor together with the extra data of σ which records the log structure on the strata.

Every fine and saturated log smooth scheme with a torus action is locally isomorphic to a log toric variety defined by a logarithmic fan. Conversely, a logarithmic fan determines a log smooth toric variety whose log structure is the divisorial log structure associated to the toric boundary plus the ghost sheaf determined by σ. The log Picard group of X(Σ) fits into an exact sequence

0 → M → Piclog(X(Σ)) → Pic(X(Δ)) → 0

where the first map sends a character to the corresponding log line bundle with its canonical log structure. The log Chow ring Alog*(X(Σ)) is generated by the log divisor classes Dρ corresponding to rays ρ of Δ together with the classes σ(ρ) in the ghost sheaf. The log intersection product is computed by the same Stanley–Reisner relations as in the classical case, but the linear equivalence relations are modified by the map σ.

Logarithmic fans also control degenerations of toric varieties: a family over Spec ℤ[ℕ] with log structure given by the divisor t = 0 corresponds to a morphism of logarithmic fans Σ → Σ0 where Σ0 is the logarithmic fan of the central fibre. The log smoothness of the total space is equivalent to the condition that the map of fans is a subdivision compatible with the monoid maps. This combinatorial criterion is used in the construction of log Calabi–Yau degenerations and in the proof of the log mirror symmetry conjecture for toric complete intersections.

Logarithmic Shimura Varieties and Logarithmic Period Domains

Logarithmic Shimura varieties arise as the log smooth compactifications of Shimura varieties associated to reductive groups over ℚ with a Hodge type embedding. Let (G, X) be a Shimura datum of Hodge type and let K ⊂ G(𝔸f) be a neat compact open subgroup. The Shimura variety ShK(G, X) carries a natural log structure coming from the toroidal compactification ShKtor constructed by Ash–Mumford–Rapoport–Tai. The boundary divisor is a normal crossings divisor, and the associated divisorial log structure makes ShKtor a log smooth scheme over Spec ℤ (after possibly inverting a finite set of primes). The log de Rham cohomology of the universal abelian scheme over ShKtor computes the log Hodge cohomology of the Shimura variety, and the log Hodge filtration coincides with the filtration induced by the Hodge decomposition on the interior.

The logarithmic period domain Dlog is the log analytic space obtained by equipping the classical period domain D with the log structure induced by the normal crossings boundary of a suitable toroidal compactification of the quotient ΓD. The log period map Φlog : ShKtor → ΓDlog is a morphism of log analytic spaces which extends the classical period map. The log Griffiths transversality theorem states that the differential of Φlog maps the log tangent bundle into the log subbundle Tlog−1,1 of the log Hodge bundle. This property is essential for defining the log mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of the boundary strata.

In the p‑adic setting, the logarithmic Faltings–Chai integral model of the Siegel modular variety provides a log smooth scheme over ℤp whose generic fibre is the Shimura variety for GSp2g. The log crystalline cohomology of this model carries a log Frobenius and a log monodromy operator, and the log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism identifies it with the log de Rham cohomology of the generic fibre. The resulting log filtered (φ, N)‑modules are the p‑adic avatars of the log mixed Hodge structures on the complex side, and they play a central role in the proof of the log version of the Fontaine–Mazur conjecture for Galois representations arising from Shimura varieties.

  • Confusing the log Chow group with the classical Chow group of the underlying scheme; the log cycle classes retain the ghost sheaf data and the rational equivalence uses log Cartier divisors.
  • Applying the classical Riemann–Roch formula without the log Todd class; the log Todd class differs by the contribution of the boundary divisor.
  • Assuming the log Hilbert scheme represents the same functor as the classical Hilbert scheme; the log structure imposes extra conditions on the families of subschemes.
  • Treating a logarithmic fan as an ordinary fan; the monoid map σ encodes the log structure on strata and cannot be ignored.
  • Identifying the log period domain with the classical period domain as analytic spaces; the log structure on the boundary is essential for the log Griffiths transversality statement.
  • Omitting the log monodromy operator N in the log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism for Shimura varieties; N is non‑zero on the boundary strata and encodes the weight filtration.
  • Using the classical virtual fundamental class on a log moduli space without the log perfect obstruction theory; the log virtual class lives in the log Chow group and differs by the log normal bundle contribution.

These advanced topics complete the research‑level toolkit for logarithmic geometry across intersection theory, enumerative geometry, toric methods, and arithmetic applications.

Logarithmic Prismatic Cohomology and the Logarithmic Prismatic Site

Prismatic cohomology, introduced by Bhatt and Scholze, provides a unified framework for p‑adic cohomology theories. In the logarithmic setting, one works with the logarithmic prismatic site (X/𝔸)₍log₎₍△₎ whose objects are logarithmic prisms (A, I, M) equipped with a map to the log scheme X. A logarithmic prism is a δ‑ring A with an ideal I = (d) such that A is (p, I)‑complete, p ∈ I + pA, and the Frobenius φ : A → A satisfies φ(d) = p·u for a unit u, together with a log structure M on Spec A compatible with the divided powers on I. The logarithmic prismatic cohomology complex △₍log₎(X/𝔸) is the derived global sections of the structure sheaf 𝒪₍△₎ on this site. It carries a natural Frobenius φ and a logarithmic Nygaard filtration N^≥• whose graded pieces are related to the logarithmic Hodge–Tate cohomology. The logarithmic prismatic comparison theorem states that for a proper log smooth scheme X over 𝒪ₖ with k a perfectoid field, there are canonical isomorphisms △₍log₎(X/𝔸) ⊗^L_𝔸 𝔸_inf ≃ RΓ₍log₎₍ét₎(X_C, ℤ_p) ⊗_ℤ_p 𝔸_inf and △₍log₎(X/𝔸) ⊗^L_𝔸 A_inf/(ξ) ≃ RΓ₍log₎₍dR₎(X/𝒪ₖ). The logarithmic prismatic site also admits a logarithmic version of the Breuil–Kisin prism, giving rise to logarithmic Breuil–Kisin cohomology which computes the logarithmic crystalline cohomology of the special fibre. The logarithmic Nygaard filtration induces the logarithmic Hodge filtration on log de Rham cohomology after base change, and the logarithmic conjugate filtration on log Hodge–Tate cohomology. This theory is essential for the logarithmic p‑adic Langlands correspondence and for the construction of logarithmic (φ, Γ)‑modules.

Logarithmic Syntomic Cohomology and the Logarithmic Fontaine–Messing Isomorphism

Logarithmic syntomic cohomology is defined as the homotopy fixed points of the logarithmic Frobenius on the logarithmic Nygaard completion of prismatic cohomology: RΓ₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(r)) := (RΓ₍△₎₍log₎(X/𝔸) ̂_N^≥r)φ=p^r. For a log smooth proper scheme X over 𝒪ₖ, the logarithmic syntomic cohomology groups H^i₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(r)) are finitely generated ℤ_p‑modules that interpolate between logarithmic étale cohomology and logarithmic de Rham cohomology. The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism provides a canonical quasi‑isomorphism between the logarithmic syntomic complex and the logarithmic crystalline complex with its logarithmic Hodge filtration: RΓ₍syn₎₍log₎(X/𝒪ₖ, r) ≃ RΓ₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗^LW(k) 𝒪ₖ ⊗ Fil^r_log Ω^•₍log₎. This isomorphism is constructed using the logarithmic prismatic site and the logarithmic Nygaard filtration, and it respects the logarithmic Frobenius and the logarithmic monodromy operator N. The logarithmic syntomic cohomology computes the logarithmic p‑adic étale cohomology via the logarithmic syntomic–étale comparison: H^i₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(r)) ⊗ ℚ_p ≃ H^i₍ét₎₍log₎(X_η, ℚ_p(r))Gal. In the semistable case, the logarithmic syntomic cohomology of the generic fibre is related to the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato cohomology of the special fibre by the logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism, and the logarithmic monodromy operator N on the log crystalline side corresponds to the logarithmic weight filtration on the log étale side. The logarithmic syntomic regulator map from logarithmic motivic cohomology to logarithmic syntomic cohomology is compatible with the logarithmic Chern classes and the logarithmic cycle class map.

Worked Comparison: Logarithmic Syntomic vs Logarithmic Crystalline
Let X be a proper log smooth scheme over 𝒪ₖ with semistable reduction. Explain how the logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism identifies the logarithmic syntomic cohomology H²₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(1)) with a subquotient of the logarithmic crystalline cohomology H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ, and describe the role of the logarithmic monodromy operator N in this identification.
The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism gives a filtered quasi‑isomorphism RΓ₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(1)) ≃ (RΓ₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ, Fil1_log). Taking cohomology, H²₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(1)) is the kernel of the map H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ → H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ / Fil1_log induced by the logarithmic Hodge filtration. The logarithmic monodromy operator N acts on H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) and satisfies N(Fil^r_log) ⊂ Filr-1_log. The logarithmic weight filtration W_• on log crystalline cohomology is defined by W_m = Im(N^m) ∩ Ker(Nm+1) shifted appropriately. Under the isomorphism, the logarithmic syntomic cohomology corresponds to the subspace where N acts nilpotently and the logarithmic Hodge filtration is compatible with the weight filtration. In particular, the logarithmic monodromy operator N encodes the extension data between the graded pieces of the logarithmic Hodge filtration, and its non‑vanishing on the boundary strata reflects the non‑triviality of the log structure.
Exam Strategy: Logarithmic Comparison Isomorphisms
When asked to compare logarithmic cohomology theories, always identify the site (prismatic, crystalline, syntomic, étale), the relevant filtration (Nygaard, Hodge, conjugate, weight), and the operators (φ, N, Galois action). The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism is the bridge between syntomic and crystalline; the logarithmic prismatic comparison is the bridge to étale and de Rham. Memorise the filtration shifts: Fil^r_log on log de Rham corresponds to N^≥r on prismatic, and the logarithmic monodromy N lowers the Hodge filtration by one. A typical trap is to forget that the log structure modifies the filtration on the boundary — the log Hodge filtration Fil^r_log Ω^•₍log₎ includes forms with logarithmic poles along the divisor.

Logarithmic Breuil–Kisin Modules and Logarithmic Crystalline Representations

Logarithmic Breuil–Kisin modules provide an integral p‑adic Hodge theory for log crystalline Galois representations. Let 𝔖 = W(k)[[u]] be the Breuil–Kisin ring with its standard log structure given by the divisor u = 0, and let 𝔖₍log₎ denote the associated log prismatic envelope. A logarithmic Breuil–Kisin module of height r is a finite free 𝔖₍log₎‑module ℳ equipped with a φ‑semilinear map φ_ℳ : φ^*ℳ → ℳ whose cokernel is killed by E(u)^r, where E(u) is the Eisenstein polynomial of a uniformiser π of K, together with a logarithmic connection ∇_log : ℳ → ℳ ⊗ Ω¹₍log₎(𝔖₍log₎/W(k)) satisfying Griffiths transversality with respect to the logarithmic Hodge filtration. The category of logarithmic Breuil–Kisin modules of height r is equivalent to the category of log crystalline Galois representations of G_K with Hodge–Tate weights in [0, r] and log monodromy operator N satisfying Nr+1 = 0. The equivalence is given by the logarithmic Kisin functor T₍log₎(ℳ) = (ℳ ⊗_𝔖 𝔸_inf)φ=1 equipped with its natural G_K‑action and logarithmic monodromy. The logarithmic Fontaine functor D₍crys₎₍log₎(V) = (V ⊗_ℚ_p B₍crys₎₍log₎)G_K recovers the logarithmic filtered (φ, N)‑module. The logarithmic Breuil–Kisin classification extends to the relative setting over a log smooth base S, giving a logarithmic version of the Breuil–Kisin–Fargues correspondence. This theory is crucial for the construction of logarithmic eigenvarieties and for the logarithmic p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GL₂(ℚ_p) with non‑trivial log structure.

Logarithmic Arakelov Theory and Logarithmic Green Functions

Logarithmic Arakelov theory extends classical Arakelov geometry to arithmetic varieties with log structures at infinity. Let X be a regular arithmetic variety over Spec ℤ with a log structure given by a normal crossings divisor D at infinity. The logarithmic Arakelov Chow group CH^p₍log,Ar₎(X) is generated by pairs (Z, g_Z) where Z is a p‑codimensional cycle on X meeting D properly, and g_Z is a logarithmic Green current for Z, i.e. a current on X(ℂ) D(ℂ) with logarithmic singularities along D(ℂ) satisfying dd^c g_Z + δ_Z = ω_Z for a smooth log form ω_Z. The logarithmic arithmetic intersection product is defined using the logarithmic *-product of Green currents, which incorporates the logarithmic singularities along the boundary. The logarithmic arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem states that for a hermitian log vector bundle Ē on X, the logarithmic arithmetic Chern character ch₍log,Ar₎(Ē) satisfies ch₍log,Ar₎(Ē) = π_*(ch₍log₎(E) · Td₍log,Ar₎(T₍log₎X)) in CH^•₍log,Ar₎(X) ⊗ ℚ, where Td₍log,Ar₎ is the logarithmic arithmetic Todd class. The logarithmic Faltings height of a log abelian variety is computed by the logarithmic arithmetic self‑intersection of the log Hodge bundle. Logarithmic Green functions for logarithmic divisors are constructed using the logarithmic heat kernel on the log Riemann surface X(ℂ) D(ℂ) with its complete hyperbolic metric. The logarithmic Kronecker limit formula expresses the value at s = 1 of the logarithmic Eisenstein series in terms of the logarithmic Faltings delta invariant. This theory underlies the logarithmic version of the Bogomolov conjecture and the logarithmic equidistribution of small points on log abelian varieties.

Logarithmic Weight Monodromy Conjecture and Logarithmic Weil Conjectures

The logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture predicts that for a proper log smooth variety X over a finite field 𝔽_q, the logarithmic monodromy operator N on the logarithmic ℓ‑adic cohomology H^i₍ét₎₍log₎(X𝔽_q, ℚ_ℓ) satisfies the logarithmic weight filtration property: the graded pieces Gr^W_m H^i₍ét₎₍log₎ are pure of weight i + m. The logarithmic Weil conjectures, proved by Kato and Nakayama for log smooth varieties, state that the logarithmic zeta function Z₍log₎(X, T) = exp(∑r≥1 |X(𝔽q^r)₍log₎| T^r / r) is a rational function whose zeros and poles have absolute value q-w/2 where w is the logarithmic weight. The logarithmic Betti numbers b^i₍log₎ = dim H^i₍ét₎₍log₎(X𝔽_q, ℚ_ℓ) satisfy the logarithmic Poincaré duality b^i₍log₎ = b2d-i_₍log₎ for d = dim X. The logarithmic hard Lefschetz theorem holds for the logarithmic ample class in the log Chow ring. The logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture is known in the semistable case via the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism and the logarithmic Rapoport–Zink spectral sequence. For a log smooth degeneration over a discrete valuation ring with perfect residue field, the logarithmic monodromy operator N on the log ℓ‑adic cohomology of the generic fibre is identified with the logarithmic monodromy on the log crystalline cohomology of the special fibre, and the logarithmic weight filtration coincides with the logarithmic monodromy filtration. The logarithmic Weil conjectures for log smooth compactifications of Shimura varieties imply the logarithmic Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for automorphic forms on the boundary strata.

  • Confusing the logarithmic prismatic site with the classical prismatic site; the log structure on the prism (A, I, M) is essential for the comparison theorems in the semistable case.
  • Assuming the logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism holds without the log smoothness hypothesis; it requires the log structure to be fine, saturated, and the morphism to be log smooth.
  • Omitting the logarithmic monodromy operator N when stating the logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture; N is the key operator linking the weight filtration to the Hodge filtration.
  • Treating logarithmic Green functions as ordinary Green functions; they must have logarithmic singularities along the boundary divisor and satisfy the logarithmic Poisson equation.
  • Identifying the logarithmic Breuil–Kisin module category with the classical one; the log connection ∇_log and the log structure on 𝔖 are mandatory for the equivalence with log crystalline representations.
  • Forgetting that the logarithmic zeta function counts points with log structure; |X(𝔽q^r)₍log₎| differs from the classical point count by the contribution of the boundary strata.
  • Applying the classical arithmetic Riemann–Roch without the logarithmic Todd class; the log Todd class contains correction terms from the normal bundle of the boundary divisor.
