Forcing and the Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis

Paul Cohen introduced forcing in 1963 to prove that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH) is independent of ZFC. The method builds a generic extension V[G] of a ground model V by adjoining a generic filter G for a partially ordered set (poset) ℙ. The elements of ℙ are called conditions; a filter G ⊆ ℙ is generic over V if it meets every dense subset of ℙ that belongs to V. The forcing relation ⊩ defines when a condition forces a statement to hold in the extension. Cohen’s original poset for adding a new subset of ω consists of finite partial functions from ω to 2 ordered by reverse inclusion. The generic filter yields a Cohen real, a new subset of ω not in V, and the extension satisfies ¬CH while preserving all cardinals and cofinalities. The Boolean-valued model approach, developed by Scott, Solovay, and Vopěnka, replaces the poset by a complete Boolean algebra ℬ and interprets formulas as Boolean truth values; generic ultrafilters on ℬ then produce the same extensions. Easton’s theorem (1970) shows that the continuum function κ ↦ 2^κ on regular cardinals can be prescribed arbitrarily subject to monotonicity and König’s lemma, demonstrating the vast flexibility of forcing. Iterated forcing with countable support preserves ω₁ and allows the construction of models where the continuum is ℵ₂, ℵ_ω₁, or any regular cardinal above ℵ₁. Proper forcing, introduced by Shelah, preserves stationary subsets of ω₁ and is essential for preserving combinatorial principles such as ◊ and □. The technique also proves the independence of the Axiom of Choice from ZF by adding a generic set of atoms (Fraenkel–Mostowski models) or by symmetric submodels of forcing extensions. Forcing has become the central tool for exploring the landscape of set‑theoretic universes and for calibrating the consistency strength of mathematical statements.

The Constructible Universe L and Inner Model Theory

Gödel’s constructible universe L, defined in 1938, is the smallest transitive class containing all ordinals and closed under definable power set operations. Formally, L₀ = ∅, Lα+1 = Def(L_α) (the set of subsets of L_α definable over ⟨L_α,∈⟩ with parameters), and L_λ = ⋃α<λ L_α for limit λ; L = ⋃α∈Ord L_α. Gödel proved that L satisfies ZFC and the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). The Condensation Lemma states that any elementary substructure of some L_α is isomorphic to some L_β, which yields fine structural control over L. Jensen’s fine structure theory (1972) introduced the Σ_n hierarchy over L, the projectum, and the master code, enabling the analysis of large cardinal properties inside L. The Covering Lemma for L asserts that every uncountable set of ordinals is covered by a constructible set of the same cardinality, provided 0^♯ does not exist. If 0^♯ exists, L is “thin” and there are many indiscernibles, leading to a rich hierarchy of inner models for measurable cardinals (the Dodd–Jensen core model K). Inner model theory builds canonical models L[U] for a measurable cardinal, L[μ] for a strong cardinal, and ultimately the core model K below a Woodin cardinal. These models satisfy ZFC and capture the large cardinal structure up to their level. The existence of 0^♯ is equivalent to the existence of a non‑trivial elementary embedding j: L → L, and its consistency strength is strictly below a measurable cardinal. Modern inner model theory, due to Steel, Mitchell, and Woodin, constructs mice (iterable premice) that serve as building blocks for models with superstrong, Woodin, and supercompact cardinals. The ultimate goal is the “ultimate inner model” that would accommodate all large cardinals and resolve the continuum problem from within a canonical universe.

Worked Example: Forcing a Cohen Real
Let ℙ be the poset of finite partial functions p: ω → 2 ordered by reverse inclusion (q ≤ p iff q ⊇ p). Show that if G is ℙ‑generic over V, then the union ⋃G is a total function f: ω → 2 and f ∉ V.
Each condition p ∈ ℙ is a finite function. For any n ∈ ω, the set D_n = {p ∈ ℙ : n ∈ dom(p)} is dense in ℙ and belongs to V. Since G meets every dense set in V, there is p_n ∈ G ∩ D_n. Because G is a filter, the conditions are compatible, so the union f = ⋃G is a function with domain ω. For each n, f(n) = p_n(n) ∈ {0,1}, so f: ω → 2. If f were in V, then the set E = {p ∈ ℙ : p ⊈ f} would be dense (any condition can be extended to disagree with f on a new coordinate). But G ∩ E = ∅ because every p ∈ G is a subset of f. This contradicts genericity. Hence f ∉ V.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a forcing construction, first identify the poset and the dense sets that guarantee the desired property. Write down the definition of genericity and verify that the generic filter meets each dense set. For inner model questions, recall the condensation lemma and the covering lemma; they are the standard tools for proving that a set is constructible or that a cardinal is preserved. Keep the distinction between symmetric submodels (for AC independence) and full generic extensions (for CH independence) clear.

Determinacy, Projective Sets, and Large Cardinals

Infinite two‑player games of perfect information on ω provide a natural setting for determinacy. A game G(A) with payoff set A ⊆ ω^ω is determined if one player has a winning strategy. Gale and Stewart (1953) proved that all open (and closed) games are determined. Martin (1975) established Borel determinacy: every Borel subset of ω^ω yields a determined game. The proof uses a transfinite induction on the Borel rank and requires the existence of iterated power sets up to ω₁, hence it cannot be carried out in Zermelo set theory alone. Projective determinacy (PD) asserts that every projective set (Σ1_n, Π1_n) is determined. Martin and Steel (1989) showed that PD follows from the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals. Conversely, Woodin proved that PD implies the existence of inner models with infinitely many Woodin cardinals. The Axiom of Determinacy (AD) states that all subsets of ω^ω are determined; AD contradicts the full Axiom of Choice but holds in L(ℝ) under large cardinal assumptions. In L(ℝ), AD is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals with a measurable above them (Woodin, 1988). Determinacy has profound regularity consequences: all projective sets are Lebesgue measurable, have the Baire property, and the perfect set property. The hierarchy of determinacy axioms calibrates the consistency strength of regularity properties for definable sets of reals and links descriptive set theory directly to the large cardinal hierarchy.

Reflection Principles and the Levy Hierarchy

The Lévy hierarchy classifies formulas of set theory by the complexity of their quantifiers: Σ₀ = Π₀ = Δ₀ are bounded formulas; Σn+1 formulas are of the form ∃x φ with φ ∈ Π_n; Πn+1 formulas are ∀x φ with φ ∈ Σ_n. The Reflection Theorem (Montague–Lévy, 1961) states that for any finite set of formulas Φ, there is a club class of ordinals α such that ⟨V_α,∈⟩ is an elementary substructure of V for all formulas in Φ. In particular, for each n there is a proper class of Σ_n‑correct cardinals κ (V_κ ≺Σ_n V). Reflection is provable in ZFC and is a key tool for constructing inner models and proving consistency results. A cardinal κ is Π^m_n‑indescribable if for every Π^m_n sentence φ and every A ⊆ V_κ, ⟨V_κ,∈,A⟩ ⊨ φ implies there is α < κ with ⟨V_α,∈,A∩V_α⟩ ⊨ φ. Indescribability strengthens reflection by allowing second‑order parameters. Π11‑indescribable cardinals are exactly the weakly compact cardinals. Higher indescribability corresponds to larger large cardinals: Π^m_n‑indescribable cardinals sit below measurable cardinals for m≥2. The Lévy hierarchy also underlies the definition of the constructible hierarchy L_α and the fine‑structure projecta. In proof theory, the ordinal analysis of theories like Kripke–Platek set theory (KP) uses Σ₁‑reflection to assign proof‑theoretic ordinals. Reflection principles thus bridge the gap between syntactic complexity, large cardinal combinatorics, and the structure of the cumulative hierarchy.

Ordinal Analysis and Proof‑Theoretic Strength

Ordinal analysis assigns to each formal theory T a proof‑theoretic ordinal |T|, the supremum of the order types of primitive recursive well‑orderings that T can prove are well‑founded. Gentzen (1936) showed that Peano Arithmetic (PA) has proof‑theoretic ordinal ε₀, the least ordinal closed under ω‑exponentiation. The consistency of PA is provable in primitive recursive arithmetic plus transfinite induction up to ε₀. For stronger theories, the ordinals grow rapidly: the system ATR₀ (arithmetical transfinite recursion) has ordinal Γ₀ (the Feferman–Schütte ordinal), while Π¹₁‑CA₀ reaches the Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal ψ₀(Ω_ω). The ordinal analysis of Kripke–Platek set theory with Σ₁‑separation (KP) yields the Bachmann–Howard ordinal. Adding Π₃‑reflection to KP reaches the ordinal of Π¹₂‑CA₀. Large cardinal axioms correspond to even larger ordinals via ordinal collapsing functions: the existence of a measurable cardinal implies the well‑foundedness of the ordinal ψ(Ω_ω) in a suitable notation system. Rathjen and others have developed ordinal analyses for theories with Mahlo, weakly compact, and Π^m_n‑indescribable cardinals, using infinitary proof systems and operator‑controlled derivations. The program of ordinal analysis provides a precise calibration of the consistency strength of mathematical theories and reveals the deep connection between proof theory, large cardinals, and the structure of the constructible hierarchy.

  • Confusing forcing with symmetric models: forcing adds generic sets, but independence of AC requires symmetric submodels, not the full generic extension.
  • Assuming L satisfies CH but not GCH: Gödel proved L satisfies GCH, so CH holds automatically in L.
  • Thinking Borel determinacy is provable in ZF alone: Martin’s proof uses replacement up to ω₁, so it needs ZFC or at least Zermelo + Σ₁‑replacement.
  • Equating projective determinacy with AD: PD only covers projective sets, while AD asserts determinacy for all sets of reals and contradicts AC.
  • Misapplying the reflection theorem: reflection gives Σ_n‑correct cardinals, but not every Σ_n‑correct cardinal is inaccessible; additional closure properties are needed.
  • Overlooking the role of ordinal collapsing functions in proof theory: the proof‑theoretic ordinal of a theory with large cardinals is not the large cardinal itself but a recursive ordinal obtained by collapsing.
  • Review these traps carefully before the exam.

Forcing Axioms and the Structure of the Continuum

Forcing axioms assert that certain families of dense sets in a partial order admit a filter meeting all of them. Martin's Axiom MA(κ) states that for any ccc partial order ℙ and any family 𝒟 of ≤ κ dense subsets of ℙ, there is a filter 𝐺 ⊆ ℙ intersecting every member of 𝒟. MA(ℵ₁) is equivalent to MA for all ccc posets and implies 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₁; in fact MA(κ) holds for all κ < 2^ℵ₀. The Proper Forcing Axiom PFA, introduced by Baumgartner, replaces ccc with proper forcing — those preserving stationary subsets of ω₁. PFA implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂, the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis, and that every Aronszajn tree is special. Martin's Maximum MM, due to Foreman, Magidor, and Shelah (1988), extends PFA to all posets preserving stationary subsets of ω₁; MM implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and that the nonstationary ideal on ω₁ is ℵ₂-saturated. The consistency strength of PFA is a supercompact cardinal; MM requires a supercompact cardinal as well. Forcing axioms decide many cardinal invariants of the continuum: under PFA, 𝔭 = 𝔱 = ℵ₂, 𝔟 = 𝔡 = ℵ₂, add(ℳ) = cov(ℳ) = ℵ₂, while 𝔞 = ℵ₁ remains independent. The hierarchy MA < PFA < MM calibrates the tension between combinatorial principles and the size of the continuum, and their equiconsistency with large cardinals anchors them in the consistency strength hierarchy.

Inner Model Theory and Core Models

Inner model theory constructs canonical transitive models of ZFC containing all ordinals, approximating V from below. The core model K, developed by Jensen, Dodd, Mitchell, and Steel, is the maximal iterable inner model not reaching a measurable cardinal. Below a measurable, K exists and satisfies the Covering Lemma: for every uncountable set X of ordinals, there is Y ∈ K with X ⊆ Y and |Y| = |X|. This fails at a measurable, where 0^♯ exists and K = L[0^♯]. For larger large cardinals, one builds mice — iterable premice with extenders. A premouse is a structure ⟨J_α[𝐸], ∈, 𝐸⟩ where 𝐸 codes extender sequences; iterability means all iteration trees have well-founded models. The core model K^DJ for a Woodin cardinal uses the Dodd-Jensen property to compare mice. Steel's core model induction shows that determinacy hypotheses imply the existence of mice with Woodin cardinals. The comparison lemma for mice (Mitchell-Steel) states that any two iterable mice are comparable via iteration. The hierarchy of core models K, K^DJ, K^c, … calibrates consistency strength: if there is no inner model with a Woodin cardinal, then K^DJ exists and satisfies covering for Σ₂ formulas. The fine structure of mice — projecta, standard parameters, solidity — mirrors the fine structure of L but with extenders replacing the Σ₁-Skolem functions. Inner model theory thus provides the "lower bounds" for consistency strength, while forcing provides "upper bounds"; their meeting at equiconsistency results (e.g., PFA ⇔ supercompact) completes the calibration.

Worked Comparison: MA vs PFA vs MM
State the exact consistency strength of each forcing axiom and one cardinal invariant it decides differently from the others.
MA(ℵ₁) is equiconsistent with ZFC (no large cardinals needed); it implies 𝔭 = 𝔱 = ℵ₁ and 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₁ but does not fix 2^ℵ₀. PFA is equiconsistent with a supercompact cardinal; it implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and 𝔭 = 𝔱 = ℵ₂. MM is also equiconsistent with a supercompact cardinal (but strictly stronger than PFA in direct implication); it implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and that the nonstationary ideal on ω₁ is ℵ₂-saturated, which PFA does not decide. The key difference: MA is a ccc axiom consistent with CH failing arbitrarily high; PFA and MM fix the continuum at ℵ₂ and require large cardinals.
Exam Strategy: Forcing Axiom Hierarchy
Memorise the triplet: MA (ccc, no large cardinals, continuum flexible) < PFA (proper, supercompact, 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂) < MM (stationary-preserving, supercompact, NS_ω₁ saturated). Examiners often ask which axiom implies the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (PFA and MM do; MA does not) or which decides the value of 𝔭 (PFA and MM give ℵ₂; MA gives ℵ₁). Link each axiom to its large cardinal equiconsistency — this is a standard "match the following" question type.

Descriptive Set Theory: Scales, Uniformization, and the Projective Hierarchy

The projective hierarchy classifies subsets of Polish spaces by quantifier complexity over ℝ: Σ¹₁ (analytic), Π¹₁ (coanalytic), Σ¹ₙ₊₁ = ∃^ℝ Π¹ₙ, Π¹ₙ₊₁ = ∀^ℝ Σ¹ₙ. A scale on a set A ⊆ X is a sequence of norms φₙ: A → Ord such that if xₖ → x and φₙ(xₖ) is eventually constant for each n, then x ∈ A. The Scale Property for a pointclass Γ means every A ∈ Γ admits a Γ-scale. Under Projective Determinacy PD, every projective set has the scale property (Moschovakis, 1971). Scales yield uniformization: if A ⊆ X × Y is in Γ and Γ has the scale property with appropriate closure, then A admits a uniformizing function in Γ. The Moschovakis Coding Lemma states that under AD, every Σ¹₂ set of reals can be coded by a real. The Wadge hierarchy refines the projective hierarchy by continuous reducibility: A ≤_W B iff A = f⁻¹(B) for continuous f. Under AD, the Wadge hierarchy of subsets of ω^ω is well-ordered of length Θ, the supremum of ordinals surjecting onto ℝ. The periodicity theorems (Martin-Monk, Steel) show that the Wadge degrees of Σ¹₂ₙ₊₁ and Π¹₂ₙ₊₁ alternate in a pattern determined by the projective ordinals δ¹ₙ. The projective ordinals δ¹ₙ = sup{length of Δ¹ₙ prewellorderings} satisfy δ¹₁ = ω₁, δ¹₂ = ω₂ under AD, and δ¹ₙ are the Suslin cardinals. The connection to large cardinals: PD is equiconsistent with infinitely many Woodin cardinals (Martin-Steel, Woodin). The scale property for Σ¹ₙ₊₁ is equivalent to the existence of a Σ¹ₙ₊₁ wellordering of ℝ, which under AD has length δ¹ₙ₊₁. Descriptive set theory thus translates determinacy into structural regularity properties — measurability, Baire property, perfect set property — and calibrates them via the projective ordinals and Wadge degrees.

Reverse Mathematics and Subsystems of Second-Order Arithmetic

Reverse mathematics, initiated by Friedman and Simpson, calibrates the logical strength of ordinary mathematical theorems by identifying the weakest subsystem of second-order arithmetic proving them. The base system RCA₀ (Recursive Comprehension Axiom) has Δ⁰₁-comprehension and Σ⁰₁-induction; its ω-models are exactly the Turing ideals. WKL₀ adds Weak König's Lemma (every infinite binary tree has a path); it is equivalent to Heine-Borel compactness of [0,1], the existence of separating hyperplanes, and the Gödel Completeness Theorem for countable languages. ACA₀ adds arithmetical comprehension; it is equivalent to the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, the existence of algebraic closures of countable fields, and the sequential completeness of ℝ. ATR₀ (Arithmetical Transfinite Recursion) allows iteration of arithmetical comprehension along any well-ordering; it is equivalent to the comparability of countable well-orderings, the existence of Σ¹₁-separating sets, and the open determinacy for countable games. Π¹₁-CA₀ adds Π¹₁-comprehension; it is equivalent to the Cantor-Bendixson theorem for closed sets, the existence of countable coded ω-models of ACA₀, and the determinacy of Π¹₁ games. The ordinal analysis of these systems: |RCA₀| = ω^ω, |WKL₀| = ω^ω, |ACA₀| = ε₀, |ATR₀| = Γ₀ (Feferman-Schütte), |Π¹₁-CA₀| = ψ₀(Ω_ω) (Takeuti-Feferman-Buchholz). The equivalence theorems are proved over RCA₀: e.g., "Every countable vector space has a basis" ⇔ ACA₀; "Every countable abelian group is a direct sum of a divisible group and a reduced group" ⇔ ACA₀; "The Hahn-Banach theorem for separable spaces" ⇔ WKL₀. Reverse mathematics thus maps the landscape of countable mathematics onto a hierarchy of five "Big Five" systems, with recent work exploring the "zoo" of principles between them (RT²₂, COH, SADS, etc.).

Cardinal Invariants of the Continuum and PCF Theory

The cardinal invariants of the continuum measure the combinatorial structure of (ω^ω, ≤*) and the ideal of meager/null sets. The dominating number 𝔡 = min{|F| : F ⊆ ω^ω dominating}, the bounding number 𝔟 = min{|F| : F ⊆ ω^ω unbounded}, the splitting number 𝔰 = min{|S| : S ⊆ [ω]^ω splitting all infinite sets}, the reaping number 𝔯 = min{|R| : R ⊆ [ω]^ω unsplit}, the almost disjointness number 𝔞 = max{|A| : A ⊆ [ω]^ω almost disjoint}, the pseudointersection number 𝔭 = min{|F| : F ⊆ [ω]^ω centred, no pseudointersection}, and the tower number 𝔱 = min{length of a tower in ([ω]^ω, ⊆*)}. ZFC proves ℵ₁ ≤ 𝔭 ≤ 𝔱 ≤ 𝔥 ≤ 𝔤 ≤ 𝔡 ≤ 𝔠 and ℵ₁ ≤ 𝔟 ≤ 𝔡 ≤ 𝔠, with 𝔭 ≤ 𝔟, 𝔱 ≤ 𝔡. The Cichoń diagram relates measure and category invariants: add(ℳ) ≤ cov(ℳ) ≤ 𝔡 ≤ cof(ℳ) ≤ 𝔠 and add(𝒩) ≤ cov(𝒩) ≤ 𝔡 ≤ cof(𝒩) ≤ 𝔠, with add(ℳ) ≤ add(𝒩) and cof(𝒩) ≤ cof(ℳ). Shelah's PCF (Possible Cofinalities) theory analyses the structure of ∏i<κ λ_i / J for singular λ = sup λ_i. The fundamental theorem: for any progressive set 𝔞 of regular cardinals, pcf(𝔞) has a maximum and |pcf(𝔞)| < |𝔞|⁺⁴. The cov vs pp theorem: cov(λ, κ, θ, σ) = sup{pp(μ) : μ ∈ pcf(𝔞)} for suitable 𝔞. PCF yields the bound 2^ℵ_ω < ℵω₄ (Shelah, 1994), improving the Galvin-Hajnal bound. The invariant 𝔭 = 𝔱 was proved by Malliaris and Shelah (2016), resolving a decades-old problem. The consistency of all Cichoń's diagram invariants being pairwise distinct was shown by Goldstern, Kellner, and Shelah (2019) using a finite support iteration of ccc posets. PCF theory thus provides the deep structural engine behind the independence results for cardinal invariants, linking singular cardinal arithmetic to the combinatorics of the continuum.

Models of Set Theory without the Axiom of Choice

Symmetric models, introduced by Cohen and refined by Jech-Sochor, produce models of ZF + ¬AC by taking a forcing extension V[G] and restricting to the class HS of hereditarily symmetric names. A name τ is symmetric if its symmetry group sym(τ) = {π ∈ Aut(ℙ) : πτ = τ} belongs to a normal filter ℱ of subgroups of Aut(ℙ); τ is hereditarily symmetric if all names in its transitive closure are symmetric. The basic Fraenkel model adds a countable set of Cohen reals with the finite-support permutation group and the filter of subgroups fixing finite sets; the resulting symmetric model satisfies ZF + "there is an infinite Dedekind-finite set of reals" + ¬AC_ω. The Feferman-Levy model collapses ℵ_ω to ℵ₁ using a symmetric collapse, yielding ZF + ℝ is a countable union of countable sets + ¬AC_ω(ℝ). Solovay's model (1970) starts with an inaccessible κ, collapses it to ω₁ via Levy collapse, and takes the symmetric submodel of sets hereditarily definable from ordinals and reals; it satisfies ZF + DC + "every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property, and the perfect set property". The Axiom of Determinacy AD holds in L(ℝ) under large cardinals (Woodin), and AD implies ¬AC but DC_ℝ. The HOD (hereditarily ordinal-definable sets) of a model of AD is a model of ZFC with a proper class of Woodin cardinals. The hierarchy of choice principles: AC ⇒ DC ⇒ AC_ω ⇒ AC_fin; none reverse in ZF. The Kinna-Wagner principle (every set embeds into a power set of a well-ordered set) is equivalent to AC. The study of ZF models reveals the precise choice strength needed for analysis: Hahn-Banach ⇔ BPI (Boolean Prime Ideal theorem) ⇔ Compactness for propositional logic; Tychonoff for Hausdorff spaces ⇔ BPI; Tychonoff for all spaces ⇔ AC. The interplay between symmetric models, inner models of determinacy, and forcing over ZF maps the geography of choice-free mathematics.

  • Confusing the consistency strength of MA (none) with PFA/MM (supercompact) — MA is a theorem of ZFC for κ < 2^ℵ₀, while PFA/MM require large cardinals.
  • Thinking the core model K exists above a measurable cardinal — K exists only below the first measurable; above it, 0^♯ exists and K = L[0^♯].
  • Equating the scale property with uniformization — scales imply uniformization only for pointclasses closed under ∃^ℝ and ∀^ℝ with appropriate coding.
  • Assuming WKL₀ proves the existence of a non-principal ultrafilter on ω — WKL₀ is conservative over RCA₀ for Π¹₁ sentences and does not prove the existence of any non-computable set.
  • Believing all cardinal invariants in Cichoń's diagram can be simultaneously distinct in ZFC — this is a consistency result (Goldstern-Kellner-Shelah), not a theorem of ZFC.
  • Thinking Solovay's model satisfies full AC — it satisfies DC but not AC_ω(ℝ); the reals cannot be well-ordered there.
  • Overlooking that PCF theory applies to singular cardinals of uncountable cofinality — the bound 2^ℵ_ω < ℵω₄ uses the structure of pcf(𝔞) for 𝔞 = {ℵ_n : n < ω}.

Ultrafilters, Ultrapowers, and Elementary Embeddings

An ultrafilter on a set X is a maximal filter in the Boolean algebra 𝒫(X): a collection 𝒰 ⊆ 𝒫(X) closed under supersets and finite intersections, containing no empty set, and for every A ⊆ X exactly one of A or X A belongs to 𝒰. Principal ultrafilters are those generated by a singleton {x}; non‑principal (free) ultrafilters exist on any infinite set by the Boolean Prime Ideal theorem (equivalent to BPI, strictly weaker than AC). Given an ultrafilter 𝒰 on I and a family of structures Mi (i ∈ I) in a common language, the ultraproduct ∏i∈I Mi / 𝒰 identifies sequences that agree on a 𝒰‑large set. Łoś’s theorem states that a first‑order formula φ holds in the ultraproduct iff the set of indices where φ holds in Mi belongs to 𝒰. When all Mi = V (the universe), the ultrapower VI/𝒰 yields an elementary embedding j : V → M where M is the transitive collapse of the ultrapower. The critical point crit(j) is the least ordinal moved by j; it is a measurable cardinal, and 𝒰 = {X ⊆ crit(j) : crit(j) ∈ j(X)} is a normal ultrafilter. Conversely, every measurable cardinal carries a normal ultrafilter giving rise to such an embedding. Iterating this construction produces the Mitchell order on normal measures and the hierarchy of α-measurable cardinals. Kunen’s inconsistency theorem (1971) shows there is no non‑trivial elementary embedding j : V → V in ZFC, but embeddings j : V → M with M ⊂ V are the central objects of large cardinal theory: strong, supercompact, and extendible cardinals are all characterised by the existence of embeddings with specific closure properties of the target model M.

Iterated Forcing, Proper Forcing, and the Proper Forcing Axiom

Cohen’s original forcing adds a single generic real. To control the continuum at higher cardinals or to preserve cardinals like ℵ1, one iterates forcing notions along an ordinal α. A finite‑support iteration of ccc posets remains ccc (hence preserves all cardinals), but a countable‑support iteration of proper posets is proper (Shelah, 1982). A forcing notion ℙ is proper if for every sufficiently large regular θ, every countable elementary submodel N ≺ H(θ) containing ℙ, and every p ∈ ℙ ∩ N, there is a condition q ≤ p that is N‑generic (i.e., meets every dense subset of ℙ in N). Properness implies ℵ1‑preservation and is preserved by countable‑support iterations. The Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA) asserts that for every proper ℙ and every family of ℵ1 dense subsets of ℙ, there is a filter meeting all of them. PFA implies 2ℵ0 = ℵ2, the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (SCH), the failure of □κ for all κ ≥ ℵ1, and that every Aronszajn tree is special. It also implies the Open Colouring Axiom (OCA) and that all ℵ1‑dense subsets of ℝ are isomorphic (Baumgartner). Martin’s Maximum (MM) strengthens PFA to posets preserving stationary subsets of ω1; MM implies the non‑stationary ideal on ω1 is ℵ2‑saturated and that the continuum is ℵ2. The consistency strength of PFA is a supercompact cardinal (Baumgartner, 1983; Shelah, 1984); MM requires a supercompact as well (Foreman‑Magidor‑Shelah, 1988). The Bounded Proper Forcing Axiom (BPFA) restricts PFA to Σ1‑definable dense sets and is equiconsistent with a reflecting cardinal. Shelah’s Proper Forcing Axiom for ℵ1 (PFAℵ1) and the Semiproper Forcing Axiom (SPFA) occupy intermediate consistency strengths. Iterated forcing with revised countable support (RCS) is used to force MM while preserving supercompactness.

Worked Example: Properness and ℵ1-Preservation
Let ℙ be the poset of countable partial functions from ω1 to 2 ordered by reverse inclusion. Show that ℙ is proper and preserves ℵ1.
Step 1: Verify properness. Fix a large regular θ and a countable N ≺ H(θ) with ℙ ∈ N. Let p ∈ ℙ ∩ N. Since N is countable, δ = N ∩ ω1 is a countable ordinal. Define q = p ∪ {(δ, 0)}. Then dom(q) = dom(p) ∪ {δ} is countable, so q ∈ ℙ and q ≤ p. For any dense D ∈ N, D ∩ N is non‑empty (by elementarity, N thinks “∃r ∈ D”). Pick r ∈ D ∩ N; then r is compatible with q because dom(r) ∩ {δ} = ∅ (as δ ∉ N). Hence q is N‑generic. Step 2: ℵ1-preservation. Proper forcing preserves stationary subsets of ω1 (Shelah). Since ℵ1 is regular, any club in ω1 remains stationary, so ω1 cannot be collapsed to ω. Thus ℵ1 is preserved in any generic extension by ℙ.
Exam Strategy: Forcing Axioms Hierarchy
Memorise the implication chain: MM ⇒ PFA ⇒ BPFA, with consistency strengths: supercompact ⇒ supercompact ⇒ reflecting cardinal. Know the key consequences: PFA ⇒ 2ℵ0 = ℵ2 + SCH + no □κ; MM ⇒ NSω1 is ℵ2-saturated. For multiple-choice questions, eliminate options that claim PFA implies CH or that MM is consistent with a measurable cardinal (it requires supercompact).

Prikry Forcing and the Singular Cardinals Problem

Prikry forcing (1970) was the first method to change the cofinality of a measurable cardinal κ to ω without adding bounded subsets of κ. Let 𝒰 be a normal ultrafilter on κ. Conditions are pairs (s, A) where s ∈ [κ]<ω is a finite increasing sequence, A ∈ 𝒰, and max(s) < min(A) (if s ≠ ∅). The order is (t, B) ≤ (s, A) iff s ⊆ t, B ⊆ A, and t s ⊆ A. The generic filter adds an ω‑sequence cofinal in κ, so cf(V[G]κ) = ω, but the Prikry property (every statement is decided by a condition with the same stem) ensures no new bounded subsets of κ are added. Consequently, cardinals ≤ κ are preserved, and 2κ can be made arbitrarily large while κ becomes singular of cofinality ω. This showed that ZFC cannot prove the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (SCH): 2cf(κ) < κ ⇒ κcf(κ) = κ+. Magidor (1976) generalised Prikry forcing to change cf(κ) to any regular λ < κ using a (κ, λ)‑extender. Gitik (1980) proved that “all uncountable cardinals are singular” is consistent relative to a proper class of strongly compact cardinals. The Singular Cardinals Problem asks which cardinal arithmetic configurations are possible at singular cardinals. Shelah’s PCF theory (1994) gave the ZFC bound 2ℵω < ℵω4 (improved from Galvin‑Hajnal’s ℵω1). The optimal bound 2ℵω < ℵω4 is sharp: Gitik‑Magidor (1992) showed 2ℵω = ℵω4 is consistent relative to a measurable cardinal of Mitchell order ω4. The Strong Hypothesis (SH) and the Local Singular Cardinals Hypothesis are weaker variants consistent with large cardinals. Prikry‑type forcings (diagonal Prikry, Magidor‑Radin, supercompact Prikry) are the primary tools for constructing models where SCH fails at a singular cardinal of uncountable cofinality.

Borel Equivalence Relations and the Glimm–Effros Dichotomy

A Borel equivalence relation on a Polish space X is an equivalence relation E ⊆ X × X that is a Borel subset. The central classification problem asks when E is smooth (Borel reducible to equality on a Polish space, i.e., admits a Borel transversal) and when it is non‑smooth. The Glimm–Effros dichotomy (1980s, Harrington‑Kechris‑Louveau 1990) states: for every Borel equivalence relation E on a Polish space, either E is smooth or E0 ⊑B E, where E0 is the relation of eventual equality on 2ω (x E0 y ⇔ ∃n ∀m ≥ n x(m) = y(m)). This is the analogue of the perfect set theorem for equivalence relations. The proof uses the Gandy–Harrington topology and the fact that E0 is a minimal non‑smooth Borel equivalence relation under Borel reducibility (⊑B). Beyond E0, the hierarchy of Borel equivalence relations is rich: E0 <B E1 <B E2 <B … where En is the orbit equivalence relation of the shift action of ℤn on 2ℤn. The Feldman–Moore theorem characterises countable Borel equivalence relations as exactly those induced by Borel actions of countable groups. Hyperfinite equivalence relations (increasing unions of finite relations) are precisely those Borel reducible to E0 (Dougherty‑Jackson‑Kechris, 1994). The treeable and amenable classes lie strictly between hyperfinite and general countable relations. For non‑countable relations, orbit equivalence relations of Polish group actions provide a vast supply: the isomorphism relations on countable graphs, groups, and linear orders are complete analytic equivalence relations (not Borel). The Burgess trichotomy for analytic equivalence relations (assuming PD) states: every analytic equivalence relation either has ≤ ℵ0 classes, exactly ℵ1 classes, or perfectly many classes. The Martin conjecture on Turing degrees and the Kechris–Louveau classification of Borel equivalence relations up to Borel bireducibility remain central open problems.

Set-Theoretic Geology: Grounds, Mantles, and the Bedrock

Set‑theoretic geology (Fuchs‑Hamkins‑Reitz, 2015) studies the structure of the universe V as a forcing extension of inner models called grounds. A ground of V is an inner model W ⊆ V such that V = W[G] for some W-generic filter G over a poset in W. The Ground Axiom (GA) asserts that V has no proper grounds (i.e., V is not a non‑trivial forcing extension of any inner model). Reitz (2006) proved GA is first‑order expressible and consistent relative to ZFC. The mantle M is the intersection of all grounds; it is a model of ZFC and is the largest forcing‑invariant definable class. The generic mantle is the intersection of all grounds of all forcing extensions of V; it equals the mantle of the mantle. The bedrock is the intersection of all grounds in the generic multiverse; it is the smallest ground of all forcing extensions. Fuchs‑Hamkins‑Reitz showed the mantle can be any model of ZFC, and the bedrock may not exist (the grounds may have no minimal element). The Downward Directed Grounds Hypothesis (DDG) states that any two grounds have a common deeper ground; this is equivalent to the mantle being a ground. Usuba (2017) proved DDG holds if there is a hyper‑huge cardinal, and that the mantle is then the unique bedrock. The Inner Mantle (intersection of all inner models that are grounds of some forcing extension) and the Outer Mantle extend the hierarchy. Geology connects to the Multiverse View (Hamkins, 2012): the universe of sets is not unique but a multiverse of models connected by forcing. The Maximality Principle (MP) asserts that any statement forceably necessary is already true; MP is equiconsistent with ZFC. The Necessary Maximality Principle (NMP) requires MP to hold in all forcing extensions; NMP is equiconsistent with a proper class of inaccessible cardinals. These principles formalise the idea that the set‑theoretic universe is “maximal” with respect to forcing.

  • Confusing Prikry forcing with Namba forcing — Namba forcing changes cf(ω2) to ω but adds new reals; Prikry forcing adds no bounded subsets and preserves all cardinals ≤ κ.
  • Thinking proper forcing preserves all cardinals — proper forcing preserves ℵ1 but can collapse ℵ2 (e.g., the standard proper forcing for □ω1 collapses ℵ2 to ℵ1).
  • Assuming PFA implies CH is false — PFA implies 2ℵ0 = ℵ2, so CH fails, but the statement “PFA implies CH is false” is a tautology; the trap is claiming PFA decides CH in the sense of proving ¬CH (it does, but the phrasing often confuses students).
  • Believing the Glimm–Effros dichotomy applies to analytic equivalence relations — it is a theorem for Borel equivalence relations; for analytic relations, the Burgess trichotomy (under PD) replaces it.
  • Equating the mantle with the core model K — the mantle is a forcing‑invariant class definable in any model; K is a fine‑structural inner model built from extenders and exists only below certain large cardinals.
  • Thinking the Ground Axiom is a large cardinal axiom — GA is a first‑order statement consistent with ZFC alone (Reitz); it asserts the universe is not a forcing extension, not that large cardinals exist.
  • Confusing the generic mantle with the mantle — the generic mantle is the intersection of grounds of all forcing extensions; it is always contained in the mantle, and they can differ (Fuchs‑Hamkins‑Reitz).

The Solovay Model and the Consistency of ZF + DC + “All Sets of Reals are Lebesgue Measurable”

In 1970 Robert Solovay constructed a model of ZF in which every set of real numbers is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property, and satisfies the perfect set property. The construction begins with a ground model V satisfying ZFC + “there exists an inaccessible cardinal κ”. One then performs the Lévy collapse Coll(ω, <κ), which makes κ become ω₁ while preserving all cardinals below κ and adding no new reals beyond those needed to collapse the cardinals. In the resulting generic extension V[G], the inner model L(ℝ)V[G] — the smallest inner model containing all reals and ordinals — satisfies ZF + DC (Dependent Choice) and the statement “every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable”.

The key points are:

  • The inaccessible cardinal is essential: Shelah later proved that if ZF + “all sets of reals are Lebesgue measurable” is consistent, then ZFC + “there exists an inaccessible cardinal” is consistent. Thus the large‑cardinal assumption cannot be removed.
  • DC holds in L(ℝ)V[G] because the collapse is ω‑closed and the reals are added by a countable support iteration; this permits the usual recursive constructions needed for analysis.
  • Full AC fails: there is no well‑ordering of the reals in this model, and Vitali‑type non‑measurable sets cannot be formed.
  • The model also satisfies that every set of reals has the Baire property and the perfect set property, so the classical regularity properties of descriptive set theory hold universally.

Solovay’s theorem shows that the pathological sets whose existence relies on AC (e.g., non‑measurable sets, Bernstein sets) are not provable in ZF alone. It also demonstrates that large cardinals are not merely “strong” assumptions but can be used to obtain natural models of determinacy‑like regularity for all sets of reals.

The Shoenfield Absoluteness Theorem and its Applications

The Shoenfield Absoluteness Theorem (1961) states that any Σ¹₂ or Π¹₂ sentence — i.e., a statement of the form ∃X ⊆ ω ∀Y ⊆ ω φ(X,Y) or its negation, where φ is arithmetical — is absolute between any two transitive models of ZF that have the same ordinals. In particular, if V ⊆ W are transitive models with Ord^V = Ord^W, then for any Σ¹₂ sentence σ, V ⊧ σ iff W ⊧ σ.

The proof proceeds by showing that Σ¹₂ statements are equivalent in ZF to statements of the form “there exists a real x such that a certain tree T_x on ω × ω₁ is well‑founded”. Well‑foundedness of a tree is a Π¹₁ property, and by Mostowski collapse the existence of a ranking function for T_x is absolute between models with the same ordinals. Consequently, the truth of Σ¹₂ sentences does not change when passing to forcing extensions that preserve ω₁.

Major applications include:

  • Independence of CH from Σ¹₂ statements: Since “CH” is a Σ²₁ statement (it quantifies over subsets of ω₁), Shoenfield absoluteness does not apply directly; however, many consequences of CH (e.g., existence of a Σ¹₂ well‑ordering of the reals) are Σ¹₂ and therefore absolute. This shows that forcing cannot change the truth value of such consequences if ω₁ is preserved.
  • Projective Determinacy: Martin and Steel used Shoenfield absoluteness as a base step in their proof that projective determinacy follows from the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals. The absoluteness of Σ¹₂ statements allows the induction to climb the projective hierarchy.
  • Consistency of “all Σ¹₂ sets are measurable”: Because measurability of a Σ¹₂ set is a Π¹₃ statement, Shoenfield absoluteness does not settle it, but the theorem clarifies exactly which regularity properties are forcing‑invariant.

The theorem is a cornerstone of modern set theory: it delineates the boundary between statements that are “local” to the reals (and thus immune to forcing that does not collapse ω₁) and those that are genuinely sensitive to the height of the universe.

Worked Example: Applying Shoenfield Absoluteness
Show that the statement “there exists a non‑principal ultrafilter on ω” cannot be decided by any forcing that preserves ω₁.
The existence of a non‑principal ultrafilter on ω is a Σ¹₂ statement: it asserts ∃U ⊆ 𝒫(ω) [U is an ultrafilter ∧ ∀n {n} ∉ U]. The property “U is an ultrafilter” is arithmetical in U, so the whole sentence is Σ¹₂. By Shoenfield absoluteness, any two transitive models with the same ordinals agree on its truth value. A forcing extension that preserves ω₁ has the same ordinals as the ground model up to ω₁, and in fact the same ordinals altogether because forcing does not add new ordinals. Therefore the truth of the Σ¹₂ sentence is unchanged. Since ZFC proves the existence of such an ultrafilter (using AC), the statement is true in the ground model and remains true in the extension; it cannot be forced false. Conversely, if one started with a model of ZF + ¬AC where no ultrafilter exists, the statement would be false and remain false. Thus the statement is forcing‑invariant under ω₁‑preserving forcing.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a given statement is absolute under forcing, first classify its logical complexity in the Levy hierarchy. If it is Σ¹₂ or Π¹₂, Shoenfield absoluteness applies provided the forcing does not collapse ω₁. If the statement is more complex (e.g., Σ²₁), absoluteness typically fails and you must look for specific forcing constructions that change its truth value.

The Axiom of Determinacy and the Structure of L(ℝ)

The Axiom of Determinacy (AD) asserts that for every two‑player game of length ω with moves in ω, one of the players has a winning strategy. AD contradicts the full Axiom of Choice but is consistent relative to large cardinals: Martin and Steel (1989) proved that if there exist infinitely many Woodin cardinals, then L(ℝ) satisfies AD. Woodin later showed that the converse holds — AD in L(ℝ) implies the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals in an inner model.

Inside L(ℝ) under AD, the following regularity properties hold for all sets of reals:

  • Lebesgue measurability
  • The Baire property
  • The perfect set property (every uncountable set contains a perfect subset)
  • Every set of reals is either countable or has a perfect subset, so the continuum hypothesis holds in the sense that there is no intermediate cardinality between ℵ₀ and 2ℵ₀.

The structure of L(ℝ) under AD is remarkably rich. The Wadge hierarchy of subsets of ω^ω has length Θ, the supremum of the ordinals that are surjective images of ℝ. The projective hierarchy collapses: every projective set is determined, and the projective ordinals δ¹_n are all below Θ. Moreover, the theory of L(ℝ) under AD is generically absolute — it is the same in all forcing extensions that preserve the relevant large cardinals. This absoluteness is a key ingredient in Woodin’s Ω‑conjecture and his analysis of the continuum problem.

AD also implies that ω₁ and ω₂ are measurable cardinals in L(ℝ), and that the club filter on ω₁ is an ultrafilter. These combinatorial consequences make L(ℝ) a canonical model for “tame” set theory where pathological sets of reals do not exist.

Generic Absoluteness and Woodin’s Ω‑Conjecture

Generic absoluteness refers to the phenomenon where certain statements have the same truth value in V and in all (or a broad class of) forcing extensions of V. The most celebrated instance is the Shoenfield absoluteness for Σ¹₂ statements, but Woodin discovered a far stronger form: assuming a proper class of Woodin cardinals, the theory of L(ℝ) is invariant under all set forcing. That is, for any sentence φ in the language of set theory, if φ holds in L(ℝ)^V then it holds in L(ℝ)V[G] for any V‑generic filter G.

Woodin formalised this by introducing Ω‑logic, a proof system whose validities capture exactly the statements that are true in all generic extensions of models with a proper class of Woodin cardinals. The Ω‑conjecture asserts that a sentence is Ω‑valid iff it is true in all such generic extensions. If the Ω‑conjecture holds, then the Continuum Hypothesis is Ω‑refutable (i.e., ¬CH is Ω‑valid), which would mean that CH is false in every “reasonable” universe of sets.

Key points:

  • Ω‑logic extends ordinary first‑order logic by allowing infinite conjunctions and disjunctions indexed by ordinals, and its semantics is defined via generic extensions.
  • The Ω‑conjecture is known to be consistent relative to a proper class of Woodin cardinals, but its truth remains open.
  • If the Ω‑conjecture is true, then the theory of L(ℝ) is “complete” in a strong sense: any statement about the reals that can be settled by forcing is already decided in L(ℝ).
  • This program connects large cardinals, descriptive set theory, and the philosophy of mathematical truth, suggesting that the universe of sets may have a unique “maximal” theory.

Supercompact Cardinals and the Strong Compactness Theorem

A cardinal κ is supercompact if for every λ ≥ κ there exists an elementary embedding j: V → M with critical point κ such that j(κ) > λ and M^λ ⊆ M (i.e., M is closed under λ‑sequences). Equivalently, κ is λ‑supercompact for all λ ≥ κ. Supercompactness is a very strong large‑cardinal notion; it implies that κ is measurable, strong, and even extendible.

The connection with compactness logic is given by the Magidor characterization: κ is supercompact iff the infinitary logic Lκ,κ satisfies the strong compactness theorem — every κ‑satisfiable set of sentences has a model. This mirrors the classical compactness theorem for first‑order logic (which corresponds to ω‑compactness).

Consequences of supercompact cardinals include:

  • The Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (SCH) holds above a supercompact cardinal (Solovay).
  • Forcing axioms such as Martin’s Maximum (MM) and the Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA) are equiconsistent with a supercompact cardinal (or slightly weaker variants).
  • Supercompactness is indestructible under certain forcing iterations (Laver preparation), allowing one to force combinatorial principles while preserving the large cardinal.
  • The existence of a supercompact cardinal implies the consistency of AD in L(ℝ) via the derived model construction.

Supercompact cardinals sit near the top of the large‑cardinal hierarchy that is still compatible with V = L[μ]‑type inner models. Their consistency strength is strictly below that of a huge cardinal but above that of a strongly compact cardinal. The interplay between supercompactness, forcing axioms, and the structure of the continuum remains a central theme in contemporary set theory.

  • Confusing the Solovay model with a model of ZFC — the Solovay model satisfies ZF + DC but not full AC; it cannot be a model of ZFC.
  • Assuming Shoenfield absoluteness applies to Σ²₁ statements — it only covers Σ¹₂ and Π¹₂; CH is Σ²₁ and is not absolute.
  • Thinking AD is consistent with ZFC — AD contradicts AC, so it can only hold in models of ZF (or ZF + DC).
  • Believing generic absoluteness holds for all statements — it is known for L(ℝ) under large cardinals, but fails for statements about the full universe (e.g., CH).
  • Equating supercompactness with strong compactness — every supercompact cardinal is strongly compact, but the converse is not provable in ZFC (it is consistent that the first strongly compact is not supercompact).
  • Overlooking the role of the Lévy collapse in Solovay’s construction — the collapse makes the inaccessible cardinal become ω₁; without it the model would not have the desired regularity properties.
  • Misapplying the Ω‑conjecture as a theorem — it remains a conjecture; its truth would settle CH, but it is not yet proved.

These advanced topics illustrate how large cardinals, forcing, and descriptive set theory intertwine to shape the modern understanding of infinity and the limits of provability.

The HOD Conjecture and the HOD Dichotomy

The class HOD (hereditarily ordinal‑definable sets) is the inner model consisting of all sets that are definable from ordinal parameters. The HOD conjecture, formulated by Woodin, asserts that if there is an extendible cardinal then HOD correctly computes the successors of all singular cardinals above that cardinal. Equivalently, the conjecture predicts that the pattern of cardinal arithmetic in HOD mirrors that of V for sufficiently large cardinals. A major breakthrough is the HOD dichotomy theorem: assuming a proper class of Woodin cardinals, either HOD is “close” to V in the sense that it computes successors of singular cardinals correctly, or there is a proper class of measurable cardinals in HOD that are not measurable in V. This dichotomy links the structure of HOD to the existence of large cardinals and has profound consequences for the analysis of inner models. For instance, if the HOD conjecture holds, then the failure of the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (SCH) at a singular strong limit cardinal of countable cofinality forces the existence of a very strong large cardinal in HOD, pushing the consistency strength far beyond a supercompact cardinal. The conjecture remains open, but it has become a central organizing principle in the search for ultimate inner models.

Key Equivalences

  • HOD conjecture ⇔ for every extendible cardinal δ, (δ⁺)ᴴᴼᴰ = δ⁺.
  • Failure of HOD conjecture ⇔ there is a proper class of cardinals that are measurable in HOD but not in V.
  • Under a proper class of Woodin cardinals, the HOD dichotomy is provable in ZFC.

These equivalences show that the HOD conjecture is not merely a statement about definability but a deep reflection principle connecting the large‑cardinal structure of V with that of its canonical inner model.

The Ultimate L Conjecture and the Search for a Canonical Inner Model

The Ultimate L programme, initiated by Woodin, aims to construct a canonical inner model that accommodates all known large cardinals and satisfies the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). The conjecture posits the existence of a fine‑structural model Ultimate L, built by iterating extenders in a manner analogous to Gödel’s L but using the full strength of extendible and supercompact cardinals. If Ultimate L exists, it would be a model of ZFC + GCH + “there is a proper class of Woodin cardinals” and would be universal for all set‑generic extensions: every set‑generic extension of V would be a generic extension of Ultimate L. This would resolve many independence phenomena by showing that the “true” universe of sets is, in a precise sense, close to a model of GCH. The construction relies on the comparison theory of mouse‑like structures (mice) and the development of iteration strategies for extenders of arbitrary length. Recent progress includes the proof that if there is a supercompact cardinal then there is an inner model with a supercompact cardinal (the “supercompactness” inner model), but the full Ultimate L remains conjectural. The programme also connects with the HOD conjecture: if Ultimate L exists, then HOD of any generic extension is a generic extension of Ultimate L, implying the HOD conjecture.

Milestones in the Programme

  1. Construction of L[E] models for measurable and strong cardinals (Mitchell, Steel).
  2. Development of the core model K up to a Woodin cardinal (Steel, Jensen).
  3. Proof of the existence of an inner model with a supercompact cardinal (Woodin, 2010s).
  4. Formulation of the Ultimate L conjecture and its equivalence to the HOD conjecture under suitable large cardinals.

The Ultimate L conjecture is arguably the most ambitious project in contemporary inner model theory; its resolution would either provide a definitive canonical universe or demonstrate inherent limits to the fine‑structural approach.

Worked Example: HOD Dichotomy Application
Assume there is a proper class of Woodin cardinals. Show that either the HOD conjecture holds or there is a proper class of cardinals that are measurable in HOD but not in V.
By the HOD dichotomy theorem (Woodin), under a proper class of Woodin cardinals exactly one of the following holds: (1) For every singular cardinal λ of uncountable cofinality, λ⁺ is correctly computed by HOD; this is precisely the HOD conjecture for extendible cardinals. (2) There is a proper class of cardinals κ such that κ is measurable in HOD but not measurable in V. The proof uses the analysis of the HOD of the derived model of a Woodin cardinal and the fact that the Σ₂ theory of HOD is absolute under set forcing. Thus the dichotomy is a direct consequence of the generic absoluteness for L(ℝ) and the structure of the extender sequence in HOD.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the relationship between large cardinals and HOD, first identify which large cardinal hypothesis is assumed (e.g., proper class of Woodin cardinals, extendible cardinal). Then recall the HOD dichotomy: it gives a clean either/or statement. If the problem asks for consistency strength, note that the failure of the HOD conjecture implies a proper class of measurable cardinals in HOD, which has strictly higher consistency strength than the large cardinals assumed in V. Use the equivalences listed in the Key Equivalences box to translate between statements about successors of singulars and measurability in HOD.

Stationary Tower Forcing and Generic Absoluteness

Stationary tower forcing, introduced by Woodin, is a class forcing notion that uses stationary subsets of [H_θ]^ω (for regular θ) as conditions. The generic filter adds a generic elementary embedding j: V → M with critical point ω₁^V, and the target model M is closed under ω‑sequences. This forcing is instrumental in proving generic absoluteness results for the theory of L(ℝ) under large cardinal assumptions. In particular, assuming a proper class of Woodin cardinals, the stationary tower forcing yields a generic embedding that makes the theory of L(ℝ) invariant under all set forcing. The key technical point is that the stationary tower is <δ‑closed for a Woodin cardinal δ, so it preserves the Woodin cardinals and the structure of L(ℝ). The generic embedding also provides a canonical way to compare models of AD⁺ and to analyze the projective hierarchy. Stationary tower forcing is also used to prove the consistency of the failure of the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis at ℵ_ω from a supercompact cardinal, by collapsing the supercompact to become ℵ_ω while preserving the stationary tower structure.

Properties of the Stationary Tower

  • Conditions are stationary subsets of [H_θ]^ω ordered by inclusion.
  • The forcing is <δ‑closed for any Woodin cardinal δ.
  • The generic embedding j: V → M satisfies M^ω ⊆ M and crit(j) = ω₁^V.
  • If G is generic, then V[G] satisfies that the theory of L(ℝ) is the same as in V.

These properties make the stationary tower a central tool for connecting large cardinals, determinacy, and the structure of the continuum.

The Consistency Strength Hierarchy: From Measurable to Rank‑into‑Rank

The large‑cardinal hierarchy is calibrated by consistency strength: a large cardinal axiom A is stronger than B if Con(ZFC + A) implies Con(ZFC + B) but not conversely. The hierarchy begins with inaccessible cardinals, then Mahlo, weakly compact, indescribable, measurable, strong, Woodin, supercompact, extendible, huge, and finally rank‑into‑rank (I₀, I₁, I₂, I₃). Each step typically adds a new level of elementary embedding: measurable gives j: V → M with crit(j) = κ; strong gives j: V → M with V_λ ⊆ M; supercompact gives j: V → M with M^λ ⊆ M for all λ ≥ κ; extendible gives j: V_λ → V_μ with crit(j) = κ; huge gives j: V → M with Mj(κ) ⊆ M; rank‑into‑rank gives j: V_λ → V_λ with crit(j) < λ. The consistency strength increases strictly at each stage. For example, the existence of a supercompact cardinal is equiconsistent with the Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA) and with Martin’s Maximum (MM). A huge cardinal is stronger than a supercompact but weaker than a rank‑into‑rank cardinal. The I₀ axiom (there is a nontrivial elementary embedding j: L(Vλ+1) → L(Vλ+1) with crit(j) < λ) sits at the very top of the known hierarchy that is still compatible with ZFC. The exact boundaries are explored via inner model theory and forcing: for instance, the consistency of I₀ implies the consistency of AD in L(ℝ) and the failure of the Axiom of Choice at high levels.

Selected Consistency Strength Comparisons

Consistency Strength Order (weakest to strongest)
Large CardinalEquiconsistent Theory
MeasurableZFC + “there is a measurable cardinal”
StrongZFC + “there is a strong cardinal”
WoodinZFC + “there is a Woodin cardinal”
SupercompactPFA, MM
ExtendibleZFC + “there is an extendible cardinal”
HugeZFC + “there is a huge cardinal”
Rank‑into‑rank (I₀)ZFC + I₀

Understanding this hierarchy is essential for evaluating the relative strength of forcing axioms, determinacy axioms, and statements about the continuum.

The Multiverse View and the Philosophy of Set‑Theoretic Truth

The multiverse view, championed by Hamkins and others, proposes that there is not a single universe of sets but a multitude of equally legitimate set‑theoretic universes, each a model of ZFC (or ZF). This perspective reframes independence results: CH is neither true nor false absolutely; it is true in some universes and false in others. The multiverse is not a formal theory but a philosophical stance that influences mathematical practice. It suggests that the goal of set theory is to explore the relationships among universes via forcing, inner models, and large cardinals, rather than to settle undecided statements by fiat. Key principles include: (1) Every universe has forcing extensions and inner models that are also universes. (2) The collection of all universes is not a set but a proper class. (3) Truth is relative to a universe; there is no absolute truth predicate for the whole multiverse. This view contrasts with the “universe” view (Gödel, Woodin) which seeks a single canonical universe (e.g., Ultimate L) that decides all statements. The debate has practical consequences: if one adopts the multiverse view, research focuses on the structure of the multiverse (e.g., the modal logic of forcing, the generic multiverse, the mantle). If one adopts the universe view, research focuses on finding axioms that uniquely determine the continuum (e.g., the Ω‑conjecture, the Ultimate L conjecture). Both perspectives have produced deep mathematics; the exam may ask you to compare their implications for the status of CH, the Axiom of Choice, and large cardinal axioms.

Multiverse vs Universe: Key Differences

  • Ontology: many universes vs one true universe.
  • Truth: relative vs absolute.
  • Methodology: study of forcing extensions and inner models as peers vs search for deciding axioms.
  • Attitude toward CH: undecided in principle vs potentially decided by new axioms.

While the multiverse view is not a formal axiom system, it provides a framework for interpreting the vast landscape of independence results and for understanding the role of forcing as a method of moving between universes.

  • Confusing the HOD conjecture with the statement that HOD satisfies GCH — the conjecture only concerns successors of singular cardinals, not full GCH.
  • Assuming the Ultimate L conjecture is proved — it remains a conjecture; only partial results (inner models for supercompact cardinals) are known.
  • Thinking stationary tower forcing is a set forcing — it is a class forcing; its generic embeddings are not definable in V.
  • Equating consistency strength with size of cardinals — a huge cardinal is larger than a supercompact, but consistency strength is measured by implication of consistency, not cardinal magnitude.
  • Believing the multiverse view resolves CH — it reframes CH as relative, but does not provide a truth value in any absolute sense.
  • Overlooking that the HOD dichotomy requires a proper class of Woodin cardinals — without that hypothesis the dichotomy is not provable in ZFC.
  • Misapplying the rank‑into‑rank axioms as compatible with V = L — they are incompatible with V = L because they imply the existence of non‑constructible sets.

Easton's Theorem and the Continuum Function on Regular Cardinals

Easton's theorem (1970) completely characterises the possible behaviour of the continuum function κ ↦ 2κ on regular cardinals in models of ZFC. The theorem states that for any function F from the class of regular cardinals to cardinals satisfying (i) κ ≤ λ implies F(κ) ≤ F(λ) (monotonicity) and (ii) cf(F(κ)) > κ (König's lemma constraint), there is a forcing extension preserving all cofinalities and cardinals in which 2κ = F(κ) for every regular κ. The forcing used is a product of Cohen forcings Add(κ, F(κ)) with Easton support: conditions are functions p whose domain is a set of regular cardinals, p(κ) ∈ Add(κ, F(κ)), and for every regular λ, |dom(p) ∩ λ| < λ. This support ensures that the forcing is κ-closed for each regular κ, hence preserves all cardinals and cofinalities. Easton's theorem shows that ZFC imposes almost no restrictions on the continuum function on regular cardinals beyond monotonicity and König's lemma. In particular, CH can fail at ℵ0 while holding at ℵ1, or 2ℵ0 = ℵ2 and 2ℵ1 = ℵω+1, or any other pattern consistent with the two constraints. The theorem does not apply to singular cardinals, where deep ZFC constraints (Shelah's pcf theory, the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis) severely restrict the possible values of 2κ. Easton's original proof used a class forcing iteration; modern presentations often use a product with Easton support. The theorem is a cornerstone of the "local" approach to the continuum problem: it shows that the behaviour of 2κ on regular cardinals is essentially independent of ZFC, motivating the search for additional axioms (large cardinals, forcing axioms) that constrain the continuum function globally.

The Singular Cardinals Hypothesis and pcf Theory

The Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (SCH) is the statement that for every singular strong limit cardinal κ, 2κ = κ+. Equivalently, if κ is singular and 2cf(κ) < κ, then κcf(κ) = κ+. SCH is a ZFC theorem for singular cardinals of uncountable cofinality (Silver's theorem: if κ is singular of uncountable cofinality and 2λ = λ+ for all sufficiently large λ < κ, then 2κ = κ+), but it is independent for singular cardinals of countable cofinality. The most famous independence result is Magidor's (1977): it is consistent relative to a supercompact cardinal that ℵω is a strong limit and 2ℵω = ℵω+2, violating SCH. Shelah's pcf theory (possible cofinalities) provides the definitive ZFC analysis of cardinal arithmetic at singular cardinals. For a set A of regular cardinals, pcf(A) is the set of all possible cofinalities of ultraproducts ∏A/D where D is an ultrafilter on A. The fundamental theorem of pcf theory: if A is a set of regular cardinals with |A| < min(A), then pcf(A) has a maximum element, denoted max pcf(A), and there is a sequence ⟨bλ : λ ∈ pcf(A)⟩ of "generators" such that for any ultrafilter D on A, cf(∏A/D) = λ iff bλ ∈ D. This yields Shelah's bound: if κ is singular, then κcf(κ) < ℵ(2cf(κ))+. In particular, if κ is a strong limit singular cardinal, then 2κ < ℵ(2cf(κ))+. For κ = ℵω, this gives 2ℵω < ℵω4, a dramatic improvement over the trivial bound ℵωω. pcf theory also proves that if ℵω is a strong limit, then 2ℵω < ℵω4, and more generally the "revised GCH" theorem: for every singular κ, there is a cofinal A ⊆ κ such that |pcf(A)| < κ. The theory has applications beyond cardinal arithmetic: it provides scales (cofinal sequences in ∏A modulo the bounded ideal) used in the construction of models with prescribed cardinal arithmetic, and it underlies the analysis of the ideal of non-stationary sets on ℵω+1.

Worked Problem: Applying Easton's Theorem and pcf Bounds
Suppose we want a model of ZFC where 2ℵ0 = ℵ2, 2ℵ1 = ℵ3, 2ℵ2 = ℵ5, and ℵω is a strong limit with 2ℵω = ℵω+2. Is this consistent with ZFC? If so, what large cardinal assumption is needed? If not, which constraint is violated?
The pattern on regular cardinals (ℵ0, ℵ1, ℵ2) satisfies Easton's conditions: monotonicity holds (ℵ2 ≤ ℵ3 ≤ ℵ5) and König's lemma holds (cf(ℵ2) = ℵ2 > ℵ0, cf(ℵ3) = ℵ3 > ℵ1, cf(ℵ5) = ℵ5 > ℵ2). So by Easton's theorem, there is a forcing extension preserving cardinals and cofinalities where 2ℵ0 = ℵ2, 2ℵ1 = ℵ3, 2ℵ2 = ℵ5. For the singular cardinal ℵω, we require it to be a strong limit (so 2ℵn < ℵω for all n < ω) and 2ℵω = ℵω+2. This violates SCH. Magidor proved that the failure of SCH at ℵω (i.e., ℵω strong limit but 2ℵω > ℵω+1) is equiconsistent with a measurable cardinal of Mitchell order ω (or a supercompact cardinal). Shelah's pcf bound gives 2ℵω < ℵω4, so ℵω+2 is allowed. Thus the full pattern is consistent relative to a supercompact cardinal (or a measurable of Mitchell order ω). The forcing construction uses a Prikry-type forcing to change the cofinality of a large cardinal to ω while controlling the continuum function below it, combined with Easton forcing for the regular cardinals.
Exam Strategy: Cardinal Arithmetic Independence
When a question asks whether a given pattern of 2κ is consistent, first check Easton's conditions on the regular cardinals involved. If they hold, the pattern is consistent on the regulars by Easton's theorem (no large cardinals needed). For singular cardinals, check Silver's theorem (uncountable cofinality) and Shelah's pcf bounds (countable cofinality). If the pattern violates SCH at a singular of countable cofinality, a large cardinal (measurable of high Mitchell order or supercompact) is required. Memorise the key bounds: 2ℵω < ℵω4 (Shelah), and Silver's theorem: if κ is singular of uncountable cofinality and GCH holds below κ, then GCH holds at κ. Distinguish between "consistent with ZFC" (no large cardinals) and "consistent relative to a large cardinal" (large cardinals needed).

Martin's Maximum and the Maximality Principle

Martin's Maximum (MM) is the strongest known forcing axiom consistent with ZFC, introduced by Foreman, Magidor, and Shelah (1988). It asserts that for every stationary set preserving (SSP) forcing notion P and every collection D of ℵ1 dense subsets of P, there is a filter G ⊆ P meeting every set in D. "Stationary set preserving" means that P does not destroy the stationarity of any stationary subset of ω1 (equivalently, of any stationary subset of any regular cardinal). MM implies PFA (the Proper Forcing Axiom) and is strictly stronger in consistency strength. The consistency of MM relative to a supercompact cardinal was proved by Foreman, Magidor, and Shelah using a sophisticated iteration of SSP forcings with revised countable support. MM has dramatic consequences: it implies 2ℵ0 = ℵ2 (so CH fails), the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis holds, the non-stationary ideal on ω1 is ℵ2-saturated, and every projective set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property, and has the perfect set property. MM also implies that the continuum is real-valued measurable (there is a countably additive probability measure on all subsets of ℝ vanishing on singletons). The Maximality Principle (MP), introduced by Hamkins (2003), is a different kind of "maximality" axiom: it asserts that if a sentence φ is forceably necessary (i.e., there is a forcing extension in which φ holds in all further forcing extensions), then φ already holds in V. In modal logic terms, MP says that the forcing modality □◇φ → φ is valid. MP is equiconsistent with ZFC (no large cardinals needed), but it implies that the universe is "maximal" with respect to forcing: any statement that can be made permanently true by forcing is already true. MP has interesting consequences: it implies that there are no inaccessible cardinals (since "there is an inaccessible" is forceably necessary but false in L), and it implies that the continuum is ℵ1 or ℵ2 (since one can force CH or ¬CH and then make it necessary by collapsing cardinals). The Boldface Maximality Principle (BMP), allowing parameters, is equiconsistent with a reflecting cardinal. MP and MM represent two different philosophies: MM is a "local" maximality principle for a specific class of forcings (SSP), while MP is a "global" maximality principle for the entire forcing multiverse. Both have been extensively studied in the context of the generic multiverse and the philosophy of set-theoretic truth.

Core Model Induction and Mouse Theory

Core model induction is a central technique in modern inner model theory, developed by Steel, Woodin, and others, for proving determinacy and regularity properties from large cardinal hypotheses. The core model K is a canonical inner model that exists below a measurable cardinal; it generalises L and captures the large cardinal structure of V up to the first measurable. A "mouse" is a small, iterable premouse — a structure M = (Jα[E], ∈, E) where E is a sequence of extenders coding elementary embeddings, satisfying certain fine-structural conditions (soundness, projectum, etc.). Mice are the building blocks of inner models for large cardinals. The core model induction proceeds by assuming a hypothesis (e.g., "every projective set is determined" or "ADL(ℝ) holds") and showing that if the hypothesis fails, one can construct a mouse with a certain large cardinal property, contradicting the assumed consistency strength. For example, to prove that projective determinacy (PD) follows from the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals, one shows that if PD fails, there is a minimal counterexample, and from it one constructs a mouse with a Woodin cardinal, then iterates to get a contradiction. The "induction" refers to the fact that the proof proceeds by induction on the complexity of the pointclass (Σ1n, Π1n), using the fact that determinacy for a pointclass implies the existence of scales and uniformization, which in turn allow the construction of mice for the next level. The core model K(X) relative to a set X is the minimal iterable inner model containing X and all its iterates. The comparison lemma for mice (any two iterable mice can be compared by iterating their extenders) is the key technical tool. Core model induction has been used to establish equiconsistencies: ZFC + "there are n Woodin cardinals" is equiconsistent with ZF + DC + "every Σ1n+1 set is determined"; ZFC + "there are infinitely many Woodin cardinals" is equiconsistent with ZF + DC + PD; ZFC + "there is a measurable Woodin cardinal" is equiconsistent with ZF + DC + ADL(ℝ). The technique also yields the "mouse capturing" theorem: under ADL(ℝ), every real x is in a mouse over x, and the mice over x are exactly the iterates of the minimal mouse M1(x). This connects descriptive set theory (determinacy, scales, uniformization) with fine structure (mice, iteration trees, comparison). The ultimate goal is to build a mouse for a supercompact cardinal, which would yield an inner model for "there is a supercompact cardinal" and resolve the inner model problem for supercompactness.

Square Principles and the Tree Property at Successors of Singulars

Jensen's square principle □κ for a cardinal κ asserts the existence of a sequence ⟨Cα : α < κ+, α limit⟩ such that each Cα is a club in α, the order-type of Cα is at most κ, and if β is a limit point of Cα then Cβ = Cα ∩ β (coherence). The weak square □κ* allows the sequence to be a sequence of sets of clubs, each of size ≤ κ. These principles are ZFC theorems in L (□κ holds for all κ) and are incompatible with certain large cardinals: if κ is supercompact, then □κ fails; if κ is weakly compact, then □κ fails. The tree property at a cardinal λ (TP(λ)) states that every λ-tree has a cofinal branch. For regular λ > ℵ1, TP(λ) is equivalent to λ being weakly compact. At successors of singulars, the situation is more subtle. The tree property at ℵω+1 is consistent relative to a supercompact cardinal (Magidor-Shelah), but it is a major open problem whether TP(ℵω+1) can hold simultaneously with the failure of SCH at ℵω. Cummings and Foreman (1998) showed that TP(ℵω+1) + 2ℵω > ℵω+1 is consistent relative to a supercompact cardinal. The interaction between square principles and the tree property is governed by the following: □κ implies the existence of a special κ+-Aronszajn tree, hence ¬TP(κ+). Conversely, if κ is singular and TP(κ+) holds, then □κ fails. The failure of □κ at a singular κ is a large cardinal property: it implies that κ is a limit of cardinals that are measurable in some inner model (Jensen, Schimmerling). The "strong square" □κ* is weaker: it can hold at successors of singulars even when large cardinals are present. The study of square principles and the tree property at successors of singulars is a central topic in the "local" analysis of the continuum and the structure of the universe below large cardinals. It connects to the approachability ideal, stationary reflection, and the structure of the non-stationary ideal on κ+.

  • Confusing Easton's theorem with the behaviour of the continuum function on singular cardinals — Easton's theorem only applies to regular cardinals; singular cardinals are constrained by Silver's theorem and Shelah's pcf bounds.
  • Assuming that the failure of SCH at ℵω requires a supercompact cardinal — it is equiconsistent with a measurable cardinal of Mitchell order ω, which is strictly weaker than supercompact.
  • Thinking that Martin's Maximum implies the failure of the Axiom of Choice — MM is a forcing axiom for ZFC; it implies AC and in fact implies 2ℵ0 = ℵ2.
  • Equating the Maximality Principle with Martin's Maximum — MP is a global modal principle equiconsistent with ZFC; MM is a local forcing axiom for SSP forcings with consistency strength of a supercompact cardinal.
  • Believing that the core model K exists above a measurable cardinal — K only exists below the first measurable; above that, one needs mice with extenders (the "core model" for larger large cardinals is not a single canonical model but a hierarchy of mice).
  • Assuming that □κ fails at a singular κ implies κ is large in V — it implies κ is a limit of cardinals measurable in an inner model, not necessarily in V.
  • Thinking that the tree property at ℵω+1 decides the value of 2ℵω — TP(ℵω+1) is consistent with both SCH and its failure at ℵω (relative to a supercompact).
