Carathéodory’s Extension Theorem – From Pre‑Measures to Full Measures

The construction of Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ is a special case of a far more general result: given a set X and an algebra 𝔄 of subsets of X, a function μ₀:𝔄→[0,∞] that is countably additive on disjoint families whose union stays in 𝔄 is called a pre‑measure. Carathéodory’s extension theorem guarantees that such a μ₀ extends uniquely to a complete measure μ on the σ‑algebra σ(𝔄) generated by 𝔄, provided μ₀ is σ‑finite (i.e., X can be written as a countable union of sets of finite μ₀‑measure). The proof proceeds by defining an outer measure μ* on all subsets of X via

μ*(E)=inf{∑ μ₀(A_i) : E⊂⋃A_i, A_i∈𝔄}. A set E is declared μ*-measurable if for every A⊂X, μ*(A)=μ*(A∩E)+μ*(A∖E). The collection of μ*-measurable sets forms a σ‑algebra containing 𝔄, and the restriction of μ* to this σ‑algebra is a complete measure extending μ₀.

Why this matters for exam‑level problems:

  • When asked to construct a measure on a product space, candidates often start from rectangles and invoke Carathéodory to justify the existence of the product measure without re‑proving countable additivity.
  • In probability, the theorem underlies the definition of distributions from cumulative distribution functions (CDFs). The CDF F defines a pre‑measure on half‑open intervals (a,b] by μ₀((a,b])=F(b)−F(a); Carathéodory then yields the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure associated with F.
  • σ‑finiteness is a frequent exam trap: if the pre‑measure is not σ‑finite, the extension may fail to be unique. Classic counter‑examples involve counting measure on an uncountable set.

Typical exam question: “Show that the counting pre‑measure on the algebra of finite subsets of an uncountable set X does not extend uniquely to a measure on the power set of X.” The answer hinges on the lack of σ‑finiteness, leading to many non‑equivalent extensions (e.g., the trivial extension that assigns ∞ to every infinite set).

Completion of Measure Spaces and Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measures

Even after Carathéodory’s theorem, a measure space (X,𝔽,μ) may miss subsets of null sets. The completion of (X,𝔽,μ) adds every subset N⊂Z where Z∈𝔽 and μ(Z)=0, forming the σ‑algebra

𝔽̂ = {A∪N : A∈𝔽, N⊂Z for some Z∈𝔽 with μ(Z)=0}.

On 𝔽̂ we define μ̂(A∪N)=μ(A). The resulting space (X,𝔽̂,μ̂) is complete: every μ̂‑null set is in 𝔽̂. Completion is essential when dealing with Lebesgue integration, because many limit processes produce sets that differ from measurable sets only by a null set.

Lebesgue–Stieltjes measures illustrate the interplay of CDFs, pre‑measures, and completion. Given a right‑continuous, non‑decreasing function F:ℝ→ℝ, define μ₀ on half‑open intervals (a,b] by μ₀((a,b])=F(b)−F(a). Carathéodory extends μ₀ to a measure μ_F on the Borel σ‑algebra. However, μ_F may assign zero measure to a Borel set B while a subset N⊂B is not Borel. After completion, N becomes measurable with μ̂_F(N)=0, allowing us to integrate functions that are only defined up to sets of μ_F‑measure zero.

Exam‑level nuance: when a problem states “let X be a random variable with distribution function F,” the implicit measure is the completed Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure. Ignoring completion can lead to incorrect statements about almost sure convergence, because convergence “a.s.” is defined with respect to the completed σ‑algebra.

Important historical note: the Lebesgue–Stieltjes construction was formalised by Henri Lebesgue (1902) and later refined by Thomas Joannes Stieltjes (1894) in the context of continued fractions. Their combined legacy provides the rigorous foundation for probability densities, discrete mass points, and mixed distributions.

Technique – Using Completion to Resolve a Measurability Issue
Let μ be Lebesgue measure on ℝ and let A⊂[0,1] be a non‑Borel set of Lebesgue measure zero (such sets exist by the axiom of choice). Define f(x)=1_A(x). Show that f is μ‑integrable and compute ∫ f dμ.
Since A has outer measure zero, μ*(A)=0. In the completed measure space (ℝ,𝔏̂,μ̂), every subset of A is measurable with μ̂‑measure zero. Hence f is measurable (its pre‑image of {1} is A, a μ̂‑null set). The integral of a non‑negative simple function equals the sum of values times the measure of the level sets: ∫ f dμ̂ = 1·μ̂(A)=0. Therefore f is integrable and its integral is 0, even though A is not Borel.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “almost surely” or “with probability 1,” immediately check whether the underlying σ‑algebra has been completed. If the problem involves a set defined via a limit (e.g., lim sup of events), assume completion; this avoids losing marks for claiming a set is non‑measurable.

Uniform Integrability and the de la Vallée‑Poussin Criterion

Uniform integrability (UI) is the bridge between convergence in measure and convergence in L¹. A family 𝔉⊂L¹(μ) is uniformly integrable if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that μ(A)<δ implies supf∈𝔉∫_A|f| dμ<ε. Intuitively, UI prevents “mass” from escaping to sets of arbitrarily small measure.

The de la Vallée‑Poussin theorem provides a practical test: 𝔉 is UI iff there exists a convex, increasing function Φ:[0,∞)→[0,∞) with Φ(t)/t→∞ as t→∞ such that supf∈𝔉∫ Φ(|f|) dμ < ∞. Common choices are Φ(t)=t·log(1+t) or Φ(t)=t^p for p>1.

Why UI appears in exams:

  • In the Vitali convergence theorem, the hypothesis “{f_n} is uniformly integrable and f_n→f in measure” yields f_n→f in L¹. Many problems ask to verify UI for a given sequence, often by exhibiting a suitable Φ.
  • In probability, UI of {X_n} is equivalent to the family {E[|X_n|]} being bounded and the tails being uniformly small. This is the key condition in the proof of the dominated convergence theorem for expectations.
  • UI also characterises relatively compact subsets of L¹ (Dunford–Pettis theorem). Exam questions may request a proof that a set is relatively compact by showing UI and tightness.

Typical trap: confusing “bounded in L¹” with UI. A sequence with ‖f_n‖₁≤C need not be UI; for example, f_n=n·χ[0,1/n] has constant L¹ norm 1 but fails UI because the mass concentrates on shrinking intervals.

Sample calculation: Let f_n(x)=n·χ[0,1/n] on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure. Choose Φ(t)=t·log(1+t). Then ∫ Φ(|f_n|) = ∫01/n n·log(1+n) dx = (1/n)·n·log(1+n)=log(1+n)→∞, so the de la Vallée‑Poussin condition fails, confirming non‑UI.

Martingale Convergence Theorem via Measure‑Theoretic Tools

Martingales are sequences {X_n} of integrable random variables adapted to an increasing filtration {𝔽_n} such that E[Xn+1|𝔽_n]=X_n a.s. The martingale convergence theorem (MCT) states: if {X_n} is a martingale that is uniformly integrable, then X_n converges a.s. and in L¹ to a limit X∞, and X∞=E[X∞|𝔽_n] for all n.

Measure‑theoretic proof outline:

  1. Define the maximal function X* = sup_n |X_n|. Doob’s maximal inequality gives μ({X*>λ}) ≤ (1/λ)·sup_n E[|X_n|] for λ>0. This inequality is derived from the sub‑martingale property of |X_n| and the optional stopping theorem.
  2. Uniform integrability of {X_n} implies that {X*} is integrable. Consequently, X*<∞ a.s., establishing almost sure boundedness of the martingale.
  3. Apply the upcrossing lemma: for any a+]−E[(X0−a)+])/(b−a). Uniform integrability forces the total expected upcrossings to be finite, which forces the limit limn→∞ X_n to exist a.s.
  4. Finally, the UI condition guarantees convergence in L¹ by the Vitali convergence theorem (a corollary of UI and a.e. convergence).

Exam relevance:

  • Problems often ask to verify the UI condition for a given martingale. Typical techniques include bounding moments (e.g., showing sup_n E[|X_n|^p] < ∞ for some p>1) and invoking the de la Vallée‑Poussin criterion.
  • In discrete‑time gambling models, the optional stopping theorem is used to compute expectations of stopped martingales; the measure‑theoretic justification rests on the σ‑algebra of the stopping time.
  • When the filtration is generated by a sequence of independent random variables, the martingale difference sequence D_n = X_n−Xn-1 often satisfies E[D_n|𝔽n-1]=0, making {X_n} a martingale. Proving convergence then reduces to checking UI of the partial sums.

Common mistake: assuming that any L²‑bounded martingale automatically converges a.s. While L²‑boundedness implies UI (by Cauchy–Schwarz), the exam setter may deliberately give a martingale that is only L¹‑bounded to test whether the candidate recognises the need for UI.

Weak Convergence of Measures, Prokhorov’s Theorem and Applications

Weak convergence (also called convergence in distribution) of probability measures μ_n→μ on a metric space (S,d) is defined by the convergence of integrals of bounded continuous functions:

μ_n ⇒ μ ⇔ ∀ f∈C_b(S), ∫ f dμ_n → ∫ f dμ.

Key characterisation tools:

  • Portmanteau theorem provides equivalent formulations: convergence of μ_n(A) for all continuity sets A, limsup inequality for closed sets, liminf for open sets, and convergence of characteristic functions when S=ℝ^k.
  • Prokhorov’s theorem links tightness and relative compactness: a family {μ_n} on a complete separable metric space (Polish space) is relatively compact in the weak topology iff it is tight, i.e., for every ε>0 there exists a compact K⊂S with μ_n(K)≥1−ε for all n.

Application to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT): Let S_n = (X₁+…+X_n)/√n where {X_i} are i.i.d. with mean 0, variance 1. The sequence of distributions μ_n of S_n is tight (by Chebyshev’s inequality) and any weak limit must have characteristic function φ(t)=e−t²/2. By Lévy’s continuity theorem, μ_n ⇒ N(0,1). The measure‑theoretic proof hinges on tightness (Prokhorov) and pointwise convergence of characteristic functions.

Exam scenarios:

  1. Given a sequence of distributions defined by densities f_n(x)=n·e−nx·χ[0,∞)(x), identify the weak limit. The densities concentrate near 0; using the change of variable y=nx shows μ_n ⇒ δ₀ (Dirac measure at 0). The candidate must justify tightness and verify convergence on continuity sets.
  2. In a problem on empirical measures, one is asked to prove that the empirical distribution of i.i.d. samples converges weakly to the true distribution almost surely (Glivenko–Cantelli). The proof uses the law of large numbers for indicator functions of continuity sets and then invokes the Portmanteau theorem.
  3. When a question mentions “the sequence {μ_n} is uniformly tight,” the examiner expects the candidate to invoke Prokhorov to claim existence of a weakly convergent subsequence, then identify the limit using additional information (e.g., moments or characteristic functions).

Typical trap: confusing weak convergence with convergence of densities in L¹. Weak convergence does not require the densities to converge pointwise or in norm; only the integrals against bounded continuous test functions must converge. Candidates who attempt to integrate the densities directly often miss the role of tightness.

  • Assuming σ‑finiteness automatically guarantees uniqueness of Carathéodory extensions; neglect the counter‑example of counting measure on an uncountable set.
  • Overlooking completion when a problem involves “almost everywhere” statements; forgetting that subsets of null sets become measurable only after completion.
  • Equating boundedness in L¹ with uniform integrability; the classic counter‑example f_n=n·χ[0,1/n] must be remembered.
  • Skipping the verification of UI in martingale convergence problems; L²‑boundedness is sufficient but not necessary, and the exam may present only L¹ bounds.
  • Treating weak convergence of measures as pointwise convergence of densities; always revert to the Portmanteau criteria or characteristic functions.
  • Neglecting tightness when applying Prokhorov’s theorem; without a tightness argument the existence of a weak limit cannot be claimed.
  • Misapplying the optional stopping theorem without checking the integrability of the stopped martingale; the theorem requires the stopped variable to be integrable.

Differentiation of Measures and the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem

The Lebesgue differentiation theorem states that for any locally integrable function f on ℝⁿ, the average of f over balls centred at x converges to f(x) for almost every x as the radius tends to zero. Formally, if B(x,r) denotes the open ball of radius r, then

limr→0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) f(y) dy = f(x) for a.e. x.

The proof rests on the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function Mf(x) = supr>0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) |f(y)| dy. The maximal inequality ‖Mf‖L¹,∞ ≤ C‖f‖L¹ yields a weak‑type (1,1) bound, which together with density of continuous functions in L¹ gives almost‑everywhere convergence. A key corollary is the Lebesgue density theorem: for any measurable set E, the density limr→0 |E∩B(x,r)|/|B(x,r)| equals 1 for a.e. x∈E and 0 for a.e. x∉E. This theorem underpins the identification of points of density with the support of a measure and is essential when proving that a Radon–Nikodym derivative can be recovered by differentiating the corresponding measure.

In the language of measures, if μ is a finite Borel measure on ℝⁿ absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure λ, the Radon–Nikodym derivative dμ/dλ coincides λ‑a.e. with the limit of μ(B(x,r))/λ(B(x,r)). For singular measures the limit is either 0 or ∞ λ‑a.e., reflecting the mutual singularity. Examiners often ask to distinguish between the behaviour of absolutely continuous and singular parts via differentiation, or to apply the density theorem to show that a set of positive measure contains points of density 1.

Conditional Expectation as a Radon–Nikodym Derivative

Let (Ω,ℱ,ℙ) be a probability space and 𝒢⊂ℱ a sub‑σ‑algebra. For an integrable random variable X, the conditional expectation E[X|𝒢] is the unique (up to ℙ‑a.s. equality) 𝒢‑measurable random variable Y satisfying ∫A Y dℙ = ∫A X dℙ for every A∈𝒢. This definition is precisely the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the signed measure ν(A)=∫A X dℙ with respect to ℙ restricted to 𝒢. The existence of Y follows from the Radon–Nikodym theorem because ν≪ℙ on 𝒢 and both are σ‑finite.

Properties such as linearity, tower property E[E[X|𝒢]|ℋ]=E[X|ℋ] for ℋ⊂𝒢, and Jensen’s inequality for convex φ (φ(E[X|𝒢]) ≤ E[φ(X)|𝒢]) are direct consequences of the measure‑theoretic construction. The martingale convergence theorem can be proved by viewing a martingale (Xₙ) as a sequence of Radon–Nikodym derivatives dμₙ/dℙ on an increasing filtration; uniform integrability of {Xₙ} is equivalent to the uniform absolute continuity of the measures μₙ, which in turn yields convergence of the derivatives in L¹.

In exam problems, candidates are frequently asked to compute E[X|𝒢] when 𝒢 is generated by a countable partition {Aₖ}. The answer is Σₖ (∫Aₖ X dℙ / ℙ(Aₖ)) 1Aₖ, provided ℙ(Aₖ)>0. When 𝒢 is generated by a random variable Y, the conditional expectation becomes a Borel function g(Y) where g(y)=E[X|Y=y] is defined via the regular conditional distribution. Recognising the Radon–Nikodym viewpoint avoids the common mistake of treating conditional expectation as an elementary average without verifying 𝒢‑measurability and the defining integral identity.

Worked Example: Conditional Expectation on a Partition
Let Ω={1,2,3,4} with ℙ({i})=1/4. Define X(i)=i². Let 𝒢 be the σ‑algebra generated by the partition {{1,2},{3,4}}. Compute E[X|𝒢].
For A₁={1,2}, ∫A₁ X dℙ = (1²+2²)/4 = 5/4. ℙ(A₁)=1/2. Hence the value on A₁ is (5/4)/(1/2)=5/2. For A₂={3,4}, ∫A₂ X dℙ = (3²+4²)/4 = 25/4. ℙ(A₂)=1/2. Value on A₂ = (25/4)/(1/2)=25/2. Therefore E[X|𝒢](ω)=5/2 for ω∈{1,2} and 25/2 for ω∈{3,4}. This function is 𝒢‑measurable and satisfies the defining integral property.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a conditional expectation, first identify the generating σ‑algebra. If it is a finite or countable partition, write the explicit formula Σ (∫Aₖ X dℙ)/ℙ(Aₖ) 1Aₖ. For σ‑algebras generated by a random variable, recall that the answer must be a Borel function of that variable; use the regular conditional distribution or the factorisation lemma. Always verify the two defining conditions: 𝒢‑measurability and equality of integrals on every 𝒢‑set.

Singular Continuous Measures and the Cantor–Lebesgue Function

A Borel measure μ on ℝ is singular continuous if it is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure λ (there exists a Borel set N with λ(N)=0 and μ(ℝN)=0) and has no atoms (μ({x})=0 for all x). The canonical example is the Cantor–Lebesgue measure μC supported on the middle‑third Cantor set C. Its distribution function F(x)=μC((−∞,x]) is the Cantor function, also called the Devil’s staircase. F is continuous, non‑decreasing, constant on each interval removed in the construction of C, and satisfies F(0)=0, F(1)=1. Despite being continuous, F′(x)=0 for λ‑a.e. x, yet μC is not absolutely continuous because μC(C)=1 while λ(C)=0.

The Lebesgue decomposition theorem states that any finite Borel measure μ can be uniquely written as μ = μac + μsc + μpp, where μac≪λ, μsc⟂λ and atomless, and μpp is pure point (a countable sum of atoms). The Cantor measure provides the singular continuous component. In Fourier analysis, the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of μC does not vanish at infinity, illustrating that Riemann–Lebesgue lemma fails for singular continuous measures. Examiners may ask to prove that the Cantor function has derivative zero almost everywhere, or to show that a given distribution function corresponds to a singular continuous measure by verifying continuity, absence of jumps, and singularity with respect to λ.

Ergodic Theory: Invariant Measures and the Birkhoff Ergodic Theorem

Let (X,ℬ,μ) be a probability space and T:X→X a measurable transformation preserving μ, i.e. μ(T⁻¹A)=μ(A) for all A∈ℬ. The system is ergodic if every T‑invariant set has measure 0 or 1. The Birkhoff ergodic theorem asserts that for any f∈L¹(μ), the time averages (1/n) Σk=0n−1 f(Tᵏx) converge μ‑a.e. to a T‑invariant function f*. If the system is ergodic, f* is constant μ‑a.e. and equals ∫ f dμ. The proof uses the maximal ergodic inequality: for λ>0, λ μ({supn≥1 (1/n) Σk=0n−1 f(Tᵏx) > λ}) ≤ ∫{f*>λ} f dμ. This inequality is the dynamical analogue of the Hardy–Littlewood maximal inequality and yields almost‑everywhere convergence via a standard density argument.

Applications include the strong law of large numbers for stationary sequences (take T as the shift on the sequence space) and the equidistribution of irrational rotations on the circle (unique ergodicity). In competitive examinations, a typical question presents a measure‑preserving map and asks whether it is ergodic; the candidate must either exhibit a non‑trivial invariant set or invoke a known criterion such as the spectral condition that the only eigenfunctions of the Koopman operator Uf=f∘T with eigenvalue 1 are constants. Another common task is to compute the limit of time averages for a specific observable, which reduces to evaluating the space average when ergodicity is established.

  • Confusing the Lebesgue differentiation theorem with the fundamental theorem of calculus; the former holds for any locally integrable function, the latter requires absolute continuity.
  • Assuming conditional expectation is always given by an elementary formula without checking σ‑finiteness or the defining integral identity.
  • Treating the Cantor function as absolutely continuous because it is continuous; remember that absolute continuity is strictly stronger.
  • Neglecting to verify the maximal ergodic inequality when applying Birkhoff’s theorem; the inequality is the key step that guarantees almost‑everywhere convergence.
  • Misidentifying the singular continuous component in a Lebesgue decomposition; a measure can be singular yet have atoms, so atomlessness must be checked separately.
  • Applying the Radon–Nikodym theorem without confirming absolute continuity; the derivative does not exist if the measure is not absolutely continuous with respect to the reference measure.
  • Overlooking the role of σ‑finiteness in the Radon–Nikodym theorem and in the construction of conditional expectations on non‑probability spaces.

These advanced topics complete the measure‑theoretic toolkit needed for rigorous analysis and probability at the highest competitive level.

Signed Measures and the Hahn Decomposition Theorem

A signed measure on a measurable space (X, Σ) is a function ν : Σ → [−∞, ∞] that is countably additive and takes at most one of the values +∞, −∞. Unlike a positive measure, ν can assign negative mass to sets. The Hahn decomposition theorem asserts that there exist disjoint measurable sets P and N such that P ∪ N = X, ν(E) ≥ 0 for every E ⊆ P, and ν(E) ≤ 0 for every E ⊆ N. The pair (P, N) is not unique, but any two such decompositions differ only by ν‑null sets. The proof proceeds by defining the positive variation ν⁺(E) = sup{ν(F) : F ⊆ E, F ∈ Σ} and the negative variation ν⁻(E) = −inf{ν(F) : F ⊆ E, F ∈ Σ}, then showing ν = ν⁺ − ν⁻ and that ν⁺, ν⁻ are mutually singular positive measures. This decomposition underlies the Jordan decomposition and the definition of total variation |ν| = ν⁺ + ν⁻.

Key consequences for examiners: (1) a signed measure is finite iff both ν⁺ and ν⁻ are finite; (2) the Hahn decomposition provides a canonical way to separate the “positive part” and “negative part” of a signed measure without invoking densities; (3) the theorem fails if ν is allowed to take both +∞ and −∞ on sets of positive measure, which is why the definition of a signed measure excludes that possibility. Typical exam questions ask to construct the Hahn decomposition for a concrete signed measure such as ν(E) = ∫_E (f − g) dμ where f, g ∈ L¹(μ), or to prove that the positive and negative variations are the smallest positive measures dominating ν and −ν respectively.

Jordan Decomposition and Total Variation of Signed Measures

The Jordan decomposition theorem states that every signed measure ν can be written uniquely as ν = ν⁺ − ν⁻ where ν⁺ and ν⁻ are positive measures, at least one of which is finite, and ν⁺ ⟂ ν⁻ (they are mutually singular). The measures ν⁺ and ν⁻ are called the positive and negative variations of ν. The total variation measure is defined by |ν| = ν⁺ + ν⁻; it is a positive measure that dominates |ν(E)| for every measurable E. Moreover, |ν| is the smallest positive measure with this property: if λ is any positive measure such that |ν(E)| ≤ λ(E) for all E, then |ν| ≤ λ.

An equivalent constructive definition uses the supremum over partitions: |ν|(E) = sup Σi=1^n |ν(E_i)| where the supremum runs over all finite measurable partitions {E_i} of E. This definition makes it clear that |ν| is a measure and that ν ≪ |ν|. The Radon–Nikodym derivative dν/d|ν| takes values in {−1, 1} |ν|‑almost everywhere, providing a measurable “sign function” for ν. In practice, the total variation norm ‖ν‖ = |ν|(X) turns the space of finite signed measures into a Banach space. Examiners often test the relationship between the Hahn decomposition (P, N) and the Jordan decomposition: ν⁺(E) = ν(E ∩ P), ν⁻(E) = −ν(E ∩ N). A common twist is to ask whether the Jordan decomposition of a complex measure (see below) coincides with the decomposition of its real and imaginary parts; the answer is yes, but the total variation of a complex measure is defined via a supremum over partitions with complex coefficients, leading to the inequality |ν| ≤ |Re ν| + |Im ν|.

Worked Example: Jordan Decomposition of a Signed Measure on ℝ
Let μ be Lebesgue measure on ℝ and define ν(E) = ∫_E (1[0,1] − 2·1[2,3]) dμ for Borel sets E. Find the Hahn decomposition (P, N), the positive and negative variations ν⁺, ν⁻, and the total variation |ν|.
The integrand f(x) = 1[0,1](x) − 2·1[2,3](x) is ≥ 0 on [0,1] and ≤ 0 on [2,3]; it is zero elsewhere. Take P = [0,1] and N = ℝ [0,1] (or more precisely N = (−∞,0) ∪ (1,2) ∪ (3,∞) ∪ [2,3]). Then for any Borel E, ν(E ∩ P) = μ(E ∩ [0,1]) ≥ 0 and ν(E ∩ N) = −2 μ(E ∩ [2,3]) ≤ 0. Hence (P, N) is a Hahn decomposition. The positive variation is ν⁺(E) = ν(E ∩ P) = μ(E ∩ [0,1]). The negative variation is ν⁻(E) = −ν(E ∩ N) = 2 μ(E ∩ [2,3]). The total variation is |ν|(E) = ν⁺(E) + ν⁻(E) = μ(E ∩ [0,1]) + 2 μ(E ∩ [2,3]). One verifies that |ν|(ℝ) = 1 + 2 = 3, which equals ‖ν‖.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for the Hahn or Jordan decomposition, first identify a measurable function f such that ν(E) = ∫_E f dμ (if ν ≪ μ). Then P = {f ≥ 0}, N = {f < 0} gives a Hahn decomposition, and ν⁺(E) = ∫E∩P f dμ, ν⁻(E) = −∫E∩N f dμ. This avoids the abstract supremum construction and is accepted as a complete answer.

Radon Measures on Locally Compact Hausdorff Spaces

A Radon measure on a locally compact Hausdorff space X is a Borel measure μ that is finite on compact sets, outer regular on all Borel sets (μ(E) = inf{μ(U) : E ⊆ U, U open}), and inner regular on open sets (μ(U) = sup{μ(K) : K ⊆ U, K compact}). These regularity properties make Radon measures the natural objects for integration on topological spaces. Every finite Borel measure on a metric space is Radon; more generally, any σ‑finite measure on a locally compact second‑countable Hausdorff space that is inner regular on all Borel sets is Radon. The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem (see next section) characterises the dual of C_c(X) (continuous functions with compact support) as the space of signed Radon measures. Important consequences: (1) the support of a Radon measure, defined as the complement of the largest open set of measure zero, is a closed set carrying the full mass; (2) convolution of two Radon measures on a locally compact group is again a Radon measure provided at least one has compact support; (3) the space of Radon measures with the vague topology (testing against C_c(X)) is a locally convex topological vector space, and the Banach–Alaoglu theorem yields compactness of bounded sets in the dual of C0(X). Examiners may ask to prove that a given Borel measure on ℝⁿ defined by a density with respect to Lebesgue measure is Radon, or to show that the Dirac delta at a point is a Radon measure but not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani Representation Theorem

Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space and C_c(X) the space of continuous real‑valued functions with compact support, equipped with the inductive limit topology. The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem states that every positive linear functional Λ : C_c(X) → ℝ corresponds uniquely to a Radon measure μ such that Λ(f) = ∫_X f dμ for all f ∈ C_c(X). If Λ is a bounded linear functional on C0(X) (continuous functions vanishing at infinity) with the supremum norm, the representing measure is a finite signed Radon measure, and the norm of Λ equals the total variation ‖μ‖ = |μ|(X). The proof constructs an outer measure μ* on all subsets by μ*(E) = inf{Λ(f) : f ∈ C_c(X), f ≥ 1_E}, then restricts to the σ‑algebra of μ*‑measurable sets (Carathéodory’s criterion) and verifies regularity. The theorem extends to complex linear functionals, yielding a complex Radon measure. A frequent examination twist: given a positive linear functional on C_c(ℝ) defined by Λ(f) = Σn=1^∞ 2−n f(n), identify the representing measure (a discrete measure with atoms of mass 2−n at the integers) and compute its total variation. Another common question asks to prove that the dual of C0(X) is isometrically isomorphic to the space of finite signed Radon measures with the total variation norm.

Disintegration of Measures and Regular Conditional Probabilities

Let (X, Σ, μ) be a σ‑finite measure space and π : X → Y a measurable map into a standard Borel space Y. A disintegration of μ with respect to π is a family {μ_y}y∈Y of probability measures on X such that (i) y ↦ μ_y(A) is measurable for each A ∈ Σ, (ii) μ_y(π⁻¹({y})) = 1 for μ∘π⁻¹‑almost every y, and (iii) μ(A) = ∫_Y μ_y(A) d(μ∘π⁻¹)(y) for all A ∈ Σ. The existence theorem (Rokhlin, 1949) guarantees a disintegration when X is a standard Borel space and μ is σ‑finite; the family is unique up to μ∘π⁻¹‑null sets. In probability theory, taking π to be a random variable or a sub‑σ‑algebra yields regular conditional probabilities: for a sub‑σ‑algebra 𝒢 ⊆ Σ, the conditional expectation E[1_A | 𝒢] can be represented as y ↦ μ_y(A) where μ_y is the disintegration of ℙ with respect to the measurable map that generates 𝒢. This provides a rigorous foundation for “conditioning on a continuous random variable”. Applications include the construction of Markov kernels, the proof of the existence of regular conditional distributions for Polish spaces, and the formulation of the martingale problem for stochastic processes. Examiners often test the distinction between a version of conditional expectation (a 𝒢‑measurable function) and a regular conditional probability (a measure‑valued map); a typical trap is to assume that a regular conditional probability exists for every measurable space, whereas counterexamples exist when Y is not a standard Borel space.

  • Confusing the Hahn decomposition (which separates a signed measure into positive and negative sets) with the Jordan decomposition (which produces mutually singular positive measures ν⁺, ν⁻); the former is a partition of the space, the latter a pair of measures.
  • Assuming that every signed measure admits a density with respect to its total variation without verifying that the measure is finite; the Radon–Nikodym derivative dν/d|ν| exists only when ν is finite or σ‑finite.
  • Treating a Radon measure as automatically inner regular on all Borel sets; the definition requires inner regularity only on open sets, and outer regularity on all Borel sets.
  • Misapplying the Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem to functionals on C_b(X) (bounded continuous functions) instead of C0(X) or C_c(X); the dual of C_b(X) is the space of finitely additive measures, not Radon measures.
  • Believing that a disintegration exists for arbitrary measurable maps between arbitrary measurable spaces; the standard Borel hypothesis on the target space is essential.
  • Overlooking that the total variation of a complex measure is defined via a supremum over partitions with complex coefficients, which is strictly larger than the sum of the total variations of its real and imaginary parts.
  • When computing conditional expectations via disintegration, forgetting to check that the conditional measure μ_y is a probability measure for almost every y; this is part of the definition and must be verified in proofs.

Bochner Integral and Vector‑Valued Lᵖ Spaces

The Bochner integral extends the Lebesgue integral to functions taking values in a Banach space B. A measurable function f : X → B is Bochner integrable iff it is strongly measurable (the pointwise limit of simple functions) and ∫‖f‖B dμ < ∞. The integral is defined as the limit in B of integrals of approximating simple functions, and it satisfies linearity, dominated convergence, and the triangle inequality ‖∫f dμ‖ ≤ ∫‖f‖ dμ. When B = ℝ the construction collapses to the ordinary Lebesgue integral.

Vector‑valued Lᵖ spaces Lᵖ(μ; B) consist of equivalence classes of strongly measurable functions with finite norm (∫‖f‖Bᵖ dμ)1/p. For 1 ≤ p < ∞ these spaces are Banach; they are reflexive exactly when B is reflexive and p ∈ (1, ∞). The dual of Lᵖ(μ; B) can be identified with Lq(μ; B*) (1/p + 1/q = 1) provided B* has the Radon–Nikodým property — a subtle condition that fails for many classical spaces such as L¹[0,1].

Key applications appear in stochastic PDEs, where solutions live in Lᵖ(Ω; C([0,T]; H)) and the Itô integral is a Bochner integral against a cylindrical Wiener process. Examiners often test the distinction between strong measurability and weak measurability (Pettis measurability theorem): a function is strongly measurable iff it is weakly measurable and essentially separably valued. A typical trap is to assume that every weakly measurable function is Bochner integrable; the separability requirement is essential.

Choquet Capacities and Analytic Sets

A Choquet capacity on a measurable space (X, Σ) is a set function c : Σ → [0,∞] that is monotone, continuous from below (for increasing sequences) and continuous from above on compact sets (when X is a compact metric space). Capacities arise naturally in potential theory and in the study of analytic (Suslin) sets. The Choquet capacitability theorem states that every analytic set A ⊂ X is capacitable: c(A) = sup{c(K) : K ⊂ A, K compact}. This result underpins the measurability of projections of Borel sets and the existence of measurable selectors for multifunctions.

Analytic sets are continuous images of Borel subsets of Polish spaces; they form a σ‑algebra containing all Borel sets but are not closed under complement. The Lusin separation theorem asserts that two disjoint analytic sets can be separated by a Borel set. In probability, capacities model outer probabilities of non‑measurable events; the Choquet integral ∫f dc = ∫₀^∞ c({f > t}) dt provides a nonlinear expectation used in robust finance and imprecise probability.

Examination questions frequently ask to prove that the projection of a Borel set in a product of Polish spaces is analytic, or to show that a given set function (e.g., outer measure) satisfies the capacity axioms. A common mistake is to treat analytic sets as Borel; the classic counterexample is the set of well‑founded trees in the Baire space, which is analytic but not Borel.

Worked Example: Capacitability of a Projection
Let X = Y = ℝ with the Borel σ‑algebra and let B ⊂ ℝ² be a Borel set. Define the capacity c(A) = λ*(π₁(A)) where λ* is Lebesgue outer measure and π₁ is the projection onto the first coordinate. Show that c is a Choquet capacity and that the projection π₁(B) is capacitable.
Monotonicity of c follows from monotonicity of λ* and π₁. For an increasing sequence Aₙ ↑ A, π₁(Aₙ) ↑ π₁(A); outer measure is continuous from below, so c(Aₙ) → c(A). For a decreasing sequence of compact sets Kₙ ↓ K, π₁(Kₙ) are compact (continuous image of compact) and decrease to π₁(K); outer measure is continuous from above on compact sets, giving c(Kₙ) → c(K). Hence c is a Choquet capacity. By the Choquet capacitability theorem, every analytic set is capacitable. Since π₁(B) is the projection of a Borel set, it is analytic, therefore capacitable: c(π₁(B)) = sup{c(K) : K ⊂ π₁(B), K compact}.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem mentions “outer measure”, “projection”, or “analytic set”, immediately recall the Choquet capacitability theorem. Write down the three capacity axioms and verify them for the given set function; this often earns full credit even if the final capacitability conclusion is only stated.

Optimal Transport: Wasserstein Distance and Kantorovich Duality

Given Polish spaces X, Y and probability measures μ ∈ 𝒫(X), ν ∈ 𝒫(Y), the Wasserstein‑p distance (p ≥ 1) is Wp(μ, ν) = (infπ ∈ Π(μ,ν) ∫ d(x,y)ᵖ dπ(x,y))1/p, where Π(μ,ν) is the set of couplings with marginals μ, ν. The infimum is attained (by Prokhorov’s theorem and lower semicontinuity of the cost) and defines a metric on the subspace of measures with finite p‑th moment.

Kantorovich duality states that Wpᵖ(μ,ν) = sup{∫ φ dμ + ∫ ψ dν : φ(x) + ψ(y) ≤ d(x,y)ᵖ}. The supremum is over bounded continuous functions; when the cost is a metric power, optimal potentials are c‑concave and satisfy the c‑transform relations. The dual formulation is the basis for numerical algorithms (Sinkhorn iterations, entropic regularization) and for proving stability of optimal maps under perturbations of the marginals.

In the quadratic case p = 2 on ℝⁿ, Brenier’s theorem shows that if μ is absolutely continuous, the optimal transport map is the gradient of a convex function, linking optimal transport to Monge–Ampère equations. Examiners often ask to derive the dual problem from the primal linear program, or to prove that W₁ metrises weak convergence plus convergence of first moments. A frequent trap is to forget that the dual supremum may not be attained without additional regularity (e.g., compact support).

Large Deviation Principles and Rate Functions

A family of probability measures {με} on a topological space X satisfies a large deviation principle (LDP) with speed a(ε) → ∞ and good rate function I : X → [0,∞] if for every measurable set A, −infx ∈ A° I(x) ≤ liminfε→0 (1/a(ε)) log με(A) ≤ limsupε→0 (1/a(ε)) log με(A) ≤ −infx ∈ Ā I(x). The rate function is lower semicontinuous and has compact level sets (goodness).

Cramér’s theorem gives the LDP for empirical means of i.i.d. real random variables with speed n and rate function the Legendre–Fenchel transform of the log‑moment generating function. The Gärtner–Ellis theorem extends this to dependent sequences under a differentiability condition on the scaled cumulant generating function. Varadhan’s lemma provides Laplace asymptotics: (1/a(ε)) log ∫ ea(ε)F(x) dμε(x) → supx {F(x) − I(x)} for bounded continuous F.

Applications include Sanov’s theorem for empirical measures (rate function = relative entropy), Freidlin–Wentzell theory for small‑noise diffusions, and the contraction principle which pushes an LDP forward through a continuous map. In exams, a typical question asks to compute the rate function for a given exponential family or to verify the LDP conditions for a sequence of Gaussian measures with shrinking variance. A common error is to confuse the speed a(ε) with the scaling of the random variable; the speed must be explicitly identified.

Entropy, Relative Entropy, and the Data Processing Inequality

For a probability measure μ ≪ ν on a measurable space, the relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence) is D(μ‖ν) = ∫ log(dμ/dν) dμ, with the convention D = ∞ if μ is not absolutely continuous. D is non‑negative, jointly convex, and lower semicontinuous in the weak topology. The chain rule D(μ‖ν) = D(μ₁‖ν₁) + ∫ D(μ₂(·|x)‖ν₂(·|x)) dμ₁(x) holds for product spaces.

The data processing inequality states that for any measurable map T, D(μ∘T⁻¹ ‖ ν∘T⁻¹) ≤ D(μ‖ν). Equality holds iff T is sufficient for the pair (μ,ν). This inequality underpins the monotonicity of mutual information I(X;Y) = D(PXY‖PX⊗PY) under Markov kernels and is central to information‑theoretic proofs of the central limit theorem (via the entropy power inequality) and to concentration of measure (via the log‑Sobolev inequality).

In the context of optimal transport, the relative entropy appears as the rate function in Sanov’s theorem and as the regularisation term in the Schrödinger bridge problem. Examiners may ask to prove the data processing inequality using Jensen’s inequality on the convex function x log x, or to show that the relative entropy is the unique (up to scaling) functional satisfying additivity, chain rule, and monotonicity. A typical trap is to apply the inequality to non‑measurable transformations or to forget the absolute continuity requirement.

  • Assuming that every weakly measurable Banach‑valued function is Bochner integrable without checking essential separability.
  • Treating analytic sets as Borel sets; the projection of a Borel set need not be Borel.
  • Using Kantorovich duality without verifying that the cost function is lower semicontinuous and the marginals have finite p‑th moments.
  • Confusing the speed a(ε) in a large deviation principle with the scaling of the underlying random variables.
  • Applying the data processing inequality to a transformation that is not measurable or to measures that are not absolutely continuous.
  • Neglecting the goodness condition (compact level sets) when stating that a rate function is good.
  • Forgetting that the Radon–Nikodým property of the dual Banach space is required for the duality (Lᵖ(μ;B))* ≅ Lq(μ;B*).
The advanced topics above complete the measure‑theoretic toolkit needed for research‑level problems in analysis, probability, and mathematical finance.

Interpolation Theory: Riesz–Thorin and Marcinkiewicz Theorems

Interpolation theory provides a systematic way to deduce boundedness of linear (or sublinear) operators on intermediate Lp spaces from known estimates at the endpoints. The classical Riesz–Thorin convexity theorem states that if a linear operator T is bounded from Lp₀ to Lq₀ with norm M₀ and from Lp₁ to Lq₁ with norm M₁, then for any θ ∈ (0,1) the operator extends boundedly from Lpθ to Lqθ where 1/pθ = (1−θ)/p₀ + θ/p₁ and 1/qθ = (1−θ)/q₀ + θ/q₁. The interpolated norm satisfies ‖T‖pθ→qθ ≤ M₀1−θ M₁θ. The proof uses the three‑lines lemma applied to an analytic family of operators Tz constructed via complex interpolation of the measure spaces.

The Marcinkiewicz interpolation theorem relaxes linearity to sublinearity and replaces strong endpoint bounds by weak‑type estimates. An operator T is of weak type (p,q) if there exists C such that μ({|Tf| > λ}) ≤ (C‖f‖p/λ)q for all λ > 0. If T is sublinear and of weak types (p₀,q₀) and (p₁,q₁) with p₀ < p₁ and q₀ ≤ q₁, then T is strong type (pθ,qθ) for every θ ∈ (0,1) with the same convex combination formulas. This theorem is the engine behind the boundedness of the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator on Lp for p > 1.

Real interpolation (the K‑method of Peetre and the J‑method) yields a finer scale of spaces, the Lorentz spaces Lp,q, which capture the exact borderline behavior. For instance, the Hilbert transform maps L1 to weak‑L1 and L∞ to BMO; real interpolation gives boundedness on Lp,q for 1 < p < ∞, 1 ≤ q ≤ ∞. Examiners often ask to verify the weak‑type (1,1) estimate for the maximal function and then invoke Marcinkiewicz to obtain strong Lp bounds, or to compute the exact Lorentz norm of a given operator.

Hardy–Littlewood Maximal Function and Differentiation of Integrals

The Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator M is defined for a locally integrable function f on ℝⁿ by Mf(x) = supr>0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) |f(y)| dy, where the supremum runs over all balls centered at x. The fundamental weak‑type (1,1) inequality states that there exists a constant Cn depending only on dimension such that |{x : Mf(x) > λ}| ≤ (Cn/λ) ‖f‖1 for every λ > 0. The proof uses the Vitali covering lemma: from any collection of balls with bounded overlap one can extract a disjoint subcollection covering a fixed fraction of the union. This geometric argument is dimension‑dependent; the best constant Cn grows like n log n.

By Marcinkiewicz interpolation, M is bounded on Lp for every 1 < p ≤ ∞, with operator norm ≤ Cp,n. The endpoint p = ∞ is trivial, while p = 1 fails for strong type (a standard counterexample uses a characteristic function of a ball). The maximal function controls the Lebesgue differentiation theorem: for f ∈ L1loc, the averages (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) f(y) dy converge to f(x) for almost every x as r → 0. The proof writes the difference between the average and f(x) as an integral of the maximal function of f−f(x) and uses the weak‑type estimate together with a density argument (approximate f by continuous functions of compact support).

A refined version, the Lebesgue differentiation theorem for locally integrable functions on metric measure spaces satisfying the doubling condition, replaces Euclidean balls by metric balls. The Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator remains weak‑type (1,1) under the doubling hypothesis, and the differentiation theorem holds. Examiners frequently test the covering lemma step: given a family of balls, construct a disjoint subfamily covering at least a fixed proportion of the measure of the union. Another common question asks to show that the centered maximal function and the uncentered maximal function (supremum over all balls containing x) are pointwise comparable up to a dimensional constant.

Worked Example: Weak‑Type Estimate for the Maximal Function
Let f = χ[0,1] on ℝ. Compute the distribution function of Mf and verify the weak‑type (1,1) inequality with an explicit constant.
For x ∈ [0,1], the ball centered at x with radius r contains [0,1] when r ≥ max(x,1−x). The average is 1/(2r) for such r, so the supremum is attained at the smallest admissible r, giving Mf(x) = 1/(2 max(x,1−x)). For x outside [0,1], the ball must stretch to cover [0,1]; the optimal radius is |x|+1/2 for x>1 and 1/2−x for x<0, yielding Mf(x) = 1/(2|x|+1). The set {Mf > λ} consists of two intervals symmetric about 1/2. Solving 1/(2 max(x,1−x)) > λ on [0,1] gives max(x,1−x) < 1/(2λ), i.e. x ∈ (1/2−1/(2λ), 1/2+1/(2λ)) intersected with [0,1]. Its length is min(1, 1/λ). Outside [0,1], 1/(2|x|+1) > λ gives |x| < (1/λ−1)/2, contributing length (1/λ−1) for λ ≤ 1. Total measure = min(1,1/λ) + max(0,1/λ−1) = 1/λ for λ ≥ 1, and = 1 for λ < 1. Hence |{Mf > λ}| ≤ 1/λ = ‖f‖₁/λ, confirming weak‑type (1,1) with constant 1.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a weak‑type estimate, first identify the level sets of the maximal function. Use the covering lemma to bound the measure of the union of balls by a constant times the sum of measures of a disjoint subfamily. Remember that the constant in the Vitali lemma is 3ⁿ for the centered maximal function and 5ⁿ for the uncentered version; state which version you are using. For interpolation questions, write down the endpoint exponents explicitly and check the convexity condition 1/pθ = (1−θ)/p₀ + θ/p₁. A quick sanity check: the interpolated norm must be ≤ the geometric mean of the endpoint norms.

BMO Space, John–Nirenberg Inequality, and Duality with H¹

The space BMO (bounded mean oscillation) consists of locally integrable functions f on ℝⁿ such that the supremum over all cubes Q of the mean oscillation (1/|Q|) ∫Q |f−fQ| dx is finite, where fQ denotes the average of f over Q. The BMO seminorm ‖f‖BMO = supQ ⨍Q |f−fQ| makes BMO a Banach space modulo constants. A fundamental result is the John–Nirenberg inequality: there exist constants c₁, c₂ > 0 depending only on dimension such that for any f ∈ BMO and any cube Q, |{x ∈ Q : |f(x)−fQ| > λ}| ≤ c₁|Q| exp(−c₂λ/‖f‖BMO). This exponential decay implies that BMO functions belong to Lploc for every finite p, and that the BMO norm is equivalent to the Lp mean oscillation norm (⨍Q |f−fQ|p)1/p for any 1 ≤ p < ∞.

The duality (H¹)* = BMO, proved by Fefferman and Stein, is a cornerstone of real‑variable harmonic analysis. The Hardy space H¹ consists of functions f ∈ L1 whose maximal function (defined via the Poisson or heat semigroup) is in L1. Every g ∈ BMO defines a bounded linear functional on H¹ by ⟨g,f⟩ = ∫ f g (interpreted via a limiting procedure because the product may not be integrable). Conversely, every continuous linear functional on H¹ arises uniquely from a BMO function. This duality fails if one replaces H¹ by L1; indeed (L1)* = L∞, which is strictly smaller than BMO. The atomic decomposition of H¹ (every f ∈ H¹ is a sum of L∞ atoms with ∑ |λk| ≈ ‖f‖H¹) is the standard tool to prove the duality.

Applications include the boundedness of singular integral operators on BMO (Calderón–Zygmund theory) and the characterization of weights for which the Hilbert transform is bounded on weighted L2 (the A₂ condition). Examiners often ask to prove that log|x| ∈ BMO(ℝ) but log|x| ∉ L∞, or to show that the John–Nirenberg inequality implies the equivalence of BMO norms defined with different powers p. A typical trap is to assume that the product of an H¹ function and a BMO function is integrable without invoking the atomic decomposition or a suitable truncation argument.

Sobolev Embedding Theorems and the Role of Capacity

Sobolev spaces Wk,p(Ω) consist of functions whose weak derivatives up to order k belong to Lp(Ω). The classical Sobolev embedding theorem states that if kp < n then Wk,p(ℝⁿ) Lp*(ℝⁿ) with p* = np/(n−kp); if kp = n the embedding holds into BMO (or exponential Orlicz class); if kp > n then functions are Hölder continuous of order k−n/p. The proof uses the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality and the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality for Riesz potentials. For bounded domains with Lipschitz boundary the same embeddings hold by extension operators.

Capacity provides a fine measure of the size of exceptional sets where Sobolev functions may be irregular. The p‑capacity of a compact set K ⊂ ℝⁿ is capp(K) = inf{‖φ‖W1,pp : φ ∈ Cc∞(ℝⁿ), φ ≥ 1 on K}. A property holds quasi‑everywhere (q.e.) if it holds outside a set of zero p‑capacity. Every function in W1,p has a quasi‑continuous representative, and two representatives coincide q.e. The capacity is the correct gauge for removable singularities: a compact set K is removable for W1,p (i.e. every W1,p function on Ω\\K extends to Ω) iff capp(K) = 0. This is the analytic counterpart of the fact that sets of zero Lebesgue measure are removable for Lp.

The Trudinger–Moser inequality sharpens the critical embedding W1,n(ℝⁿ) BMO: for any α ≤ αn = nωn−11/(n−1) the exponential integral ∫ exp(α|u|n/(n−1)) dx is uniformly bounded on the unit ball of W1,n. This borderline case appears in geometric analysis (prescribed curvature equations) and in the study of the Jacobian determinant of W1,n maps. Examiners may ask to prove the embedding W1,p Lp* via the representation u(x) = ∫ ∇u(y)·(x−y)/|x−y|n dy and the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality, or to show that a function in W1,p can be modified on a set of arbitrarily small capacity to become continuous.

Gaussian Measures on Separable Banach Spaces and the Cameron–Martin Theorem

A centered Gaussian measure γ on a separable Banach space B is a Borel probability measure such that every continuous linear functional ℓ ∈ B* induces a centered Gaussian random variable ℓ#γ on ℝ. The covariance operator Q : B* → B** is defined by ⟨Qℓ₁, ℓ₂⟩ = ∫ ℓ₁(x)ℓ₂(x) dγ(x). The Cameron–Martin space H ⊂ B is the completion of Q(B*) under the inner product ⟨Qℓ₁, Qℓ₂⟩H = ⟨ℓ₁, Qℓ₂⟩. It is a separable Hilbert space densely and continuously embedded in B. The Cameron–Martin theorem states that for any h ∈ H, the translated measure γh(A) = γ(A−h) is absolutely continuous with respect to γ, with Radon–Nikodym derivative dγh/dγ(x) = exp(⟨x, h⟩H − ½‖h‖H²), where ⟨x, h⟩H denotes the Paley–Wiener integral. If h ∉ H, then γh and γ are mutually singular.

This result underpins the Malliavin calculus: the derivative operator D acts on smooth cylinder functions F(x) = f(ℓ₁(x),…,ℓm(x)) by DF(x) = ∑ ∂if(ℓ(x)) Qℓi, taking values in H. The integration‑by‑parts formula ∫ ⟨DF, h⟩H dγ = ∫ F ⟨x, h⟩H dγ follows directly from the Cameron–Martin density. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup Pt = e−tL with generator L = −δD (where δ is the divergence) is symmetric in L²(γ) and satisfies the hypercontractivity estimate ‖Pt‖L²→Lq ≤ 1 for q = 1+e2t. This is the infinite‑dimensional analogue of Nelson’s hypercontractivity for the Gaussian measure on ℝⁿ.

On an abstract Wiener space (i.e. a Gaussian measure on a separable Banach space with Cameron–Martin space H), the Gross–Malliavin–Sobolev spaces Dk,p are defined as the closures of smooth cylinder functions under the norm (‖F‖Lᵖᵖ + ∑j=1k ‖DjF‖Lᵖ(H⊗j)ᵖ)1/p. The Meyer inequalities give equivalence of norms defined via the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator. Examiners often test the absolute continuity criterion: given a shift h in a concrete Wiener space (e.g. B = C[0,1] with Wiener measure), decide whether h belongs to the Cameron–Martin space (it does iff h is absolutely continuous with square‑integrable derivative). Another common question asks to derive the integration‑by‑parts formula for the Malliavin derivative from the Cameron–Martin density.

  • Confusing the weak‑type (1,1) constant for the centered maximal function with that for the uncentered version; the constants differ by a factor of 3ⁿ versus 5ⁿ.
  • Applying Marcinkiewicz interpolation without verifying sublinearity of the operator; the theorem fails for merely linear operators that are not sublinear.
  • Assuming that BMO functions are bounded; log|x| is the standard counterexample.
  • Using the duality (H¹)* = BMO without the atomic decomposition or a truncation argument to justify the pairing ∫ f g.
  • Forgetting that the Sobolev embedding W1,n BMO is sharp and does not improve to L∞; the Trudinger–Moser exponential integrability is the correct replacement.
  • Treating capacity zero sets as Lebesgue null sets; there are compact sets of positive Lebesgue measure but zero p‑capacity for p > n.
  • Assuming that every shift of a Gaussian measure on a Banach space is absolutely continuous; the Cameron–Martin theorem restricts absolute continuity to shifts in the Cameron–Martin Hilbert space.

Kolmogorov Extension Theorem and Construction of Stochastic Processes

The Kolmogorov extension theorem provides the measure‑theoretic foundation for building stochastic processes with prescribed finite‑dimensional distributions. Let (Ω, ℱ, ℙ) be a probability space and let {X_t}t∈T be a family of random variables indexed by a set T (often ℝ₊ or ℕ). The finite‑dimensional distributions are the push‑forward measures μt₁,…,t_k = ℙ ∘ (Xt₁,…,Xt_k)⁻¹ on ℝ^k. Kolmogorov’s theorem states that if a consistent family of probability measures {μt₁,…,t_k} on ℝ^k satisfies the compatibility conditions (marginalisation and permutation invariance), then there exists a probability space and a process with exactly those finite‑dimensional distributions. The proof constructs the product space ℝ^T equipped with the cylinder σ‑algebra and defines a pre‑measure on cylinder sets; Carathéodory’s extension theorem then yields a unique probability measure on the product σ‑algebra. This result underpins the existence of Brownian motion, Poisson processes, and Lévy processes. A crucial refinement is the Kolmogorov continuity criterion: if there exist constants α, β, C > 0 such that 𝔼[|X_t − X_s|^α] ≤ C |t − s|1+β for all s, t, then the process admits a modification with Hölder‑continuous sample paths of any order γ < β/α. This criterion is the standard tool for proving that Brownian motion has continuous paths.

Key Steps in the Construction

  1. Specify the index set T and the state space E (usually ℝ^d).
  2. Define a consistent family of finite‑dimensional distributions on E^k.
  3. Verify the Kolmogorov consistency conditions (projective limits).
  4. Apply Carathéodory’s extension to obtain a measure on the cylinder σ‑algebra of E^T.
  5. If path regularity is needed, check the continuity criterion to get a continuous modification.

Examiners often ask to verify consistency for a given covariance function (e.g., the Brownian covariance min(s,t)) or to derive the continuity exponent from a moment bound. The theorem also extends to processes taking values in Polish spaces, where Prokhorov’s theorem replaces the finite‑dimensional argument.

Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities and Hypercontractivity

Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (LSI) quantify the rate at which a probability measure smooths functions under a diffusion semigroup. For the standard Gaussian measure γ on ℝ^n, Gross’s LSI states that for every smooth f with ∫ f² dγ = 1,

∫ f² log f² dγ ≤ 2 ∫ |∇f|² dγ.

The constant 2 is sharp and is attained by linear functions. This inequality is equivalent to the hypercontractivity of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup P_t = e−tL where L = −Δ + x·∇ is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator. Hypercontractivity means that for 1 < p < q < ∞ and t ≥ ½ log((q−1)/(p−1)), the operator norm satisfies ‖P_t‖L^p(γ)→L^q(γ) ≤ 1. The equivalence is proved via the entropy method: differentiate the map t ↦ ‖P_t f‖Lp(t) with a suitably chosen p(t) and use the LSI to show the derivative is non‑positive. LSI also implies a Poincaré inequality (spectral gap) with constant 1 for the Gaussian measure, and it tensorises: if μ_i satisfy LSI with constants C_i, then the product measure satisfies LSI with constant max C_i. This tensorisation is crucial for high‑dimensional concentration phenomena. In the context of Markov chains, a modified LSI (with Dirichlet form ℰ(f,f) = ½ ∑x,y (f(x)−f(y))² π(x)P(x,y)) yields exponential convergence in relative entropy: Ent_π(P_t f) ≤ e−2ρ t Ent_π(f) where ρ is the LSI constant. Examiners may ask to derive the Gaussian LSI from the heat kernel representation, to prove hypercontractivity for the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup, or to show that the LSI constant for the uniform measure on the discrete cube {−1,1}^n is 1/2 (Bobkov–Götze).

Worked Example: Hypercontractivity Exponent
Let P_t be the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup on ℝ with invariant Gaussian measure γ. For p=2 and q=4, find the minimal t such that ‖P_t f‖L4(γ) ≤ ‖f‖L2(γ) for all f ∈ L2(γ).
The hypercontractivity condition requires t ≥ ½ log((q−1)/(p−1)). Here p=2, q=4, so (q−1)/(p−1) = 3/1 = 3. Hence t ≥ ½ log 3. The minimal time is t = ½ log 3. At this time the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup maps L2(γ) contractively into L4(γ).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the hypercontractivity time, always write the formula t = ½ log((q−1)/(p−1)) and substitute the given p,q. Do not confuse the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup with the heat semigroup; the latter satisfies ‖etΔ‖L^p→L^q ≤ 1 for t ≥ (1/4) log((q−1)/(p−1)) on ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure. The constants differ because the invariant measure is Gaussian versus Lebesgue.

Fractional Sobolev Spaces and the Gagliardo Seminorm

For s ∈ (0,1) and p ∈ [1,∞), the fractional Sobolev space Ws,p(ℝ^n) consists of functions f ∈ L^p(ℝ^n) for which the Gagliardo seminorm

[f]Ws,p = (∫ℝ^n∫ℝ^n |f(x)−f(y)|^p / |x−y|n+sp dx dy)1/p

is finite. The full norm is ‖f‖Ws,p = (‖f‖L^p^p + [f]Ws,p^p)1/p. These spaces interpolate between L^p (s=0) and W1,p (s=1) and are the natural domain of the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s/2. The embedding theorems mirror the integer‑order case: if sp < n, then Ws,p(ℝ^n) Lp* with p* = np/(n−sp) (Sobolev exponent); if sp = n, the critical embedding is into BMO or exponential Orlicz spaces (Trudinger–Moser type); if sp > n, functions are Hölder continuous of order s−n/p. The Gagliardo seminorm is also the quadratic form of the fractional Laplacian: for p=2, [f]Ws,22 = Cn,s ∫ |ξ|2s |ℱf(ξ)|2 dξ. This Fourier representation shows that Ws,2 = H^s (Bessel potential spaces) with equivalent norms. On bounded domains, extension operators exist for Lipschitz boundaries, allowing the same seminorm definition via restriction. Examiners frequently test the scaling argument: under f_λ(x) = f(λx), the seminorm scales as [f_λ]Ws,p = λs−n/p [f]Ws,p, which immediately yields the critical exponent p* = np/(n−sp). Another common question asks to prove the compact embedding Ws,p(Ω) L^p(Ω) for bounded Ω using the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem and the fact that the seminorm controls translations.

Besov and Triebel–Lizorkin Spaces via Real Interpolation

Besov spaces B^sp,q and Triebel–Lizorkin spaces F^sp,q refine the Sobolev scale by measuring smoothness with two indices p (integrability) and q (fine‑tuning of the dyadic decomposition). Let φ be a smooth radial function supported in an annulus such that ∑j∈ℤ φ(2−jξ) = 1 for ξ ≠ 0. The Littlewood–Paley blocks are Δ_j f = ℱ⁻¹[φ(2−j·) ℱf]. Then

‖f‖B^sp,q = (‖Δ−1f‖L^p^q + ∑j≥0 2jsq ‖Δ_j f‖L^p^q)1/q (with the usual modification for q=∞),

‖f‖F^sp,q = ‖(∑j≥−1 2jsq |Δ_j f|^q)1/q‖L^p.

These spaces coincide with classical ones for special parameters: B^s2,2 = F^s2,2 = H^s, B^sp,2 = F^sp,2 for 1

, and B^sp,∞ captures borderline regularity (e.g., B0∞,∞ = BMO). Real interpolation gives (L^p, W1,p)θ,q = B^θp,q for 0<θ<1, while complex interpolation yields [L^p, W1,p]_θ = F^θp,2. The embedding B^sp,q₁ B^sp,q₂ holds for q₁ ≤ q₂, and F^sp,q₁ F^sp,q₂ for q₁ ≥ q₂. The duality (B^sp,q)' = B−sp',q' (with 1/p+1/p'=1, 1/q+1/q'=1) is valid for 1

. Examiners may ask to identify the Besov space corresponding to the trace of a Sobolev function on a hyperplane (answer: Bs−1/pp,p) or to prove that the solution of the heat equation with initial data in B^sp,q stays in the same space with norm controlled by the initial norm. The atomic decomposition of Besov spaces (using smooth atoms with moment conditions) is a powerful tool for nonlinear PDEs.

Concentration of Measure on the Sphere and Gaussian Isoperimetry

Concentration of measure describes the phenomenon that Lipschitz functions on high‑dimensional metric probability spaces are sharply concentrated around their median. On the Euclidean sphere Sn−1 with uniform probability measure σ_n, Lévy’s lemma states that for any 1‑Lipschitz function f : Sn−1 → ℝ and any t > 0,

σ_n({|f − M_f| ≥ t}) ≤ 2 exp(−(n−1)t²/2),

where M_f is a median of f. The Gaussian analogue (Tsirelson–Ibragimov–Sudakov) says that for the standard Gaussian measure γ_n on ℝ^n and any 1‑Lipschitz f,

γ_n({|f − M_f| ≥ t}) ≤ 2 exp(−t²/2).

Both inequalities are consequences of the isoperimetric profile: among sets of given measure, half‑spaces (for Gaussian) or spherical caps (for the sphere) minimise the boundary measure. The Gaussian isoperimetric inequality states that for any Borel set A ⊂ ℝ^n with γ_n(A) = Φ(a) (where Φ is the standard normal CDF), the Minkowski content satisfies γ_n+(A) ≥ φ(a) where φ is the Gaussian density. This yields the concentration bound via the Herbst argument: the log‑Sobolev inequality for γ_n implies Entγ_n(eλf) ≤ λ²/2 ∫ eλf dγ_n for 1‑Lipschitz f, which after optimisation gives the sub‑Gaussian tail. On the sphere, the same argument uses the Bakry–Émery curvature‑dimension condition CD(n−1, n−1). Concentration of measure underpins many results in high‑dimensional probability: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, Dvoretzky’s theorem, and the existence of almost Euclidean sections of convex bodies. Examiners often ask to derive the Gaussian concentration inequality from the log‑Sobolev inequality, or to compute the median of the norm ‖X‖ for X ∼ γ_n (it is √n + O(1/√n)) and then bound the deviation ℙ(|‖X‖ − √n| ≥ t).

  • Confusing the Gagliardo seminorm scaling exponent; the correct homogeneity is s − n/p, not s − n.
  • Applying the Kolmogorov continuity criterion without checking that the moment bound holds uniformly in the index set; the constants must be independent of s,t.
  • Assuming that hypercontractivity holds for the heat semigroup on ℝ^n with the same time exponent as the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup; the Gaussian invariant measure changes the constant.
  • Using the Besov norm B^sp,q with q=∞ as if it were a Hilbert space; duality fails at the endpoints q=1,∞.
  • Forgetting that the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality gives the optimal constant 1/2 in the exponent of the concentration bound; any larger constant would contradict the half‑space extremals.
  • Treating the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s/2 as a local operator; its non‑local nature is essential for the Gagliardo seminorm representation.
  • Overlooking that the Kolmogorov extension theorem only guarantees existence on the product σ‑algebra; path regularity requires a separate modification argument.
