It also connects to the arbitrarily varying channel (AVC) when the state sequence can change arbitrarily from symbol to symbol; the AVC capacity with deterministic codes is either zero or equals the random‑code capacity, a dichotomy known as the AVC “capacity dichotomy” (Ericson, 1985).

The Arbitrarily Varying Channel: Deterministic and Random Code Capacities

An arbitrarily varying channel (AVC) is a family of channels {Ws : s ∈ 𝒮} where the state s may vary arbitrarily from one channel use to the next, possibly chosen by an adversary who knows the codebook but not the transmitted codeword. Two coding paradigms are studied: deterministic codes (fixed encoder/decoder) and random codes (encoder and decoder share a random key unknown to the adversary). The deterministic‑code capacity Cdet is either zero or equals the random‑code capacity Cran = maxp(x) minq(s) I(X; Y) where the minimisation is over state distributions q(s) on 𝒮. This dichotomy was proved by Ericson (1985) and later refined by Ahlswede (1986) using the “elimination technique”. If the AVC is symmetrizable — i.e., there exists a stochastic matrix q(s|x) such that ∑s Ws(y|x) q(s|x′) = ∑s Ws(y|x′) q(s|x) for all x, x′, y — then the adversary can mimic the channel output distribution of any other input, forcing Cdet = 0. Otherwise, Cdet = Cran. For the binary AVC with state set 𝒮 = {0,1} and transition W0 = BSC(δ), W1 = BSC(1−δ), the channel is symmetrizable for any δ ≠ ½, so deterministic capacity is zero. With a shared random key of rate o(n), the random‑code capacity is 1 − h₂(δ) (the worst‑case BSC). The AVC model captures jamming, adversarial noise, and the limits of deterministic error correction without shared randomness. It also connects to the concept of “list decoding” where the decoder outputs a list of size L; for symmetrizable AVCs, list decoding with L ≥ 2 can achieve positive rates even with deterministic codes. The AVC framework extends to channels with input and state constraints (e.g., power limits on the jammer), leading to the “constrained AVC” capacity formulas of Hughes and Narayan (1987).

Information‑Theoretic Limits of Private Information Retrieval and Secure Multiparty Computation

Private information retrieval (PIR) allows a user to retrieve a record from a replicated database without revealing which record is requested. In the information‑theoretic setting with k non‑colluding servers each holding the full database of n bits, the classic result of Chor, Goldreich, Kushilevitz, and Sudan (1998) shows that the total download cost (communication from servers to user) is at least n + O(log n) bits for perfect privacy, and a scheme achieving n + O(log n) exists using polynomial interpolation over a finite field. When servers may collude up to t < k, the optimal download cost becomes n·k/(k−t) + O(log n) (Sun and Jafar, 2017), establishing the PIR capacity C = 1 − t/k. This capacity formula mirrors the capacity of a k-user multiple‑access channel with t eavesdroppers, highlighting a deep duality between PIR and secure distributed storage. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) generalises PIR: m parties each hold a private input and wish to compute a function f without revealing their inputs beyond what the output reveals. In the information‑theoretic model with honest‑but‑curious parties and a threshold t of colluding parties, the communication complexity of perfectly secure MPC for arbitrary functions is characterised by the “MPC capacity” which equals the reciprocal of the optimal rate of a secret‑sharing scheme with privacy threshold t and reconstruction threshold t+1. For linear functions over a finite field, the optimal communication is O(m·n) field elements, achieved by Shamir secret sharing combined with Beaver’s multiplication triples. The connection to network coding is explicit: the MPC protocol can be viewed as a network coding problem on a complete graph where each edge carries a share, and the cut‑set bound yields the same capacity expression. Recent work on “capacity of private computation” (e.g., Kadhe et al., 2020) shows that for a single server with side information, the optimal download cost equals the conditional entropy of the desired message given the side information, generalising the PIR capacity to the setting where the user already knows a correlated random variable. These results demonstrate that information‑theoretic privacy metrics (mutual information, conditional entropy) directly quantify the fundamental communication overhead of cryptographic tasks, and they provide benchmarks for evaluating the efficiency of practical protocols.

  • Trap 1: Assuming the compound channel capacity is simply the minimum of individual capacities; the minimax theorem requires the input distribution to be chosen before the worst‑case channel is revealed, so the order of inf and sup matters unless a saddle point exists.
  • Trap 2: Confusing symmetrizability of an AVC with the existence of a zero‑capacity deterministic code; symmetrizability is a sufficient condition for zero deterministic capacity, but not necessary for all alphabets — check the exact definition.
  • Trap 3: Using the random‑code capacity formula for an AVC when the problem explicitly asks for deterministic codes; the two capacities coincide only for non‑symmetrizable AVCs.
  • Trap 4: Forgetting that PIR capacity with colluding servers is 1 − t/k, not 1/k; the download cost scales with k/(k−t), which reduces to the classic n + O(log n) only when t = 0.
  • Trap 5: Treating the MPC communication complexity as independent of the function being computed; for arbitrary functions the complexity can be exponential, while for linear functions it is linear in the input size.
  • Trap 6: Applying the Gaussian MAC sum‑capacity formula to a fading MAC without averaging over the fading distribution; ergodic capacity requires expectation of the instantaneous polymatroid, not the polymatroid of the expectations.
  • Trap 7: Assuming Marton’s inner bound is tight for all broadcast channels; it is known to be tight only for degraded, less‑noisy, more‑capable, deterministic, and semi‑deterministic BCs — the general BC capacity remains open.

These advanced topics illustrate how information theory extends beyond point‑to‑point links to multi‑user networks, adversarial models, and cryptographic primitives, providing exact capacity characterisations or tight bounds that guide the design of modern communication and privacy‑preserving systems.

Bayesian Games and Incomplete Information

In many strategic situations players do not know the exact payoff functions of their opponents. A Bayesian game models this by introducing a finite set of types for each player, a common prior probability distribution over type profiles, and payoff functions that depend on both actions and types. Each player observes his own type but not the types of others, and chooses a strategy that maps his type to an action. A Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) is a profile of type‑contingent strategies such that, for every player and every possible type, the prescribed action maximizes expected payoff given the strategies of the other players and the posterior beliefs derived from the prior.

The classic example is a first‑price sealed‑bid auction with private values. Each bidder’s valuation is his type, drawn independently from a known distribution. In a symmetric BNE each bidder shades his bid below his valuation according to a bidding function that solves a differential equation derived from the first‑order condition of expected utility maximization. The equilibrium bidding function is increasing and strictly below the valuation, reflecting the trade‑off between winning probability and payment.

Existence of a BNE in finite Bayesian games follows from the same fixed‑point arguments used for complete‑information games, after expanding the strategy space to include type‑contingent mappings. However, the equilibrium may not be unique, and refinement concepts such as perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) are often employed in dynamic settings where players update beliefs after observing actions.

Applications extend beyond auctions: mechanism design with private information, signaling games in labor markets, and models of regulatory capture all rely on Bayesian analysis. The key computational challenge is that the strategy space grows exponentially with the number of types, motivating approximation algorithms and the use of interim correlated rationalizability as a tractable solution concept.

Correlated Equilibrium and Public Signals

A correlated equilibrium generalizes Nash equilibrium by allowing players to condition their actions on a public random signal drawn from a known distribution. Formally, a probability distribution over action profiles is a correlated equilibrium if, for every player and every action in the support of his marginal distribution, the expected payoff from following the recommendation is at least as high as the expected payoff from any unilateral deviation, given the conditional distribution over opponents’ actions.

The set of correlated equilibria is a convex polytope described by linear inequalities, making it computationally easier to characterize than the set of Nash equilibria, which requires solving a non‑convex problem. In many games — such as the game of Chicken — correlated equilibria achieve higher total welfare than any mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium because the correlation device can recommend “safe” action pairs with positive probability while avoiding the worst outcomes.

Public signals arise naturally in many economic environments: traffic lights, price announcements, or central bank communications. The revelation principle for correlated equilibria states that any outcome implementable by a correlation device can be implemented by a direct mechanism where the mediator simply recommends actions and players have no incentive to misreport their private information (if any). This principle underlies the design of mediated communication protocols in multi‑agent systems.

An important distinction is between coarse correlated equilibrium (where players must commit to following the recommendation before seeing it) and the standard correlated equilibrium (where players may deviate after observing the recommendation). The former corresponds to learning dynamics such as regret‑minimization algorithms, which converge to the set of coarse correlated equilibria in repeated play.

Worked Example: Correlated Equilibrium in Chicken
Consider the Chicken game with payoff matrix (row player first):
    Swerve  Straight
Swerve  (0,0)  (-1,1)
Straight (1,-1) (-5,-5)
Find a correlated equilibrium that yields higher expected sum of payoffs than the mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium.
The mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium has each player playing Straight with probability 2/3, giving expected payoff -1/3 each, total -2/3. Consider a correlation device that recommends (Swerve, Straight) with probability 1/2 and (Straight, Swerve) with probability 1/2. If a player receives “Swerve”, the opponent is playing Straight, so deviating to Straight yields -5 versus 0 from obeying — no incentive to deviate. If a player receives “Straight”, the opponent is playing Swerve, so deviating to Swerve yields 0 versus 1 from obeying — again no incentive. Expected payoffs are (1+(-1))/2 = 0 for each player, total 0, which Pareto‑dominates the Nash outcome.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a correlated equilibrium, first write down the linear incentive constraints for each player and each recommended action. Because the constraints are linear, you can often guess a symmetric distribution over a small support and verify it satisfies all inequalities. This is faster than solving for mixed‑strategy Nash equilibria, which require solving polynomial equations.

Optimal Auction Design and Revenue Maximization

Myerson’s optimal auction theory characterizes the revenue‑maximizing mechanism for selling a single indivisible good to risk‑neutral bidders with independent private values drawn from known distributions. The key insight is the introduction of virtual values: for a bidder with value v drawn from distribution F with density f, the virtual value is φ(v) = v - (1 - F(v))/f(v). The optimal auction allocates the good to the bidder with the highest non‑negative virtual value and charges the critical payment that makes truthful reporting a dominant strategy.

When value distributions are regular (virtual value increasing), the optimal auction reduces to a second‑price auction with a reserve price r* that solves φ(r*) = 0. This reserve price is independent of the number of bidders and exceeds the seller’s own valuation, reflecting the trade‑off between higher revenue from shading bids and the risk of no sale. For irregular distributions, ironing — replacing the virtual value function by its concave envelope — restores monotonicity and yields a deterministic allocation rule.

The revenue equivalence theorem states that any two standard auction formats (first‑price, second‑price, all‑pay, etc.) that allocate the good to the highest bidder and give zero expected payoff to the lowest type generate the same expected revenue. Myerson’s result shows that the optimal mechanism is essentially a second‑price auction with an appropriately chosen reserve price, and no other mechanism can extract more expected revenue under the same information structure.

Extensions to multi‑unit auctions, budget‑constrained bidders, and interdependent values (e.g., the Cremer‑McLean mechanism) demonstrate that full surplus extraction is possible when bidders’ signals are sufficiently correlated. However, the Myerson‑Satterthwaite theorem proves that in bilateral trade with independent private values, no mechanism can be simultaneously efficient, individually rational, and budget‑balanced — a fundamental impossibility result for market design.

Repeated Games with Imperfect Monitoring

In the standard repeated game model, players observe the entire action profile after each period. Imperfect monitoring relaxes this: each player receives a private signal correlated with the action profile, such as a noisy price observation in a collusive oligopoly. The set of equilibrium payoffs is characterized by the folk theorem for imperfect monitoring, which requires that the signal structure be sufficiently informative — formally, that the monitoring structure satisfy individual full rank or pairwise full rank conditions.

When monitoring is imperfect, players cannot condition strategies directly on opponents’ actions; instead they use belief‑based strategies that map histories of private signals to actions. The self‑generating set approach (Abreu, Pearce, Stacchetti) constructs equilibrium payoff sets recursively: a set of payoff vectors is self‑generating if each vector can be decomposed into a current payoff plus a continuation value drawn from the set, with incentive constraints satisfied given the signal distribution.

A central result is that as the discount factor δ approaches 1, any feasible and individually rational payoff vector can be approximated by a sequential equilibrium provided the monitoring structure is almost perfect (signals become arbitrarily informative). However, with fixed noise, the equilibrium payoff set may be strictly smaller than the feasible set, and the value of information can be quantified by the size of the self‑generating set.

Applications include relational contracts in labor markets, where effort is observed only through noisy output, and tacit collusion where firms observe market prices but not individual quantities. The Green‑Porter model shows that price wars can be an equilibrium phenomenon triggered by low price signals, even when all firms are cooperating.

Price of Anarchy in Congestion Games

Congestion games model situations where many agents share resources — roads, communication links, server capacity — and each agent’s cost on a resource increases with the number of users. Rosenthal proved that every finite congestion game possesses a pure‑strategy Nash equilibrium, and the game is a potential game with Rosenthal’s potential function Φ = Σₑ Σk=1xₑ cₑ(k), where cₑ is the cost function of resource e and xₑ the number of users.

The price of anarchy (PoA) measures the inefficiency of selfish routing: PoA = maxequilibrium (total cost at equilibrium) / (minimum possible total cost). For affine cost functions cₑ(x) = aₑ x + bₑ with aₑ, bₑ ≥ 0, the PoA is exactly 4/3, a tight bound proved by Roughgarden and Tardos. This means selfish routing increases total latency by at most 33 % compared to a centrally optimized flow.

For general polynomial cost functions of degree d, the PoA grows as Θ(d / log d). In contrast, the price of stability (best equilibrium / optimum) is 1 for congestion games because the potential minimizer is always a Nash equilibrium. This dichotomy highlights that while the worst equilibrium can be bad, there always exists an equilibrium as good as the optimum.

Algorithmic implications: computing a pure Nash equilibrium in congestion games is PLS‑complete in general, but best‑response dynamics converge quickly in practice. Mechanism design interventions — such as marginal‑cost pricing (Pigouvian tolls) — can internalize externalities and achieve the social optimum, effectively reducing the PoA to 1 at the cost of implementing tolls.

  • Confusing Bayesian Nash equilibrium with perfect Bayesian equilibrium — the latter requires sequential rationality and consistent beliefs after every history, not just at the interim stage.
  • Assuming every correlated equilibrium can be implemented without a mediator — some require a trusted correlation device; the revelation principle only guarantees a direct mechanism if players have no private information beyond the recommendation.
  • Forgetting that Myerson’s optimal auction assumes independent private values and risk neutrality; with interdependent values or risk aversion the virtual‑value formula changes and revenue equivalence may fail.
  • Treating the folk theorem for imperfect monitoring as unconditional — it holds only under specific rank conditions on the signal distribution; without them the equilibrium set can be dramatically smaller.
  • Misapplying the price of anarchy bound of 4/3 to non‑affine cost functions — the bound is tight only for affine latencies; for higher‑degree polynomials the PoA is larger and must be computed case by case.
  • Overlooking that the price of stability equals 1 in congestion games because the potential minimizer is a Nash equilibrium — this does not generalize to all potential games with non‑exact potentials.
  • Confusing coarse correlated equilibrium with correlated equilibrium — the former allows deviation only before seeing the signal, the latter after; learning dynamics converge to the former, not necessarily the latter.

Coalitional Games and the Shapley Value

Coalitional (or cooperative) game theory studies how groups of players can form binding agreements and how the resulting surplus should be divided. A coalitional game is a pair (N, v) where N = {1,…,n} is the set of players and v : 2^N → ℝ is the characteristic function with v(∅)=0. The core is the set of payoff vectors x ∈ ℝ^n such that Σi∈N x_i = v(N) and Σi∈S x_i ≥ v(S) for every coalition S ⊆ N. When the core is non‑empty it contains all stable allocations, but many games have an empty core. The Shapley value φ(v) provides a unique single‑valued solution that satisfies four axioms: efficiency (Σ_i φ_i = v(N)), symmetry (players with identical marginal contributions receive equal payoffs), dummy player (a player who adds nothing to any coalition receives zero), and additivity (the value of the sum of two games equals the sum of their values). The explicit formula is φ_i(v) = Σ_{S⊆N{i}} (|S|! (n−|S|−1)! / n!) [v(S∪{i}) − v(S)]. This weights each marginal contribution by the probability that the players in S appear before i in a random ordering. The Shapley‑Shubik power index applies this to voting games where v(S)=1 if S is a winning coalition and 0 otherwise. In cost‑sharing problems such as airport runway allocation or multicast tree construction, the Shapley value yields a fair division that is also budget‑balanced and strategy‑proof under certain conditions. Computing the Shapley value is #P‑complete in general, but for weighted voting games and network cost games polynomial‑time algorithms exist using generating functions or marginal contribution sampling.

Stochastic Games and Markov Perfect Equilibrium

A stochastic game (Shapley, 1953) extends repeated games by allowing the stage‑game payoff matrix to depend on a state variable that evolves according to a transition probability controlled by the players’ actions. Formally, a stochastic game is a tuple (N, S, {A_i}, u, P, δ) where N is the player set, S a finite state space, A_i the action set of player i, u_i(s, a) the stage payoff, P(s' | s, a) the transition kernel, and δ ∈ (0,1) the discount factor. A Markov strategy for player i maps the current state s to a mixed action σ_i(s) ∈ Δ(A_i), ignoring the full history. A Markov perfect equilibrium (MPE) is a profile of Markov strategies that constitutes a subgame‑perfect equilibrium in every subgame starting from any state. The Bellman optimality condition for player i given opponents’ strategies σ−i is V_i(s) = maxa_i∈A_i [ u_i(s, a_i, σ−i(s)) + δ Σs' P(s' | s, a_i, σ−i(s)) V_i(s') ]. Existence of an MPE in finite stochastic games with discounted payoffs follows from the contraction mapping property of the Bellman operator; however, multiple MPEs are common. In applications such as oligopoly with capacity investment, the state is the vector of installed capacities, and the MPE captures the dynamic strategic effect of today’s investment on future competition. Computation of MPE typically uses value iteration or policy iteration on the joint Bellman system; the problem is PPAD‑hard in general, but for two‑player zero‑sum stochastic games it reduces to a linear program. The concept of “state‑space reduction” via ergodic sets is often used to simplify analysis in macroeconomic models with stochastic games.

Worked Example: Markov Perfect Equilibrium in a Duopoly Investment Game
Two firms choose investment levels a₁, a₂ ∈ {0,1} each period. The state s = (k₁, k₂) records cumulative capacity. Stage profit for firm i is π_i = (10 − k₁ − k₂) k_i − 2 a_i. Capacity evolves as k_i' = k_i + a_i. Discount factor δ = 0.9. Find a symmetric MPE where both firms use a threshold rule: invest if k_i ≤ K* and not otherwise.
Because of symmetry, look for a threshold K* such that the value function V(k) satisfies the Bellman equation for a representative firm when the opponent also uses the threshold. For k ≤ K*, the firm invests (a=1) and receives immediate profit (10 − 2k − 1)k − 2 plus discounted continuation V(k+1). For k > K*, the firm does not invest (a=0) and receives (10 − 2k)k + δ V(k). At the threshold K*, the firm must be indifferent: (10 − 2K* − 1)K* − 2 + δ V(K*+1) = (10 − 2K*)K* + δ V(K*). Using the fact that for k > K* the value function follows V(k) = (10 − 2k)k + δ V(k) ⇒ V(k) = (10 − 2k)k / (1−δ). Substituting and solving numerically yields K* = 2. Thus each firm invests until its capacity reaches 2, then stops. The symmetric MPE is fully characterized by this threshold.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a Markov perfect equilibrium, first identify the state variable and write the Bellman equation for a generic player. Look for structural simplifications such as symmetry, monotonicity, or threshold policies. If the game is zero‑sum, convert to a linear program; otherwise, argue existence via contraction and describe the equilibrium qualitatively (e.g., threshold rule) rather than solving a high‑dimensional system explicitly.

Information Design and Bayesian Persuasion

Information design studies how a sender can influence the actions of receivers by choosing a signal structure (experiment) that maps states of the world to distributions over messages. The canonical model (Kamenica & Gentzkow, 2011) has a sender and a receiver with a common prior μ ∈ Δ(Ω) over a finite state space Ω. The receiver chooses an action a ∈ A after observing a message m ∈ M; the sender’s payoff is v(a, ω) and the receiver’s payoff is u(a, ω). A signaling policy is a mapping π : Ω → Δ(M). The receiver forms a posterior belief β(m) ∈ Δ(Ω) via Bayes’ rule and selects a best‑response action a*(β). The sender’s problem is to choose π to maximize Σ_ω μ(ω) Σ_m π(m|ω) v(a*(β(m)), ω). The concavification method solves this: define the sender’s indirect utility V(β) = max_a Σ_ω β(ω) v(a, ω). The optimal value is the concave envelope of V evaluated at the prior μ, i.e., cav V(μ). An optimal policy corresponds to a decomposition of μ into a distribution over posteriors that are extreme points of the concave envelope. In the binary‑state, binary‑action case, the optimal policy is either full revelation, no revelation, or a “partial pooling” that induces two posteriors, one where the receiver is indifferent and one where the sender’s preferred action is strictly optimal. Applications include stress‑test disclosure by regulators, prosecutor‑judge interactions, and platform design of recommendation algorithms. The framework extends to multiple receivers (public vs. private signals), dynamic persuasion, and settings where the sender also has private information (Bayesian persuasion with informed sender).

Algorithmic Game Theory: Complexity of Equilibrium Computation

Algorithmic game theory analyses the computational difficulty of finding equilibria and the efficiency of decentralized dynamics. The central complexity classes are PPAD (Polynomial Parity Arguments on Directed graphs) for Nash equilibrium in finite games, PLS (Polynomial Local Search) for pure Nash equilibria in potential games, and FIXP for fixed‑point problems with algebraic circuits. Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou (2009) proved that computing a Nash equilibrium in a 3‑player normal‑form game is PPAD‑complete; for 2‑player games the problem is also PPAD‑complete (Chen & Deng, 2006). In contrast, zero‑sum games reduce to linear programming and are solvable in polynomial time. For congestion games, Rosenthal’s potential guarantees existence of pure equilibria, but finding one is PLS‑complete (Fabrikant, Papadimitriou, Talwar, 2004). The price of anarchy bounds the worst‑case inefficiency of equilibria; for affine latency functions the PoA is exactly 4/3, while for degree‑d polynomials it grows as Θ(d / log d). Learning dynamics such as best‑response, fictitious play, and no‑regret algorithms converge to coarse correlated equilibria in polynomial time, but convergence to a Nash equilibrium can require exponential time. The smoothed‑complexity analysis shows that for generic payoffs the Lemke‑Howson algorithm runs in expected polynomial time. Mechanism design algorithms (e.g., VCG, Myerson’s optimal auction) are polynomial for single‑parameter domains but become NP‑hard for multi‑parameter settings such as combinatorial auctions. Approximation algorithms and communication‑complexity lower bounds are active research frontiers.

Matching Markets and the Deferred Acceptance Algorithm

Two‑sided matching markets model assignments where agents on both sides have preferences over each other, such as medical residents to hospitals, students to schools, or kidney donors to patients. A matching μ is a bijection between subsets of the two sides such that each agent is matched to at most one partner. Stability requires that no blocking pair (i, j) exists with i preferring j to μ(i) and j preferring i to μ(j). The Gale‑Shapley deferred acceptance (DA) algorithm produces a stable matching: one side proposes sequentially to their most preferred acceptable partner not yet rejected; the other side holds the best proposal and rejects the rest. The algorithm terminates in at most n² steps and yields the proposer‑optimal stable matching (every proposer gets their best partner among all stable matchings) and the reviewer‑pessimal stable matching. The lattice structure of stable matchings (Knuth, 1976) implies that the set of stable matchings forms a distributive lattice under the partial order “proposer prefers”. In school choice, the student‑proposing DA is strategy‑proof for students (truthful reporting is a dominant strategy) but not for schools. The top‑trading‑cycles (TTC) mechanism achieves Pareto efficiency and strategy‑proofness when priorities are not strict. With couples or complementarities, stable matchings may not exist; the problem becomes NP‑complete. Recent work on matching with contracts (Hatfield & Milgrom, 2005) generalizes DA to settings where terms (wages, schedules) are part of the offer, preserving stability under substitutability and law of aggregate demand. Empirical evaluations of the NRMP (National Resident Matching Program) show that the switch to student‑proposing DA in 1998 increased the proportion of residents matched to their first choice from 50% to over 70%.

  • Confusing the Shapley value with the core — the Shapley value is a single point that may lie outside the core, while the core is a set of all stable allocations.
  • Assuming every stochastic game has a unique Markov perfect equilibrium — multiplicity is generic; selection criteria such as Pareto dominance or risk dominance are needed for predictions.
  • Treating Bayesian persuasion as a standard signaling game — the sender commits to a signal structure ex‑ante, which fundamentally changes the equilibrium concept from perfect Bayesian equilibrium to a constrained optimization.
  • Believing that computing a Nash equilibrium in a two‑player general‑sum game is polynomial — it is PPAD‑complete, and no polynomial‑time algorithm is known unless PPAD = P.
  • Thinking the Gale‑Shapley algorithm is strategy‑proof for both sides — only the proposing side has a dominant‑strategy incentive to report truthfully.
  • Overlooking that the price of anarchy bound of 4/3 applies only to affine latency functions; for higher‑degree polynomials the bound is larger and must be derived case by case.

Dynamic Mechanism Design and Intertemporal Incentives

Dynamic mechanism design extends static mechanism theory to environments where agents’ private information evolves over time and the designer can condition current allocations on past reports. The central object is a direct revelation mechanism that specifies, for each period t, an allocation rule xt(θt) and a payment rule pt(θt) as functions of the history of reported types θt = (θ1,…,θt). Incentive compatibility now requires that truthful reporting in every period forms a perfect Bayesian equilibrium of the induced dynamic game. The envelope theorem generalises to a dynamic envelope condition: the derivative of the agent’s continuation value with respect to the current type equals the expected marginal allocation, integrated over future type distributions. This yields a necessary and sufficient condition for implementability known as the dynamic incentive compatibility (DIC) constraint.

A key result by Pavan, Segal, and Toikka (2014) shows that under a Markovian type process and quasilinear utilities, the optimal dynamic mechanism can be characterised by a sequence of static “virtual value” functions that incorporate the information rent from future periods. The virtual value at time t is φt(θt) = θt − (1−Ft(θt))/ft(θt) − ∂/∂θt E[ future rent | θt ]. The extra term captures how today’s report influences the distribution of future types and thus future rents. When types are independent across periods, the future‑rent term vanishes and the problem decomposes into a series of independent Myerson auctions. With persistence (e.g., AR(1) processes), the optimal mechanism typically distorts current allocations downward to reduce the agent’s incentive to misreport today in order to manipulate tomorrow’s information rent.

Implementation often uses a bank account or score that tracks the agent’s cumulative transfers, allowing the designer to smooth payments over time while preserving incentive compatibility. The bank account evolves as Bt+1 = Bt + pt − c(xt), where c is the cost of allocation. The designer can then offer a menu of contracts indexed by the current bank balance, achieving the same allocation as the direct mechanism but with simpler messaging. Applications include optimal procurement with learning‑by‑doing, dynamic spectrum auctions, and long‑term insurance contracts where risk types evolve.

Learning in Games: Fictitious Play, Regret Minimization, and Convergence

Learning dynamics model how boundedly rational players might reach equilibrium through repeated interaction. Fictitious play assumes each player best‑responds to the empirical frequency of opponents’ past actions. In two‑player zero‑sum games, Brown (1951) proved that the empirical frequencies converge to the set of Nash equilibria. For general‑sum games, convergence is not guaranteed; Shapley (1964) constructed a 3×3 game where fictitious play cycles indefinitely. However, in potential games and supermodular games, fictitious play converges to a pure Nash equilibrium.

No‑regret learning provides a stronger guarantee: if every player uses an algorithm whose average regret grows sublinearly (e.g., multiplicative weights, hedge, or follow‑the‑perturbed‑leader), the empirical joint distribution of play converges to the set of coarse correlated equilibria (CCE). The regret bound for multiplicative weights after T rounds is O(√(log N / T)) for N actions, yielding an ε-CCE in O(log N / ε²) rounds. This polynomial‑time convergence contrasts with the PPAD‑hardness of computing a Nash equilibrium, explaining why learning dynamics are computationally attractive.

Convergence to a Nash equilibrium rather than a CCE requires additional structure. In zero‑sum games, the time‑average of no‑regret dynamics converges to the minimax value. In games with a variational stability property (e.g., congestion games with convex costs), the empirical distribution converges to a Nash equilibrium. Recent work on optimistic mirror descent and extra‑gradient methods achieves last‑iterate convergence to Nash equilibrium in monotone games (including bilinear zero‑sum games) at a rate O(1/T). These results bridge the gap between learning theory and equilibrium computation, showing that simple adaptive rules can efficiently find equilibria in large classes of economically relevant games.

Worked Example: Regret Bound for Multiplicative Weights
Consider a player with three actions facing an adversarial loss sequence ℓt ∈ [0,1]³. The player runs the multiplicative weights algorithm with learning rate η = √(2 log 3 / T). Derive the upper bound on the player’s average regret after T rounds.
The standard regret bound for multiplicative weights with learning rate η is RegretT ≤ (log N)/η + η T/8, where N = 3. Substituting η = √(2 log 3 / T) gives RegretT ≤ (log 3) / √(2 log 3 / T) + √(2 log 3 / T) · T/8 = √(T log 3 / 2) + √(T log 3 / 2) / 4 = (5/4) √(T log 3 / 2). Dividing by T yields average regret ≤ (5/4) √(log 3 / (2T)) = O(√(log N / T)). For T = 10⁴, average regret ≤ 0.012, confirming an ε‑CCE with ε ≈ 0.012.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the convergence class of a learning dynamic, first identify the game class (zero‑sum, potential, monotone, general‑sum). Then match the dynamic: fictitious play → Nash in zero‑sum/potential; no‑regret → CCE in all games, Nash in monotone/variationally stable games; optimistic gradient → last‑iterate Nash in monotone games. Memorise the regret bound O(√(log N / T)) for multiplicative weights; it appears in quantitative comparison questions.

Mean Field Games and Large Population Limits

Mean field game (MFG) theory, developed independently by Lasry & Lions (2007) and Huang, Caines & Malhamé (2006), analyses strategic interaction among a continuum of infinitesimal agents. Each agent solves a stochastic control problem where the state dynamics depend on the aggregate distribution of all agents’ states, denoted mt. In the limit N → ∞, the interaction term becomes deterministic, yielding a coupled system: a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation for the value function v(t,x) backward in time, and a Fokker–Planck (FP) equation for the density m(t,x) forward in time. The pair (v,m) satisfying the HJB–FP system constitutes a mean field equilibrium.

Existence of a classical solution requires regularity conditions on the Hamiltonian H(x,α,m) and the coupling cost F(x,m). Lasry & Lions proved existence under monotonicity of F (i.e., ∫ (F(x,m₁)−F(x,m₂))(m₁−m₂) dx ≥ 0) and convexity of H in the control. Uniqueness follows from the same monotonicity condition. When monotonicity fails, multiple equilibria can arise, leading to coordination problems reminiscent of multiple Nash equilibria in finite games.

MFG has been applied to crowd motion, optimal execution in financial markets, and demand‑side management in power grids. In the linear‑quadratic setting, the HJB–FP system reduces to a Riccati ODE for the value function and a linear FP equation, admitting closed‑form solutions. The master equation, a PDE on the space of probability measures, characterises the value function for any initial distribution and provides a propagation‑of‑chaos justification: the empirical distribution of N agents converges to the mean field limit at rate O(1/√N) in Wasserstein distance. Numerical methods include finite‑difference schemes for the HJB–FP system and deep‑learning‑based solvers for high‑dimensional master equations.

Robust Mechanism Design under Ambiguity

Classical mechanism design assumes the designer knows the exact prior distribution of agents’ types. Robust mechanism design relaxes this by modelling the designer’s uncertainty as a set of possible priors 𝒫 (an ambiguity set). The designer seeks a mechanism that maximises the worst‑case expected objective over 𝒫, while agents best‑respond to their true type and the mechanism. This leads to a max‑min problem: maxmechanism minP∈𝒫 EP[objective].

Bergemann and Morris (2005) introduced the robust implementation concept: a social choice function is robustly implementable if it can be implemented for every prior in 𝒫. For single‑parameter environments, the optimal robust auction is a prior‑independent mechanism that achieves a constant‑factor approximation to the optimal revenue for any prior in a broad class (e.g., regular distributions). Dhangwatnotai, Roughgarden, and Yan (2010) showed that the Vickrey auction with a random reserve drawn from the prior‑free distribution yields a 2‑approximation to the optimal Myerson revenue for any regular prior.

When agents are ambiguity‑averse (max‑min expected utility à la Gilboa–Schmeidler), the equilibrium concept becomes robust Bayesian Nash equilibrium. The designer’s problem can be reformulated as a zero‑sum game between the designer and nature, where nature chooses a prior from 𝒫 after seeing the mechanism. Under convexity of 𝒫 and compactness, a saddle‑point exists by Sion’s minimax theorem. Computationally, robust mechanism design often reduces to a convex optimisation over the mechanism’s allocation and payment rules, with constraints that are linear in the worst‑case prior. Recent work on distributionally robust mechanism design uses Wasserstein balls around an empirical distribution to construct data‑driven mechanisms with finite‑sample guarantees.

  • Confusing dynamic incentive compatibility with static IC — the dynamic envelope condition includes a future‑rent term that vanishes only under independent types.
  • Assuming fictitious play converges in all games — Shapley’s 3×3 counterexample shows cycling; convergence holds only in zero‑sum, potential, or supermodular games.
  • Treating coarse correlated equilibrium as equivalent to Nash equilibrium — CCE allows correlation through the empirical distribution, while Nash requires independent mixed strategies.
  • Believing mean field games always have a unique equilibrium — monotonicity of the coupling cost is essential; without it multiple equilibria are generic.
  • Thinking robust mechanism design simply replaces the prior with a worst‑case point — the designer must optimise over a set of priors, leading to a max‑min problem that may require saddle‑point computation.
  • Overlooking that the price of anarchy bound of 4/3 applies only to affine latency functions; for higher‑degree polynomials the bound is larger and must be derived case by case.

Quantal Response Equilibrium and Bounded Rationality

Nash equilibrium assumes players best‑respond with perfect rationality and common knowledge of rationality. Quantal Response Equilibrium (QRE), introduced by McKelvey and Palfrey (1995), relaxes this by modelling choice probabilities as a smooth function of expected payoffs. In a normal‑form game with payoff matrix ui(si, s−i), the logit QRE specifies that player i chooses pure strategy si with probability proportional to exp(λ ui(si, σ−i)), where λ ≥ 0 is a precision parameter. As λ → ∞, QRE converges to Nash equilibrium; as λ → 0, play approaches uniform randomisation. The parameter λ captures the degree of rationality: higher λ means players are more sensitive to payoff differences. QRE is a fixed point of the quantal response mapping Qi(σ−i) = (exp(λ ui(si, σ−i)) / ∑s'i exp(λ ui(s'i, σ−i))). Existence follows from Brouwer's fixed‑point theorem since Q is continuous and maps the simplex to itself. Uniqueness is not guaranteed; multiple QRE can exist for a given λ, and the equilibrium correspondence can exhibit bifurcations as λ varies. The logit QRE is the most common specification, but other choice rules (probit, power) yield different equilibrium concepts. Empirically, QRE explains systematic deviations from Nash in experiments: over‑play of dominated strategies, own‑payoff effects, and the "centipede game" pattern where players exit earlier than backward induction predicts. Goeree, Holt, and Palfrey (2000) showed that QRE fits data from constant‑sum games, ultimatum games, and auction experiments better than Nash. In estimation, λ is treated as a structural parameter; maximum likelihood estimation of λ from choice data requires solving the QRE fixed point for each candidate λ. Computationally, homotopy methods trace the equilibrium correspondence from λ = 0 (unique uniform equilibrium) to the target λ, avoiding local convergence issues. QRE also provides a foundation for level‑k thinking and cognitive hierarchy models: a level‑0 player randomises uniformly, level‑1 best‑responds to level‑0, etc., and the Poisson‑weighted mixture approximates QRE for appropriate λ. For examiners, the key distinction is that QRE is a statistical equilibrium concept — it predicts choice distributions, not deterministic outcomes — and it nests Nash as a limiting case rather than replacing it.

Global Games and Equilibrium Selection in Coordination Games

Coordination games with multiple Nash equilibria — such as the Stag Hunt or Bank Run game — pose an equilibrium selection problem. Global games, introduced by Carlsson and van Damme (1993) and popularised by Morris and Shin (1998, 2003), resolve this by embedding the game in a setting of incomplete information about a payoff‑relevant state θ. In the canonical binary‑action global game, two players choose between Invest (I) and Not Invest (N). Payoffs are: u(I, I; θ) = θ, u(I, N; θ) = −1, u(N, I; θ) = 0, u(N, N; θ) = 0. The state θ is drawn from a diffuse prior on ℝ. Each player observes a private signal xi = θ + εi, where εi ~ Uniform[−ε, ε] (or Normal) independently. A strategy is a threshold rule: invest iff xi ≥ x*. The unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium in monotone strategies is characterised by a critical signal x* and a critical state θ* such that: (i) a player with signal x* is indifferent between I and N given the opponent uses threshold x*, and (ii) the state θ* is the unique state where the mass of players investing equals the threshold for investment to be profitable. The indifference condition yields ∫θ*−εθ*+ε (θ − 1) dθ = 0, giving θ* = 1. The critical signal satisfies x* = θ* + ε = 1 + ε. As ε → 0 (vanishing noise), the equilibrium converges to a unique limit: invest iff θ > 1. This selects the risk‑dominant equilibrium (Harsanyi and Selten, 1988) — the equilibrium with the larger basin of attraction under uniform trembles. The global‑games selection is robust: it survives iterated deletion of dominated strategies and coincides with the unique rationalisable strategy profile. The key insight is that even arbitrarily small incomplete information destroys common knowledge of the payoff structure, unravelling the multiplicity. The technique extends to n‑player games with strategic complementarities (supermodular games). Frankel, Morris, and Pauzner (2003) showed that for a broad class of games with strategic complementarities and a "limit dominance" condition (each action is dominant for sufficiently extreme θ), the set of rationalisable strategies shrinks to a unique equilibrium as noise vanishes. Applications include currency crises (Morris and Shin, 1998), debt pricing (Rochet and Vives, 2004), and technology adoption. For examiners, the critical steps are: (a) specify the state‑dependent payoff game, (b) define the signal structure, (c) conjecture monotone threshold strategies, (d) derive the indifference condition at the margin, (e) take the limit as noise vanishes, and (f) verify limit dominance. A common trap is assuming global games always select the risk‑dominant equilibrium; this holds only for symmetric binary‑action games with uniform limit dominance. In asymmetric games or with non‑uniform priors, the selected equilibrium depends on the relative precision of signals and the shape of the prior.

Worked Example: Global Game Threshold Calculation
Consider a 2‑player investment game with payoffs: u(I,I;θ) = θ, u(I,N;θ) = −c, u(N,I;θ) = 0, u(N,N;θ) = 0, where c > 0 is the cost of failed investment. The state θ ~ Uniform[0, 10]. Each player observes xi = θ + εi, εi ~ Uniform[−ε, ε] independent. Find the limiting equilibrium threshold as ε → 0.
Step 1: Conjecture symmetric threshold strategy: invest iff xi ≥ x*. Step 2: Given opponent uses x*, a player with signal x invests iff E[θ | x, opponent invests] > c. Opponent invests iff xj ≥ x* ⇔ θ + εj ≥ x* ⇔ εj ≥ x* − θ. Since εj ~ Uniform[−ε, ε], Pr(opponent invests | θ) = 1 if θ ≥ x* + ε, 0 if θ ≤ x* − ε, and (θ − (x* − ε)) / (2ε) if θ ∈ (x* − ε, x* + ε). Step 3: Indifference at x = x*: E[θ | x*, opponent invests] = c. By symmetry, the posterior of θ given x* is Uniform[x* − ε, x* + ε]. The event "opponent invests" further restricts θ. In the limit ε → 0, the conditioning event becomes θ = x*. Thus the limiting indifference condition is x* = c. Step 4: Limit dominance: for θ > c, I is dominant; for θ < 0, N is dominant (since θ < 0 < c). The unique limit equilibrium is: invest iff θ > c. The critical state is θ* = c, critical signal x* = c.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for equilibrium selection in a coordination game with incomplete information, first check whether the game has strategic complementarities (supermodular payoffs). If yes, the global‑games method applies: write the indifference condition at the marginal signal, take the vanishing‑noise limit, and verify limit dominance. The selected equilibrium is almost always the risk‑dominant one in symmetric binary‑action games. Memorise the formula θ* = c for the canonical investment game with cost c — it appears frequently in currency‑crisis and bank‑run applications.

Network Games: Strategic Complements and Substitutes

Network games model situations where a player's payoff depends on the actions of their neighbours in a graph G = (N, E). The canonical linear‑quadratic specification (Ballester, Calvó‑Armengol, and Zenou, 2006) has payoff ui(xi, x−i) = ai xi − ½ xi2 + φ xi ∑j∈Ni gij xj, where xi ∈ ℝ+ is effort, ai > 0 is marginal return, φ captures strategic interaction, and gij = 1 if (i, j) ∈ E. If φ > 0, actions are strategic complements (higher neighbour effort raises marginal return); if φ < 0, strategic substitutes. The best‑response is xi = max{0, ai + φ ∑j gij xj}. In vector form, x = max{0, a + φ Gx}, where G is the adjacency matrix. For φ > 0 (complements), a unique interior Nash equilibrium exists iff φ λmax(G) < 1, where λmax is the largest eigenvalue of G. The equilibrium is x* = (I − φ G)−1 a = ∑k=0∞ φk Gk a. The term (Gk a)i sums aj over all walks of length k from i to j; thus equilibrium effort is proportional to Bonacich centrality with decay factor φ. This is the key result: in games of strategic complements, equilibrium effort is proportional to Bonacich centrality. For φ < 0 (substitutes), the best‑response mapping is a contraction if |φ| λmax(G) < 1, guaranteeing a unique equilibrium. However, with substitutes, effort is lower for more central players — they free‑ride on neighbours' efforts. The condition φ λmax(G) < 1 is also necessary and sufficient for the equilibrium to be stable under best‑response dynamics. Extensions include: (i) heterogeneous φij (weighted networks), (ii) incomplete information about G (Bayesian network games), (iii) endogenous network formation (players choose links at cost), and (iv) games on directed graphs (asymmetric influence). Galeotti et al. (2010) studied Bayesian network games where players know only their degree distribution; they showed that equilibrium is monotone in degree for complements but not necessarily for substitutes. Bramoullé, Kranton, and D'Amours (2014) characterised equilibria in games with strategic substitutes on arbitrary networks, showing that specialised equilibria (where some players exert zero effort) are generic. For examiners, the central results are: (a) the spectral radius condition for existence/uniqueness, (b) the Bonacich centrality formula for complements, (c) the free‑riding effect for substitutes, and (d) the distinction between degree centrality (local) and Bonacich centrality (global, incorporating neighbours' neighbours). A frequent exam question asks to compute the equilibrium effort vector for a given small network (e.g., a star or line) and interpret the centrality ranking.

Bargaining Theory: Rubinstein Alternating Offers and Nash Bargaining Solution

Bargaining theory analyses how two or more players divide a surplus. The two foundational models are the axiomatic Nash Bargaining Solution (NBS) and the strategic Rubinstein Alternating‑Offers game. The NBS (Nash, 1950) assumes a feasible set S ⊂ ℝ2 of utility pairs (closed, convex, bounded) and a disagreement point d ∈ S. The solution is the unique pair (u1*, u2*) ∈ S maximising the Nash product (u1 − d1)(u2 − d2) subject to u ≥ d. The axioms are: Pareto efficiency, symmetry, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and invariance to affine transformations of utility. For a pie of size 1 with linear utilities and d = (0,0), NBS gives (½, ½). With asymmetric bargaining power (weights α, 1−α), the generalised NBS maximises (u1 − d1)α(u2 − d2)1−α. The Rubinstein (1982) game provides a non‑cooperative foundation. Two players bargain over a pie of size 1. Player 1 offers x ∈ [0,1] in period 1; player 2 accepts or rejects. If rejected, player 2 offers y in period 2, etc. Players discount future payoffs by δ1, δ2 ∈ (0,1). The unique subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE) has player 1 offering x* = (1 − δ2) / (1 − δ1δ2) in period 1, which player 2 accepts immediately. Player 1's share is x*, player 2's is 1 − x*. As δ1, δ2 → 1 (patient players), x* → ½ if δ1 = δ2; if δ1 ≠ δ2, the limit depends on the relative discount factors. Binmore, Rubinstein, and Wolinsky (1986) showed that if the time between offers Δ → 0 and discount factors are δi = e−riΔ, the SPE converges to the NBS with bargaining powers proportional to 1/ri. This is the "Nash program" — the strategic model implements the axiomatic solution. Extensions include: (i) outside options (Shaked and Sutton, 1984): if a player can exit and receive a payoff wi, the equilibrium share is max{NBS share, wi}; (ii) incomplete information (Abreu and Gul, 2000; Ausubel and Deneckere, 1989): types with different discount factors or outside options lead to screening and delay; (iii) multi‑party bargaining (Okada, 1996): the core of the cooperative game coincides with the set of SPE payoffs under certain protocols. For examiners, the key computations are: (a) derive the SPE offer in the two‑period Rubinstein game by backward induction, (b) solve the infinite‑horizon fixed point x = 1 − δ2(1 − δ1x), (c) compute the NBS for a given feasible set (e.g., S = {(u1, u2) : u1 + u2 ≤ 1, ui ≥ 0}), (d) explain the relationship between δi and bargaining power. A common trap is confusing the NBS (which depends on the disagreement point and feasible set) with the Rubinstein SPE (which depends on discount factors and the order of offers). They coincide only in the limit of vanishing friction and equal discount factors.

Security Games and Stackelberg Leadership in Defense Applications

Security games model a defender (leader) allocating limited resources to protect targets against an attacker (follower) who observes the defender's mixed strategy and best‑responds. This is a Stackelberg game with commitment: the defender commits to a mixed strategy σ ∈ Δ(X), where X is the set of pure allocations (e.g., which targets to patrol). The attacker observes σ and chooses a target t to attack. Payoffs: defender gets Ud(c, t) if target t is covered (c = 1) and Ud(u, t) if uncovered (c = 0); attacker gets Ua(c, t). Typically Ud(c, t) > Ud(u, t) and Ua(u, t) > Ua(c, t). The defender's problem is maxσ ∑t [σt Ud(c, t) + (1 − σt) Ud(u, t)] subject to the attacker best‑responding: t ∈ argmaxt' [σt' Ua(c, t') + (1 − σt') Ua(u, t')]. This is a bilevel optimisation. For a single attacker and multiple targets, the problem can be formulated as a mixed‑integer linear program (MILP) or solved via the DOBSS (Decomposed Optimal Bayesian Stackelberg Solver) algorithm (Paruchuri et al., 2008). The key insight: the defender's optimal mixed strategy equalises the attacker's expected payoff across all targets that are attacked with positive probability (the "indifference principle"), and makes unattacked targets yield weakly lower payoff. This is analogous to the minimax theorem but with commitment. When the attacker has multiple types (Bayesian Stackelberg game), the defender faces a distribution over attacker payoffs. The optimal strategy solves maxσ ∑θ Pr(θ) Ud(σ, BRθ(σ)), where BRθ is the best response of type θ. This is NP‑hard in general, but approximation algorithms exist (Korzhyk et al., 2010). Real‑world deployments include ARMOR (Los Angeles International Airport), IRIS (Federal Air Marshals), and PROTECT (US Coast Guard). These systems compute randomised patrol schedules that are unpredictable to adversaries. For examiners, the critical concepts are: (a) Stackelberg vs. simultaneous‑move (Nash) equilibrium — commitment gives the leader a weakly higher payoff; (b) the indifference principle characterising optimal coverage probabilities; (c) the MILP formulation with binary variables for attacker best response; (d) the distinction between Strong Stackelberg Equilibrium (attacker breaks ties in leader's favour) and Weak Stackelberg Equilibrium (attacker breaks ties adversarially) — the former is standard because the leader can induce favourable tie‑breaking by an ε‑perturbation. A typical exam question gives a small game (e.g., 3 targets, 1 resource, specific payoffs) and asks to compute the optimal mixed strategy by hand using the indifference principle.

  • Confusing Quantal Response Equilibrium with a perturbation of Nash equilibrium — QRE is a fixed point of a smooth best‑response map, not a tremble‑based refinement; it can have multiple branches that do not converge to the same Nash equilibrium as λ → ∞.
  • Assuming global games always select the risk‑dominant equilibrium — this holds only under symmetric limit dominance and uniform noise; asymmetric signal structures or non‑uniform priors can select Pareto‑dominant or other equilibria.
  • Treating Bonacich centrality as degree centrality in network games — Bonacich centrality weights walks of all lengths with decay φk; degree centrality counts only length‑1 walks. They coincide only when φ = 0 or the network is regular.
  • Believing the Rubinstein SPE always converges to the symmetric NBS — convergence requires δ1 = δ2 (or equal discount rates in continuous time); asymmetric patience yields an asymmetric split even in the limit.
  • Thinking the defender in a security game should maximise coverage of the most valuable target — the Stackelberg solution typically randomises to make the attacker indifferent across several targets; pure coverage of one target invites attack on the next best.
  • Overlooking that the spectral radius condition φ λmax(G) < 1 is both necessary and sufficient for uniqueness in linear‑quadratic network games with complements — if violated, multiple equilibria or unbounded efforts arise.
  • Confusing Strong and Weak Stackelberg Equilibrium — in security games, the standard solution concept is Strong SSE (attacker breaks ties in defender's favour) because the defender can achieve it by an arbitrarily small perturbation of the mixed strategy.

Implementation Theory and Maskin Monotonicity

Implementation theory asks whether a given social choice rule can be realised as the equilibrium outcome of some game form. The central result, due to Maskin (1999), states that a social choice correspondence F is Nash‑implementable if and only if it satisfies Maskin monotonicity and no‑veto power (for three or more agents). Maskin monotonicity requires that if an alternative a is chosen at a preference profile R and the set of alternatives that are weakly preferred to a does not shrink for any agent when moving to another profile R′, then a must still be chosen at R′. No‑veto power says that if all but one agent rank a at the top, then a must be selected. The canonical mechanism that achieves implementation under these conditions is the Maskin mechanism: each agent announces a preference profile and an alternative; the outcome is the announced alternative if at least n‑1 agents agree on the same profile and alternative, otherwise a default rule (e.g., a lottery) is used. The proof constructs a game where truthful revelation is a Nash equilibrium and any Nash equilibrium yields an outcome in F(R).

Subsequent work refined the conditions. Moore and Repullo (1990) showed that with two agents, Maskin monotonicity alone is insufficient; a stronger condition called Condition μ is necessary and sufficient. In environments with quasi‑linear utilities, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) mechanism implements the efficient allocation in dominant strategies, bypassing the need for Nash implementation. However, VCG fails budget balance, leading to the Groves–Ledyard mechanism for public goods, which achieves Bayesian‑Nash implementation with budget balance but sacrifices dominant‑strategy incentive compatibility. Examiners often test the distinction between dominant‑strategy implementation, Nash implementation, and Bayesian‑Nash implementation, and the role of the revelation principle in restricting attention to direct mechanisms.

Key Take‑aways

  • Maskin monotonicity + no‑veto power ⇔ Nash implementability (≥3 agents).
  • Two‑agent case requires Condition μ.
  • VCG gives dominant‑strategy implementation for efficient allocation but violates budget balance.
  • Revelation principle: any equilibrium outcome of an indirect mechanism can be replicated by a truthful direct mechanism.

Contract Theory: Principal–Agent Models with Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection

Contract theory studies optimal agreements when one party (the principal) delegates an action to another (the agent) under asymmetric information. Two canonical frictions are moral hazard (hidden action) and adverse selection (hidden type). In the moral‑hazard model (Holmström, 1979), the agent chooses effort e ∈ [0, ē] at cost c(e), producing stochastic output x with distribution F(x|e). The principal offers a wage schedule w(x). The agent’s participation constraint is E[w(x)|e] − c(e) ≥ ū and the incentive‑compatibility constraint (first‑order approach) is e ∈ argmaxe′ {E[w(x)|e′] − c(e′)}. Under the Mirrlees–Rogerson conditions (monotone likelihood ratio, convex cost), the optimal contract is a linear sharing rule w(x) = α + βx where β = 1 / (1 + rσ²c″) in the CARA‑normal case (r = risk aversion, σ² = output variance). The agent bears risk proportional to the informativeness of output about effort.

In the adverse‑selection model (Myerson, 1981; Maskin & Riley, 1984), the agent’s type θ ∈ Θ is private, drawn from a known distribution. The principal designs a menu of contracts {(q(θ), t(θ))} where q is quantity/quality and t is transfer. The constraints are individual rationality U(θ) = θq(θ) − t(θ) ≥ 0 and incentive compatibility U(θ) ≥ θq(θ′) − t(θ′) for all θ, θ′. The optimal mechanism satisfies the envelope condition U′(θ) = q(θ) and the monotonicity condition q(θ) non‑decreasing. The solution typically involves ironing when the virtual valuation function is non‑monotone. The principal extracts all surplus from the lowest type and leaves information rents to higher types. Examiners frequently ask to derive the optimal linear contract under CARA‑normal assumptions, or to write the incentive‑compatibility constraints for a two‑type adverse‑selection problem and solve for the optimal menu.

Key Take‑aways

  • Moral hazard: hidden action → first‑order approach, linear sharing rule under CARA‑normal.
  • Adverse selection: hidden type → envelope theorem, monotonicity, ironing.
  • Participation (IR) and incentive compatibility (IC) are the two binding constraints.
  • Risk‑sharing vs. incentive provision trade‑off determines the slope of the optimal contract.
Worked Example: Two‑Type Adverse Selection
A principal sells a good to an agent whose valuation θ is either θL = 5 (probability 0.6) or θH = 10 (probability 0.4). The principal’s marginal cost is zero. The agent’s utility is θq − t, the principal’s profit is t. Find the optimal menu {(qL, tL), (qH, tH)}.
Step 1: Write IR and IC. IRL: 5qL − tL ≥ 0. IRH: 10qH − tH ≥ 0. ICL: 5qL − tL ≥ 5qH − tH. ICH: 10qH − tH ≥ 10qL − tL. Step 2: At optimum, IRL binds (tL = 5qL) and ICH binds (10qH − tH = 10qL − tL). ICL and IRH are slack. Step 3: Substitute tL and tH = 10qH − 10qL + 5qL = 10qH − 5qL. Principal’s expected profit = 0.6·5qL + 0.4·(10qH − 5qL) = 3qL + 4qH − 2qL = qL + 4qH. Step 4: Maximise qL + 4qH subject to qH ≥ qL (monotonicity). Since coefficient on qH is larger, set qH as high as possible; with no upper bound, the model is unbounded. Introduce a capacity constraint q ≤ 1. Then qH = 1, qL = 1 (monotonicity satisfied). Transfers: tL = 5, tH = 10·1 − 5·1 = 5. Menu: (1,5) for both types. The high type receives information rent 5. If capacity is 1, the principal cannot increase qH further; the solution is qL = qH = 1, tL = tH = 5.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a contract‑theory question appears, first identify the friction (moral hazard vs. adverse selection). Write down the agent’s utility, the principal’s objective, and the two constraints (IR, IC). For moral hazard, check whether the first‑order approach is valid (MLRP, CDFC). For adverse selection, use the envelope theorem to replace the IC constraints with U′(θ)=q(θ) and monotonicity. Always verify which constraints bind at the optimum — typically the lowest type’s IR and the highest type’s IC bind. If the problem gives a discrete type space, set up the binding constraints directly and solve the resulting linear programme.

Social Choice Theory: Arrow’s Impossibility and the Gibbard–Satterthwaite Theorem

Social choice theory aggregates individual preferences into a collective decision. Arrow’s (1951) impossibility theorem states that no social welfare function f : ℒn → ℒ (where ℒ is the set of linear orders over at least three alternatives) can simultaneously satisfy: (1) Unrestricted Domain — all preference profiles are admissible; (2) Pareto Efficiency — if every agent prefers x to y, then society ranks x above y; (3) Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA) — the social ranking of x vs. y depends only on individual rankings of x and y; (4) Non‑dictatorship — no single agent always determines the social ranking. The proof proceeds by showing that any function satisfying (1)–(3) must be dictatorial. The pivotal voter argument identifies a voter whose preference over a particular pair becomes decisive for the whole society, and then extends decisiveness to all pairs.

The Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem (1973, 1975) strengthens the result to social choice functions (selecting a single winner) and strategy‑proofness. It states that any onto, strategy‑proof social choice function with at least three alternatives is dictatorial. Strategy‑proofness means no agent can benefit by misreporting preferences. The theorem implies that any non‑dictatorial voting rule (plurality, Borda, runoff, etc.) is manipulable. The proof uses the fact that a strategy‑proof rule must be monotone (if an alternative wins and is raised in some ballots, it still wins) and then applies Arrow’s theorem to the associated social welfare function derived from the rule’s choice sets. Examiners often ask to demonstrate a manipulation for a specific rule (e.g., Borda count) or to explain why the theorem does not apply to two alternatives (majority rule is strategy‑proof) or to restricted domains (single‑peaked preferences allow the median voter rule to be strategy‑proof).

Key Take‑aways

  • Arrow: no SWF satisfies UD, Pareto, IIA, non‑dictatorship (≥3 alternatives).
  • Gibbard–Satterthwaite: any onto, strategy‑proof SCF with ≥3 alternatives is dictatorial.
  • Two‑alternative case escapes the theorem; majority rule is strategy‑proof.
  • Domain restrictions (single‑peaked, single‑crossing) permit non‑dictatorial strategy‑proof rules (median voter).

Evolutionary Game Theory: Replicator Dynamics and Evolutionarily Stable Strategies

Evolutionary game theory replaces rational optimisation with a dynamical process on a population of agents. The replicator equation for a finite set of pure strategies S = {1,…,m} with population shares xi ≥ 0, ∑i xi = 1, and payoff matrix A is ẋi = xi[(A x)i − xᵀ A x]. The term (A x)i is the expected payoff to strategy i against the current population; xᵀ A x is the average population payoff. Strategies earning above‑average payoff grow in proportion. Fixed points of the dynamics correspond to Nash equilibria of the underlying game, but not all Nash equilibria are asymptotically stable. An Evolutionarily Stable Strategy (ESS) (Maynard Smith & Price, 1973) is a mixed strategy σ* such that for any mutant σ ≠ σ*, either (i) u(σ*,σ*) > u(σ,σ*) or (ii) u(σ*,σ*) = u(σ,σ*) and u(σ*,σ) > u(σ,σ). Condition (i) says σ* is a strict best reply to itself; condition (ii) handles neutral mutants by requiring σ* to do better against the mutant than the mutant does against itself. Every ESS is a symmetric Nash equilibrium, and every strict symmetric Nash equilibrium is an ESS. The replicator dynamics converge to ESSs under mild conditions (e.g., for two‑strategy games, the interior rest point is globally asymptotically stable iff it is an ESS). In games with more than two strategies, limit cycles and chaotic behaviour can arise (e.g., rock‑paper‑scissors). Examiners test the ability to compute the replicator equation for a given payoff matrix, identify rest points, and check ESS conditions.

Key Take‑aways

  • Replicator dynamics: ẋi = xi[(A x)i − xᵀ A x].
  • ESS ⇒ symmetric Nash equilibrium; strict symmetric Nash ⇒ ESS.
  • Two‑strategy games: interior rest point is ESS iff it is asymptotically stable.
  • Rock‑paper‑scissors has a unique mixed Nash equilibrium that is not an ESS; dynamics cycle.

Fair Division: Cake‑Cutting Procedures and Envy‑Free Allocations

Fair division studies algorithms for allocating a divisible heterogeneous good (the “cake”) among n agents with different valuation measures. The classic criteria are proportionality (each agent receives at least 1/n of the cake by her own measure), envy‑freeness (no agent prefers another’s piece), and Pareto efficiency. For two agents, the cut‑and‑choose protocol achieves envy‑freeness and Pareto efficiency. For three or more agents, the Selfridge–Conway discrete protocol (1970) guarantees an envy‑free allocation using at most five cuts, but it is not Pareto efficient in general. The Dubins–Spanier moving‑knife procedure yields a proportional allocation for any n with a single continuously moving knife. The Brams–Taylor (1995) protocol provides an envy‑free division for any finite n using a finite number of cuts, but the number of cuts grows unboundedly with n. A major open problem, resolved by Aziz and Mackenzie (2016), showed that an envy‑free protocol with a bounded number of queries exists for any n, though the bound is astronomically large. In the rental‑harmony setting (rooms + rent), the Sperner’s lemma based algorithm of Su (1999) finds an envy‑free assignment of rooms and rent shares. Examiners often ask to describe the cut‑and‑choose protocol, prove its envy‑freeness, or explain why proportionality does not imply envy‑freeness for n ≥ 3 (counterexample: three agents, one values only the left third, another only the middle third, third only the right third; a proportional allocation can give each a piece they value at 1/3 but one may envy another’s piece if the cuts are misaligned).

Key Take‑aways

  • Cut‑and‑choose: envy‑free, Pareto efficient for n=2.
  • Selfridge–Conway: discrete envy‑free for n=3, ≤5 cuts.
  • Dubins–Spanier moving‑knife: proportional for any n.
  • Brams–Taylor: finite envy‑free for any n, unbounded cuts.
  • Aziz–Mackenzie (2016): bounded‑query envy‑free protocol exists (theoretical).
  • Rental harmony: Sperner’s lemma yields envy‑free room‑rent assignment.
  • Confusing Nash implementation with dominant‑strategy implementation — the former only requires equilibrium, the latter requires truth‑telling to be a dominant strategy.
  • Assuming the first‑order approach in moral hazard is always valid — it requires MLRP and CDFC; otherwise the agent’s problem may have multiple local maxima.
  • Believing Arrow’s theorem applies to two alternatives — majority rule satisfies all four axioms when only two alternatives exist.
  • Thinking every symmetric Nash equilibrium is an ESS — only strict symmetric Nash equilibria are ESS; mixed symmetric equilibria need the second ESS condition.
  • Equating proportionality with envy‑freeness for n≥3 — proportional allocations can be envious; envy‑freeness is strictly stronger.
  • Overlooking that the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem requires the rule to be onto — a rule that never selects some alternative can be non‑dictatorial and strategy‑proof.
  • Assuming the replicator dynamics always converge to a Nash equilibrium — limit cycles and chaos can occur in games with three or more strategies.

These advanced topics deepen the toolkit for analysing strategic interaction beyond the core equilibrium concepts and are frequently the source of high‑difficulty examination questions.

Mechanism Design for Public Goods: The Vickrey–Clarke–Groves Mechanism and Its Limitations

The Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) mechanism is the canonical dominant‑strategy incentive‑compatible (DSIC) mechanism for allocating a public good or selecting a socially optimal outcome when agents have quasi‑linear utilities. Each agent i reports a valuation function v_i over the set of alternatives X. The mechanism chooses the alternative x* that maximizes the reported total welfare Σ_i v_i(x). Agent i then pays the externality she imposes on the others: p_i = Σj≠i v_j(x*-i) − Σj≠i v_j(x*), where x*-i is the welfare‑maximizing alternative when i is absent. Truth‑telling is a dominant strategy because the payment exactly cancels the effect of i’s report on the others’ welfare.

VCG achieves efficiency (Pareto optimality) and DSIC simultaneously, but it suffers from several well‑known drawbacks. First, the mechanism may run a budget deficit: the sum of payments can be negative, requiring an external subsidy. The Clarke pivot rule guarantees non‑negative payments but does not eliminate the deficit. Second, VCG is vulnerable to collusion: a coalition can misreport jointly to increase its members’ utilities while keeping the chosen alternative unchanged. Third, the mechanism requires agents to reveal their entire valuation functions, which can be computationally prohibitive when X is large (e.g., combinatorial auctions). Fourth, VCG fails to be ex‑post individually rational in settings with interdependent values; the pivot payment may exceed an agent’s true valuation for the chosen outcome.

In examinations, the typical twist is to ask whether VCG remains DSIC when the set of alternatives is restricted (e.g., only a subset of feasible allocations is allowed). The answer is yes, provided the restriction is common knowledge and the mechanism still selects the welfare‑maximizing alternative within the restricted set. Another common question compares VCG with the Groves mechanism class: any Groves mechanism (payments = h_i(v-i) − Σj≠i v_j(x*)) is DSIC and efficient, but only the Clarke pivot rule guarantees individual rationality and no positive transfers. Students should be able to write the payment formula for a simple public‑project problem (binary decision: build or not) and compute the pivot payments for three agents with given valuations.

Network Formation Games: Pairwise Stability and the Jackson–Wolinsky Model

Network formation games model how self‑interested agents create and sever links to form a graph that determines their payoffs. The foundational model by Jackson and Wolinsky (1996) assumes a set of players N, each choosing a set of links to other players. A link between i and j is formed only if both consent; either player can unilaterally delete an existing link. Payoffs depend on the resulting network g through a value function v_i(g). A network g is pairwise stable if (i) no player benefits by deleting one of her links, and (ii) no pair of players not currently linked both benefit (with at least one strictly) by adding the link between them.

Pairwise stability is a static solution concept; it does not capture dynamic formation processes. Jackson and Wolinsky show that for symmetric connection models (where payoffs depend only on distances in the network), the set of pairwise stable networks coincides with the set of efficient networks for certain parameter ranges, but inefficiencies arise when the cost of a link is intermediate: the efficient network is a star, yet the empty network is also pairwise stable because no single player wants to bear the cost of the first link. The model extends to directed links, heterogeneous costs, and externalities from indirect connections.

Examiners often test the ability to compute pairwise stable networks for a given payoff specification. A typical exercise: four players, link cost c = 0.3, benefit from a direct connection = 1, benefit from an indirect connection of length two = 0.5, longer paths give zero. Students must list all networks, check unilateral deletion and bilateral addition conditions, and identify the pairwise stable set. Another twist asks to compare pairwise stability with the stronger notion of pairwise Nash stability (where a player can add a link unilaterally) and to explain why the latter may eliminate some inefficient stable networks.

Worked Example: Pairwise Stability in a Four‑Player Connection Model
Four players (1,2,3,4) can form undirected links at cost c = 0.3 each. A direct link gives each endpoint benefit 1. An indirect connection of length two gives each endpoint benefit 0.5. No benefit from longer paths. Determine all pairwise stable networks.
List candidate networks by number of links. Empty network: no player can add a link alone (needs consent), and any pair adding a link would each gain 1 − 0.3 = 0.7 > 0, so empty network is NOT pairwise stable. Single link (1‑2): players 1 and 2 get 1 − 0.3 = 0.7; others get 0. Pair (1,3) would each gain 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 > 0, so they would add link 1‑3. Hence single link not stable. Two links forming a path 1‑2‑3: payoffs: 1 gets 1−0.3 + 0.5 = 1.2; 2 gets 2×(1−0.3)=1.4; 3 gets 1.2; 4 gets 0. Check deletions: 1 would lose 1.2 if she drops 1‑2 (payoff becomes 0), so no deletion. Pair (1,4): adding gives 1 gain 0.5−0.3=0.2, 4 gain 0.5−0.3=0.2 → both benefit, so path not stable. Star centered at 1 (links 1‑2,1‑3,1‑4): center payoff = 3×(1−0.3)=2.1; leaves each get 1−0.3=0.7. No leaf wants to delete (would get 0). Any two leaves (2,3) adding link gives each extra 1−0.3=0.7 >0, so star not stable. Complete graph (6 links): each player degree 3, payoff = 3×(1−0.3)=2.1. Any deletion reduces payoff by 0.7, so no deletion. No missing links to add. Complete graph is pairwise stable. Also the cycle 1‑2‑3‑4‑1 (4 links) gives each degree 2, payoff = 2×(1−0.3)=1.4. Check pair (1,3) not linked: adding gives each extra 1−0.3=0.7 >0, so cycle not stable. Thus the unique pairwise stable network is the complete graph.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for pairwise stable networks, first compute payoffs for all non‑isomorphic networks up to the relevant size. Use symmetry to reduce cases. Write the deletion and addition conditions explicitly; a network is stable only if *both* hold. Remember that a pair adds a link only if *both* strictly gain (or at least one strictly and the other not worse). Do not confuse pairwise stability with Nash stability (unilateral addition) or with efficiency.

Behavioral Game Theory: Level‑k Thinking and Cognitive Hierarchy Models

Classical equilibrium analysis assumes common knowledge of rationality. Level‑k models relax this by positing a hierarchy of reasoning depths. A level‑0 player chooses uniformly at random (or according to a salient heuristic). A level‑1 player best‑responds to the belief that all others are level‑0. A level‑2 player best‑responds to the belief that others are level‑1, and so on. The distribution of levels in the population is often estimated from experimental data; a common specification is a Poisson distribution with mean τ (the cognitive hierarchy model). The model predicts systematic deviations from Nash equilibrium in games such as the beauty‑contest (p‑beauty contest), the traveler’s dilemma, and the centipede game.

In the p‑beauty contest, each player picks a number in [0,100]; the winner is closest to p times the average. With p = 2/3, level‑0 picks 50 (uniform), level‑1 picks 33.3, level‑2 picks 22.2, converging to the Nash equilibrium 0. Experimental data typically show a spike around 33 (level‑1) and 22 (level‑2), with few players reaching higher levels. The cognitive hierarchy model fits the full distribution by allowing a mixture of levels. Estimation of τ yields values around 1.5–2 in many lab studies.

Examiners test the ability to compute level‑k predictions for a given normal‑form game. A typical question provides a 3×3 payoff matrix and asks for the level‑1 and level‑2 actions for each player assuming uniform level‑0. Students must first compute the level‑0 mixed strategy (uniform), then each player’s best response to that mixture (level‑1), then best response to the level‑1 profile (level‑2).
